EN101\"﻿I can hardly describe the mood in which I was left by this harrowing episode--an episode at once mad and pitiful
column2: grotesque and terrifying. The grocery boy had prepared me for it
column3: yet the reality left me none the less bewildered and disturbed. Puerile though the story was
column4: old Zadok's insane earnestness and horror had communicated to me a mounting unrest which joined with my earlier sense of loathing for the town and its blight of intangible shadow.

column1: Later I might sift the tale and extract some nucleus of historic allegory; just now I wished to put it out of my head. The hour grown perilously late--my watch said 7:15
column2: and the Arkham bus left Town Square at eight--so I tried to give my thoughts as neutral and practical a cast as possible
column3: meanwhile walking rapidly through the deserted streets of gaping roofs and leaning houses toward the hotel where I had checked my valise and would find my bus.

column1: Though the golden light of late afternoon gave the ancient roofs and decrepit chimneys an air of mystic loveliness and peace
column2: I could not help glancing over my shoulder now and then. I would surely be very glad to get out of malodorous and fear-shadowed Innsmouth
column3: and wished there were some other vehicle than the bus driven by that sinister-looking fellow Sargent. Yet I did not hurry too precipitately
column4: for there were architectural details worth viewing at every silent corner; and I could easily
column5: I calculated
column6: cover the necessary distance in a half-hour.

column1: Studying the grocery youth's map and seeking a route I had not traversed before
column2: I chose Marsh Street instead of State for my approach to Town Square. Near the corner of Fall Street I began to see scattered groups of furtive whisperers
column3: and when I finally reached the Square I saw that almost all the loiterers were congregated around the door of the Gilman House. It seemed as if many bulging
column4: watery
column5: unwinking eyes looked oddly at me as I claimed my valise in the lobby
column6: and I hoped that none of these unpleasant creatures would be my fellow-passengers on the coach.

column1: The bus
column2: rather early
column3: rattled in with three passengers somewhat before eight
column4: and an evil-looking fellow on the sidewalk muttered a few indistinguishable words to the driver. Sargent threw out a mail-bag and a roll of newspapers
column5: and entered the hotel; while the passengers--the same men whom I had seen arriving in Newburyport that morning--shambled to the sidewalk and exchanged some faint guttural words with a loafer in a language I could have sworn was not English. I boarded the empty coach and took the seat I had taken before
column6: but was hardly settled before Sargent re-appeared and began mumbling in a throaty voice of peculiar repulsiveness.

column1: I was
column2: it appeared
column3: in very bad luck. There had been something wrong with the engine
column4: despite the excellent time made from Newburyport
column5: and the bus could not complete the journey to Arkham. No
column6: it could not possibly be repaired that night
column7: nor was there any other way of getting transportation out of Innsmouth either to Arkham or elsewhere. Sargent was sorry
column8: but I would have to stop over at the Gilman. Probably the clerk would make the price easy for me
column9: but there was nothing else to do. Almost dazed by this sudden obstacle
column10: and violently dreading the fall of night in this decaying and half-unlighted town
column11: I left the bus and reentered the hotel lobby; where the sullen queer-looking night clerk told me I could have Room 428 on next the top floor--large
column12: but without running water--for a dollar.

column1: Despite what I had heard of this hotel in Newburyport
column2: I signed the register
column3: paid my dollar
column4: let the clerk take my valise
column5: and followed that sour
column6: solitary attendant up three creaking flights of stairs past dusty corridors which seemed wholly devoid of life. My room was a dismal rear one with two windows and bare
column7: cheap furnishings
column8: overlooked a dingy court-yard otherwise hemmed in by low
column9: deserted brick blocks
column10: and commanded a view of decrepit westward-stretching roofs with a marshy countryside beyond. At the end of the corridor was a bathroom--a discouraging relique with ancient marble bowl
column11: tin tub
column12: faint electric light
column13: and musty wooded paneling around all the plumbing fixtures.

column1: It being still daylight
column2: I descended to the Square and looked around for a dinner of some sort; noticing as I did so the strange glances I received from the unwholesome loafers. Since the grocery was closed
column3: I was forced to patronise the restaurant I had shunned before; a stooped
column4: narrow-headed man with staring
column5: unwinking eyes
column6: and a flat-nosed wench with unbelievably thick
column7: clumsy hands being in attendance. The service was all of the counter type
column8: and it relieved me to find that much was evidently served from cans and packages. A bowl of vegetable soup with crackers was enough for me
column9: and I soon headed back for my cheerless room at the Gilman; getting a evening paper and a fly-specked magazine from the evil-visaged clerk at the rickety stand beside his desk.

column1: As twilight deepened I turned on the one feeble electric bulb over the cheap
column2: iron-framed bed
column3: and tried as best I could to continue the reading I had begun. I felt it advisable to keep my mind wholesomely occupied
column4: for it would not do to brood over the abnormalities of this ancient
column5: blight-shadowed town while I was still within its borders. The insane yarn I had heard from the aged drunkard did not promise very pleasant dreams
column6: and I felt I must keep the image of his wild
column7: watery eyes as far as possible from my imagination.

column1: Also
column2: I must not dwell on what that factory inspector had told the Newburyport ticket-agent about the Gilman House and the voices of its nocturnal tenants--not on that
column3: nor on the face beneath the tiara in the black church doorway; the face for whose horror my conscious mind could not account. It would perhaps have been easier to keep my thoughts from disturbing topics had the room not been so gruesomely musty. As it was
column4: the lethal mustiness blended hideously with the town's general fishy odour and persistently focussed one's fancy on death and decay.

column1: Another thing that disturbed me was the absence of a bolt on the door of my room. One had been there
column2: as marks clearly shewed
column3: but there were signs of recent removal. No doubt it had been out of order
column4: like so many other things in this decrepit edifice. In my nervousness I looked around and discovered a bolt on the clothes press which seemed to be of the same size
column5: judging from the marks
column6: as the one formerly on the door. To gain a partial relief from the general tension I busied myself by transferring this hardware to the vacant place with the aid of a handy three-in-one device including a screwdriver which I kept on my key-ring. The bolt fitted perfectly
column7: and I was somewhat relieved when I knew that I could shoot it firmly upon retiring. Not that I had any real apprehension of its need
column8: but that any symbol of security was welcome in an environment of this kind. There were adequate bolts on the two lateral doors to connecting rooms
column9: and these I proceeded to fasten.

column1: I did not undress
column2: but decided to read till I was sleepy and then lie down with only my coat
column3: collar
column4: and shoes off. Taking a pocket flash light from my valise
column5: I placed it in my trousers
column6: so that I could read my watch if I woke up later in the dark. Drowsiness
column7: however
column8: did not come; and when I stopped to analyse my thoughts I found to my disquiet that I was really unconsciously listening for something--listening for something which I dreaded but could not name. That inspector's story must have worked on my imagination more deeply than I had suspected. Again I tried to read
column9: but found that I made no progress.

column1: After a time I seemed to hear the stairs and corridors creak at intervals as if with footsteps
column2: and wondered if the other rooms were beginning to fill up. There were no voices
column3: however
column4: and it struck me that there was something subtly furtive about the creaking. I did not like it
column5: and debated whether I had better try to sleep at all. This town had some queer people
column6: and there had undoubtedly been several disappearances. Was this one of those inns where travelers were slain for their money? Surely I had no look of excessive prosperity. Or were the towns folk really so resentful about curious visitors? Had my obvious sightseeing
column7: with its frequent map-consultations
column8: aroused unfavorable notice. It occurred to me that I must be in a highly nervous state to let a few random creakings set me off speculating in this fashion--but I regretted none the less that I was unarmed.

column1: At length
column2: feeling a fatigue which had nothing of drowsiness in it
column3: I bolted the newly outfitted hall door
column4: turned off the light
column5: and threw myself down on the hard
column6: uneven bed--coat
column7: collar
column8: shoes
column9: and all. In the darkness every faint noise of the night seemed magnified
column10: and a flood of doubly unpleasant thoughts swept over me. I was sorry I had put out the light
column11: yet was too tired to rise and turn it on again. Then
column12: after a long
column13: dreary interval
column14: and prefaced by a fresh creaking of stairs and corridor
column15: there came that soft
column16: damnably unmistakable sound which seemed like a malign fulfillment of all my apprehensions. Without the least shadow of a doubt
column17: the lock of my door was being tried--cautiously
column18: furtively
column19: tentatively--with a key.

column1: My sensations upon recognising this sign of actual peril were perhaps less rather than more tumultuous because of my previous vague fears. I had been
column2: albeit without definite reason
column3: instinctively on my guard--and that was to my advantage in the new and real crisis
column4: whatever it might turn out to be. Nevertheless the change in the menace from vague premonition to immediate reality was a profound shock
column5: and fell upon me with the force of a genuine blow. It never once occurred to me that the fumbling might be a mere mistake. Malign purpose was all I could think of
column6: and I kept deathly quiet
column7: awaiting the would-be intruder's next move.

column1: After a time the cautious rattling ceased
column2: and I heard the room to the north entered with a pass-key. Then the lock of the connecting door to my room was softly tried. The bolt held
column3: of course
column4: and I heard the floor creak as the prowler left the room. After a moment there came another soft rattling
column5: and I knew that the room to the south of me was being entered. Again a furtive trying of a bolted connecting door
column6: and again a receding creaking. This time the creaking went along the hall and down the stairs
column7: so I knew that the prowler had realised the bolted condition of my doors and was giving up his attempt for a greater or lesser time
column8: as the future would shew.

column1: The readiness with which I fell into a plan of action proves that I must have been subconsciously fearing some menace and considering possible avenues of escape for hours. From the first I felt that the unseen fumbler meant a danger not to be met or dealt with
column2: but only to be fled from as precipitately as possible. The one thing to do was to get out of that hotel alive as quickly as I could
column3: and through some channel other than the front stairs and lobby.

column1: Rising softly and throwing my flashlight on the switch
column2: I sought to light the bulb over my bed in order to choose and pocket some belongings for a swift
column3: valiseless flight. Nothing
column4: however
column5: happened; and I saw that the power had been cut off. Clearly
column6: some cryptic
column7: evil movement was afoot on a large scale--just what
column8: I could not say. As I stood pondering with my hand on the now useless switch I heard a muffled creaking on the floor below
column9: and thought I could barely distinguish voices in conversation. A moment later I felt less sure that the deeper sounds were voices
column10: since the apparent hoarse barkings and loose-syllabled croakings bore so little resemblance to recognized human speech. Then I thought with renewed force of what the factory inspector had heard in the night in this mouldering and pestilential building.

column1: Having filled my pockets with the flashlight's aid
column2: I put on my hat and tiptoed to the windows to consider chances of descent. Despite the state's safety regulations there was no fire escape on this side of the hotel
column3: and I saw that my windows commanded only a sheer three story drop to the cobbled courtyard. On the right and left
column4: however
column5: some ancient brick business blocks abutted on the hotel; their slant roofs coming up to a reasonable jumping distance from my fourth-story level. To reach either of these lines of buildings I would have to be in a room two from my own--in one case on the north and in the other case on the south--and my mind instantly set to work what chances I had of making the transfer.

column1: I could not
column2: I decided
column3: risk an emergence into the corridor; where my footsteps would surely be heard
column4: and where the difficulties of entering the desired room would be insuperable. My progress
column5: if it was to be made at all
column6: would have to be through the less solidly-built connecting doors of the rooms; the locks and bolts of which I would have to force violently
column7: using my shoulder as a battering-ram whenever they were set against me. This
column8: I thought
column9: would be possible owing to the rickety nature of the house and its fixtures; but I realised I could not do it noiselessly. I would have to count on sheer speed
column10: and the chance of getting to a window before any hostile forces became coordinated enough to open the right door toward me with a pass-key. My own outer door I reinforced by pushing the bureau against it--little by little
column11: in order to make a minimum of sound.

column1: I perceived that my chances were very slender
column2: and was fully prepared for any calamity. Even getting to another roof would not solve the problem for there would then remain the task of reaching the ground and escaping from the town. One thing in my favour was the deserted and ruinous state of the abutting building and the number of skylights gaping blackly open in each row.

column1: Gathering from the grocery boy's map that the best route out of town was southward
column2: I glanced first at the connecting door on the south side of the room. It was designed to open in my direction
column3: hence I saw--after drawing the bolt and finding other fastening in place--it was not a favorable one for forcing. Accordingly abandoning it as a route
column4: I cautiously moved the bedstead against it to hamper any attack which might be made on it later from the next room. The door on the north was hung to open away from me
column5: and this--though a test proved it to be locked or bolted from the other side--I knew must be my route. If I could gain the roofs of the buildings in Paine Street and descend successfully to the ground level
column6: I might perhaps dart through the courtyard and the adjacent or opposite building to Washington or Bates--or else emerge in Paine and edge around southward into Washington. In any case
column7: I would aim to strike Washington somehow and get quickly out of the Town Square region. My preference would be to avoid Paine
column8: since the fire station there might be open all night.

column1: As I thought of these things I looked out over the squalid sea of decaying roofs below me
column2: now brightened by the beams of a moon not much past full. On the right the black gash of the river-gorge clove the panorama; abandoned factories and railway station clinging barnacle-like to its sides. Beyond it the rusted railway and the Rowley road led off through a flat marshy terrain dotted with islets of higher and dryer scrub-grown land. On the left the creek-threaded country-side was nearer
column3: the narrow road to Ipswich gleaming white in the moonlight. I could not see from my side of the hotel the southward route toward Arkham which I had determined to take.

column1: I was irresolutely speculating on when I had better attack the northward door
column2: and on how I could least audibly manage it
column3: when I noticed that the vague noises underfoot had given place to a fresh and heavier creaking of the stairs. A wavering flicker of light shewed through my transom
column4: and the boards of the corridor began to groan with a ponderous load. Muffled sounds of possible vocal origin approached
column5: and at length a firm knock came at my outer door.

column1: For a moment I simply held my breath and waited. Eternities seemed to elapse
column2: and the nauseous fishy odour of my environment seemed to mount suddenly and spectacularly. Then the knocking was repeated--continuously
column3: and with growing insistence. I knew that the time for action had come
column4: and forthwith drew the bolt of the northward connecting door
column5: bracing myself for the task of battering it open. The knocking waxed louder
column6: and I hoped that its volume would cover the sound of my efforts. At last beginning my attempt
column7: I lunged again and again at the thin paneling with my left shoulder
column8: heedless of shock or pain. The door resisted even more than I expected
column9: but I did not give in. And all the while the clamour at the outer door increased.

column1: Finally the connecting door gave
column2: but with such a crash that I knew those outside must have heard. Instantly the outside knocking became a violent battering
column3: while keys sounded ominously in the hall doors of the rooms on both sides of me. Rushing through the newly opened connexion
column4: I succeeded in bolting the northerly hall door before the lock could be turned; but even as I did so I heard the hall door of the third room--the one from whose window I had hoped to reach the roof below--being tried with a pass-key.

column1: For an instant I felt absolute despair
column2: since my trapping in a chamber with no window egress seemed complete. A wave of almost abnormal horror swept over me
column3: and invested with a terrible but unexplainable singularity the flashlight-glimpsed dust prints made by the intruder who had lately tried my door from this room. Then
column4: with a dazed automatism which persisted despite hopelessness
column5: I made for the next connecting door and performed the blind motion of pushing at it in an effort to get through and--granting that fastenings might be as providentially intact as in this second room--bolt the hall door beyond before the lock could be turned from outside.

column1: Sheer fortunate chance gave me my reprieve--for the connecting door before me was not only unlocked but actually ajar. In a second I was though
column2: and had my right knee and shoulder against a hall door which was visibly opening inward. My pressure took the opener off guard
column3: for the thing shut as I pushed
column4: so that I could slip the well-conditioned bolt as I had done with the other door. As I gained this respite I heard the battering at the two other doors abate
column5: while a confused clatter came from the connecting door I had shielded with the bedstead. Evidently the bulk of my assailants had entered the southerly room and were massing in a lateral attack. But at the same moment a pass-key sounded in the next door to the north
column6: and I knew that a nearer peril was at hand.

column1: The northward connecting door was wide open
column2: but there was no time to think about checking the already turning lock in the hall. All I could do was to shut and bolt the open connecting door
column3: as well as its mate on the opposite side--pushing a bedstead against the one and a bureau against the other
column4: and moving a washstand in front of the hall door. I must
column5: I saw
column6: trust to such makeshift barriers to shield me till I could get out the window and on the roof of the Paine Street block. But even in this acute moment my chief horror was something apart from the immediate weakness of my defenses. I was shuddering because not one of my pursuers
column7: despite some hideous panting
column8: grunting
column9: and subdued barkings at odd intervals
column10: was uttering an unmuffled or intelligible vocal sound.

column1: As I moved the furniture and rushed toward the windows I heard a frightful scurrying along the corridor toward the room north of me
column2: and perceived that the southward battering had ceased. Plainly
column3: most of my opponents were about to concentrate against the feeble connecting door which they knew must open directly on me. Outside
column4: the moon played on the ridgepole of the block below
column5: and I saw that the jump would be desperately hazardous because of the steep surface on which I must land.

column1: Surveying the conditions
column2: I chose the more southerly of the two windows as my avenue of escape; planning to land on the inner slope of the roof and make for the nearest sky-light. Once inside one of the decrepit brick structures I would have to reckon with pursuit; but I hoped to descend and dodge in and out of yawning doorways along the shadowed courtyard
column3: eventually getting to Washington Street and slipping out of town toward the south.

column1: The clatter at the northerly connecting door was now terrific
column2: and I saw that the weak panelling was beginning to splinter. Obviously
column3: the besiegers had brought some ponderous object into play as a battering-ram. The bedstead
column4: however
column5: still held firm; so that I had at least a faint chance of making good my escape. As I opened the window I noticed that it was flanked by heavy velour draperies suspended from a pole by brass rings
column6: and also that there was a large projecting catch for the shutters on the exterior. Seeing a possible means of avoiding the dangerous jump
column7: I yanked at the hangings and brought them down
column8: pole and all; then quickly hooking two of the rings in the shutter catch and flinging the drapery outside. The heavy folds reached fully to the abutting roof
column9: and I saw that the rings and catch would be likely to bear my weight. So
column10: climbing out of the window and down the improvised rope ladder
column11: I left behind me forever the morbid and horror-infested fabric of the Gilman House.

column1: I landed safely on the loose slates of the steep roof
column2: and succeeded in gaining the gaping black skylight without a slip. Glancing up at the window I had left
column3: I observed it was still dark
column4: though far across the crumbling chimneys to the north I could see lights ominously blazing in the Order of Dagon Hall
column5: the Baptist church
column6: and the Congregational church which I recalled so shiveringly. There had seemed to be no one in the courtyard below
column7: and I hoped there would be a chance to get away before the spreading of a general alarm. Flashing my pocket lamp into the skylight
column8: I saw that there were no steps down. The distance was slight
column9: however
column10: so I clambered over the brink and dropped; striking a dusty floor littered with crumbling boxes and barrels.

column1: The place was ghoulish-looking
column2: but I was past minding such impressions and made at once for the staircase revealed by my flashlight--after a hasty glance at my watch
column3: which shewed the hour to be 2 a.m. The steps creaked
column4: but seemed tolerably sound; and I raced down past a barnlike second storey to the ground floor. The desolation was complete
column5: and only echoes answered my footfalls. At length I reached the lower hall at the end of which I saw a faint luminous rectangle marking the ruined Paine Street doorway. Heading the other way
column6: I found the back door also open; and darted out and down five stone steps to the grass-grown cobblestones of the courtyard.

column1: The moonbeams did not reach down here
column2: but I could just see my way about without using the flashlight. Some of the windows on the Gilman House side were faintly glowing
column3: and I thought I heard confused sounds within. Walking softly over to the Washington Street side I perceived several open doorways
column4: and chose the nearest as my route out. The hallway inside was black
column5: and when I reached the opposite end I saw that the street door was wedged immovably shut. Resolved to try another building
column6: I groped my way back toward the courtyard
column7: but stopped short when close to the doorway.

column1: For out of an opened door in the Gilman House a large crowd of doubtful shapes was pouring--lanterns bobbing in the darkness
column2: and horrible croaking voices exchanging low cries in what was certainly not English. The figures moved uncertainly
column3: and I realized to my relief that they did not know where I had gone; but for all that they sent a shiver of horror through my frame. Their features were indistinguishable
column4: but their crouching
column5: shambling gait was abominably repellent. And worst of all
column6: I perceived that one figure was strangely robed
column7: and unmistakably surmounted by a tall tiara of a design altogether too familiar. As the figures spread throughout the courtyard
column8: I felt my fears increase. Suppose I could find no egress from this building on the street side? The fishy odour was detestable
column9: and I wondered I could stand it without fainting. Again groping toward the street
column10: I opened a door off the hall and came upon an empty room with closely shuttered but sashless windows. Fumbling in the rays of my flashlight
column11: I found I could open the shutters; and in another moment had climbed outside and was fully closing the aperture in its original manner.

column1: I was now in Washington Street
column2: and for the moment saw no living thing nor any light save that of the moon. From several directions in the distance
column3: however
column4: I could hear the sound of hoarse voices
column5: of footsteps
column6: and of a curious kind of pattering which did not sound quite like footsteps. Plainly I had no time to lose. The points of the compass were clear to me
column7: and I was glad that all the street lights were turned off
column8: as is often the custom on strongly moonlit nights in prosperous rural regions. Some of the sounds came from the south
column9: yet I retained my design of escaping in that direction. There would
column10: I knew
column11: be plenty of deserted doorways to shelter me in case I met any person or group who looked like pursuers.

column1: I walked rapidly
column2: softly
column3: and close to the ruined houses. While hatless and dishevelled after my arduous climb
column4: I did not look especially noticeable; and stood a good chance of passing unheeded if forced to encounter any casual wayfarer.

column1: At Bates Street I drew into a yawning vestibule while two shambling figures crossed in front of me
column2: but was soon on my way again and approaching the open space where Eliot Street obliquely crosses Washington at the intersection of South. Though I had never seen this space
column3: it had looked dangerous to me on the grocery youth's map; since the moonlight would have free play there. There was no use trying to evade it
column4: for any alternative course would involve detours of possibly disastrous visibility and delaying effect. The only thing to do was to cross it boldly and openly; imitating the typical shamble of the Innsmouth folk as best I could
column5: and trusting that no one--or at least no pursuer of mine--would be there.

column1: Just how fully the pursuit was organised--and indeed
column2: just what its purpose might be--I could form no idea. There seemed to be unusual activity in the town
column3: but I judged that the news of my escape from the Gilman had not yet spread. I would
column4: of course
column5: soon have to shift from Washington to some other southward street; for that party from the hotel would doubtless be after me. I must have left dust prints in that last old building
column6: revealing how I had gained the street.

column1: The open space was
column2: as I had expected
column3: strongly moonlit; and I saw the remains of a parklike
column4: iron-railed green in its center. Fortunately no one was about though a curious sort of buzz or roar seemed to be increasing in the direction of Town Square. South Street was very wide
column5: leading directly down a slight declivity to the waterfront and commanding a long view out to sea; and I hoped that no one would be glancing up it from afar as I crossed in the bright moonlight.

column1: My progress was unimpeded
column2: and no fresh sound arose to hint that I had been spied. Glancing about me
column3: I involuntarily let my pace slacken for a second to take in the sight of the sea
column4: gorgeous in the burning moonlight at the street's end. Far out beyond the breakwater was the dim
column5: dark line of Devil Reef
column6: and as I glimpsed it I could not help thinking of all the hideous legends I had heard in the last twenty-four hours--legends which portrayed this ragged rock as a veritable gateway to realms of unfathomed horror and inconceivable abnormality.

column1: Then
column2: without warning
column3: I saw the intermittent flashes of light on the distant reef. They were definite and unmistakable
column4: and awaked in my mind a blind horror beyond all rational proportion. My muscles tightened for panic flight
column5: held in only by a certain unconscious caution and half-hypnotic fascination. And to make matters worse
column6: there now flashed forth from the lofty cupola of the Gilman House
column7: which loomed up to the northeast behind me
column8: a series of analogous though differently spaced gleams which could be nothing less than an answering signal.

column1: Controlling my muscles
column2: and realising afresh--how plainly visible I was
column3: I resumed my brisker and feignedly shambling pace; though keeping my eyes on that hellish and ominous reef as long as the opening of South Street gave me a seaward view. What the whole proceeding meant
column4: I could not imagine; unless it involved some strange rite connected with Devil Reef
column5: or unless some party had landed from a ship on that sinister rock. I now bent to the left around the ruinous green; still gazing toward the ocean as it blazed in the spectral summer moonlight
column6: and watching the cryptical flashing of those nameless
column7: unexplainable beacons.

column1: It was then that the most horrible impression of all was borne in upon me--the impression which destroyed my last vestige of self-control and sent me running frantically southward past the yawning black doorways and fishily staring windows of that deserted nightmare street. For at a closer glance I saw that the moonlit waters between the reef and the shore were far from empty. They were alive with a teeming horde of shapes swimming inward toward the town; and even at my vast distance and in my single moment of perception I could tell that the bobbing heads and flailing arms were alien and aberrant in a way scarcely to be expressed or consciously formulated.
My frantic running ceased before I had covered a block
column2: for at my left I began to hear something like the hue and cry of organised pursuit. There were footsteps and guttural sounds
column3: and a rattling motor wheezed south along Federal Street. In a second all my plans were utterly changed--for if the southward highway were blocked ahead of me
column4: I must clearly find another egress from Innsmouth. I paused and drew into a gaping doorway
column5: reflecting how lucky I was to have left the moonlit open space before these pursuers came down the parallel street.

column1: A second reflection was less comforting. Since the pursuit was down another street
column2: it was plain that the party was not following me directly. It had not seen me
column3: but was simply obeying a general plan of cutting off my escape. This

column7: her eldest son. He had shot himself after a trip to New England--the same trip

column9: which had caused him to be recalled at the Arkham Historical Society.

column1: This uncle had resembled her
column2: and I had never liked him either. Something about the staring
column3: unwinking expression of both of them had given me a vague
column4: unaccountable uneasiness. My mother and Uncle Walter had not looked like that. They were like their father
column5: though poor little cousin Lawrence--Walter's son--had been almost perfect duplicate of his grandmother before his condition took him to the permanent seclusion of a sanitarium at Canton. I had not seen him in four years

column1: My grandfather and his widowed son Walter now comprised the Cleveland household

column6: letters
column7: cuttings
column8: heirlooms

column1: It was in going over the letters and pictures on the Orne side that I began to acquire a kind of terror of my own ancestry. As I have said
column2: my grandmother and Uncle Douglas had always disturbed me. Now
column3: years after their passing
column4: I gazed at their pictured faces with a measurably heightened feeling of repulsion and alienation. I could not at first understand the change

It was clear that the typical expression of these faces now suggested something it had not suggested before--something which would bring stark panic if too openly thought of.

column1: But the worst shock came when my uncle shewed me the Orne jewellery in a downtown safe deposit vault. Some of the items were delicate and inspiring enough
column2: but there was one box of strange old pieces descended from my mysterious great-grandmother which my uncle was almost reluctant to produce. They were
column3: he said
column4: of very grotesque and almost repulsive design
column5: and had never to his knowledge been publicly worn; though my grandmother used to enjoy looking at them. Vague legends of bad luck clustered around them
column6: and my great-grandmother's French governess had said they ought not to be worn in New England
column7: though it would be quite safe to wear them in Europe.

column1: As my uncle began slowly and grudgingly to unwrap the things he urged me not to be shocked by the strangeness and frequent hideousness of the designs. Artists and archaeologists who had seen them pronounced their workmanship superlatively and exotically exquisite
column2: though no one seemed able to define their exact material or assign them to any specific art tradition. There were two armlets
column3: a tiara
column4: and a kind of pectoral; the latter having in high relief certain figures of almost unbearable extravagance.

column1: During this description I had kept a tight rein on my emotions
column2: but my face must have betrayed my mounting fears. My uncle looked concerned
column3: and paused in his unwrapping to study my countenance. I motioned to him to continue
column4: which he did with renewed signs of reluctance. He seemed to expect some demonstration when the first piece--the tiara--became visible
column5: but I doubt if he expected quite what actually happened. I did not expect it
column6: either
column7: for I thought I was thoroughly forewarned regarding what the jewellery would turn out to be. What I did was to faint silently away
column8: just as I had done in that brier-choked railway cut a year before.

column1: From that day on my life has been a nightmare of brooding and apprehension nor do I know how much is hideous truth and how much madness. My great-grandmother had been a Marsh of unknown source whose husband lived in Arkham--and did not old Zadok say that the daughter of Obed Marsh by a monstrous mother was married to an Arkham man through trick? What was it the ancient toper had muttered about the line of my eyes to Captain Obed's? In Arkham
column2: too
column3: the curator had told me I had the true Marsh eyes. Was Obed Marsh my own great-great-grandfather? Who--or what--then
column4: was my great-great-grandmother? But perhaps this was all madness. Those whitish-gold ornaments might easily have been bought from some Innsmouth sailor by the father of my great-grandmother
column5: whoever he was. And that look in the staring-eyed faces of my grandmother and self-slain uncle might be sheer fancy on my part--sheer fancy
column6: bolstered up by the Innsmouth shadow which had so darkly coloured my imagination. But why had my uncle killed himself after an ancestral quest in New England?

column1: For more than two years I fought off these reflections with partial success. My father secured me a place in an insurance office
column2: and I buried myself in routine as deeply as possible. In the winter of 1930-31
column3: however
column4: the dreams began. They were very sparse and insidious at first
column5: but increased in frequency and vividness as the weeks went by. Great watery spaces opened out before me
column6: and I seemed to wander through titanic sunken porticos and labyrinths of weedy cyclopean walls with grotesque fishes as my companions. Then the other shapes began to appear
column7: filling me with nameless horror the moment I awoke. But during the dreams they did not horrify me at all--I was one with them; wearing their unhuman trappings
column8: treading their aqueous ways
column9: and praying monstrously at their evil sea-bottom temples.

column1: There was much more than I could remember
column2: but even what I did remember each morning would be enough to stamp me as a madman or a genius if ever I dared write it down. Some frightful influence
column3: I felt
column4: was seeking gradually to drag me out of the sane world of wholesome life into unnamable abysses of blackness and alienage; and the process told heavily on me. My health and appearance grew steadily worse
column5: till finally I was forced to give up my position and adopt the static
column6: secluded life of an invalid. Some odd nervous affliction had me in its grip
column7: and I found myself at times almost unable to shut my eyes.

column1: It was then that I began to study the mirror with mounting alarm. The slow ravages of disease are not pleasant to watch
column2: but in my case there was something subtler and more puzzling in the background. My father seemed to notice it
column3: too
column4: for he began looking at me curiously and almost affrightedly. What was taking place in me? Could it be that I was coming to resemble my grandmother and uncle Douglas?

column1: One night I had a frightful dream in which I met my grandmother under the sea. She lived in a phosphorescent palace of many terraces
column2: with gardens of strange leprous corals and grotesque brachiate efflorescences
column3: and welcomed me with a warmth that may have been sardonic. She had changed--as those who take to the water change--and told me she had never died. Instead
column4: she had gone to a spot her dead son had learned about
column5: and had leaped to a realm whose wonders-- destined for him as well--he had spurned with a smoking pistol. This was to be my realm
column6: too--I could not escape it. I would never die
column7: but would live with those who had lived since before man ever walked the earth.

column1: I met also that which had been her grandmother. For eighty thousand years Pth'thya-l'yi had lived in Y'ha-nthlei
column2: and thither she had gone back after Obed Marsh was dead. Y'ha-nthlei was not destroyed when the upper-earth men shot death into the sea. It was hurt
column3: but not destroyed. The Deep Ones could never be destroyed
column4: even though the palaeogean magic of the forgotten Old Ones might sometimes check them. For the present they would rest; but some day
column5: if they remembered
column6: they would rise again for the tribute Great Cthulhu craved. It would be a city greater than Innsmouth next time. They had planned to spread
column7: and had brought up that which would help them
column8: but now they must wait once more. For bringing the upper-earth men's death I must do a penance
column9: but that would not be heavy. This was the dream in which I saw a shoggoth for the first time
column10: and the sight set me awake in a frenzy of screaming. That morning the mirror definitely told me I had acquired the Innsmouth look.

column1: So far I have not shot myself as my uncle Douglas did. I bought an automatic and almost took the step
column2: but certain dreams deterred me. The tense extremes of horror are lessening
column3: and I feel queerly drawn toward the unknown sea-deeps instead of fearing them. I hear and do strange things in sleep
column4: and awake with a kind of exaltation instead of terror. I do not believe I need to wait for the full change as most have waited. If I did
column5: my father would probably shut me up in a sanitarium as my poor little cousin is shut up. Stupendous and unheard-of splendors await me below
column6: and I shall seek them soon. Ia-R'lyehl Cihuiha flgagnl id Ia! No
column7: I shall not shoot myself--I cannot be made to shoot myself!

column1: I shall plan my cousin's escape from that Canton mad-house
column2: and together we shall go to marvel-shadowed Innsmouth. We shall swim out to that brooding reef in the sea and dive down through black abysses to Cyclopean and many-columned Y'ha-nthlei
column3: and in that lair of the Deep Ones we shall dwell amidst wonder and glory for ever.

I.
The Horror in Clay.
The most merciful thing in the world
column2: I think
column3: is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents. We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity
column4: and it was not meant that we should voyage far. The sciences
column5: each straining in its own direction
column6: have hitherto harmed us little; but some day the piecing together of dissociated knowledge will open up such terrifying vistas of reality
column7: and of our frightful position therein
column8: that we shall either go mad from the revelation or flee from the deadly light into the peace and safety of a new dark age.

column1: Theosophists have guessed at the awesome grandeur of the cosmic cycle wherein our world and human race form transient incidents. They have hinted at strange survivals in terms which would freeze the blood if not masked by a bland optimism. But it is not from them that there came the single glimpse of forbidden aeons which chills me when I think of it and maddens me when I dream of it. That glimpse
column2: like all dread glimpses of truth
column3: flashed out from an accidental piecing together of separated things—in this case an old newspaper item and the notes of a dead professor. I hope that no one else will accomplish this piecing out; certainly
column4: if I live
column5: I shall never knowingly supply a link in so hideous a chain. I think that the professor
column6: too
column7: intended to keep silent regarding the part he knew
column8: and that he would have destroyed his notes had not sudden death seized him.

column1: My knowledge of the thing began in the winter of 1926–27 with the death of my grand-uncle George Gammell Angell
column2: Professor Emeritus of Semitic Languages in Brown University
column3: Providence
column4: Rhode Island. Professor Angell was widely known as an authority on ancient inscriptions
column5: and had frequently been resorted to by the heads of prominent museums; so that his passing at the age of ninety-two may be recalled by many. Locally
column6: interest was intensified by the obscurity of the cause of death. The professor had been stricken whilst returning from the Newport boat; falling suddenly
column7: as witnesses said
column8: after having been jostled by a nautical-looking negro who had come from one of the queer dark courts on the precipitous hillside which formed a short cut from the waterfront to the deceased’s home in Williams Street. Physicians were unable to find any visible disorder
column9: but concluded after perplexed debate that some obscure lesion of the heart
column10: induced by the brisk ascent of so steep a hill by so elderly a man
column11: was responsible for the end. At the time I saw no reason to dissent from this dictum
column12: but latterly I am inclined to wonder—and more than wonder.

column1: As my grand-uncle’s heir and executor
column2: for he died a childless widower
column3: I was expected to go over his papers with some thoroughness; and for that purpose moved his entire set of files and boxes to my quarters in Boston. Much of the material which I correlated will be later published by the American Archaeological Society
column4: but there was one box which I found exceedingly puzzling
column5: and which I felt much averse from shewing to other eyes. It had been locked
column6: and I did not find the key till it occurred to me to examine the personal ring which the professor carried always in his pocket. Then indeed I succeeded in opening it
column7: but when I did so seemed only to be confronted by a greater and more closely locked barrier. For what could be the meaning of the queer clay bas-relief and the disjointed jottings
column8: ramblings
column9: and cuttings which I found? Had my uncle
column10: in his latter years
column11: become credulous of the most superficial impostures? I resolved to search out the eccentric sculptor responsible for this apparent disturbance of an old man’s peace of mind.

column1: The bas-relief was a rough rectangle less than an inch thick and about five by six inches in area; obviously of modern origin. Its designs
column2: however
column3: were far from modern in atmosphere and suggestion; for although the vagaries of cubism and futurism are many and wild
column4: they do not often reproduce that cryptic regularity which lurks in prehistoric writing. And writing of some kind the bulk of these designs seemed certainly to be; though my memory
column5: despite much familiarity with the papers and collections of my uncle
column6: failed in any way to identify this particular species
column7: or even to hint at its remotest affiliations.

column1: Above these apparent hieroglyphics was a figure of evidently pictorial intent
column2: though its impressionistic execution forbade a very clear idea of its nature. It seemed to be a sort of monster
column3: or symbol representing a monster
column4: of a form which only a diseased fancy could conceive. If I say that my somewhat extravagant imagination yielded simultaneous pictures of an octopus
column5: a dragon
column6: and a human caricature
column7: I shall not be unfaithful to the spirit of the thing. A pulpy
column8: tentacled head surmounted a grotesque and scaly body with rudimentary wings; but it was the general outline of the whole which made it most shockingly frightful. Behind the figure was a vague suggestion of a Cyclopean architectural background.

column5: 7 Thomas St.
column6: Providence
column7: R.I.”

column18: with references to passages in such mythological and anthropological source-books as Frazer’s Golden Bough and Miss Murray’s Witch-Cult in Western Europe. The cuttings largely alluded to outré mental illnesses and outbreaks of group folly or mania in the spring of 1925.

column1: The first half of the principal manuscript told a very peculiar tale. It appears that on March 1st
column3: a thin
column4: dark young man of neurotic and excited aspect had called upon Professor Angell bearing the singular clay bas-relief
column5: which was then exceedingly damp and fresh. His card bore the name of Henry Anthony Wilcox
column6: and my uncle had recognised him as the youngest son of an excellent family slightly known to him
column7: who had latterly been studying sculpture at the Rhode Island School of Design and living alone at the Fleur-de-Lys Building near that institution. Wilcox was a precocious youth of known genius but great eccentricity
column8: and had from childhood excited attention through the strange stories and odd dreams he was in the habit of relating. He called himself “psychically hypersensitive”
column9: but the staid folk of the ancient commercial city dismissed him as merely “queer”. Never mingling much with his kind
column10: he had dropped gradually from social visibility
column11: and was now known only to a small group of aesthetes from other towns. Even the Providence Art Club
column12: anxious to preserve its conservatism
column13: had found him quite hopeless.

column1: On the occasion of the visit
column2: ran the professor’s manuscript
column3: the sculptor abruptly asked for the benefit of his host’s archaeological knowledge in identifying the hieroglyphics on the bas-relief. He spoke in a dreamy
column4: stilted manner which suggested pose and alienated sympathy; and my uncle shewed some sharpness in replying
column5: for the conspicuous freshness of the tablet implied kinship with anything but archaeology. Young Wilcox’s rejoinder
column6: which impressed my uncle enough to make him recall and record it verbatim
column7: was of a fantastically poetic cast which must have typified his whole conversation
column8: and which I have since found highly characteristic of him. He said
column9: “It is new
column10: indeed
column11: for I made it last night in a dream of strange cities; and dreams are older than brooding Tyre
column12: or the contemplative Sphinx
column13: or garden-girdled Babylon.”

column1: It was then that he began that rambling tale which suddenly played upon a sleeping memory and won the fevered interest of my uncle. There had been a slight earthquake tremor the night before
column2: the most considerable felt in New England for some years; and Wilcox’s imagination had been keenly affected. Upon retiring
column3: he had had an unprecedented dream of great Cyclopean cities of titan blocks and sky-flung monoliths
column4: all dripping with green ooze and sinister with latent horror. Hieroglyphics had covered the walls and pillars
column5: and from some undetermined point below had come a voice that was not a voice; a chaotic sensation which only fancy could transmute into sound
column6: but which he attempted to render by the almost unpronounceable jumble of letters
column7: “Cthulhu fhtagn”.

column1: This verbal jumble was the key to the recollection which excited and disturbed Professor Angell. He questioned the sculptor with scientific minuteness; and studied with almost frantic intensity the bas-relief on which the youth had found himself working
column2: chilled and clad only in his night-clothes
column3: when waking had stolen bewilderingly over him. My uncle blamed his old age
column4: Wilcox afterward said
column5: for his slowness in recognising both hieroglyphics and pictorial design. Many of his questions seemed highly out-of-place to his visitor
column6: especially those which tried to connect the latter with strange cults or societies; and Wilcox could not understand the repeated promises of silence which he was offered in exchange for an admission of membership in some widespread mystical or paganly religious body. When Professor Angell became convinced that the sculptor was indeed ignorant of any cult or system of cryptic lore
column7: he besieged his visitor with demands for future reports of dreams. This bore regular fruit
column8: for after the first interview the manuscript records daily calls of the young man
column9: during which he related startling fragments of nocturnal imagery whose burden was always some terrible Cyclopean vista of dark and dripping stone
column10: with a subterrene voice or intelligence shouting monotonously in enigmatical sense-impacts uninscribable save as gibberish. The two sounds most frequently repeated are those rendered by the letters “Cthulhu” and “R’lyeh”.

column1: On March 23d

column5: and had manifested since then only alternations of unconsciousness and delirium. My uncle at once telephoned the family

column8: apparently

column14: the doctor added
column15: was invariably a prelude to the young man’s subsidence into lethargy. His temperature
column16: oddly enough
column17: was not greatly above normal; but his whole condition was otherwise such as to suggest true fever rather than mental disorder.

column1: On April 2nd at about 3 p.m. every trace of Wilcox’s malady suddenly ceased. He sat upright in bed

column1: Here the first part of the manuscript ended

column5: it seems
column6: had quickly instituted a prodigiously far-flung body of inquiries amongst nearly all the friends whom he could question without impertinence

column1: The press cuttings
column2: as I have intimated
column3: touched on cases of panic
column4: mania
column5: and eccentricity during the given period. Professor Angell must have employed a cutting bureau
column6: for the number of extracts was tremendous and the sources scattered throughout the globe. Here was a nocturnal suicide in London

column8: where a fanatic deduces a dire future from visions he has seen. A despatch from California describes a theosophist colony as donning white robes en masse for some “glorious fulfilment” which never arrives
column9: whilst items from India speak guardedly of serious native unrest toward the end of March. Voodoo orgies multiply in Hayti

column16: all told; and I can at this date scarcely envisage the callous rationalism with which I set them aside. But I was then convinced that young Wilcox had known of the older matters mentioned by the professor.

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.
The older matters which had made the sculptor’s dream and bas-relief so significant to my uncle formed the subject of the second half of his long manuscript. Once before
column2: it appears
column3: Professor Angell had seen the hellish outlines of the nameless monstrosity
column4: puzzled over the unknown hieroglyphics
column5: and heard the ominous syllables which can be rendered only as “Cthulhu”; and all this in so stirring and horrible a connexion that it is small wonder he pursued young Wilcox with queries and demands for data.

column1: The earlier experience had come in 1908
column2: seventeen years before
column3: when the American Archaeological Society held its annual meeting in St. Louis. Professor Angell
column4: as befitted one of his authority and attainments
column5: had had a prominent part in all the deliberations; and was one of the first to be approached by the several outsiders who took advantage of the convocation to offer questions for correct answering and problems for expert solution.

column1: The chief of these outsiders
column2: and in a short time the focus of interest for the entire meeting
column3: was a commonplace-looking middle-aged man who had travelled all the way from New Orleans for certain special information unobtainable from any local source. His name was John Raymond Legrasse
column4: and he was by profession an Inspector of Police. With him he bore the subject of his visit
column5: a grotesque
column6: repulsive
column7: and apparently very ancient stone statuette whose origin he was at a loss to determine. It must not be fancied that Inspector Legrasse had the least interest in archaeology. On the contrary
column8: his wish for enlightenment was prompted by purely professional considerations. The statuette
column9: idol
column10: fetish
column11: or whatever it was
column12: had been captured some months before in the wooded swamps south of New Orleans during a raid on a supposed voodoo meeting; and so singular and hideous were the rites connected with it
column13: that the police could not but realise that they had stumbled on a dark cult totally unknown to them
column14: and infinitely more diabolic than even the blackest of the African voodoo circles. Of its origin
column15: apart from the erratic and unbelievable tales extorted from the captured members
column16: absolutely nothing was to be discovered; hence the anxiety of the police for any antiquarian lore which might help them to place the frightful symbol
column17: and through it track down the cult to its fountain-head.

column1: Inspector Legrasse was scarcely prepared for the sensation which his offering created. One sight of the thing had been enough to throw the assembled men of science into a state of tense excitement
column2: and they lost no time in crowding around him to gaze at the diminutive figure whose utter strangeness and air of genuinely abysmal antiquity hinted so potently at unopened and archaic vistas. No recognised school of sculpture had animated this terrible object
column3: yet centuries and even thousands of years seemed recorded in its dim and greenish surface of unplaceable stone.

column4: and of exquisitely artistic workmanship. It represented a monster of vaguely anthropoid outline
column5: but with an octopus-like head whose face was a mass of feelers
column6: a scaly
column7: rubbery-looking body

column9: and long
column10: narrow wings behind. This thing
column11: which seemed instinct with a fearsome and unnatural malignancy
column12: was of a somewhat bloated corpulence
column13: and squatted evilly on a rectangular block or pedestal covered with undecipherable characters. The tips of the wings touched the back edge of the block
column14: the seat occupied the centre
column15: whilst the long
column16: curved claws of the doubled-up

column1: They worshipped

column1: III.
The Madness from the Sea.
If heaven ever wishes to grant me a boon

column8: then
column9: for my subsequent dreams and emotional impressions to become coloured and moulded by what my memory subtly held over from my secondary state? A few of the myths had significant connexions with other cloudy legends of the pre-human world

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape

Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years
column4: and linkages with other galaxies and universes
column5: were freely spoken of. Indeed
column6: there was no such thing as time in its humanly accepted sense.

column1: But most of the tales and impressions concerned a relatively late race

column4: they indicated

column3: their achievements
column4: their languages
column5: and their psychologies. With this aeon-embracing knowledge

column7: arts

column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off
column2: and when (assuming that it came from a body vastly different from the Great Race’s) it had lost its horror at its unfamiliar temporary form
column3: it was permitted to study its new environment and experience a wonder and wisdom approximating that of its displacer. With suitable precautions
column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen
column7: and to such minds the unveiling of hidden mysteries of earth—closed chapters of inconceivable pasts and dizzying vortices of future time which include the years ahead of their own natural ages—forms always
column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times

column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated

column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be
column7: while the myriad minds sent backward were left to die in the horror of strange shapes. Later the race would again face death
column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Such was the background of intertwined legend and hallucination. When

column7: plainly

column1: At times the parallelism of so many cases in so many distant ages continued to worry me as it had at first

Probably all the other victims whose cases were like mine had had a long and familiar knowledge of the tales I had learned only when in my secondary state. When these victims had lost their memory
column3: they had associated themselves with the creatures of their household myths—the fabulous invaders supposed to displace men’s minds—and had thus embarked upon quests for knowledge which they thought they could take back to a fancied
column4: non-human past. Then when their memory returned
column5: they reversed the associative process and thought of themselves as the former captive minds instead of as the displacers. Hence the dreams and pseudo-memories following the conventional myth-pattern.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations
column2: they came finally to supersede all others in my mind—largely because of the greater weakness of any rival theory. And a substantial number of eminent psychologists and anthropologists gradually agreed with me. The more I reflected
column3: the more convincing did my reasoning seem; till in the end I had a really effective bulwark against the visions and impressions which still assailed me. Suppose I did see strange things at night? These were only what I had heard and read of. Suppose I did have odd loathings and perspectives and pseudo-memories? These
column4: too
column5: were only echoes of myths absorbed in my secondary state. Nothing that I might dream
column6: nothing that I might feel

column1: Fortified by this philosophy

column4: and put my newly gained knowledge to practical use by accepting an instructorship in psychology at the university. My old chair of political economy had long been adequately filled—besides which

I continued

column4: though

column2: though harmless

column1: Afterward I saw them everywhere; swarming in all the great chambers and corridors
column2: tending monstrous machines in vaulted crypts
column3: and racing along the vast roads in gigantic boat-shaped cars. I ceased to be afraid of them

column6: though shewing no physical variation

column8: but very largely from one another. They wrote a great deal in what seemed to my cloudy vision a vast variety of characters—never the typical curvilinear hieroglyphs of the majority. A few
column9: I fancied
column10: used our own familiar alphabet. Most of them worked much more slowly than the general mass of the entities.

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August
column4: did any suggestions of bodily existence begin to harass me. I say harass
column5: because the first phase was a purely abstract though infinitely terrible association of my previously noted body-loathing with the scenes of my visions. For a while my chief concern during dreams was to avoid looking down at myself

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking
column8: I could recall only minute and meaningless scraps of the unknown tongues which my dream-self had mastered
column9: though whole phrases of the history stayed with me.

column1: I learned—even before my waking self had studied the parallel cases or the old myths from which the dreams doubtless sprang—that the entities around me were of the world’s greatest race
column2: which had conquered time and had sent exploring minds into every age. I knew
column3: too

column5: and that a few of the other strange forms housed similarly captured minds. I seemed to talk
column6: in some odd language of claw-clickings
column7: with exiled intellects from every corner of the solar system.

column1: There was a mind from the planet we know as Venus

column1: I awaked each morning in a fever
column2: sometimes frantically trying to verify or discredit such information as fell within the range of modern human knowledge. Traditional facts took on new and doubtful aspects
column3: and I marvelled at the dream-fancy which could invent such surprising addenda to history and science. I shivered at the mysteries the past may conceal
column4: and trembled at the menaces the future may bring forth. What was hinted in the speech of post-human entities of the fate of mankind produced such an effect on me that I will not set it down here. After man there would be the mighty beetle civilisation
column5: the bodies of whose members the cream of the Great Race would seize when the monstrous doom overtook the elder world. Later
column6: as the earth’s span closed
column7: the transferred minds would again migrate through time and space—to another stopping-place in the bodies of the bulbous vegetable entities of Mercury. But there would be races after them
column8: clinging pathetically to the cold planet and burrowing to its horror-filled core
column9: before the utter end.

column1: Meanwhile
column2: in my dreams

column1: The Great Race seemed to form a single loosely knit nation or league

column1: According to these scraps of information

column4: their senses did not include that of sight; their mental world being a strange
column5: non-visual pattern of impressions. They were
column6: however

column1: When these things had come to the earth they had built mighty basalt cities of windowless towers

column1: But as the aeons passed

column1: It was evident that the coming doom so desperately feared by the Great Race—the doom that was one day to send millions of keen minds across the chasm of time to strange bodies in the safer future—had to do with a final successful irruption of the Elder Beings. Mental projections down the ages had clearly foretold such a horror

column11: windowless elder towers.

column1: V.
That is the world of which my dreams brought me dim
column2: scattered echoes every night. I cannot hope to give any true idea of the horror and dread contained in such echoes

column6: creeping terror would return momentarily now and then. It did not

column1: My dear Sir:—
A recent conversation with Dr. E. M. Boyle of Perth
column2: and some papers with your articles which he has just sent me
column3: make it advisable for me to tell you about certain things I have seen in the Great Sandy Desert east of our gold field here. It would seem
column4: in view of the peculiar legends about old cities with huge stonework and strange designs and hieroglyphs which you describe

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: But what I have to tell is more than this. Two years ago
column2: when I was prospecting about 500 miles east in the desert

column4: and weathered and pitted to the very limit. At first I couldn’t find any of the marks the blackfellows told about
column5: but when I looked close enough I could make out some deeply carved lines in spite of the weathering. They were peculiar curves

column1: When I saw some

column3: and made a careful reckoning of the place with my instruments. I also took pictures of 10 or 12 of the most typical blocks
column4: and will enclose the prints for you to see. I turned my information and pictures over to the government at Perth
column5: but they have done nothing with them. Then I met Dr. Boyle
column6: who had read your articles in the Journal of the American Psychological Society
column7: and in time happened to mention the stones. He was enormously interested
column8: and became quite excited when I shewed him my snapshots
column9: saying that the stones and markings were just like those of the masonry you had dreamed about and seen described in legends. He meant to write you
column10: but was delayed. Meanwhile he sent me most of the magazines with your articles

column1: Now I can understand how important all this will be to you. Without question we are faced with the remains of an unknown civilisation older than any dreamed of before
column2: and forming a basis for your legends. As a mining engineer
column3: I have some knowledge of geology
column4: and can tell you that these blocks are so ancient they frighten me. They are mostly sandstone and granite

column1: In view of your previous diligent work in tracking down the legends and everything connected with them
column2: I cannot doubt but that you will want to lead an expedition to the desert and make some archaeological excavations. column1: The place can be reached from Pilbarra in about 4 days by motor tractor—which we’d need for our apparatus. It is somewhat west and south of Warburton’s path of 1873

column4: 125° 0' 39"" East Longitude. The climate is tropical

column6: and am keenly eager to assist in any plan you may devise. After studying your articles I am deeply impressed with the profound significance of the whole matter. Dr. Boyle will write later. When rapid communication is needed

column1: Hoping profoundly for an early message
Believe me
Most faithfully yours
Robert B. F. Mackenzie.

column1: VI.

I come now to the crucial and most difficult part of my narrative—all the more difficult because I cannot be quite certain of its reality. At times I feel uncomfortably sure that I was not dreaming or deluded; and it is this feeling—in view of the stupendous implications which the objective truth of my experience would raise—which impels me to make this record. My son—a trained psychologist with the fullest and most sympathetic knowledge of my whole case—shall be the primary judge of what I have to tell.

column4: and by noon he had conquered the impulse to stare at vacancy. About two o’clock he went out for lunch

column1: He would have to consult a nerve specialist after all—perhaps there was a connexion with his somnambulism—but meanwhile he might at least try to break the morbid spell himself. Undoubtedly he could still manage to walk away from the pull; so with great resolution he headed against it and dragged himself deliberately north along Garrison Street. By the time he had reached the bridge over the Miskatonic he was in a cold perspiration
column2: and he clutched at the iron railing as he gazed upstream at the ill-regarded island whose regular lines of ancient standing stones brooded sullenly in the afternoon sunlight.

column3: too
column4: as if some other living thing were crawling close to the ground. When the old woman began to turn toward him he fled precipitately off the bridge and into the shelter of the town’s labyrinthine waterfront alleys. Distant though the island was

column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held
column2: and only with tremendous resolution could Gilman drag himself into the old house and up the rickety stairs. For hours he sat silent and aimless
column3: with his eyes shifting gradually westward. About six o’clock his sharpened ears caught the whining prayers of Joe Mazurewicz two floors below

column6: with the glimmering spring stars shining ahead. The urge to walk was gradually changing to an urge to leap mystically into space
