column1: It was in the sky. A definite point among the stars had a claim on him and was calling him. Apparently it was a point somewhere between Hydra and Argo Navis

column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door

column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses

column5: Joe said
column6: he had not—but he must check up on this. Perhaps Frank Elwood could tell him something

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column2: see a nerve specialist
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest

column6: slanting ceiling.

column1: That night as Gilman slept the violet light broke upon him with heightened intensity
column2: and the old witch and small furry thing—getting closer than ever before—mocked him with inhuman squeals and devilish gestures. He was glad to sink into the vaguely roaring twilight abysses
column3: though the pursuit of that iridescent bubble-congeries and that kaleidoscopic little polyhedron was menacing and irritating. Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles

column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame

column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify

column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought

column7: like the whole balustrade

column11: flat

column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed

column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste

column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished

column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room

column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged

column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration

column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling

column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall

column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench

Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall

column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. column3: Gilman added
column4: might lead to dangerous and unthinkable situations; for who could foretell the conditions pervading an adjacent but normally inaccessible dimension? On the other hand

column5: too

column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him

column7: muddy

column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The first half of the principal manuscript told a very peculiar tale. It appears that on March 1st

column1: On the occasion of the visit

column9: “It is new

column12: or the contemplative Sphinx

column1: It was then that he began that rambling tale which suddenly played upon a sleeping memory and won the fevered interest of my uncle. There had been a slight earthquake tremor the night before

column5: and from some undetermined point below had come a voice that was not a voice; a chaotic sensation which only fancy could transmute into sound

column7: “Cthulhu fhtagn”.

column2: chilled and clad only in his night-clothes
column3: when waking had stolen bewilderingly over him. My uncle blamed his old age
column4: Wilcox afterward said
column5: for his slowness in recognising both hieroglyphics and pictorial design. Many of his questions seemed highly out-of-place to his visitor
column6: especially those which tried to connect the latter with strange cults or societies; and Wilcox could not understand the repeated promises of silence which he was offered in exchange for an admission of membership in some widespread mystical or paganly religious body. When Professor Angell became convinced that the sculptor was indeed ignorant of any cult or system of cryptic lore

column1: Here the first part of the manuscript ended

column5: it seems

column17: however

column1: The press cuttings
column2: as I have intimated
column3: touched on cases of panic
column4: mania
column5: and eccentricity during the given period. Professor Angell must have employed a cutting bureau
column6: for the number of extracts was tremendous and the sources scattered throughout the globe. Here was a nocturnal suicide in London
column7: where a lone sleeper had leaped from a window after a shocking cry. Here likewise a rambling letter to the editor of a paper in South America
column8: where a fanatic deduces a dire future from visions he has seen. A despatch from California describes a theosophist colony as donning white robes en masse for some “glorious fulfilment” which never arrives
column9: whilst items from India speak guardedly of serious native unrest toward the end of March. Voodoo orgies multiply in Hayti
column10: and African outposts report ominous mutterings. American officers in the Philippines find certain tribes bothersome about this time

column15: that only a miracle can have stopped the medical fraternity from noting strange parallelisms and drawing mystified conclusions. A weird bunch of cuttings
column16: all told; and I can at this date scarcely envisage the callous rationalism with which I set them aside. But I was then convinced that young Wilcox had known of the older matters mentioned by the professor.

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.
The older matters which had made the sculptor’s dream and bas-relief so significant to my uncle formed the subject of the second half of his long manuscript. Once before
column2: it appears
column3: Professor Angell had seen the hellish outlines of the nameless monstrosity
column4: puzzled over the unknown hieroglyphics
column5: and heard the ominous syllables which can be rendered only as “Cthulhu”; and all this in so stirring and horrible a connexion that it is small wonder he pursued young Wilcox with queries and demands for data.

column1: The earlier experience had come in 1908
column2: seventeen years before
column3: when the American Archaeological Society held its annual meeting in St. Louis. Professor Angell
column4: as befitted one of his authority and attainments
column5: had had a prominent part in all the deliberations; and was one of the first to be approached by the several outsiders who took advantage of the convocation to offer questions for correct answering and problems for expert solution.

column1: The chief of these outsiders
column2: and in a short time the focus of interest for the entire meeting
column3: was a commonplace-looking middle-aged man who had travelled all the way from New Orleans for certain special information unobtainable from any local source. His name was John Raymond Legrasse
column4: and he was by profession an Inspector of Police. With him he bore the subject of his visit
column5: a grotesque
column6: repulsive
column7: and apparently very ancient stone statuette whose origin he was at a loss to determine. It must not be fancied that Inspector Legrasse had the least interest in archaeology. On the contrary
column8: his wish for enlightenment was prompted by purely professional considerations. The statuette
column9: idol
column10: fetish
column11: or whatever it was
column12: had been captured some months before in the wooded swamps south of New Orleans during a raid on a supposed voodoo meeting; and so singular and hideous were the rites connected with it
column13: that the police could not but realise that they had stumbled on a dark cult totally unknown to them
column14: and infinitely more diabolic than even the blackest of the African voodoo circles. Of its origin
column15: apart from the erratic and unbelievable tales extorted from the captured members
column16: absolutely nothing was to be discovered; hence the anxiety of the police for any antiquarian lore which might help them to place the frightful symbol
column17: and through it track down the cult to its fountain-head.

column1: Inspector Legrasse was scarcely prepared for the sensation which his offering created. One sight of the thing had been enough to throw the assembled men of science into a state of tense excitement
column2: and they lost no time in crowding around him to gaze at the diminutive figure whose utter strangeness and air of genuinely abysmal antiquity hinted so potently at unopened and archaic vistas. No recognised school of sculpture had animated this terrible object
column3: yet centuries and even thousands of years seemed recorded in its dim and greenish surface of unplaceable stone.

column1: The figure
column2: which was finally passed slowly from man to man for close and careful study
column3: was between seven and eight inches in height
column4: and of exquisitely artistic workmanship. It represented a monster of vaguely anthropoid outline
column5: but with an octopus-like head whose face was a mass of feelers
column6: a scaly
column7: rubbery-looking body
column8: prodigious claws on hind and fore feet
column9: and long
column10: narrow wings behind. This thing
column11: which seemed instinct with a fearsome and unnatural malignancy
column12: was of a somewhat bloated corpulence
column13: and squatted evilly on a rectangular block or pedestal covered with undecipherable characters. The tips of the wings touched the back edge of the block
column14: the seat occupied the centre
column15: whilst the long
column16: curved claws of the doubled-up
column17: crouching hind legs gripped the front edge and extended a quarter of the way down toward the bottom of the pedestal. The cephalopod head was bent forward
column18: so that the ends of the facial feelers brushed the backs of huge fore paws which clasped the croucher’s elevated knees. The aspect of the whole was abnormally life-like
column19: and the more subtly fearful because its source was so totally unknown. Its vast
column21: and incalculable age was unmistakable; yet not one link did it shew with any known type of art belonging to civilisation’s youth—or indeed to any other time. Totally separate and apart
column22: its very material was a mystery; for the soapy
column23: greenish-black stone with its golden or iridescent flecks and striations resembled nothing familiar to geology or mineralogy. The characters along the base were equally baffling; and no member present
column24: despite a representation of half the world’s expert learning in this field
column25: could form the least notion of even their remotest linguistic kinship. They
column27: belonged to something horribly remote and distinct from mankind as we know it; something frightfully suggestive of old and unhallowed cycles of life in which our world and our conceptions have no part.

column1: And yet
column2: as the members severally shook their heads and confessed defeat at the Inspector’s problem
column3: there was one man in that gathering who suspected a touch of bizarre familiarity in the monstrous shape and writing
column4: and who presently told with some diffidence of the odd trifle he knew. This person was the late William Channing Webb
column5: Professor of Anthropology in Princeton University
column6: and an explorer of no slight note. Professor Webb had been engaged
column7: forty-eight years before
column8: in a tour of Greenland and Iceland in search of some Runic inscriptions which he failed to unearth; and whilst high up on the West Greenland coast had encountered a singular tribe or cult of degenerate Esquimaux whose religion
column9: a curious form of devil-worship
column10: chilled him with its deliberate bloodthirstiness and repulsiveness. It was a faith of which other Esquimaux knew little
column11: and which they mentioned only with shudders
column12: saying that it had come down from horribly ancient aeons before ever the world was made. Besides nameless rites and human sacrifices there were certain queer hereditary rituals addressed to a supreme elder devil or tornasuk; and of this Professor Webb had taken a careful phonetic copy from an aged angekok or wizard-priest
column13: expressing the sounds in Roman letters as best he knew how. But just now of prime significance was the fetish which this cult had cherished
column14: and around which they danced when the aurora leaped high over the ice cliffs. It was
column15: the professor stated
column16: a very crude bas-relief of stone
column17: comprising a hideous picture and some cryptic writing. And so far as he could tell
column18: it was a rough parallel in all essential features of the bestial thing now lying before the meeting.

column1: This data
column2: received with suspense and astonishment by the assembled members
column3: proved doubly exciting to Inspector Legrasse; and he began at once to ply his informant with questions. Having noted and copied an oral ritual among the swamp cult-worshippers his men had arrested
column4: he besought the professor to remember as best he might the syllables taken down amongst the diabolist Esquimaux. There then followed an exhaustive comparison of details
column5: and a moment of really awed silence when both detective and scientist agreed on the virtual identity of the phrase common to two hellish rituals so many worlds of distance apart. What
column6: in substance

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Legrasse had one point in advance of Professor Webb

column3: as given
column4: ran something like this:

column1: “In his house at R’lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.”
And now
column2: in response to a general and urgent demand
column3: Inspector Legrasse related as fully as possible his experience with the swamp worshippers; telling a story to which I could see my uncle attached profound significance. It savoured of the wildest dreams of myth-maker and theosophist

column1: On November 1st
column3: there had come to the New Orleans police a frantic summons from the swamp and lagoon country to the south. The squatters there

column5: were in the grip of stark terror from an unknown thing which had stolen upon them in the night. It was voodoo

column8: soul-chilling chants and dancing devil-flames; and
column9: the frightened messenger added
column10: the people could stand it no more.

column1: So a body of twenty police
column2: filling two carriages and an automobile
column3: had set out in the late afternoon with the shivering squatter as a guide. At the end of the passable road they alighted

column5: and now and then a pile of dank stones or fragment of a rotting wall intensified by its hint of morbid habitation a depression which every malformed tree and every fungous islet combined to create. At length the squatter settlement
column6: a miserable huddle of huts
column7: hove in sight; and hysterical dwellers ran out to cluster around the group of bobbing lanterns. The muffled beat of tom-toms was now faintly audible far
column8: far ahead; and a curdling shriek came at infrequent intervals when the wind shifted. A reddish glare
column9: too
column10: seemed to filter through the pale undergrowth beyond endless avenues of forest night. Reluctant even to be left alone again

column1: The region now entered by the police was one of traditionally evil repute
column2: substantially unknown and untraversed by white men. There were legends of a hidden lake unglimpsed by mortal sight
column3: in which dwelt a huge
column4: formless white polypous thing with luminous eyes; and squatters whispered that bat-winged devils flew up out of caverns in inner earth to worship it at midnight. They said it had been there before D’Iberville
column5: before La Salle
column6: before the Indians
column7: and before even the wholesome beasts and birds of the woods. It was nightmare itself
column8: and to see it was to die. But it made men dream
column9: and so they knew enough to keep away. The present voodoo orgy was
column10: indeed
column11: on the merest fringe of this abhorred area
column12: but that location was bad enough; hence perhaps the very place of the worship had terrified the squatters more than the shocking sounds and incidents.

column1: Only poetry or madness could do justice to the noises heard by Legrasse’s men as they ploughed on through the black morass toward the red glare and the muffled tom-toms. There are vocal qualities peculiar to men
column2: and vocal qualities peculiar to beasts; and it is terrible to hear the one when the source should yield the other. Animal fury and orgiastic licence here whipped themselves to daemoniac heights by howls and squawking ecstasies that tore and reverberated through those nighted woods like pestilential tempests from the gulfs of hell. Now and then the less organised ululation would cease
column3: and from what seemed a well-drilled chorus of hoarse voices would rise in sing-song chant that hideous phrase or ritual:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Then the men
column2: having reached a spot where the trees were thinner
column3: came suddenly in sight of the spectacle itself. Four of them reeled
column4: one fainted
column5: and two were shaken into a frantic cry which the mad cacophony of the orgy fortunately deadened. Legrasse dashed swamp water on the face of the fainting man
column6: and all stood trembling and nearly hypnotised with horror.

column1: In a natural glade of the swamp stood a grassy island of perhaps an acre’s extent
column2: clear of trees and tolerably dry. On this now leaped and twisted a more indescribable horde of human abnormality than any but a Sime or an Angarola could paint. Void of clothing
column3: this hybrid spawn were braying
column4: bellowing
column5: and writhing about a monstrous ring-shaped bonfire; in the centre of which
column6: revealed by occasional rifts in the curtain of flame
column7: stood a great granite monolith some eight feet in height; on top of which
column8: incongruous with its diminutiveness
column9: rested the noxious carven statuette. From a wide circle of ten scaffolds set up at regular intervals with the flame-girt monolith as a centre hung
column10: head downward
column11: the oddly marred bodies of the helpless squatters who had disappeared. It was inside this circle that the ring of worshippers jumped and roared
column12: the general direction of the mass motion being from left to right in endless Bacchanal between the ring of bodies and the ring of fire.

column1: It may have been only imagination and it may have been only echoes which induced one of the men
column2: an excitable Spaniard
column3: to fancy he heard antiphonal responses to the ritual from some far and unillumined spot deeper within the wood of ancient legendry and horror. This man
column4: Joseph D. Galvez
column5: I later met and questioned; and he proved distractingly imaginative. He indeed went so far as to hint of the faint beating of great wings
column6: and of a glimpse of shining eyes and a mountainous white bulk beyond the remotest trees—but I suppose he had been hearing too much native superstition.

column1: Actually
column2: the horrified pause of the men was of comparatively brief duration. Duty came first; and although there must have been nearly a hundred mongrel celebrants in the throng
column3: the police relied on their firearms and plunged determinedly into the nauseous rout. For five minutes the resultant din and chaos were beyond description. Wild blows were struck
column4: shots were fired
column5: and escapes were made; but in the end Legrasse was able to count some forty-seven sullen prisoners
column6: whom he forced to dress in haste and fall into line between two rows of policemen. Five of the worshippers lay dead

column8: of course
column9: was carefully removed and carried back by Legrasse.

column1: Examined at headquarters after a trip of intense strain and weariness
column2: the prisoners all proved to be men of a very low
column3: mixed-blooded
column4: and mentally aberrant type. Most were seamen
column5: and a sprinkling of negroes and mulattoes

column7: gave a colouring of voodooism to the heterogeneous cult. But before many questions were asked

column1: They worshipped
column2: so they said
column3: the Great Old Ones who lived ages before there were any men
column4: and who came to the young world out of the sky. Those Old Ones were gone now
column5: inside the earth and under the sea; but their dead bodies had told their secrets in dreams to the first men
column6: who formed a cult which had never died. This was that cult

column1: It was then that the most horrible impression of all was borne in upon me--the impression which destroyed my last vestige of self-control and sent me running frantically southward past the yawning black doorways and fishily staring windows of that deserted nightmare street. They were alive with a teeming horde of shapes swimming inward toward the town; and even at my vast distance and in my single moment of perception I could tell that the bobbing heads and flailing arms were alien and aberrant in a way scarcely to be expressed or consciously formulated.
My frantic running ceased before I had covered a block

column4: however

column1: No one was stirring in that dead street beside the river-gorge

column1: The vast
column2: barnlike length of the old bridge gleamed spectrally in the moonlight

column1: The marshy region began very abruptly

At the end of the cut it would cross the track and swerve off to a safer distance; but meanwhile I must be exceedingly careful. column1: Just before entering the cut I glanced behind me
column2: but saw no pursuer. The ancient spires and roofs of decaying Innsmouth gleamed lovely and ethereal in the magic yellow moonlight
column3: and I thought of how they must have looked in the old days before the shadow fell. Then
column4: as my gaze circled inland from the town
column5: something less tranquil arrested my notice and held me immobile for a second.

The distance was great and I could distinguish nothing in detail; but I did not at all like the look of that moving column. It undulated too much

column3: too

column1: Whence could come the dense personnel of such a column as I now beheld? Did those ancient

column3: uncatalogued

column1: The stench waxed overpowering

column4: haunted

column2: baying entities of unknown source flopped noisomely past
column3: scarcely more than a hundred yards away?

column1: I thought I was prepared for the worst

Then I knew that a long section of them must be plainly in sight where the sides of the cut flattened out and the road crossed the track--and I could no longer keep myself from sampling whatever horror that leering yellow moon might have to shew.
It was the end

column7: as objective flesh

column4: prolately spheroidal bubbles and a very much smaller polyhedron of unknown colours and rapidly shifting surface angles—seemed to take notice of him and follow him about or float ahead as he changed position among the titan prisms
column5: labyrinths

column3: diffused green light. He was barefooted and in his night-clothes

column1: He was good for nothing that morning

column1: He would have to consult a nerve specialist after all—perhaps there was a connexion with his somnambulism—but meanwhile he might at least try to break the morbid spell himself. Undoubtedly he could still manage to walk away from the pull; so with great resolution he headed against it and dragged himself deliberately north along Garrison Street. By the time he had reached the bridge over the Miskatonic he was in a cold perspiration
column2: and he clutched at the iron railing as he gazed upstream at the ill-regarded island whose regular lines of ancient standing stones brooded sullenly in the afternoon sunlight.

column3: too
column4: as if some other living thing were crawling close to the ground. When the old woman began to turn toward him he fled precipitately off the bridge and into the shelter of the town’s labyrinthine waterfront alleys. Distant though the island was

column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held
column2: and only with tremendous resolution could Gilman drag himself into the old house and up the rickety stairs. For hours he sat silent and aimless
column3: with his eyes shifting gradually westward. About six o’clock his sharpened ears caught the whining prayers of Joe Mazurewicz two floors below

column1: It was in the sky. A definite point among the stars had a claim on him and was calling him. Apparently it was a point somewhere between Hydra and Argo Navis

column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door

column5: Joe said

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column2: see a nerve specialist
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest

column6: slanting ceiling.

Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles

column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame

column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify

column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought

column11: flat

column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed

column6: and propelling themselves by a spider-like wriggling of their lower set of starfish-arms.

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed

column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste

column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished

column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant

column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged

column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed

column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No

column7: and she waddled in. Yes

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil

column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged

column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head

column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling

column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench

Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall

column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. column2: was still to be seen. Success
column3: Gilman added
column4: might lead to dangerous and unthinkable situations; for who could foretell the conditions pervading an adjacent but normally inaccessible dimension? On the other hand

column1: Piecing together the scattered records
column2: ancient and modern
column3: anthropological and medical
column4: I found a fairly consistent mixture of myth and hallucination whose scope and wildness left me utterly dazed. Only one thing consoled me—the fact that the myths were of such early existence. What lost knowledge could have brought pictures of the Palaeozoic or Mesozoic landscape into these primitive fables
column5: I could not even guess
column6: but the pictures had been there. Thus

Cases of amnesia no doubt created the general myth-pattern—but afterward the fanciful accretions of the myths must have reacted on amnesia sufferers and coloured their pseudo-memories. I myself had read and heard all the early tales during my memory lapse—my quest had amply proved that. Was it not natural
column8: then

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape
column2: they implied
column3: had reared towers to the sky and delved into every secret of Nature before the first amphibian forbear of man had crawled out of the hot sea three hundred million years ago. Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years
column4: and linkages with other galaxies and universes
column5: were freely spoken of. Indeed
column6: there was no such thing as time in its humanly accepted sense.

column1: But most of the tales and impressions concerned a relatively late race
column2: of a queer and intricate shape resembling no life-form known to science
column3: which had lived till only fifty million years before the advent of man. This
column4: they indicated
column5: was the greatest race of all; because it alone had conquered the secret of time. It had learned all things that ever were known or ever would be known on the earth
column6: through the power of its keener minds to project themselves into the past and future
column7: even through gulfs of millions of years
column8: and study the lore of every age. From the accomplishments of this race arose all legends of prophets
column9: including those in human mythology.

column1: In its vast libraries were volumes of texts and pictures holding the whole of earth’s annals—histories and descriptions of every species that had ever been or that ever would be
column2: with full records of their arts
column3: their achievements
column4: their languages
column5: and their psychologies. With this aeon-embracing knowledge
column6: the Great Race chose from every era and life-form such thoughts
column7: arts
column8: and processes as might suit its own nature and situation. Knowledge of the past
column9: secured through a kind of mind-casting outside the recognised senses
column10: was harder to glean than knowledge of the future.

column1: In the latter case the course was easier and more material. With suitable mechanical aid a mind would project itself forward in time
column2: feeling its dim
column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then
column4: after preliminary trials
column5: it would seize on the best discoverable representative of the highest of that period’s life-forms; entering the organism’s brain and setting up therein its own vibrations while the displaced mind would strike back to the period of the displacer
column6: remaining in the latter’s body till a reverse process was set up. The projected mind
column7: in the body of the organism of the future
column8: would then pose as a member of the race whose outward form it wore; learning as quickly as possible all that could be learned of the chosen age and its massed information and techniques.

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body
column3: would be carefully guarded. It would be kept from harming the body it occupied
column4: and would be drained of all its knowledge by trained questioners. Often it could be questioned in its own language
column5: when previous quests into the future had brought back records of that language. If the mind came from a body whose language the Great Race could not physically reproduce
column6: clever machines would be made
column7: on which the alien speech could be played as on a musical instrument. The Great Race’s members were immense rugose cones ten feet high
column8: and with head and other organs attached to foot-thick
column9: distensible limbs spreading from the apexes. They spoke by the clicking or scraping of huge paws or claws attached to the end of two of their four limbs
column10: and walked by the expansion and contraction of a viscous layer attached to their vast ten-foot bases.

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off
column2: and when (assuming that it came from a body vastly different from the Great Race’s) it had lost its horror at its unfamiliar temporary form
column3: it was permitted to study its new environment and experience a wonder and wisdom approximating that of its displacer. With suitable precautions
column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen
column7: and to such minds the unveiling of hidden mysteries of earth—closed chapters of inconceivable pasts and dizzying vortices of future time which include the years ahead of their own natural ages—forms always
column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times
column4: great disasters. And it was largely in consequence of two cases of the kind (said the old myths) that mankind had learned what it had concerning the Great Race. Of all things surviving physically and directly from that aeon-distant world
column5: there remained only certain ruins of great stones in far places and under the sea
column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated
column2: so that in most cases only a dream-shadowed blank stretched back to the time of the first exchange. Some minds recalled more than others
column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be
column7: while the myriad minds sent backward were left to die in the horror of strange shapes. Later the race would again face death
column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Such was the background of intertwined legend and hallucination. When
column2: around 1920
column3: I had my researches in coherent shape
column4: I felt a slight lessening of the tension which their earlier stages had increased. After all
column5: and in spite of the fancies prompted by blind emotions
column6: were not most of my phenomena readily explainable? Any chance might have turned my mind to dark studies during the amnesia—and then I read the forbidden legends and met the members of ancient and ill-regarded cults. That
column7: plainly
column8: supplied the material for the dreams and disturbed feelings which came after the return of memory. As for the marginal notes in dream-hieroglyphs and languages unknown to me

column10: while the hieroglyphs were doubtless coined by my fancy from descriptions in old legends
column11: and afterward woven into my dreams. I tried to verify certain points through conversation with known cult-leaders
column12: but never succeeded in establishing the right connexions.

column1: At times the parallelism of so many cases in so many distant ages continued to worry me as it had at first
column2: but on the other hand I reflected that the excitant folklore was undoubtedly more universal in the past than in the present. Probably all the other victims whose cases were like mine had had a long and familiar knowledge of the tales I had learned only when in my secondary state. When these victims had lost their memory
column3: they had associated themselves with the creatures of their household myths—the fabulous invaders supposed to displace men’s minds—and had thus embarked upon quests for knowledge which they thought they could take back to a fancied
column4: non-human past. Then when their memory returned
column5: they reversed the associative process and thought of themselves as the former captive minds instead of as the displacers. Hence the dreams and pseudo-memories following the conventional myth-pattern.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations
column2: they came finally to supersede all others in my mind—largely because of the greater weakness of any rival theory. And a substantial number of eminent psychologists and anthropologists gradually agreed with me. The more I reflected
column3: the more convincing did my reasoning seem; till in the end I had a really effective bulwark against the visions and impressions which still assailed me. Suppose I did see strange things at night? These were only what I had heard and read of. Suppose I did have odd loathings and perspectives and pseudo-memories? These
column4: too
column5: were only echoes of myths absorbed in my secondary state. Nothing that I might dream
column6: nothing that I might feel
column7: could be of any actual significance.

column1: Fortified by this philosophy
column2: I greatly improved in nervous equilibrium
column3: even though the visions (rather than the abstract impressions) steadily became more frequent and more disturbingly detailed. In 1922 I felt able to undertake regular work again
column4: and put my newly gained knowledge to practical use by accepting an instructorship in psychology at the university. My old chair of political economy had long been adequately filled—besides which
column5: methods of teaching economics had changed greatly since my heyday. My son was at this time just entering on the post-graduate studies leading to his present professorship
column6: and we worked together a great deal.

column1: IV.
I continued
column2: however
column3: to keep a careful record of the outré dreams which crowded upon me so thickly and vividly. Such a record
column4: I argued
column5: was of genuine value as a psychological document. The glimpses still seemed damnably like memories

column1: Of my visions after 1914 I will here mention only a few
column2: since fuller accounts and records are at the disposal of the serious student. It is evident that with time the curious inhibitions somewhat waned
column3: for the scope of my visions vastly increased. They have never
column4: though
column5: become other than disjointed fragments seemingly without clear motivation. Within the dreams I seemed gradually to acquire a greater and greater freedom of wandering. I floated through many strange buildings of stone
column6: going from one to the other along mammoth underground passages which seemed to form the common avenues of transit. Sometimes I encountered those gigantic sealed trap-doors in the lowest level
column7: around which such an aura of fear and forbiddenness clung. I saw tremendous tessellated pools
column8: and rooms of curious and inexplicable utensils of myriad sorts. Then there were colossal caverns of intricate machinery whose outlines and purpose were wholly strange to me

column1: The real horror began in May

column4: in view of the myths and case histories
column5: to expect. As mental barriers wore down

column7: till at last I could trace their monstrous outlines with uncomfortable ease. They seemed to be enormous iridescent cones
column8: about ten feet high and ten feet wide at the base
column9: and made up of some ridgy
column10: scaly

column12: cylindrical members

column14: and of a ridgy substance like that of the cones themselves. These members were sometimes contracted almost to nothing

column18: grey substance which moved the whole entity through expansion and contraction.

column1: Their actions
column2: though harmless
column3: horrified me even more than their appearance—for it is not wholesome to watch monstrous objects doing what one has known only human beings to do. These objects moved intelligently around the great rooms
column4: getting books from the shelves and taking them to the great tables
column5: or vice versa
column6: and sometimes writing diligently with a peculiar rod gripped in the greenish head-tentacles. The huge nippers were used in carrying books and in conversation—speech consisting of a kind of clicking and scraping. The objects had no clothing

column8: although it was frequently raised or lowered. The other three great members tended to rest downward on the sides of the cone
column9: contracted to about five feet each
column10: when not in use. From their rate of reading
column11: writing
column12: and operating their machines (those on the tables seemed somehow connected with thought) I concluded that their intelligence was enormously greater than man’s.

column1: Afterward I saw them everywhere; swarming in all the great chambers and corridors
column2: tending monstrous machines in vaulted crypts
column3: and racing along the vast roads in gigantic boat-shaped cars. I ceased to be afraid of them
column4: for they seemed to form supremely natural parts of their environment. Individual differences amongst them began to be manifest
column5: and a few appeared to be under some kind of restraint. These latter
column6: though shewing no physical variation
column7: had a diversity of gestures and habits which marked them off not only from the majority
column8: but very largely from one another. They wrote a great deal in what seemed to my cloudy vision a vast variety of characters—never the typical curvilinear hieroglyphs of the majority. A few
column9: I fancied
column10: used our own familiar alphabet. Most of them worked much more slowly than the general mass of the entities.

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August
column4: did any suggestions of bodily existence begin to harass me. I say harass
column5: because the first phase was a purely abstract though infinitely terrible association of my previously noted body-loathing with the scenes of my visions. For a while my chief concern during dreams was to avoid looking down at myself
column6: and I recall how grateful I was for the total absence of large mirrors in the strange rooms. I was mightily troubled by the fact that I always saw the great tables—whose height could not be under ten feet—from a level not below that of their surfaces.

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking
column8: I could recall only minute and meaningless scraps of the unknown tongues which my dream-self had mastered
column9: though whole phrases of the history stayed with me.

column1: I learned—even before my waking self had studied the parallel cases or the old myths from which the dreams doubtless sprang—that the entities around me were of the world’s greatest race
column2: which had conquered time and had sent exploring minds into every age. I knew
column3: too
column4: that I had been snatched from my age while another used my body in that age
column5: and that a few of the other strange forms housed similarly captured minds. I seemed to talk
column6: in some odd language of claw-clickings
column7: with exiled intellects from every corner of the solar system.

column1: There was a mind from the planet we know as Venus
column2: which would live incalculable epochs to come
column3: and one from an outer moon of Jupiter six million years in the past. Of earthly minds there were some from the winged
column4: star-headed

column1: I talked with the mind of Yiang-Li
column2: a philosopher from the cruel empire of Tsan-Chan
column3: which is to come in A.D. 5000; with that of a general of the great-headed brown people who held South Africa in B.C. 50

column5: 000 years before the squat
column6: yellow Inutos came from the west to engulf it; with that of Nug-Soth
column7: a magician of the dark conquerors of A.D. 16

column9: who had been a quaestor in Sulla’s time; with that of Khephnes

column11: James Woodville; with that of a court astronomer of pre-Inca Peru; with that of the Australian physicist Nevil Kingston-Brown
column12: who will die in A.D. 2518; with that of an archimage of vanished Yhe in the Pacific; with that of Theodotides
column13: a Graeco-Bactrian official of B.C. 200; with that of an aged Frenchman of Louis XIII’s time named Pierre-Louis Montmagny; with that of Crom-Ya

column1: I awaked each morning in a fever
column2: sometimes frantically trying to verify or discredit such information as fell within the range of modern human knowledge. Traditional facts took on new and doubtful aspects
column3: and I marvelled at the dream-fancy which could invent such surprising addenda to history and science. I shivered at the mysteries the past may conceal
column4: and trembled at the menaces the future may bring forth. What was hinted in the speech of post-human entities of the fate of mankind produced such an effect on me that I will not set it down here. After man there would be the mighty beetle civilisation
column5: the bodies of whose members the cream of the Great Race would seize when the monstrous doom overtook the elder world. Later
column6: as the earth’s span closed
column7: the transferred minds would again migrate through time and space—to another stopping-place in the bodies of the bulbous vegetable entities of Mercury. But there would be races after them
column8: clinging pathetically to the cold planet and burrowing to its horror-filled core
column9: before the utter end.

column1: Meanwhile
column2: in my dreams
column3: I wrote endlessly in that history of my own age which I was preparing—half voluntarily and half through promises of increased library and travel opportunities—for the Great Race’s central archives. The archives were in a colossal subterranean structure near the city’s centre
column4: which I came to know well through frequent labours and consultations. Meant to last as long as the race
column5: and to withstand the fiercest of earth’s convulsions
column6: this titan repository surpassed all other buildings in the massive
column7: mountain-like firmness of its construction.

column1: The records
column2: written or printed on great sheets of a curiously tenacious cellulose fabric
column3: were bound into books that opened from the top
column4: and were kept in individual cases of a strange
column5: extremely light rustless metal of greyish hue

column7: locked shelves—wrought of the same rustless metal and fastened by knobs with intricate turnings. My own history was assigned a specific place in the vaults of the lowest or vertebrate level—the section devoted to the culture of mankind and of the furry and reptilian races immediately preceding it in terrestrial dominance.

column3: and crocodiles

column14: however

column1: Markedly defective individuals were quietly disposed of as soon as their defects were noticed. Disease and the approach of death were
column2: in the absence of a sense of touch or of physical pain

column1: The Great Race seemed to form a single loosely knit nation or league

column4: with major resources rationally distributed

column5: unspecialised urges common to all organic life. A few added likenesses came through conscious adoption as the Great Race probed the future and copied what it liked. Industry
column6: highly mechanised

column11: imposed by the prodigious geologic upheavals of those primal days.

column1: Crime was surprisingly scanty

column6: star-headed Old Ones who centred in the Antarctic

column8: using camera-like weapons which produced tremendous electrical effects

column11: windowless elder ruins and of the great sealed trap-doors in the lowest subterrene levels.

column1: This fear of the basalt ruins and trap-doors was largely a matter of unspoken suggestion—or
column2: at most
column3: of furtive quasi-whispers. Everything specific which bore on it was significantly absent from such books as were on the common shelves. It was the one subject lying altogether under a taboo among the Great Race
column4: and seemed to be connected alike with horrible bygone struggles
column5: and with that future peril which would some day force the race to send its keener minds ahead en masse in time. Imperfect and fragmentary as were the other things presented by dreams and legends

column1: According to these scraps of information
column2: the basis of the fear was a horrible elder race of half-polypous
column3: utterly alien entities which had come through space from immeasurably distant universes and had dominated the earth and three other solar planets about six hundred million years ago. They were only partly material—as we understand matter—and their type of consciousness and media of perception differed wholly from those of terrestrial organisms. For example
column4: their senses did not include that of sight; their mental world being a strange
column5: non-visual pattern of impressions. They were
column6: however
column7: sufficiently material to use implements of normal matter when in cosmic areas containing it; and they required housing—albeit of a peculiar kind. Though their senses could penetrate all material barriers
column8: their substance could not; and certain forms of electrical energy could wholly destroy them. They had the power of aërial motion despite the absence of wings or any other visible means of levitation. Their minds were of such texture that no exchange with them could be effected by the Great Race.

column1: When these things had come to the earth they had built mighty basalt cities of windowless towers
column2: and had preyed horribly upon the beings they found. Thus it was when the minds of the Great Race sped across the void from that obscure trans-galactic world known in the disturbing and debatable Eltdown Shards as Yith. The newcomers
column3: with the instruments they created
column4: had found it easy to subdue the predatory entities and drive them down to those caverns of inner earth which they had already joined to their abodes and begun to inhabit. Then they had sealed the entrances and left them to their fate
column5: afterward occupying most of their great cities and preserving certain important buildings for reasons connected more with superstition than with indifference
column6: boldness
column7: or scientific and historical zeal.

column1: But as the aeons passed
column2: there came vague
column3: evil signs that the Elder Things were growing strong and numerous in the inner world. There were sporadic irruptions of a particularly hideous character in certain small and remote cities of the Great Race
column4: and in some of the deserted elder cities which the Great Race had not peopled—places where the paths to the gulfs below had not been properly sealed or guarded. After that greater precautions were taken
column5: and many of the paths were closed for ever—though a few were left with sealed trap-doors for strategic use in fighting the Elder Things if ever they broke forth in unexpected places; fresh rifts caused by that selfsame geologic change which had choked some of the paths and had slowly lessened the number of outer-world structures and ruins surviving from the conquered entities.

column1: The irruptions of the Elder Things must have been shocking beyond all description
column2: since they had permanently coloured the psychology of the Great Race. Such was the fixed mood of horror that the very aspect of the creatures was left unmentioned—at no time was I able to gain a clear hint of what they looked like. There were veiled suggestions of a monstrous plasticity
column3: and of temporary lapses of visibility
column4: while other fragmentary whispers referred to their control and military use of great winds. Singular whistling noises
column5: and colossal footprints made up of five circular toe-marks
column6: seemed also to be associated with them.

column1: It was evident that the coming doom so desperately feared by the Great Race—the doom that was one day to send millions of keen minds across the chasm of time to strange bodies in the safer future—had to do with a final successful irruption of the Elder Beings. Mental projections down the ages had clearly foretold such a horror
column2: and the Great Race had resolved that none who could escape should face it. That the foray would be a matter of vengeance
column3: rather than an attempt to reoccupy the outer world
column4: they knew from the planet’s later history—for their projections shewed the coming and going of subsequent races untroubled by the monstrous entities. Perhaps these entities had come to prefer earth’s inner abysses to the variable
column5: storm-ravaged surface
column6: since light meant nothing to them. Perhaps
column7: too
column8: they were slowly weakening with the aeons. Indeed
column9: it was known that they would be quite dead in the time of the post-human beetle race which the fleeing minds would tenant. Meanwhile the Great Race maintained its cautious vigilance
column10: with potent weapons ceaselessly ready despite the horrified banishing of the subject from common speech and visible records. And always the shadow of nameless fear hung about the sealed trap-doors and the dark
column11: windowless elder towers.

column1: V.
That is the world of which my dreams brought me dim
column2: scattered echoes every night. I cannot hope to give any true idea of the horror and dread contained in such echoes
column3: for it was upon a wholly intangible quality—the sharp sense of pseudo-memory—that such feelings mainly depended. As I have said
column4: my studies gradually gave me a defence against these feelings
column5: in the form of rational psychological explanations; and this saving influence was augmented by the subtle touch of accustomedness which comes with the passage of time. Yet in spite of everything the vague
column6: creeping terror would return momentarily now and then. It did not
column7: however
column8: engulf me as it had before; and after 1922 I lived a very normal life of work and recreation.

column1: In the course of years I began to feel that my experience—together with the kindred cases and the related folklore—ought to be definitely summarised and published for the benefit of serious students; hence I prepared a series of articles briefly covering the whole ground and illustrated with crude sketches of some of the shapes
column2: scenes
column3: decorative motifs
column4: and hieroglyphs remembered from the dreams. These appeared at various times during 1928 and 1929 in the Journal of the American Psychological Society
column5: but did not attract much attention. Meanwhile I continued to record my dreams with the minutest care
column6: even though the growing stack of reports attained troublesomely vast proportions.

column1: My dear Sir:—
A recent conversation with Dr. E. M. Boyle of Perth
column2: and some papers with your articles which he has just sent me
column3: make it advisable for me to tell you about certain things I have seen in the Great Sandy Desert east of our gold field here. It would seem
column4: in view of the peculiar legends about old cities with huge stonework and strange designs and hieroglyphs which you describe
column5: that I have come upon something very important.

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: But what I have to tell is more than this. Two years ago
column2: when I was prospecting about 500 miles east in the desert
column3: I came on a lot of queer pieces of dressed stone perhaps 3 × 2 × 2 feet in size
column4: and weathered and pitted to the very limit. At first I couldn’t find any of the marks the blackfellows told about
column5: but when I looked close enough I could make out some deeply carved lines in spite of the weathering. They were peculiar curves
column6: just like what the blacks had tried to describe. I imagine there must have been 30 or 40 blocks
column7: some nearly buried in the sand
column8: and all within a circle perhaps a quarter of a mile’s diameter.

column1: When I saw some
column2: I looked around closely for more
column3: and made a careful reckoning of the place with my instruments. I also took pictures of 10 or 12 of the most typical blocks
column4: and will enclose the prints for you to see. I turned my information and pictures over to the government at Perth
column5: but they have done nothing with them. Then I met Dr. Boyle
column6: who had read your articles in the Journal of the American Psychological Society
column7: and in time happened to mention the stones. He was enormously interested
column8: and became quite excited when I shewed him my snapshots
column9: saying that the stones and markings were just like those of the masonry you had dreamed about and seen described in legends. He meant to write you
column10: but was delayed. Meanwhile he sent me most of the magazines with your articles
column11: and I saw at once from your drawings and descriptions that my stones are certainly the kind you mean. You can appreciate this from the enclosed prints. Later on you will hear directly from Dr. Boyle.

column1: Now I can understand how important all this will be to you. Without question we are faced with the remains of an unknown civilisation older than any dreamed of before
column2: and forming a basis for your legends. As a mining engineer
column3: I have some knowledge of geology
column4: and can tell you that these blocks are so ancient they frighten me. They are mostly sandstone and granite
column5: though one is almost certainly made of a queer sort of cement or concrete. They bear evidence of water action
column6: as if this part of the world had been submerged and come up again after long ages—all since these blocks were made and used. It is a matter of hundreds of thousands of years—or heaven knows how much more. I don’t like to think about it.

column1: In view of your previous diligent work in tracking down the legends and everything connected with them
column2: I cannot doubt but that you will want to lead an expedition to the desert and make some archaeological excavations. Both Dr. Boyle and I are prepared to coöperate in such work if you—or organisations known to you—can furnish the funds. I can get together a dozen miners for the heavy digging—the blacks would be of no use
column3: for I’ve found that they have an almost maniacal fear of this particular spot. Boyle and I are saying nothing to others
column4: for you very obviously ought to have precedence in any discoveries or credit.

column1: The place can be reached from Pilbarra in about 4 days by motor tractor—which we’d need for our apparatus. It is somewhat west and south of Warburton’s path of 1873
column2: and 100 miles southeast of Joanna Spring. We could float things up the De Grey River instead of starting from Pilbarra—but all that can be talked over later. Roughly
column3: the stones lie at a point about 22° 3' 14"" South Latitude
column4: 125° 0' 39"" East Longitude. The climate is tropical
column5: and the desert conditions are trying. Any expedition had better be made in winter—June or July or August. I shall welcome further correspondence upon this subject
column6: and am keenly eager to assist in any plan you may devise. After studying your articles I am deeply impressed with the profound significance of the whole matter. Dr. Boyle will write later. When rapid communication is needed
column7: a cable to Perth can be relayed by wireless.

column1: Hoping profoundly for an early message
Believe me
Most faithfully yours
Robert B. F. Mackenzie.
Of the immediate aftermath of this letter

column5: printed reports were sparing; but enough appeared to tell of our quest for reported Australian ruins and to chronicle our various preparatory steps.

column1: Discomfort and expectancy were oddly mingled in most of us when at length our party of eighteen rattled forth over the arid leagues of sand and rock. On Friday
column2: May 31st

A certain positive terror grew on me as we advanced to this actual site of the elder world behind the legends—a terror of course abetted by the fact that my disturbing dreams and pseudo-memories still beset me with unabated force.

column1: It was on Monday
column2: June 3
column3: that we saw the first of the half-buried blocks. I cannot describe the emotions with which I actually touched—in objective reality—a fragment of Cyclopean masonry in every respect like the blocks in the walls of my dream-buildings. There was a distinct trace of carving—and my hands trembled as I recognised part of a curvilinear decorative scheme made hellish to me through years of tormenting nightmare and baffling research.

column1: A month of digging brought a total of some 1250 blocks in varying stages of wear and disintegration. Most of these were carven megaliths with curved tops and bottoms. A minority were smaller
column2: flatter
column3: plain-surfaced

column1: VI.

I come now to the crucial and most difficult part of my narrative—all the more difficult because I cannot be quite certain of its reality. At times I feel uncomfortably sure that I was not dreaming or deluded; and it is this feeling—in view of the stupendous implications which the objective truth of my experience would raise—which impels me to make this record. My son—a trained psychologist with the fullest and most sympathetic knowledge of my whole case—shall be the primary judge of what I have to tell.
First let me outline the externals of the matter
column2: as those at the camp know them. On the night of July 17–18
column3: after a windy day
column4: I retired early but could not sleep. Rising shortly before eleven
column5: and afflicted as usual with that strange feeling regarding the northeastward terrain
column6: I set out on one of my typical nocturnal walks; seeing and greeting only one person—an Australian miner named Tupper—as I left our precincts. The moon
column7: slightly past full
column8: shone from a clear sky and drenched the ancient sands with a white
column9: leprous radiance which seemed to me somehow infinitely evil. There was no longer any wind
column10: nor did any return for nearly five hours
column11: as amply attested by Tupper and others who did not sleep through the night. The Australian last saw me walking rapidly across the pallid
column12: secret-guarding hillocks toward the northeast.

column1: About 3:30 a.m. a violent wind blew up
column2: waking everyone in camp and felling three of the tents. The sky was unclouded
column3: and the desert still blazed with that leprous moonlight. As the party saw to the tents my absence was noted
column4: but in view of my previous walks this circumstance gave no one alarm. And yet as many as three men—all Australians—seemed to feel something sinister in the air. Mackenzie explained to Prof. Freeborn that this was a fear picked up from blackfellow folklore—the natives having woven a curious fabric of malignant myth about the high winds which at long intervals sweep across the sands under a clear sky. Such winds

column6: blow out of the great stone huts under the ground where terrible things have happened—and are never felt except near places where the big marked stones are scattered. Close to four the gale subsided as suddenly as it had begun
column7: leaving the sand hills in new and unfamiliar shapes.

column2: with the bloated
column3: fungoid moon sinking in the west
column4: when I staggered into camp—hatless
column5: tattered
column6: features scratched and ensanguined
column7: and without my electric torch. Most of the men had returned to bed
column8: but Prof. Dyer was smoking a pipe in front of his tent. Seeing my winded and almost frenzied state

column10: and the two of them got me on my cot and made me comfortable. My son

column1: But there was no sleep for me. My psychological state was very extraordinary—different from anything I had previously suffered. After a time I insisted upon talking—nervously and elaborately explaining my condition. I told them I had become fatigued
column2: and had lain down in the sand for a nap. There had
column3: I said
column4: been dreams even more frightful than usual—and when I was awaked by the sudden high wind my overwrought nerves had snapped. I had fled in panic

column1: Of anything strange either seen or experienced I hinted absolutely nothing—exercising the greatest self-control in that respect. But I spoke of a change of mind regarding the whole work of the expedition
column2: and earnestly urged a halt in all digging toward the northeast. My reasoning was patently weak—for I mentioned a dearth of blocks
column3: a wish not to offend the superstitious miners

column2: but took no part in the excavations. Seeing that I could not stop the work
column3: I decided to return home as soon as possible for the sake of my nerves

column5: I reflected
column6: the thing I had seen was still visible

It was the case of the anomalous basalt block all over again—the shifting sand had wiped out every trace. For an instant I half regretted having lost a certain awesome object in my stark fright—but now I know that the loss was merciful. I can still believe my whole experience an illusion—especially if

column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses

column5: Joe said

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column2: see a nerve specialist
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest
