column1: VI.

I come now to the crucial and most difficult part of my narrative—all the more difficult because I cannot be quite certain of its reality. At times I feel uncomfortably sure that I was not dreaming or deluded; and it is this feeling—in view of the stupendous implications which the objective truth of my experience would raise—which impels me to make this record. My son—a trained psychologist with the fullest and most sympathetic knowledge of my whole case—shall be the primary judge of what I have to tell.
First let me outline the externals of the matter
column2: as those at the camp know them. On the night of July 17–18
column3: after a windy day

Mackenzie explained to Prof. Freeborn that this was a fear picked up from blackfellow folklore—the natives having woven a curious fabric of malignant myth about the high winds which at long intervals sweep across the sands under a clear sky. Such winds

column1: It seemed that a maternal uncle of mine had been there many years before on a quest much like my own; and that my grandmother's family was a topic of some local curiosity. There had
column2: Mr. Peabody said
column3: been considerable discussion about the marriage of her father
column4: Benjamin Orne
column5: just after the Civil War; since the ancestry of the bride was peculiarly puzzling. That bride was understood to have been an orphaned Marsh of New Hampshire--a cousin of the Essex County Marshes--but her education had been in France and she knew very little of her family. A guardian had deposited funds in a Boston bank to maintain her and her French governess; but that guardian's name was unfamiliar to Arkham people
column6: and in time he dropped out of sight
column7: so that the governess assumed the role by court appointment. The Frenchwoman--now long dead--was very taciturn
column8: and there were those who said she could have told more than she did.

column1: But the most baffling thing was the inability of anyone to place the recorded parents of the young woman--Enoch and Lydia (Meserve) Marsh--among the known families of New Hampshire. Possibly
column2: many suggested
column3: she was the natural daughter of some Marsh of prominence--she certainly had the true Marsh eyes. Most of the puzzling was done after her early death
column4: which took place at the birth of my grandmother--her only child. Having formed some disagreeable impressions connected with the name of Marsh
column5: I did not welcome the news that it belonged on my own ancestral tree; nor was I pleased by Mr. Peabody's suggestion that I had the true Marsh eyes myself. However
column6: I was grateful for data which I knew would prove valuable; and took copious notes and lists of book references regarding the well-documented Orne family.

column1: I went directly home to Toledo from Boston
column2: and later spent a month at Maumee recuperating from my ordeal. In September I entered Oberlin for my final year
column3: and from then till the next June was busy with studies and other wholesome activities--reminded of the bygone terror only by occasional official visits from government men in connexion with the campaign which my pleas and evidence had started. Around the middle of July--just a year after the Innsmouth experience--I spent a week with my late mother's family in Cleveland; checking some of my new genealogical data with the various notes
column4: traditions
column5: and bits of heirloom material in existence there
column6: and seeing what kind of a connected chart I could construct.

column1: I did not exactly relish this task
column2: for the atmosphere of the Williamson home had always depressed me. There was a strain of morbidity there
column3: and my mother had never encouraged my visiting her parents as a child
column4: although she always welcomed her father when he came to Toledo. My Arkham-born grandmother had seemed strange and almost terrifying to me
column5: and I do not think I grieved when she disappeared. I was eight years old then
column6: and it was said that she had wandered off in grief after the suicide of my Uncle Douglas
column7: her eldest son. He had shot himself after a trip to New England--the same trip
column8: no doubt
column9: which had caused him to be recalled at the Arkham Historical Society.

column1: This uncle had resembled her
column2: and I had never liked him either. Something about the staring
column3: unwinking expression of both of them had given me a vague
column4: unaccountable uneasiness. My mother and Uncle Walter had not looked like that. They were like their father
column5: though poor little cousin Lawrence--Walter's son--had been almost perfect duplicate of his grandmother before his condition took him to the permanent seclusion of a sanitarium at Canton. I had not seen him in four years
column6: but my uncle once implied that his state
column7: both mental and physical
column8: was very bad. This worry had probably been a major cause of his mother's death two years before.

column1: My grandfather and his widowed son Walter now comprised the Cleveland household
column2: but the memory of older times hung thickly over it. I still disliked the place
column3: and tried to get my researches done as quickly as possible. Williamson records and traditions were supplied in abundance by my grandfather; though for Orne material I had to depend on my uncle Walter
column4: who put at my disposal the contents of all his files
column5: including notes
column6: letters
column7: cuttings
column8: heirlooms
column9: photographs
column10: and miniatures.

column1: It was in going over the letters and pictures on the Orne side that I began to acquire a kind of terror of my own ancestry. As I have said
column2: my grandmother and Uncle Douglas had always disturbed me. Now
column3: years after their passing
column4: I gazed at their pictured faces with a measurably heightened feeling of repulsion and alienation. I could not at first understand the change
column5: but gradually a horrible sort of comparison began to obtrude itself on my unconscious mind despite the steady refusal of my consciousness to admit even the least suspicion of it. It was clear that the typical expression of these faces now suggested something it had not suggested before--something which would bring stark panic if too openly thought of.

column1: But the worst shock came when my uncle shewed me the Orne jewellery in a downtown safe deposit vault. Some of the items were delicate and inspiring enough
column2: but there was one box of strange old pieces descended from my mysterious great-grandmother which my uncle was almost reluctant to produce. They were
column3: he said
column4: of very grotesque and almost repulsive design
column5: and had never to his knowledge been publicly worn; though my grandmother used to enjoy looking at them. Vague legends of bad luck clustered around them
column6: and my great-grandmother's French governess had said they ought not to be worn in New England
column7: though it would be quite safe to wear them in Europe.

column1: As my uncle began slowly and grudgingly to unwrap the things he urged me not to be shocked by the strangeness and frequent hideousness of the designs. Artists and archaeologists who had seen them pronounced their workmanship superlatively and exotically exquisite
column2: though no one seemed able to define their exact material or assign them to any specific art tradition. There were two armlets
column3: a tiara
column4: and a kind of pectoral; the latter having in high relief certain figures of almost unbearable extravagance.

column1: During this description I had kept a tight rein on my emotions
column2: but my face must have betrayed my mounting fears. My uncle looked concerned
column3: and paused in his unwrapping to study my countenance. I motioned to him to continue
column4: which he did with renewed signs of reluctance. He seemed to expect some demonstration when the first piece--the tiara--became visible
column5: but I doubt if he expected quite what actually happened. I did not expect it
column6: either
column7: for I thought I was thoroughly forewarned regarding what the jewellery would turn out to be. What I did was to faint silently away
column8: just as I had done in that brier-choked railway cut a year before.

column1: From that day on my life has been a nightmare of brooding and apprehension nor do I know how much is hideous truth and how much madness. My great-grandmother had been a Marsh of unknown source whose husband lived in Arkham--and did not old Zadok say that the daughter of Obed Marsh by a monstrous mother was married to an Arkham man through trick? What was it the ancient toper had muttered about the line of my eyes to Captain Obed's? In Arkham
column2: too
column3: the curator had told me I had the true Marsh eyes. Was Obed Marsh my own great-great-grandfather? Who--or what--then
column4: was my great-great-grandmother? But perhaps this was all madness. Those whitish-gold ornaments might easily have been bought from some Innsmouth sailor by the father of my great-grandmother
column5: whoever he was. And that look in the staring-eyed faces of my grandmother and self-slain uncle might be sheer fancy on my part--sheer fancy
column6: bolstered up by the Innsmouth shadow which had so darkly coloured my imagination. But why had my uncle killed himself after an ancestral quest in New England?

column1: For more than two years I fought off these reflections with partial success. My father secured me a place in an insurance office
column2: and I buried myself in routine as deeply as possible. In the winter of 1930-31
column3: however
column4: the dreams began. They were very sparse and insidious at first
column5: but increased in frequency and vividness as the weeks went by. Great watery spaces opened out before me
column6: and I seemed to wander through titanic sunken porticos and labyrinths of weedy cyclopean walls with grotesque fishes as my companions. Then the other shapes began to appear
column7: filling me with nameless horror the moment I awoke. But during the dreams they did not horrify me at all--I was one with them; wearing their unhuman trappings
column8: treading their aqueous ways
column9: and praying monstrously at their evil sea-bottom temples.

column1: There was much more than I could remember
column2: but even what I did remember each morning would be enough to stamp me as a madman or a genius if ever I dared write it down. Some frightful influence
column3: I felt
column4: was seeking gradually to drag me out of the sane world of wholesome life into unnamable abysses of blackness and alienage; and the process told heavily on me. My health and appearance grew steadily worse
column5: till finally I was forced to give up my position and adopt the static
column6: secluded life of an invalid. Some odd nervous affliction had me in its grip
column7: and I found myself at times almost unable to shut my eyes.

column1: It was then that I began to study the mirror with mounting alarm. The slow ravages of disease are not pleasant to watch
column2: but in my case there was something subtler and more puzzling in the background. My father seemed to notice it
column3: too
column4: for he began looking at me curiously and almost affrightedly. What was taking place in me? Could it be that I was coming to resemble my grandmother and uncle Douglas?

column1: One night I had a frightful dream in which I met my grandmother under the sea. She lived in a phosphorescent palace of many terraces
column2: with gardens of strange leprous corals and grotesque brachiate efflorescences
column3: and welcomed me with a warmth that may have been sardonic. She had changed--as those who take to the water change--and told me she had never died. Instead
column4: she had gone to a spot her dead son had learned about
column5: and had leaped to a realm whose wonders-- destined for him as well--he had spurned with a smoking pistol. This was to be my realm
column6: too--I could not escape it. I would never die
column7: but would live with those who had lived since before man ever walked the earth.

column1: I met also that which had been her grandmother. For eighty thousand years Pth'thya-l'yi had lived in Y'ha-nthlei
column2: and thither she had gone back after Obed Marsh was dead. Y'ha-nthlei was not destroyed when the upper-earth men shot death into the sea. It was hurt
column3: but not destroyed. The Deep Ones could never be destroyed
column4: even though the palaeogean magic of the forgotten Old Ones might sometimes check them. For the present they would rest; but some day
column5: if they remembered
column6: they would rise again for the tribute Great Cthulhu craved. It would be a city greater than Innsmouth next time. They had planned to spread
column7: and had brought up that which would help them
column8: but now they must wait once more. For bringing the upper-earth men's death I must do a penance
column9: but that would not be heavy. This was the dream in which I saw a shoggoth for the first time
column10: and the sight set me awake in a frenzy of screaming. That morning the mirror definitely told me I had acquired the Innsmouth look.

column1: So far I have not shot myself as my uncle Douglas did. I bought an automatic and almost took the step
column2: but certain dreams deterred me. The tense extremes of horror are lessening
column3: and I feel queerly drawn toward the unknown sea-deeps instead of fearing them. I hear and do strange things in sleep
column4: and awake with a kind of exaltation instead of terror. I do not believe I need to wait for the full change as most have waited. If I did
column5: my father would probably shut me up in a sanitarium as my poor little cousin is shut up. Stupendous and unheard-of splendors await me below
column6: and I shall seek them soon. Ia-R'lyehl Cihuiha flgagnl id Ia! No
column7: I shall not shoot myself--I cannot be made to shoot myself!

column1: I shall plan my cousin's escape from that Canton mad-house
column2: and together we shall go to marvel-shadowed Innsmouth. We shall swim out to that brooding reef in the sea and dive down through black abysses to Cyclopean and many-columned Y'ha-nthlei
column3: and in that lair of the Deep Ones we shall dwell amidst wonder and glory for ever.

column1: \﻿Searchers after horror haunt strange
column2: far places. For them are the catacombs of Ptolemais
column3: and the carven mausolea of the nightmare countries. They climb to the moonlit towers of ruined Rhine castles
column4: and falter down black cobwebbed steps beneath the scattered stones of forgotten cities in Asia. The haunted wood and the desolate mountain are their shrines
column5: and they linger around the sinister monoliths on uninhabited islands. But the true epicure in the terrible
column6: to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence
column7: esteems most of all the ancient
column8: lonely farmhouses of backwoods New England; for there the dark elements of strength
column9: solitude
column10: grotesqueness
column11: and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous.

column1: Most horrible of all sights are the little unpainted wooden houses remote from travelled ways
column2: usually squatted upon some damp
column3: grassy slope or leaning against some gigantic outcropping of rock. Two hundred years and more they have leaned or squatted there
column4: while the vines have crawled and the trees have swelled and spread. They are almost hidden now in lawless luxuriances of green and guardian shrouds of shadow; but the small-paned windows still stare shockingly
column5: as if blinking through a lethal stupor which wards off madness by dulling the memory of unutterable things.

column1: In such houses have dwelt generations of strange people
column2: whose like the world has never seen. Seized with a gloomy and fanatical belief which exiled them from their kind
column3: their ancestors sought the wilderness for freedom. There the scions of a conquering race indeed flourished free from the restrictions of their fellows
column4: but cowered in an appalling slavery to the dismal phantasms of their own minds. Divorced from the enlightenment of civilisation
column5: the strength of these Puritans turned into singular channels; and in their isolation
column6: morbid self-repression
column7: and struggle for life with relentless Nature
column8: there came to them dark furtive traits from the prehistoric depths of their cold Northern heritage. By necessity practical and by philosophy stern
column9: these folk were not beautiful in their sins. Erring as all mortals must
column10: they were forced by their rigid code to seek concealment above all else; so that they came to use less and less taste in what they concealed. Only the silent
column11: sleepy
column12: staring houses in the backwoods can tell all that has lain hidden since the early days; and they are not communicative
column13: being loath to shake off the drowsiness which helps them forget. Sometimes one feels that it would be merciful to tear down these houses
column14: for they must often dream.

column1: It was to a time-battered edifice of this description that I was driven one afternoon in November
column3: by a rain of such chilling copiousness that any shelter was preferable to exposure. I had been travelling for some time amongst the people of the Miskatonic Valley in quest of certain genealogical data; and from the remote
column4: devious
column5: and problematical nature of my course
column6: had deemed it convenient to employ a bicycle despite the lateness of the season. Now I found myself upon an apparently abandoned road which I had chosen as the shortest cut to Arkham; overtaken by the storm at a point far from any town
column7: and confronted with no refuge save the antique and repellent wooden building which blinked with bleared windows from between two huge leafless elms near the foot of a rocky hill. Distant though it was from the remnant of a road
column8: the house none the less impressed me unfavourably the very moment I espied it. Honest
column9: wholesome structures do not stare at travellers so slyly and hauntingly
column10: and in my genealogical researches I had encountered legends of a century before which biassed me against places of this kind. Yet the force of the elements was such as to overcome my scruples
column11: and I did not hesitate to wheel my machine up the weedy rise to the closed door which seemed at once so suggestive and secretive.

column1: I had somehow taken it for granted that the house was abandoned
column2: yet as I approached it I was not so sure; for though the walks were indeed overgrown with weeds
column3: they seemed to retain their nature a little too well to argue complete desertion. Therefore instead of trying the door I knocked
column4: feeling as I did so a trepidation I could scarcely explain. As I waited on the rough
column5: mossy rock which served as a doorstep
column6: I glanced at the neighbouring windows and the panes of the transom above me
column7: and noticed that although old
column8: rattling
column9: and almost opaque with dirt
column10: they were not broken. The building
column11: then
column12: must still be inhabited
column13: despite its isolation and general neglect. However
column14: my rapping evoked no response
column15: so after repeating the summons I tried the rusty latch and found the door unfastened. Inside was a little vestibule with walls from which the plaster was falling
column16: and through the doorway came a faint but peculiarly hateful odour. I entered
column17: carrying my bicycle
column18: and closed the door behind me. Ahead rose a narrow staircase
column19: flanked by a small door probably leading to the cellar
column20: while to the left and right were closed doors leading to rooms on the ground floor.

column1: Leaning my cycle against the wall I opened the door at the left
column2: and crossed into a small low-ceiled chamber but dimly lighted by its two dusty windows and furnished in the barest and most primitive possible way. It appeared to be a kind of sitting-room
column3: for it had a table and several chairs
column4: and an immense fireplace above which ticked an antique clock on a mantel. Books and papers were very few
column5: and in the prevailing gloom I could not readily discern the titles. What interested me was the uniform air of archaism as displayed in every visible detail. Most of the houses in this region I had found rich in relics of the past
column6: but here the antiquity was curiously complete; for in all the room I could not discover a single article of definitely post-revolutionary date. Had the furnishings been less humble
column7: the place would have been a collector’s paradise.

column1: As I surveyed this quaint apartment
column2: I felt an increase in that aversion first excited by the bleak exterior of the house. Just what it was that I feared or loathed
column3: I could by no means define; but something in the whole atmosphere seemed redolent of unhallowed age
column4: of unpleasant crudeness
column5: and of secrets which should be forgotten. I felt disinclined to sit down
column6: and wandered about examining the various articles which I had noticed. The first object of my curiosity was a book of medium size lying upon the table and presenting such an antediluvian aspect that I marvelled at beholding it outside a museum or library. It was bound in leather with metal fittings
column7: and was in an excellent state of preservation; being altogether an unusual sort of volume to encounter in an abode so lowly. When I opened it to the title page my wonder grew even greater
column8: for it proved to be nothing less rare than Pigafetta’s account of the Congo region
column9: written in Latin from the notes of the sailor Lopez and printed at Frankfort in 1598. I had often heard of this work
column10: with its curious illustrations by the brothers De Bry
column11: hence for a moment forgot my uneasiness in my desire to turn the pages before me. The engravings were indeed interesting
column12: drawn wholly from imagination and careless descriptions
column13: and represented negroes with white skins and Caucasian features; nor would I soon have closed the book had not an exceedingly trivial circumstance upset my tired nerves and revived my sensation of disquiet. What annoyed me was merely the persistent way in which the volume tended to fall open of itself at Plate XII
column14: which represented in gruesome detail a butcher’s shop of the cannibal Anziques. I experienced some shame at my susceptibility to so slight a thing
column15: but the drawing nevertheless disturbed me
column16: especially in connexion with some adjacent passages descriptive of Anzique gastronomy.

column1: I had turned to a neighbouring shelf and was examining its meagre literary contents—an eighteenth-century Bible
column2: a Pilgrim’s Progress of like period
column3: illustrated with grotesque woodcuts and printed by the almanack-maker Isaiah Thomas
column4: the rotting bulk of Cotton Mather’s Magnalia Christi Americana
column5: and a few other books of evidently equal age—when my attention was aroused by the unmistakable sound of walking in the room overhead. At first astonished and startled
column6: considering the lack of response to my recent knocking at the door
column7: I immediately afterward concluded that the walker had just awakened from a sound sleep; and listened with less surprise as the footsteps sounded on the creaking stairs. The tread was heavy
column8: yet seemed to contain a curious quality of cautiousness; a quality which I disliked the more because the tread was heavy. When I had entered the room I had shut the door behind me. Now
column9: after a moment of silence during which the walker may have been inspecting my bicycle in the hall
column10: I heard a fumbling at the latch and saw the panelled portal swing open again.

column1: In the doorway stood a person of such singular appearance that I should have exclaimed aloud but for the restraints of good breeding. Old
column2: white-bearded
column3: and ragged
column4: my host possessed a countenance and physique which inspired equal wonder and respect. His height could not have been less than six feet
column5: and despite a general air of age and poverty he was stout and powerful in proportion. His face
column6: almost hidden by a long beard which grew high on the cheeks
column7: seemed abnormally ruddy and less wrinkled than one might expect; while over a high forehead fell a shock of white hair little thinned by the years. His blue eyes
column8: though a trifle bloodshot
column9: seemed inexplicably keen and burning. But for his horrible unkemptness the man would have been as distinguished-looking as he was impressive. This unkemptness
column10: however
column11: made him offensive despite his face and figure. Of what his clothing consisted I could hardly tell
column12: for it seemed to me no more than a mass of tatters surmounting a pair of high
column13: heavy boots; and his lack of cleanliness surpassed description.

column1: The appearance of this man
column2: and the instinctive fear he inspired
column3: prepared me for something like enmity; so that I almost shuddered through surprise and a sense of uncanny incongruity when he motioned me to a chair and addressed me in a thin
column4: weak voice full of fawning respect and ingratiating hospitality. His speech was very curious
column5: an extreme form of Yankee dialect I had thought long extinct; and I studied it closely as he sat down opposite me for conversation.

column1: “Ketched in the rain
column2: be ye?” he greeted. “Glad ye was nigh the haouse en’ hed the sense ta come right in. I calc’late I was asleep
column3: else I’d a heerd ye—I ain’t as young as I uster be
column4: an’ I need a paowerful sight o’ naps naowadays. Trav’lin’ fur? I hain’t seed many folks ’long this rud sence they tuk off the Arkham stage.”

column1: I replied that I was going to Arkham
column2: and apologised for my rude entry into his domicile
column3: whereupon he continued.

column1: “Glad ta see ye
column2: young Sir—new faces is scurce arount here
column3: an’ I hain’t got much ta cheer me up these days. Guess yew hail from Bosting
column4: don’t ye? I never ben thar
column5: but I kin tell a taown man when I see ’im—we hed one fer deestrick schoolmaster in ’eighty-four
column6: but he quit suddent an’ no one never heerd on ’im sence—” Here the old man lapsed into a kind of chuckle
column7: and made no explanation when I questioned him. He seemed to be in an aboundingly good humour
column8: yet to possess those eccentricities which one might guess from his grooming. For some time he rambled on with an almost feverish geniality
column9: when it struck me to ask him how he came by so rare a book as Pigafetta’s Regnum Congo. The effect of this volume had not left me
column10: and I felt a certain hesitancy in speaking of it; but curiosity overmastered all the vague fears which had steadily accumulated since my first glimpse of the house. To my relief
column11: the question did not seem an awkward one; for the old man answered freely and volubly.

column1: “Oh
column2: thet Afriky book? Cap’n Ebenezer Holt traded me thet in ’sixty-eight—him as was kilt in the war.” Something about the name of Ebenezer Holt caused me to look up sharply. I had encountered it in my genealogical work
column3: but not in any record since the Revolution. I wondered if my host could help me in the task at which I was labouring
column4: and resolved to ask him about it later on. He continued.

column1: “Ebenezer was on a Salem merchantman for years
column2: an’ picked up a sight o’ queer stuff in every port. He got this in London
column3: I guess—he uster like ter buy things at the shops. I was up ta his haouse onct
column4: on the hill
column5: tradin’ hosses
column6: when I see this book. I relished the picters
column7: so he give it in on a swap. ’Tis a queer book—here
column8: leave me git on my spectacles—” The old man fumbled among his rags
column9: producing a pair of dirty and amazingly antique glasses with small octagonal lenses and steel bows. Donning these
column10: he reached for the volume on the table and turned the pages lovingly.

column1: “Ebenezer cud read a leetle o’ this—’tis Latin—but I can’t. I hed two er three schoolmasters read me a bit
column2: and Passon Clark
column3: him they say got draownded in the pond—kin yew make anything outen it?” I told him that I could
column4: and translated for his benefit a paragraph near the beginning. If I erred
column5: he was not scholar enough to correct me; for he seemed childishly pleased at my English version. His proximity was becoming rather obnoxious
column6: yet I saw no way to escape without offending him. I was amused at the childish fondness of this ignorant old man for the pictures in a book he could not read
column7: and wondered how much better he could read the few books in English which adorned the room. This revelation of simplicity removed much of the ill-defined apprehension I had felt
column8: and I smiled as my host rambled on:

column1: “Queer haow picters kin set a body thinkin’. Take this un here near the front. Hev yew ever seed trees like thet
column2: with big leaves a-floppin’ over an’ daown? And them men—them can’t be niggers—they dew beat all. Kinder like Injuns
column3: I guess
column4: even ef they be in Afriky. Some o’ these here critters looks like monkeys
column5: or half monkeys an’ half men
column6: but I never heerd o’ nothing like this un.” Here he pointed to a fabulous creature of the artist
column7: which one might describe as a sort of dragon with the head of an alligator.

column1: “But naow I’ll shew ye the best un—over here nigh the middle—” The old man’s speech grew a trifle thicker and his eyes assumed a brighter glow; but his fumbling hands
column2: though seemingly clumsier than before
column3: were entirely adequate to their mission. The book fell open
column4: almost of its own accord and as if from frequent consultation at this place
column5: to the repellent twelfth plate shewing a butcher’s shop amongst the Anzique cannibals. My sense of restlessness returned
column6: though I did not exhibit it. The especially bizarre thing was that the artist had made his Africans look like white men—the limbs and quarters hanging about the walls of the shop were ghastly
column7: while the butcher with his axe was hideously incongruous. But my host seemed to relish the view as much as I disliked it.

column1: “What d’ye think o’ this—ain’t never see the like hereabouts
column2: eh? When I see this I telled Eb Holt
column3: ‘That’s suthin’ ta stir ye up an’ make yer blood tickle!’ When I read in Scripter about slayin’—like them Midianites was slew—I kinder think things
column4: but I ain’t got no picter of it. Here a body kin see all they is to it—I s’pose ’tis sinful
column5: but ain’t we all born an’ livin’ in sin?—Thet feller bein’ chopped up gives me a tickle every time I look at ’im—I hev ta keep lookin’ at ’im—see whar the butcher cut off his feet? Thar’s his head on thet bench
column6: with one arm side of it
column7: an’ t’other arm’s on the graound side o’ the meat block.”

column1: As the man mumbled on in his shocking ecstasy the expression on his hairy
column2: spectacled face became indescribable
column3: but his voice sank rather than mounted. My own sensations can scarcely be recorded. All the terror I had dimly felt before rushed upon me actively and vividly
column4: and I knew that I loathed the ancient and abhorrent creature so near me with an infinite intensity. His madness
column5: or at least his partial perversion
column6: seemed beyond dispute. He was almost whispering now
column7: with a huskiness more terrible than a scream
column8: and I trembled as I listened.

column1: “As I says
column2: ’tis queer haow picters sets ye thinkin’. D’ye know
column3: young Sir
column4: I’m right sot on this un here. Arter I got the book off Eb I uster look at it a lot
column5: especial when I’d heerd Passon Clark rant o’ Sundays in his big wig. Onct I tried suthin’ funny—here
column6: young Sir
column7: don’t git skeert—all I done was ter look at the picter afore I kilt the sheep for market—killin’ sheep was kinder more fun arter lookin’ at it—” The tone of the old man now sank very low
column8: sometimes becoming so faint that his words were hardly audible. I listened to the rain
column9: and to the rattling of the bleared
column10: small-paned windows
column11: and marked a rumbling of approaching thunder quite unusual for the season. Once a terrific flash and peal shook the frail house to its foundations

column3: I was expected to go over his papers with some thoroughness; and for that purpose moved his entire set of files and boxes to my quarters in Boston. Much of the material which I correlated will be later published by the American Archaeological Society
column4: but there was one box which I found exceedingly puzzling
column5: and which I felt much averse from shewing to other eyes. It had been locked
column6: and I did not find the key till it occurred to me to examine the personal ring which the professor carried always in his pocket. Then indeed I succeeded in opening it
column7: but when I did so seemed only to be confronted by a greater and more closely locked barrier. For what could be the meaning of the queer clay bas-relief and the disjointed jottings
column8: ramblings
column9: and cuttings which I found? Had my uncle
column10: in his latter years
column11: become credulous of the most superficial impostures? I resolved to search out the eccentric sculptor responsible for this apparent disturbance of an old man’s peace of mind.

column1: The bas-relief was a rough rectangle less than an inch thick and about five by six inches in area; obviously of modern origin. Its designs
column2: however
column3: were far from modern in atmosphere and suggestion; for although the vagaries of cubism and futurism are many and wild
column4: they do not often reproduce that cryptic regularity which lurks in prehistoric writing. And writing of some kind the bulk of these designs seemed certainly to be; though my memory
column5: despite much familiarity with the papers and collections of my uncle
column6: failed in any way to identify this particular species
column7: or even to hint at its remotest affiliations.

column1: Above these apparent hieroglyphics was a figure of evidently pictorial intent
column2: though its impressionistic execution forbade a very clear idea of its nature. It seemed to be a sort of monster
column3: or symbol representing a monster
column4: of a form which only a diseased fancy could conceive. If I say that my somewhat extravagant imagination yielded simultaneous pictures of an octopus
column5: a dragon
column6: and a human caricature
column7: I shall not be unfaithful to the spirit of the thing. A pulpy
column8: tentacled head surmounted a grotesque and scaly body with rudimentary wings; but it was the general outline of the whole which made it most shockingly frightful. Behind the figure was a vague suggestion of a Cyclopean architectural background.

column1: The writing accompanying this oddity was
column2: aside from a stack of press cuttings

column4: the first of which was headed “1925—Dream and Dream Work of H. A. Wilcox
column5: 7 Thomas St.
column6: Providence
column7: R.I.”
column8: and the second
column9: “Narrative of Inspector John R. Legrasse
column10: 121 Bienville St.
column11: New Orleans
column12: La.
column13: at 1908 A. A. S. Mtg.—Notes on Same
column14: & Prof. Webb’s Acct.” The other manuscript papers were all brief notes
column15: some of them accounts of the queer dreams of different persons
column16: some of them citations from theosophical books and magazines (notably W. Scott-Elliot’s Atlantis and the Lost Lemuria)
column17: and the rest comments on long-surviving secret societies and hidden cults
column18: with references to passages in such mythological and anthropological source-books as Frazer’s Golden Bough and Miss Murray’s Witch-Cult in Western Europe. The cuttings largely alluded to outré mental illnesses and outbreaks of group folly or mania in the spring of 1925.

column1: The first half of the principal manuscript told a very peculiar tale. It appears that on March 1st
column3: a thin
column4: dark young man of neurotic and excited aspect had called upon Professor Angell bearing the singular clay bas-relief
column5: which was then exceedingly damp and fresh. His card bore the name of Henry Anthony Wilcox
column6: and my uncle had recognised him as the youngest son of an excellent family slightly known to him
column7: who had latterly been studying sculpture at the Rhode Island School of Design and living alone at the Fleur-de-Lys Building near that institution. Wilcox was a precocious youth of known genius but great eccentricity
column8: and had from childhood excited attention through the strange stories and odd dreams he was in the habit of relating. He called himself “psychically hypersensitive”
column9: but the staid folk of the ancient commercial city dismissed him as merely “queer”. Never mingling much with his kind
column10: he had dropped gradually from social visibility
column11: and was now known only to a small group of aesthetes from other towns. Even the Providence Art Club
column12: anxious to preserve its conservatism
column13: had found him quite hopeless.

column1: On the occasion of the visit
column2: ran the professor’s manuscript
column3: the sculptor abruptly asked for the benefit of his host’s archaeological knowledge in identifying the hieroglyphics on the bas-relief. He spoke in a dreamy
column4: stilted manner which suggested pose and alienated sympathy; and my uncle shewed some sharpness in replying
column5: for the conspicuous freshness of the tablet implied kinship with anything but archaeology. Young Wilcox’s rejoinder
column6: which impressed my uncle enough to make him recall and record it verbatim
column7: was of a fantastically poetic cast which must have typified his whole conversation
column8: and which I have since found highly characteristic of him. He said
column9: “It is new
column10: indeed
column11: for I made it last night in a dream of strange cities; and dreams are older than brooding Tyre
column12: or the contemplative Sphinx
column13: or garden-girdled Babylon.”

column1: It was then that he began that rambling tale which suddenly played upon a sleeping memory and won the fevered interest of my uncle. There had been a slight earthquake tremor the night before
column2: the most considerable felt in New England for some years; and Wilcox’s imagination had been keenly affected. Upon retiring
column3: he had had an unprecedented dream of great Cyclopean cities of titan blocks and sky-flung monoliths
column4: all dripping with green ooze and sinister with latent horror. Hieroglyphics had covered the walls and pillars
column5: and from some undetermined point below had come a voice that was not a voice; a chaotic sensation which only fancy could transmute into sound
column6: but which he attempted to render by the almost unpronounceable jumble of letters
column7: “Cthulhu fhtagn”.

column1: This verbal jumble was the key to the recollection which excited and disturbed Professor Angell. He questioned the sculptor with scientific minuteness; and studied with almost frantic intensity the bas-relief on which the youth had found himself working
column2: chilled and clad only in his night-clothes
column3: when waking had stolen bewilderingly over him. My uncle blamed his old age
column4: Wilcox afterward said
column5: for his slowness in recognising both hieroglyphics and pictorial design. Many of his questions seemed highly out-of-place to his visitor
column6: especially those which tried to connect the latter with strange cults or societies; and Wilcox could not understand the repeated promises of silence which he was offered in exchange for an admission of membership in some widespread mystical or paganly religious body. When Professor Angell became convinced that the sculptor was indeed ignorant of any cult or system of cryptic lore
column7: he besieged his visitor with demands for future reports of dreams. This bore regular fruit
column8: for after the first interview the manuscript records daily calls of the young man
column9: during which he related startling fragments of nocturnal imagery whose burden was always some terrible Cyclopean vista of dark and dripping stone
column10: with a subterrene voice or intelligence shouting monotonously in enigmatical sense-impacts uninscribable save as gibberish. The two sounds most frequently repeated are those rendered by the letters “Cthulhu” and “R’lyeh”.

column1: On March 23d
column2: the manuscript continued
column3: Wilcox failed to appear; and inquiries at his quarters revealed that he had been stricken with an obscure sort of fever and taken to the home of his family in Waterman Street. He had cried out in the night
column4: arousing several other artists in the building
column5: and had manifested since then only alternations of unconsciousness and delirium. My uncle at once telephoned the family
column6: and from that time forward kept close watch of the case; calling often at the Thayer Street office of Dr. Tobey
column7: whom he learned to be in charge. The youth’s febrile mind
column8: apparently
column9: was dwelling on strange things; and the doctor shuddered now and then as he spoke of them. They included not only a repetition of what he had formerly dreamed
column10: but touched wildly on a gigantic thing “miles high” which walked or lumbered about. He at no time fully described this object
column11: but occasional frantic words
column12: as repeated by Dr. Tobey
column13: convinced the professor that it must be identical with the nameless monstrosity he had sought to depict in his dream-sculpture. Reference to this object
column14: the doctor added
column15: was invariably a prelude to the young man’s subsidence into lethargy. His temperature
column16: oddly enough
column17: was not greatly above normal; but his whole condition was otherwise such as to suggest true fever rather than mental disorder.

column1: On April 2nd at about 3 p.m. every trace of Wilcox’s malady suddenly ceased. He sat upright in bed
column2: astonished to find himself at home and completely ignorant of what had happened in dream or reality since the night of March 22nd. Pronounced well by his physician
column3: he returned to his quarters in three days; but to Professor Angell he was of no further assistance. All traces of strange dreaming had vanished with his recovery
column4: and my uncle kept no record of his night-thoughts after a week of pointless and irrelevant accounts of thoroughly usual visions.

column1: Here the first part of the manuscript ended
column2: but references to certain of the scattered notes gave me much material for thought—so much
column3: in fact
column4: that only the ingrained scepticism then forming my philosophy can account for my continued distrust of the artist. The notes in question were those descriptive of the dreams of various persons covering the same period as that in which young Wilcox had had his strange visitations. My uncle
column5: it seems
column6: had quickly instituted a prodigiously far-flung body of inquiries amongst nearly all the friends whom he could question without impertinence
column7: asking for nightly reports of their dreams
column8: and the dates of any notable visions for some time past. The reception of his request seems to have been varied; but he must
column9: at the very least
column10: have received more responses than any ordinary man could have handled without a secretary. This original correspondence was not preserved
column11: but his notes formed a thorough and really significant digest. Average people in society and business—New England’s traditional “salt of the earth”—gave an almost completely negative result
column12: though scattered cases of uneasy but formless nocturnal impressions appear here and there
column13: always between March 23d and April 2nd—the period of young Wilcox’s delirium. Scientific men were little more affected
column14: though four cases of vague description suggest fugitive glimpses of strange landscapes
column15: and in one case there is mentioned a dread of something abnormal.

column1: It was from the artists and poets that the pertinent answers came
column2: and I know that panic would have broken loose had they been able to compare notes. As it was
column3: lacking their original letters
column4: I half suspected the compiler of having asked leading questions
column5: or of having edited the correspondence in corroboration of what he had latently resolved to see. That is why I continued to feel that Wilcox
column6: somehow cognisant of the old data which my uncle had possessed
column7: had been imposing on the veteran scientist. These responses from aesthetes told a disturbing tale. From February 28th to April 2nd a large proportion of them had dreamed very bizarre things
column8: the intensity of the dreams being immeasurably the stronger during the period of the sculptor’s delirium. Over a fourth of those who reported anything
column9: reported scenes and half-sounds not unlike those which Wilcox had described; and some of the dreamers confessed acute fear of the gigantic nameless thing visible toward the last. One case
column10: which the note describes with emphasis
column11: was very sad. The subject
column12: a widely known architect with leanings toward theosophy and occultism
column13: went violently insane on the date of young Wilcox’s seizure
column14: and expired several months later after incessant screamings to be saved from some escaped denizen of hell. Had my uncle referred to these cases by name instead of merely by number
column15: I should have attempted some corroboration and personal investigation; but as it was
column16: I succeeded in tracing down only a few. All of these
column17: however
column18: bore out the notes in full. I have often wondered if all the objects of the professor’s questioning felt as puzzled as did this fraction. It is well that no explanation shall ever reach them.

column1: The press cuttings
column2: as I have intimated
column3: touched on cases of panic
column4: mania
column5: and eccentricity during the given period. Professor Angell must have employed a cutting bureau
column6: for the number of extracts was tremendous and the sources scattered throughout the globe. Here was a nocturnal suicide in London
column7: where a lone sleeper had leaped from a window after a shocking cry. Here likewise a rambling letter to the editor of a paper in South America
column8: where a fanatic deduces a dire future from visions he has seen. A despatch from California describes a theosophist colony as donning white robes en masse for some “glorious fulfilment” which never arrives
column9: whilst items from India speak guardedly of serious native unrest toward the end of March. Voodoo orgies multiply in Hayti
column10: and African outposts report ominous mutterings. American officers in the Philippines find certain tribes bothersome about this time
column11: and New York policemen are mobbed by hysterical Levantines on the night of March 22–23. The west of Ireland
column12: too
column13: is full of wild rumour and legendry
column14: and a fantastic painter named Ardois-Bonnot hangs a blasphemous “Dream Landscape” in the Paris spring salon of 1926. And so numerous are the recorded troubles in insane asylums
column15: that only a miracle can have stopped the medical fraternity from noting strange parallelisms and drawing mystified conclusions. A weird bunch of cuttings
column16: all told; and I can at this date scarcely envisage the callous rationalism with which I set them aside. But I was then convinced that young Wilcox had known of the older matters mentioned by the professor.

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.
The older matters which had made the sculptor’s dream and bas-relief so significant to my uncle formed the subject of the second half of his long manuscript. Once before
column2: it appears
column3: Professor Angell had seen the hellish outlines of the nameless monstrosity
column4: puzzled over the unknown hieroglyphics
column5: and heard the ominous syllables which can be rendered only as “Cthulhu”; and all this in so stirring and horrible a connexion that it is small wonder he pursued young Wilcox with queries and demands for data.

column1: The earlier experience had come in 1908
column2: seventeen years before
column3: when the American Archaeological Society held its annual meeting in St. Louis. Professor Angell
column4: as befitted one of his authority and attainments
column5: had had a prominent part in all the deliberations; and was one of the first to be approached by the several outsiders who took advantage of the convocation to offer questions for correct answering and problems for expert solution.

column1: The chief of these outsiders
column2: and in a short time the focus of interest for the entire meeting
column3: was a commonplace-looking middle-aged man who had travelled all the way from New Orleans for certain special information unobtainable from any local source. His name was John Raymond Legrasse
column4: and he was by profession an Inspector of Police. With him he bore the subject of his visit
column5: a grotesque
column6: repulsive
column7: and apparently very ancient stone statuette whose origin he was at a loss to determine. It must not be fancied that Inspector Legrasse had the least interest in archaeology. On the contrary
column8: his wish for enlightenment was prompted by purely professional considerations. The statuette
column9: idol
column10: fetish
column11: or whatever it was
column12: had been captured some months before in the wooded swamps south of New Orleans during a raid on a supposed voodoo meeting; and so singular and hideous were the rites connected with it
column13: that the police could not but realise that they had stumbled on a dark cult totally unknown to them
column14: and infinitely more diabolic than even the blackest of the African voodoo circles. Of its origin
column15: apart from the erratic and unbelievable tales extorted from the captured members
column16: absolutely nothing was to be discovered; hence the anxiety of the police for any antiquarian lore which might help them to place the frightful symbol
column17: and through it track down the cult to its fountain-head.

column1: Inspector Legrasse was scarcely prepared for the sensation which his offering created. One sight of the thing had been enough to throw the assembled men of science into a state of tense excitement
column2: and they lost no time in crowding around him to gaze at the diminutive figure whose utter strangeness and air of genuinely abysmal antiquity hinted so potently at unopened and archaic vistas. No recognised school of sculpture had animated this terrible object
column3: yet centuries and even thousands of years seemed recorded in its dim and greenish surface of unplaceable stone.

column1: The figure
column2: which was finally passed slowly from man to man for close and careful study
column3: was between seven and eight inches in height
column4: and of exquisitely artistic workmanship. It represented a monster of vaguely anthropoid outline
column5: but with an octopus-like head whose face was a mass of feelers
column6: a scaly
column7: rubbery-looking body
column8: prodigious claws on hind and fore feet
column9: and long
column10: narrow wings behind. This thing
column11: which seemed instinct with a fearsome and unnatural malignancy
column12: was of a somewhat bloated corpulence
column13: and squatted evilly on a rectangular block or pedestal covered with undecipherable characters. The tips of the wings touched the back edge of the block
column14: the seat occupied the centre
column15: whilst the long
column16: curved claws of the doubled-up
column17: crouching hind legs gripped the front edge and extended a quarter of the way down toward the bottom of the pedestal. The cephalopod head was bent forward
column18: so that the ends of the facial feelers brushed the backs of huge fore paws which clasped the croucher’s elevated knees. The aspect of the whole was abnormally life-like
column19: and the more subtly fearful because its source was so totally unknown. Its vast
column21: and incalculable age was unmistakable; yet not one link did it shew with any known type of art belonging to civilisation’s youth—or indeed to any other time. Totally separate and apart
column22: its very material was a mystery; for the soapy
column23: greenish-black stone with its golden or iridescent flecks and striations resembled nothing familiar to geology or mineralogy. The characters along the base were equally baffling; and no member present
column24: despite a representation of half the world’s expert learning in this field
column25: could form the least notion of even their remotest linguistic kinship. They
column27: belonged to something horribly remote and distinct from mankind as we know it; something frightfully suggestive of old and unhallowed cycles of life in which our world and our conceptions have no part.

column1: And yet
column2: as the members severally shook their heads and confessed defeat at the Inspector’s problem
column3: there was one man in that gathering who suspected a touch of bizarre familiarity in the monstrous shape and writing
column4: and who presently told with some diffidence of the odd trifle he knew. This person was the late William Channing Webb
column5: Professor of Anthropology in Princeton University
column6: and an explorer of no slight note. Professor Webb had been engaged
column7: forty-eight years before
column8: in a tour of Greenland and Iceland in search of some Runic inscriptions which he failed to unearth; and whilst high up on the West Greenland coast had encountered a singular tribe or cult of degenerate Esquimaux whose religion
column9: a curious form of devil-worship
column10: chilled him with its deliberate bloodthirstiness and repulsiveness. It was a faith of which other Esquimaux knew little
column11: and which they mentioned only with shudders
column12: saying that it had come down from horribly ancient aeons before ever the world was made. Besides nameless rites and human sacrifices there were certain queer hereditary rituals addressed to a supreme elder devil or tornasuk; and of this Professor Webb had taken a careful phonetic copy from an aged angekok or wizard-priest
column13: expressing the sounds in Roman letters as best he knew how. But just now of prime significance was the fetish which this cult had cherished
column14: and around which they danced when the aurora leaped high over the ice cliffs. It was
column15: the professor stated
column16: a very crude bas-relief of stone
column17: comprising a hideous picture and some cryptic writing. And so far as he could tell
column18: it was a rough parallel in all essential features of the bestial thing now lying before the meeting.

column1: This data
column2: received with suspense and astonishment by the assembled members
column3: proved doubly exciting to Inspector Legrasse; and he began at once to ply his informant with questions. Having noted and copied an oral ritual among the swamp cult-worshippers his men had arrested
column4: he besought the professor to remember as best he might the syllables taken down amongst the diabolist Esquimaux. There then followed an exhaustive comparison of details
column5: and a moment of really awed silence when both detective and scientist agreed on the virtual identity of the phrase common to two hellish rituals so many worlds of distance apart. What
column6: in substance
column7: both the Esquimau wizards and the Louisiana swamp-priests had chanted to their kindred idols was something very like this—the word-divisions being guessed at from traditional breaks in the phrase as chanted aloud:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Legrasse had one point in advance of Professor Webb
column2: for several among his mongrel prisoners had repeated to him what older celebrants had told them the words meant. This text
column3: as given
column4: ran something like this:

column1: “In his house at R’lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.”
And now
column2: in response to a general and urgent demand
column3: Inspector Legrasse related as fully as possible his experience with the swamp worshippers; telling a story to which I could see my uncle attached profound significance. It savoured of the wildest dreams of myth-maker and theosophist
column4: and disclosed an astonishing degree of cosmic imagination among such half-castes and pariahs as might be least expected to possess it.

column1: On November 1st
column3: there had come to the New Orleans police a frantic summons from the swamp and lagoon country to the south. The squatters there
column4: mostly primitive but good-natured descendants of Lafitte’s men
column5: were in the grip of stark terror from an unknown thing which had stolen upon them in the night. It was voodoo
column6: apparently
column7: but voodoo of a more terrible sort than they had ever known; and some of their women and children had disappeared since the malevolent tom-tom had begun its incessant beating far within the black haunted woods where no dweller ventured. There were insane shouts and harrowing screams
column8: soul-chilling chants and dancing devil-flames; and
column9: the frightened messenger added
column10: the people could stand it no more.

column1: So a body of twenty police
column2: filling two carriages and an automobile
column3: had set out in the late afternoon with the shivering squatter as a guide. At the end of the passable road they alighted
column4: and for miles splashed on in silence through the terrible cypress woods where day never came. Ugly roots and malignant hanging nooses of Spanish moss beset them
column5: and now and then a pile of dank stones or fragment of a rotting wall intensified by its hint of morbid habitation a depression which every malformed tree and every fungous islet combined to create. At length the squatter settlement
column6: a miserable huddle of huts
column7: hove in sight; and hysterical dwellers ran out to cluster around the group of bobbing lanterns. The muffled beat of tom-toms was now faintly audible far
column8: far ahead; and a curdling shriek came at infrequent intervals when the wind shifted. A reddish glare
column9: too
column10: seemed to filter through the pale undergrowth beyond endless avenues of forest night. Reluctant even to be left alone again
column11: each one of the cowed squatters refused point-blank to advance another inch toward the scene of unholy worship
column12: so Inspector Legrasse and his nineteen colleagues plunged on unguided into black arcades of horror that none of them had ever trod before.

column1: The region now entered by the police was one of traditionally evil repute
column2: substantially unknown and untraversed by white men. There were legends of a hidden lake unglimpsed by mortal sight
column3: in which dwelt a huge
column4: formless white polypous thing with luminous eyes; and squatters whispered that bat-winged devils flew up out of caverns in inner earth to worship it at midnight. They said it had been there before D’Iberville
column5: before La Salle
column6: before the Indians
column7: and before even the wholesome beasts and birds of the woods. It was nightmare itself
column8: and to see it was to die. But it made men dream
column9: and so they knew enough to keep away. The present voodoo orgy was
column10: indeed
column11: on the merest fringe of this abhorred area
column12: but that location was bad enough; hence perhaps the very place of the worship had terrified the squatters more than the shocking sounds and incidents.

column1: Only poetry or madness could do justice to the noises heard by Legrasse’s men as they ploughed on through the black morass toward the red glare and the muffled tom-toms. There are vocal qualities peculiar to men
column2: and vocal qualities peculiar to beasts; and it is terrible to hear the one when the source should yield the other. Animal fury and orgiastic licence here whipped themselves to daemoniac heights by howls and squawking ecstasies that tore and reverberated through those nighted woods like pestilential tempests from the gulfs of hell. Now and then the less organised ululation would cease
column3: and from what seemed a well-drilled chorus of hoarse voices would rise in sing-song chant that hideous phrase or ritual:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Then the men
column2: having reached a spot where the trees were thinner
column3: came suddenly in sight of the spectacle itself. Four of them reeled
column4: one fainted
column5: and two were shaken into a frantic cry which the mad cacophony of the orgy fortunately deadened. Legrasse dashed swamp water on the face of the fainting man
column6: and all stood trembling and nearly hypnotised with horror.

column1: In a natural glade of the swamp stood a grassy island of perhaps an acre’s extent
column2: clear of trees and tolerably dry. On this now leaped and twisted a more indescribable horde of human abnormality than any but a Sime or an Angarola could paint. Void of clothing
column3: this hybrid spawn were braying
column4: bellowing
column5: and writhing about a monstrous ring-shaped bonfire; in the centre of which
column6: revealed by occasional rifts in the curtain of flame
column7: stood a great granite monolith some eight feet in height; on top of which
column8: incongruous with its diminutiveness
column9: rested the noxious carven statuette. From a wide circle of ten scaffolds set up at regular intervals with the flame-girt monolith as a centre hung
column10: head downward
column11: the oddly marred bodies of the helpless squatters who had disappeared. It was inside this circle that the ring of worshippers jumped and roared
column12: the general direction of the mass motion being from left to right in endless Bacchanal between the ring of bodies and the ring of fire.

column1: It may have been only imagination and it may have been only echoes which induced one of the men
column2: an excitable Spaniard
column3: to fancy he heard antiphonal responses to the ritual from some far and unillumined spot deeper within the wood of ancient legendry and horror. This man
column4: Joseph D. Galvez
column5: I later met and questioned; and he proved distractingly imaginative. He indeed went so far as to hint of the faint beating of great wings
column6: and of a glimpse of shining eyes and a mountainous white bulk beyond the remotest trees—but I suppose he had been hearing too much native superstition.

column1: Actually
column2: the horrified pause of the men was of comparatively brief duration. Duty came first; and although there must have been nearly a hundred mongrel celebrants in the throng
column3: the police relied on their firearms and plunged determinedly into the nauseous rout. For five minutes the resultant din and chaos were beyond description. Wild blows were struck
column4: shots were fired
column5: and escapes were made; but in the end Legrasse was able to count some forty-seven sullen prisoners
column6: whom he forced to dress in haste and fall into line between two rows of policemen. Five of the worshippers lay dead
column7: and two severely wounded ones were carried away on improvised stretchers by their fellow-prisoners. The image on the monolith
column8: of course
column9: was carefully removed and carried back by Legrasse.

column1: Examined at headquarters after a trip of intense strain and weariness
column2: the prisoners all proved to be men of a very low
column3: mixed-blooded
column4: and mentally aberrant type. Most were seamen
column5: and a sprinkling of negroes and mulattoes
column6: largely West Indians or Brava Portuguese from the Cape Verde Islands
column7: gave a colouring of voodooism to the heterogeneous cult. But before many questions were asked
column8: it became manifest that something far deeper and older than negro fetichism was involved. Degraded and ignorant as they were
column9: the creatures held with surprising consistency to the central idea of their loathsome faith.

column1: They worshipped
column2: so they said
column3: the Great Old Ones who lived ages before there were any men
column4: and who came to the young world out of the sky. Those Old Ones were gone now
column5: inside the earth and under the sea; but their dead bodies had told their secrets in dreams to the first men
column6: who formed a cult which had never died. This was that cult
column7: and the prisoners said it had always existed and always would exist
column8: hidden in distant wastes and dark places all over the world until the time when the great priest Cthulhu
column9: from his dark house in the mighty city of R’lyeh under the waters
column10: should rise and bring the earth again beneath his sway. Some day he would call
column11: when the stars were ready
column12: and the secret cult would always be waiting to liberate him.

column1: Meanwhile no more must be told. There was a secret which even torture could not extract. Mankind was not absolutely alone among the conscious things of earth
column2: for shapes came out of the dark to visit the faithful few. But these were not the Great Old Ones. No man had ever seen the Old Ones. The carven idol was great Cthulhu
column3: but none might say whether or not the others were precisely like him. No one could read the old writing now

column1: Here the old man faltered
column2: mumbled
column3: and lapsed into a moody and apprehensive silence; glancing nervously over his shoulder and then turning back to stare fascinatedly at the distant black reef. When I spoke to him he did not answer
column4: so I knew I would have to let him finish the bottle. The insane yarn I was hearing interested me profoundly
column5: for I fancied there was contained within it a sort of crude allegory based upon the strangeness of Innsmouth and elaborated by an imagination at once creative and full of scraps of exotic legend. Not for a moment did I believe that the tale had any really substantial foundation; but none the less the account held a hint of genuine terror if only because it brought in references to strange jewels clearly akin to the malign tiara I had seen at Newburyport. Perhaps the ornaments had
column6: after all
column7: come from some strange island; and possibly the wild stories were lies of the bygone Obed himself rather than of this antique toper.

column1: So I say that I have not murdered Edward Derby. Rather have I avenged him

column1: I have known Edward Pickman Derby all his life. Eight years my junior

column4: fantastic

column8: secretive inner life in the boy

column1: As for the Innsmouth people--the youth hardly knew what to make of them. They were as furtive and seldom seen as animals that live in burrows

Perhaps--judging from the quantities of bootleg liquor they consumed--they lay for most of the daylight hours in an alcoholic stupor. They seemed sullenly banded together in some sort of fellowship and understanding--despising the world as if they had access to other and preferable spheres of entity. Their appearance--especially those staring
column3: unwinking eyes which one never saw shut--was certainly shocking enough; and their voices were disgusting. It was awful to hear them chanting in their churches at night

column1: They were very fond of the water

column1: Only a very rare affliction

column6: curtained car.

column1: There were all sorts of rumors about how Marsh had come to look. He had once been a great dandy; and people said he still wore the frock-coated finery of the Edwardian age curiously adapted to certain deformities. His son had formerly conducted the office in the square

column5: or whatever they were called nowadays--also wore this kind of ornament as a headdress; but one seldom caught glimpses of them. Other specimens the youth had not seen

column1: The Marshes

column1: Thus I began my systematic though half-bewildered tour of Innsmouth's narrow
column2: shadow-blighted ways. Crossing the bridge and turning toward the roar of the lower falls

column1: Re-crossing the gorge on the Main Street bridge

column3: above which rose the ghoulish

column5: but most were tightly boarded up. Down unpaved side streets I saw the black
column6: gaping windows of deserted hovels

column8: the terror of a deserted house swells in geometrical rather than arithmetical progression as houses multiply to form a city of stark desolation. The sight of such endless avenues of fishy-eyed vacancy and death
column9: and the thought of such linked infinities of black

column11: start up vestigial fears and aversions that not even the stoutest philosophy can disperse.

column1: Fish Street was as deserted as Main

column6: according to the sketch
column7: was in ruins.

column3: scurryings
column4: and hoarse doubtful noises; and I thought uncomfortably about the hidden tunnels suggested by the grocery boy. Suddenly I found myself wondering what the voices of those denizens would be like. I had heard no speech so far in this quarter
column5: and was unaccountably anxious not to do so.

column6: Lafayette

column9: most of them decrepit and boarded up amidst neglected grounds
column10: but one or two in each street shewing signs of occupancy. In Washington Street there was a row of four or five in excellent repair and with finely-tended lawns and gardens. The most sumptuous of these--with wide terraced parterres extending back the whole way to Lafayette Street--I took to be the home of Old Man Marsh

column6: staring eyes that never shut.

column3: and seeing others
column4: with the traces of an old railway station and covered railway bridge beyond
column5: up the gorge on my right.

column2: but I took the risk and crossed again to the south bank where traces of life reappeared. Furtive
column3: shambling creatures stared cryptically in my direction
column4: and more normal faces eyed me coldly and curiously. Innsmouth was rapidly becoming intolerable
column5: and I turned down Paine Street toward the Square in the hope of getting some vehicle to take me to Arkham before the still-distant starting-time of that sinister bus.

column1: I.
It is true that I have sent six bullets through the head of my best friend
column2: and yet I hope to shew by this statement that I am not his murderer. At first I shall be called a madman—madder than the man I shot in his cell at the Arkham Sanitarium. Later some of my readers will weigh each statement
column3: correlate it with the known facts
column4: and ask themselves how I could have believed otherwise than as I did after facing the evidence of that horror—that thing on the doorstep.

column1: Until then I also saw nothing but madness in the wild tales I have acted on. Even now I ask myself whether I was misled—or whether I am not mad after all. I do not know—but others have strange things to tell of Edward and Asenath Derby
column2: and even the stolid police are at their wits’ ends to account for that last terrible visit. They have tried weakly to concoct a theory of a ghastly jest or warning by discharged servants
column3: yet they know in their hearts that the truth is something infinitely more terrible and incredible.

column1: So I say that I have not murdered Edward Derby. Rather have I avenged him
column2: and in so doing purged the earth of a horror whose survival might have loosed untold terrors on all mankind. There are black zones of shadow close to our daily paths
column3: and now and then some evil soul breaks a passage through. When that happens
column4: the man who knows must strike before reckoning the consequences.

column1: I have known Edward Pickman Derby all his life. Eight years my junior
column2: he was so precocious that we had much in common from the time he was eight and I sixteen. He was the most phenomenal child scholar I have ever known
column3: and at seven was writing verse of a sombre
column4: fantastic
column5: almost morbid cast which astonished the tutors surrounding him. Perhaps his private education and coddled seclusion had something to do with his premature flowering. An only child
column6: he had organic weaknesses which startled his doting parents and caused them to keep him closely chained to their side. He was never allowed out without his nurse
column7: and seldom had a chance to play unconstrainedly with other children. All this doubtless fostered a strange
column8: secretive inner life in the boy
column9: with imagination as his one avenue of freedom.

column1: At any rate
column2: his juvenile learning was prodigious and bizarre; and his facile writings such as to captivate me despite my greater age. About that time I had leanings toward art of a somewhat grotesque cast
column3: and I found in this younger child a rare kindred spirit. What lay behind our joint love of shadows and marvels was
column4: no doubt
column5: the ancient
column6: mouldering
column7: and subtly fearsome town in which we lived—witch-cursed
column8: legend-haunted Arkham
column9: whose huddled
column10: sagging gambrel roofs and crumbling Georgian balustrades brood out the centuries beside the darkly muttering Miskatonic.

column1: As time went by I turned to architecture and gave up my design of illustrating a book of Edward’s daemoniac poems
column2: yet our comradeship suffered no lessening. Young Derby’s odd genius developed remarkably
column3: and in his eighteenth year his collected nightmare-lyrics made a real sensation when issued under the title Azathoth and Other Horrors. He was a close correspondent of the notorious Baudelairean poet Justin Geoffrey
column4: who wrote The People of the Monolith and died screaming in a madhouse in 1926 after a visit to a sinister
column5: ill-regarded village in Hungary.

column1: In self-reliance and practical affairs
column2: however
column3: Derby was greatly retarded because of his coddled existence. His health had improved
column4: but his habits of childish dependence were fostered by overcareful parents; so that he never travelled alone
column5: made independent decisions
column6: or assumed responsibilities. It was early seen that he would not be equal to a struggle in the business or professional arena
column7: but the family fortune was so ample that this formed no tragedy. As he grew to years of manhood he retained a deceptive aspect of boyishness. Blond and blue-eyed
column8: he had the fresh complexion of a child; and his attempts to raise a moustache were discernible only with difficulty. His voice was soft and light
column9: and his pampered
column10: unexercised life gave him a juvenile chubbiness rather than the paunchiness of premature middle age. He was of good height
column11: and his handsome face would have made him a notable gallant had not his shyness held him to seclusion and bookishness.

column1: Derby’s parents took him abroad every summer
column2: and he was quick to seize on the surface aspects of European thought and expression. His Poe-like talents turned more and more toward the decadent
column3: and other artistic sensitivenesses and yearnings were half-aroused in him. We had great discussions in those days. I had been through Harvard
column4: had studied in a Boston architect’s office
column5: had married
column6: and had finally returned to Arkham to practice my profession—settling in the family homestead in Saltonstall St. since my father had moved to Florida for his health. Edward used to call almost every evening
column7: till I came to regard him as one of the household. He had a characteristic way of ringing the doorbell or sounding the knocker that grew to be a veritable code signal
column8: so that after dinner I always listened for the familiar three brisk strokes followed by two more after a pause. Less frequently I would visit at his house and note with envy the obscure volumes in his constantly growing library.

column1: Derby went through Miskatonic University in Arkham
column2: since his parents would not let him board away from them. He entered at sixteen and completed his course in three years
column3: majoring in English and French literature and receiving high marks in everything but mathematics and the sciences. He mingled very little with the other students
column4: though looking enviously at the “daring” or “Bohemian” set—whose superficially “smart” language and meaninglessly ironic pose he aped
column5: and whose dubious conduct he wished he dared adopt.

column1: What he did do was to become an almost fanatical devotee of subterranean magical lore
column2: for which Miskatonic’s library was and is famous. Always a dweller on the surface of phantasy and strangeness
column3: he now delved deep into the actual runes and riddles left by a fabulous past for the guidance or puzzlement of posterity. He read things like the frightful Book of Eibon
column4: the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt
column5: and the forbidden Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred
column6: though he did not tell his parents he had seen them. Edward was twenty when my son and only child was born
column7: and seemed pleased when I named the newcomer Edward Derby Upton
column8: after him.

column1: By the time he was twenty-five Edward Derby was a prodigiously learned man and a fairly well-known poet and fantaisiste
column2: though his lack of contacts and responsibilities had slowed down his literary growth by making his products derivative and overbookish. I was perhaps his closest friend—finding him an inexhaustible mine of vital theoretical topics
column3: while he relied on me for advice in whatever matters he did not wish to refer to his parents. He remained single—more through shyness
column4: inertia
column5: and parental protectiveness than through inclination—and moved in society only to the slightest and most perfunctory extent. When the war came both health and ingrained timidity kept him at home. I went to Plattsburg for a commission
column6: but never got overseas.

column1: So the years wore on. Edward’s mother died when he was thirty-four
column2: and for months he was incapacitated by some odd psychological malady. His father took him to Europe
column3: however
column4: and he managed to pull out of his trouble without visible effects. Afterward he seemed to feel a sort of grotesque exhilaration
column5: as if of partial escape from some unseen bondage. He began to mingle in the more “advanced” college set despite his middle age
column6: and was present at some extremely wild doings—on one occasion paying heavy blackmail (which he borrowed of me) to keep his presence at a certain affair from his father’s notice. Some of the whispered rumours about the wild Miskatonic set were extremely singular. There was even talk of black magic and of happenings utterly beyond credibility.
