Edward was thirty-eight when he met Asenath Waite. She was
column2: I judge
column3: about twenty-three at the time; and was taking a special course in mediaeval metaphysics at Miskatonic. The daughter of a friend of mine had met her before—in the Hall School at Kingsport—and had been inclined to shun her because of her odd reputation. She was dark

column4: and that strange sounds sometimes floated from within as evening drew on. The old man was known to have been a prodigious magical student in his day

column1: The friend whose daughter had gone to school with Asenath Waite repeated many curious things when the news of Edward’s acquaintance with her began to spread about. Asenath
column2: it seemed

column5: and she could make any dog howl by certain motions of her right hand. There were times when she displayed snatches of knowledge and language very singular—and very shocking—for a young girl; when she would frighten her schoolmates with leers and winks of an inexplicable kind
column6: and would seem to extract an obscene and zestful irony from her present situation.

column1: Most unusual
column2: though

column4: beyond question
column5: a genuine hypnotist. By gazing peculiarly at a fellow-student she would often give the latter a distinct feeling of exchanged personality—as if the subject were placed momentarily in the magician’s body and able to stare half across the room at her real body
column6: whose eyes blazed and protruded with an alien expression. Asenath often made wild claims about the nature of consciousness and about its independence of the physical frame—or at least from the life-processes of the physical frame. Her crowning rage
column7: however

column9: she declared

column4: and recalled casual references only faintly

column7: he said

column2: though they agreed that he did not look even nearly his actual age
column3: or seem at all inappropriate as an escort for his bizarre divinity. He was only a trifle paunchy despite his indolence and self-indulgence
column4: and his face was absolutely without lines. Asenath

column5: my wife
column6: my son

column1: When Edward called on me after the honeymoon I thought he looked slightly changed. Asenath had made him get rid of the undeveloped moustache
column2: but there was more than that. He looked soberer and more thoughtful
column3: his habitual pout of childish rebelliousness being exchanged for a look almost of genuine sadness. I was puzzled to decide whether I liked or disliked the change. Certainly
column4: he seemed for the moment more normally adult than ever before. Perhaps the marriage was a good thing—might not the change of dependence form a start toward actual neutralisation
column5: leading ultimately to responsible independence? He came alone
column6: for Asenath was very busy. She had brought a vast store of books and apparatus from Innsmouth (Derby shuddered as he spoke the name)
column7: and was finishing the restoration of the Crowninshield house and grounds.

column1: Her home in—that town—was a rather disquieting place
column2: but certain objects in it had taught him some surprising things. He was progressing fast in esoteric lore now that he had Asenath’s guidance. Some of the experiments she proposed were very daring and radical—he did not feel at liberty to describe them—but he had confidence in her powers and intentions. The three servants were very queer—an incredibly aged couple who had been with old Ephraim and referred occasionally to him and to Asenath’s dead mother in a cryptic way
column3: and a swarthy young wench who had marked anomalies of feature and seemed to exude a perpetual odour of fish.

column1: III.

Their appearance--especially those staring

column11: too

column1: Assuming that I was sane and awake
column2: my experience on that night was such as has befallen no man before. It was
column3: moreover
column4: a frightful confirmation of all I had sought to dismiss as myth and dream. Mercifully there is no proof

column6: but chance and the shifting sand have so far saved them from finding it. Now I must formulate some definitive statement—not only for the sake of my own mental balance
column7: but to warn such others as may read it seriously.

column1: These pages—much in whose earlier parts will be familiar to close readers of the general and scientific press—are written in the cabin of the ship that is bringing me home. I shall give them to my son
column2: Prof. Wingate Peaslee of Miskatonic University—the only member of my family who stuck to me after my queer amnesia of long ago
column3: and the man best informed on the inner facts of my case. Of all living persons

column5: because I think he had better have the revelation in written form. Reading and re-reading at leisure will leave with him a more convincing picture than my confused tongue could hope to convey. He can do as he thinks best with this account—shewing it
column6: with suitable comment
column7: to any quarters where it will be likely to accomplish good. It is for the sake of such readers as are unfamiliar with the earlier phases of my case that I am prefacing the revelation itself with a fairly ample summary of its background.

column1: My name is Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee
column2: and those who recall the newspaper tales of a generation back—or the letters and articles in psychological journals six or seven years ago—will know who and what I am. The press was filled with the details of my strange amnesia in 1908–13
column3: and much was made of the traditions of horror
column4: madness
column5: and witchcraft which lurk behind the ancient Massachusetts town then and now forming my place of residence. Yet I would have it known that there is nothing whatever of the mad or sinister in my heredity and early life. This is a highly important fact in view of the shadow which fell so suddenly upon me from outside sources. It may be that centuries of dark brooding had given to crumbling
column6: whisper-haunted Arkham a peculiar vulnerability as regards such shadows—though even this seems doubtful in the light of those other cases which I later came to study. But the chief point is that my own ancestry and background are altogether normal. What came
column7: came from somewhere else—where
column8: I even now hesitate to assert in plain words.

column1: I am the son of Jonathan and Hannah (Wingate) Peaslee
column2: both of wholesome old Haverhill stock. I was born and reared in Haverhill—at the old homestead in Boardman Street near Golden Hill—and did not go to Arkham till I entered Miskatonic University at the age of eighteen. That was in 1889. After my graduation I studied economics at Harvard
column3: and came back to Miskatonic as Instructor of Political Economy in 1895. For thirteen years more my life ran smoothly and happily. I married Alice Keezar of Haverhill in 1896
column4: and my three children
column5: Robert K.
column6: Wingate
column7: and Hannah
column8: were born in 1898
column10: and 1903
column11: respectively. In 1898 I became an associate professor
column12: and in 1902 a full professor. At no time had I the least interest in either occultism or abnormal psychology.

column1: It was on Thursday
column2: May 14
column4: that the queer amnesia came. The thing was quite sudden
column5: though later I realised that certain brief
column6: glimmering visions of several hours previous—chaotic visions which disturbed me greatly because they were so unprecedented—must have formed premonitory symptoms. My head was aching
column7: and I had a singular feeling—altogether new to me—that someone else was trying to get possession of my thoughts.

column1: The collapse occurred about 10:20 a.m.
column2: while I was conducting a class in Political Economy VI—history and present tendencies of economics—for juniors and a few sophomores. I began to see strange shapes before my eyes
column3: and to feel that I was in a grotesque room other than the classroom. My thoughts and speech wandered from my subject
column4: and the students saw that something was gravely amiss. Then I slumped down
column5: unconscious in my chair
column6: in a stupor from which no one could arouse me. Nor did my rightful faculties again look out upon the daylight of our normal world for five years

column8: and thirteen days.

column1: It is
column2: of course
column3: from others that I have learned what followed. I shewed no sign of consciousness for sixteen and a half hours
column4: though removed to my home at 27 Crane St. and given the best of medical attention. At 3 a.m. May 15 my eyes opened and I began to speak
column5: but before long the doctors and my family were thoroughly frightened by the trend of my expression and language. It was clear that I had no remembrance of my identity or of my past
column6: though for some reason I seemed anxious to conceal this lack of knowledge. My eyes gazed strangely at the persons around me

column1: Even my speech seemed awkward and foreign. I used my vocal organs clumsily and gropingly
column2: and my diction had a curiously stilted quality
column3: as if I had laboriously learned the English language from books. The pronunciation was barbarously alien
column4: whilst the idiom seemed to include both scraps of curious archaism and expressions of a wholly incomprehensible cast. Of the latter one in particular was very potently—even terrifiedly—recalled by the youngest of the physicians twenty years afterward. For at that late period such a phrase began to have an actual currency—first in England and then in the United States—and though of much complexity and indisputable newness
column5: it reproduced in every least particular the mystifying words of the strange Arkham patient of 1908.

column4: and bodily apparatus in general. Because of this and other handicaps inherent in the mnemonic lapse

column10: art

column1: As soon as permitted

column1: Of real friendliness
column2: however
column3: I encountered little. Something in my aspect and speech seemed to excite vague fears and aversions in everyone I met

column4: and today at thirty-five he is a professor of psychology at Miskatonic. But I do not wonder at the horror I caused—for certainly
column5: the mind

column7: and facial expression of the being that awaked on May 15

column1: I will not attempt to tell much of my life from 1908 to 1913
column2: since readers may glean all the outward essentials—as I largely had to do—from files of old newspapers and scientific journals. I was given charge of my funds

column4: in travel and in study at various centres of learning. My travels
column5: however

column8: afterward shewing signs of disappointment. Later in that year I spent weeks alone beyond the limits of previous or subsequent exploration in the vast limestone cavern systems of western Virginia—black labyrinths so complex that no retracing of my steps could even be considered.

column1: My sojourns at the universities were marked by abnormally rapid assimilation
column2: as if the secondary personality had an intelligence enormously superior to my own. I have found

I could master every detail of a book merely by glancing over it as fast as I could turn the leaves; while my skill at interpreting complex figures in an instant was veritably awesome. At times there appeared almost ugly reports of my power to influence the thoughts and acts of others

column1: When the doctor reached my house he found me unconscious in the sitting-room—in an easy-chair with a table drawn up before it. On the polished table-top were scratches shewing where some heavy object had rested. The queer machine was gone

column2: and some papers with your articles which he has just sent me
column3: make it advisable for me to tell you about certain things I have seen in the Great Sandy Desert east of our gold field here. It would seem
column4: in view of the peculiar legends about old cities with huge stonework and strange designs and hieroglyphs which you describe
column5: that I have come upon something very important.

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: But what I have to tell is more than this. Two years ago
column2: when I was prospecting about 500 miles east in the desert
column3: I came on a lot of queer pieces of dressed stone perhaps 3 × 2 × 2 feet in size
column4: and weathered and pitted to the very limit. At first I couldn’t find any of the marks the blackfellows told about
column5: but when I looked close enough I could make out some deeply carved lines in spite of the weathering. They were peculiar curves
column6: just like what the blacks had tried to describe. I imagine there must have been 30 or 40 blocks
column7: some nearly buried in the sand
column8: and all within a circle perhaps a quarter of a mile’s diameter.

column1: When I saw some
column2: I looked around closely for more
column3: and made a careful reckoning of the place with my instruments. I also took pictures of 10 or 12 of the most typical blocks
column4: and will enclose the prints for you to see. I turned my information and pictures over to the government at Perth
column5: but they have done nothing with them. Then I met Dr. Boyle
column6: who had read your articles in the Journal of the American Psychological Society
column7: and in time happened to mention the stones. He was enormously interested
column8: and became quite excited when I shewed him my snapshots
column9: saying that the stones and markings were just like those of the masonry you had dreamed about and seen described in legends. He meant to write you
column10: but was delayed. Meanwhile he sent me most of the magazines with your articles
column11: and I saw at once from your drawings and descriptions that my stones are certainly the kind you mean. You can appreciate this from the enclosed prints. Later on you will hear directly from Dr. Boyle.

column1: Now I can understand how important all this will be to you. Without question we are faced with the remains of an unknown civilisation older than any dreamed of before
column2: and forming a basis for your legends. As a mining engineer
column3: I have some knowledge of geology
column4: and can tell you that these blocks are so ancient they frighten me. They are mostly sandstone and granite
column5: though one is almost certainly made of a queer sort of cement or concrete. They bear evidence of water action
column6: as if this part of the world had been submerged and come up again after long ages—all since these blocks were made and used. It is a matter of hundreds of thousands of years—or heaven knows how much more. I don’t like to think about it.

column1: In view of your previous diligent work in tracking down the legends and everything connected with them
column2: I cannot doubt but that you will want to lead an expedition to the desert and make some archaeological excavations. Both Dr. Boyle and I are prepared to coöperate in such work if you—or organisations known to you—can furnish the funds. I can get together a dozen miners for the heavy digging—the blacks would be of no use
column3: for I’ve found that they have an almost maniacal fear of this particular spot. Boyle and I are saying nothing to others
column4: for you very obviously ought to have precedence in any discoveries or credit.

column1: The place can be reached from Pilbarra in about 4 days by motor tractor—which we’d need for our apparatus. It is somewhat west and south of Warburton’s path of 1873
column2: and 100 miles southeast of Joanna Spring. We could float things up the De Grey River instead of starting from Pilbarra—but all that can be talked over later. Roughly
column3: the stones lie at a point about 22° 3' 14"" South Latitude
column4: 125° 0' 39"" East Longitude. The climate is tropical
column5: and the desert conditions are trying. Any expedition had better be made in winter—June or July or August. I shall welcome further correspondence upon this subject
column6: and am keenly eager to assist in any plan you may devise. After studying your articles I am deeply impressed with the profound significance of the whole matter. Dr. Boyle will write later. When rapid communication is needed
column7: a cable to Perth can be relayed by wireless.

column1: Hoping profoundly for an early message
Believe me
Most faithfully yours
Robert B. F. Mackenzie.
Of the immediate aftermath of this letter
column2: much can be learned from the press. My good fortune in securing the backing of Miskatonic University was great
column3: and both Mr. Mackenzie and Dr. Boyle proved invaluable in arranging matters at the Australian end. We were not too specific with the public about our objects
column4: since the whole matter would have lent itself unpleasantly to sensational and jocose treatment by the cheaper newspapers. As a result
column5: printed reports were sparing; but enough appeared to tell of our quest for reported Australian ruins and to chronicle our various preparatory steps.

column1: Professors William Dyer of the college’s geology department (leader of the Miskatonic Antarctic Expedition of 1930–31)
column2: Ferdinand C. Ashley of the department of ancient history
column3: and Tyler M. Freeborn of the department of anthropology—together with my son Wingate—accompanied me. My correspondent Mackenzie came to Arkham early in 1935 and assisted in our final preparations. He proved to be a tremendously competent and affable man of about fifty
column4: admirably well-read
column5: and deeply familiar with all the conditions of Australian travel. He had tractors waiting at Pilbarra
column6: and we chartered a tramp steamer of sufficiently light draught to get up the river to that point. We were prepared to excavate in the most careful and scientific fashion
column7: sifting every particle of sand
column8: and disturbing nothing which might seem to be in or near its original situation.

column1: Sailing from Boston aboard the wheezy Lexington on March 28
column3: we had a leisurely trip across the Atlantic and Mediterranean
column4: through the Suez Canal
column5: down the Red Sea
column6: and across the Indian Ocean to our goal. I need not tell how the sight of the low
column7: sandy West Australian coast depressed me
column8: and how I detested the crude mining town and dreary gold fields where the tractors were given their last loads. Dr. Boyle
column9: who met us
column10: proved to be elderly
column11: pleasant
column12: and intelligent—and his knowledge of psychology led him into many long discussions with my son and me.

column1: Discomfort and expectancy were oddly mingled in most of us when at length our party of eighteen rattled forth over the arid leagues of sand and rock. On Friday
column2: May 31st
column3: we forded a branch of the De Grey and entered the realm of utter desolation. A certain positive terror grew on me as we advanced to this actual site of the elder world behind the legends—a terror of course abetted by the fact that my disturbing dreams and pseudo-memories still beset me with unabated force.

column1: It was on Monday
column2: June 3
column3: that we saw the first of the half-buried blocks. I cannot describe the emotions with which I actually touched—in objective reality—a fragment of Cyclopean masonry in every respect like the blocks in the walls of my dream-buildings. There was a distinct trace of carving—and my hands trembled as I recognised part of a curvilinear decorative scheme made hellish to me through years of tormenting nightmare and baffling research.

column1: A month of digging brought a total of some 1250 blocks in varying stages of wear and disintegration. Most of these were carven megaliths with curved tops and bottoms. A minority were smaller
column2: flatter
column3: plain-surfaced
column4: and square or octagonally cut—like those of the floors and pavements in my dreams—while a few were singularly massive and curved or slanted in such a manner as to suggest use in vaulting or groining
column5: or as parts of arches or round window casings. The deeper—and the farther north and east—we dug
column6: the more blocks we found; though we still failed to discover any trace of arrangement among them. Professor Dyer was appalled at the measureless age of the fragments
column7: and Freeborn found traces of symbols which fitted darkly into certain Papuan and Polynesian legends of infinite antiquity. The condition and scattering of the blocks told mutely of vertiginous cycles of time and geologic upheavals of cosmic savagery.

column1: We had an aëroplane with us
column2: and my son Wingate would often go up to different heights and scan the sand-and-rock waste for signs of dim
column3: large-scale outlines—either differences of level or trails of scattered blocks. His results were virtually negative; for whenever he would one day think he had glimpsed some significant trend
column4: he would on his next trip find the impression replaced by another equally insubstantial—a result of the shifting
column5: wind-blown sand. One or two of these ephemeral suggestions
column6: though
column7: affected me queerly and disagreeably. They seemed
column8: after a fashion
column9: to dovetail horribly with something which I had dreamed or read
column10: but which I could no longer remember. There was a terrible pseudo-familiarity about them—which somehow made me look furtively and apprehensively over the abominable
column11: sterile terrain toward the north and northeast.

column1: Around the first week in July I developed an unaccountable set of mixed emotions about that general northeasterly region. There was horror
column2: and there was curiosity—but more than that
column3: there was a persistent and perplexing illusion of memory. I tried all sorts of psychological expedients to get these notions out of my head
column4: but met with no success. Sleeplessness also gained upon me
column5: but I almost welcomed this because of the resultant shortening of my dream-periods. I acquired the habit of taking long
column6: lone walks in the desert late at night—usually to the north or northeast
column7: whither the sum of my strange new impulses seemed subtly to pull me.

column1: Sometimes
column2: on these walks
column3: I would stumble over nearly buried fragments of the ancient masonry. Though there were fewer visible blocks here than where we had started
column4: I felt sure that there must be a vast abundance beneath the surface. The ground was less level than at our camp
column5: and the prevailing high winds now and then piled the sand into fantastic temporary hillocks—exposing some traces of the elder stones while it covered other traces. I was queerly anxious to have the excavations extend to this territory
column6: yet at the same time dreaded what might be revealed. Obviously
column7: I was getting into a rather bad state—all the worse because I could not account for it.

column1: An indication of my poor nervous health can be gained from my response to an odd discovery which I made on one of my nocturnal rambles. It was on the evening of July 11th
column2: when a gibbous moon flooded the mysterious hillocks with a curious pallor. Wandering somewhat beyond my usual limits
column3: I came upon a great stone which seemed to differ markedly from any we had yet encountered. It was almost wholly covered
column4: but I stooped and cleared away the sand with my hands
column5: later studying the object carefully and supplementing the moonlight with my electric torch. Unlike the other very large rocks
column6: this one was perfectly square-cut
column7: with no convex or concave surface. It seemed
column8: too
column9: to be of a dark basaltic substance wholly dissimilar to the granite and sandstone and occasional concrete of the now familiar fragments.

column1: Suddenly I rose
column2: turned
column3: and ran for the camp at top speed. It was a wholly unconscious and irrational flight
column4: and only when I was close to my tent did I fully realise why I had run. Then it came to me. The queer dark stone was something which I had dreamed and read about
column5: and which was linked with the uttermost horrors of the aeon-old legendry. It was one of the blocks of that basaltic elder masonry which the fabled Great Race held in such fear—the tall
column6: windowless ruins left by those brooding
column7: half-material
column8: alien Things that festered in earth’s nether abysses and against whose wind-like
column9: invisible forces the trap-doors were sealed and the sleepless sentinels posted.

column1: I remained awake all that night
column2: but by dawn realised how silly I had been to let the shadow of a myth upset me. Instead of being frightened
column3: I should have had a discoverer’s enthusiasm. The next forenoon I told the others about my find
column4: and Dyer
column5: Freeborn
column6: Boyle
column7: my son
column8: and I set out to view the anomalous block. Failure
column9: however
column10: confronted us. I had formed no clear idea of the stone’s location
column11: and a late wind had wholly altered the hillocks of shifting sand.

column1: VI.

I come now to the crucial and most difficult part of my narrative—all the more difficult because I cannot be quite certain of its reality. At times I feel uncomfortably sure that I was not dreaming or deluded; and it is this feeling—in view of the stupendous implications which the objective truth of my experience would raise—which impels me to make this record. My son—a trained psychologist with the fullest and most sympathetic knowledge of my whole case—shall be the primary judge of what I have to tell.
First let me outline the externals of the matter
column2: as those at the camp know them. On the night of July 17–18
column3: after a windy day
column4: I retired early but could not sleep. Rising shortly before eleven
column5: and afflicted as usual with that strange feeling regarding the northeastward terrain
column6: I set out on one of my typical nocturnal walks; seeing and greeting only one person—an Australian miner named Tupper—as I left our precincts. The moon
column7: slightly past full
column8: shone from a clear sky and drenched the ancient sands with a white
column9: leprous radiance which seemed to me somehow infinitely evil. There was no longer any wind
column10: nor did any return for nearly five hours
column11: as amply attested by Tupper and others who did not sleep through the night. The Australian last saw me walking rapidly across the pallid
column12: secret-guarding hillocks toward the northeast.

column1: About 3:30 a.m. a violent wind blew up
column2: waking everyone in camp and felling three of the tents. The sky was unclouded
column3: and the desert still blazed with that leprous moonlight. As the party saw to the tents my absence was noted
column4: but in view of my previous walks this circumstance gave no one alarm. And yet as many as three men—all Australians—seemed to feel something sinister in the air. Mackenzie explained to Prof. Freeborn that this was a fear picked up from blackfellow folklore—the natives having woven a curious fabric of malignant myth about the high winds which at long intervals sweep across the sands under a clear sky. Such winds
column5: it is whispered
column6: blow out of the great stone huts under the ground where terrible things have happened—and are never felt except near places where the big marked stones are scattered. Close to four the gale subsided as suddenly as it had begun
column7: leaving the sand hills in new and unfamiliar shapes.

column1: It was just past five
column2: with the bloated
column3: fungoid moon sinking in the west
column4: when I staggered into camp—hatless
column5: tattered
column6: features scratched and ensanguined
column7: and without my electric torch. Most of the men had returned to bed
column8: but Prof. Dyer was smoking a pipe in front of his tent. Seeing my winded and almost frenzied state
column9: he called Dr. Boyle
column10: and the two of them got me on my cot and made me comfortable. My son
column11: roused by the stir
column12: soon joined them
column13: and they all tried to force me to lie still and attempt sleep.

column1: But there was no sleep for me. My psychological state was very extraordinary—different from anything I had previously suffered. After a time I insisted upon talking—nervously and elaborately explaining my condition. I told them I had become fatigued
column2: and had lain down in the sand for a nap. There had
column3: I said
column4: been dreams even more frightful than usual—and when I was awaked by the sudden high wind my overwrought nerves had snapped. I had fled in panic
column5: frequently falling over half-buried stones and thus gaining my tattered and bedraggled aspect. I must have slept long—hence the hours of my absence.

column1: Of anything strange either seen or experienced I hinted absolutely nothing—exercising the greatest self-control in that respect. But I spoke of a change of mind regarding the whole work of the expedition
column2: and earnestly urged a halt in all digging toward the northeast. My reasoning was patently weak—for I mentioned a dearth of blocks
column3: a wish not to offend the superstitious miners
column4: a possible shortage of funds from the college
column5: and other things either untrue or irrelevant. Naturally
column6: no one paid the least attention to my new wishes—not even my son
column7: whose concern for my health was very obvious.

column1: The next day I was up and around the camp
column2: but took no part in the excavations. Seeing that I could not stop the work
column3: I decided to return home as soon as possible for the sake of my nerves
column4: and made my son promise to fly me in the plane to Perth—a thousand miles to the southwest—as soon as he had surveyed the region I wished let alone. If
column5: I reflected
column6: the thing I had seen was still visible
column7: I might decide to attempt a specific warning even at the cost of ridicule. It was just conceivable that the miners who knew the local folklore might back me up. Humouring me
column8: my son made the survey that very afternoon; flying over all the terrain my walk could possibly have covered. Yet nothing of what I had found remained in sight. It was the case of the anomalous basalt block all over again—the shifting sand had wiped out every trace. For an instant I half regretted having lost a certain awesome object in my stark fright—but now I know that the loss was merciful. I can still believe my whole experience an illusion—especially if
column9: as I devoutly hope
column10: that hellish abyss is never found.

column1: Wingate took me to Perth July 20
column2: though declining to abandon the expedition and return home. He stayed with me until the 25th
column3: when the steamer for Liverpool sailed. Now
column4: in the cabin of the Empress
column5: I am pondering long and frantically on the entire matter
column6: and have decided that my son at least must be informed. It shall rest with him whether to diffuse the matter more widely. In order to meet any eventuality I have prepared this summary of my background—as already known in a scattered way to others—and will now tell as briefly as possible what seemed to happen during my absence from the camp that hideous night.

column1: Nerves on edge
column2: and whipped into a kind of perverse eagerness by that inexplicable
column3: dread-mingled
column4: pseudo-mnemonic urge toward the northeast
column5: I plodded on beneath the evil
column6: burning moon. Here and there I saw
column7: half-shrouded by the sand
column8: those primal Cyclopean blocks left from nameless and forgotten aeons. The incalculable age and brooding horror of this monstrous waste began to oppress me as never before
column9: and I could not keep from thinking of my maddening dreams
column10: of the frightful legends which lay behind them
column11: and of the present fears of natives and miners concerning the desert and its carven stones.

column1: And yet I plodded on as if to some eldritch rendezvous—more and more assailed by bewildering fancies
column2: compulsions
column3: and pseudo-memories. I thought of some of the possible contours of the lines of stones as seen by my son from the air
column4: and wondered why they seemed at once so ominous and so familiar. Something was fumbling and rattling at the latch of my recollection
column5: while another unknown force sought to keep the portal barred.

column1: The night was windless
column2: and the pallid sand curved upward and downward like frozen waves of the sea. I had no goal
column3: but somehow ploughed along as if with fate-bound assurance. My dreams welled up into the waking world
column4: so that each sand-embedded megalith seemed part of endless rooms and corridors of pre-human masonry
column5: carved and hieroglyphed with symbols that I knew too well from years of custom as a captive mind of the Great Race. At moments I fancied I saw those omniscient conical horrors moving about at their accustomed tasks
column6: and I feared to look down lest I find myself one with them in aspect. Yet all the while I saw the sand-covered blocks as well as the rooms and corridors; the evil
column7: burning moon as well as the lamps of luminous crystal; the endless desert as well as the waving ferns and cycads beyond the windows. I was awake and dreaming at the same time.

column1: I do not know how long or how far—or indeed
column2: in just what direction—I had walked when I first spied the heap of blocks bared by the day’s wind. It was the largest group in one place that I had so far seen
column3: and so sharply did it impress me that the visions of fabulous aeons faded suddenly away. Again there were only the desert and the evil moon and the shards of an unguessed past. I drew close and paused
column4: and cast the added light of my electric torch over the tumbled pile. A hillock had blown away
column5: leaving a low
column6: irregularly round mass of megaliths and smaller fragments some forty feet across and from two to eight feet high.

column1: From the very outset I realised that there was some utterly unprecedented quality about these stones. Not only was the mere number of them quite without parallel
column2: but something in the sand-worn traces of design arrested me as I scanned them under the mingled beams of the moon and my torch. Not that any one differed essentially from the earlier specimens we had found. It was something subtler than that. The impression did not come when I looked at one block alone
column3: but only when I ran my eye over several almost simultaneously. Then
column4: at last
column5: the truth dawned upon me. The curvilinear patterns on many of these blocks were closely related—parts of one vast decorative conception. For the first time in this aeon-shaken waste I had come upon a mass of masonry in its old position—tumbled and fragmentary
column6: it is true
column7: but none the less existing in a very definite sense.

column1: Mounting at a low place
column2: I clambered laboriously over the heap; here and there clearing away the sand with my fingers
column3: and constantly striving to interpret varieties of size
column4: shape
column5: and style
column6: and relationships of design. After a while I could vaguely guess at the nature of the bygone structure
column7: and at the designs which had once stretched over the vast surfaces of the primal masonry. The perfect identity of the whole with some of my dream-glimpses appalled and unnerved me. This was once a Cyclopean corridor thirty feet tall
column8: paved with octagonal blocks and solidly vaulted overhead. There would have been rooms opening off on the right
column9: and at the farther end one of those strange inclined planes would have wound down to still lower depths.

column1: I started violently as these conceptions occurred to me
column2: for there was more in them than the blocks themselves had supplied. How did I know that this level should have been far underground? How did I know that the plane leading upward should have been behind me? How did I know that the long subterrene passage to the Square of Pillars ought to lie on the left one level above me? How did I know that the room of machines
column3: and the rightward-leading tunnel to the central archives
column4: ought to lie two levels below? How did I know that there would be one of those horrible
column5: metal-banded trap-doors at the very bottom
column6: four levels down? Bewildered by this intrusion from the dream-world
column7: I found myself shaking and bathed in a cold perspiration.

column1: Then
column2: as a last
column3: intolerable touch
column4: I felt that faint
column5: insidious stream of cool air trickling upward from a depressed place near the centre of the huge heap. Instantly
column6: as once before
column7: my visions faded
column8: and I saw again only the evil moonlight
column9: the brooding desert
column10: and the spreading tumulus of palaeogean masonry. Something real and tangible
column11: yet fraught with infinite suggestions of nighted mystery
column12: now confronted me. For that stream of air could argue but one thing—a hidden gulf of great size beneath the disordered blocks on the surface.

column1: My first thought was of the sinister blackfellow legends of vast underground huts among the megaliths where horrors happen and great winds are born. Then thoughts of my own dreams came back
column2: and I felt dim pseudo-memories tugging at my mind. What manner of place lay below me? What primal
column3: inconceivable source of age-old myth-cycles and haunting nightmares might I be on the brink of uncovering? It was only for a moment that I hesitated
column4: for more than curiosity and scientific zeal was driving me on and working against my growing fear.

column1: I seemed to move almost automatically
column2: as if in the clutch of some compelling fate. Pocketing my torch
column3: and struggling with a strength that I had not thought I possessed
column4: I wrenched aside first one titan fragment of stone and then another
column5: till there welled up a strong draught whose dampness contrasted oddly with the desert’s dry air. A black rift began to yawn
column6: and at length—when I had pushed away every fragment small enough to budge—the leprous moonlight blazed on an aperture of ample width to admit me.

column1: I drew out my torch and cast a brilliant beam into the opening. Below me was a chaos of tumbled masonry
column2: sloping roughly down toward the north at an angle of about forty-five degrees
column3: and evidently the result of some bygone collapse from above. Between its surface and the ground level was a gulf of impenetrable blackness at whose upper edge were signs of gigantic
column4: stress-heaved vaulting. At this point
column5: it appeared
column6: the desert’s sands lay directly upon a floor of some titan structure of earth’s youth—how preserved through aeons of geologic convulsion I could not then and cannot now even attempt to guess.

column1: In retrospect
column2: the barest idea of a sudden
column3: lone descent into such a doubtful abyss—and at a time when one’s whereabouts were unknown to any living soul—seems like the utter apex of insanity. Perhaps it was—yet that night I embarked without hesitancy upon such a descent. Again there was manifest that lure and driving of fatality which had all along seemed to direct my course. With torch flashing intermittently to save the battery
column4: I commenced a mad scramble down the sinister
column5: Cyclopean incline below the opening—sometimes facing forward as I found good hand and foot holds
column6: and at other times turning to face the heap of megaliths as I clung and fumbled more precariously. In two directions beside me
column7: distant walls of carven
column8: crumbling masonry loomed dimly under the direct beams of my torch. Ahead
column9: however
column10: was only unbroken blackness.

column1: I kept no track of time during my downward scramble. So seething with baffling hints and images was my mind
column2: that all objective matters seemed withdrawn into incalculable distances. Physical sensation was dead
column3: and even fear remained as a wraith-like
column4: inactive gargoyle leering impotently at me. Eventually I reached a level floor strown with fallen blocks
column5: shapeless fragments of stone
column6: and sand and detritus of every kind. On either side—perhaps thirty feet apart—rose massive walls culminating in huge groinings. That they were carved I could just discern
column7: but the nature of the carvings was beyond my perception. What held me the most was the vaulting overhead. The beam from my torch could not reach the roof
column8: but the lower parts of the monstrous arches stood out distinctly. And so perfect was their identity with what I had seen in countless dreams of the elder world
column9: that I trembled actively for the first time.

column1: Behind and high above
column2: a faint luminous blur told of the distant moonlit world outside. Some vague shred of caution warned me that I should not let it out of my sight
column3: lest I have no guide for my return. I now advanced toward the wall on my left
column4: where the traces of carving were plainest. The littered floor was nearly as hard to traverse as the downward heap had been
column5: but I managed to pick my difficult way. At one place I heaved aside some blocks and kicked away the detritus to see what the pavement was like
column6: and shuddered at the utter
column7: fateful familiarity of the great octagonal stones whose buckled surface still held roughly together.

column1: Reaching a convenient distance from the wall
column2: I cast the torchlight slowly and carefully over its worn remnants of carving. Some bygone influx of water seemed to have acted on the sandstone surface
column3: while there were curious incrustations which I could not explain. In places the masonry was very loose and distorted
column4: and I wondered how many aeons more this primal
column5: hidden edifice could keep its remaining traces of form amidst earth’s heavings.

column1: But it was the carvings themselves that excited me most. Despite their time-crumbled state
column2: they were relatively easy to trace at close range; and the complete
column3: intimate familiarity of every detail almost stunned my imagination. That the major attributes of this hoary masonry should be familiar
column4: was not beyond normal credibility. Powerfully impressing the weavers of certain myths
column5: they had become embodied in a stream of cryptic lore which
column6: somehow coming to my notice during the amnesic period
column7: had evoked vivid images in my subconscious mind. But how could I explain the exact and minute fashion in which each line and spiral of these strange designs tallied with what I had dreamt for more than a score of years? What obscure
column8: forgotten iconography could have reproduced each subtle shading and nuance which so persistently
column9: exactly
column10: and unvaryingly besieged my sleeping vision night after night?

column1: For this was no chance or remote resemblance. Definitely and absolutely
column2: the millennially ancient
column3: aeon-hidden corridor in which I stood was the original of something I knew in sleep as intimately as I knew my own house in Crane Street
column4: Arkham. True
column5: my dreams shewed the place in its undecayed prime; but the identity was no less real on that account. I was wholly and horribly oriented. The particular structure I was in was known to me. Known

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.

column4: though not without hope of making up lost ground before the end of the term. It was in March when the fresh element entered his lighter preliminary dreaming
column5: and the nightmare shape of Brown Jenkin began to be companioned by the nebulous blur which grew more and more to resemble a bent old woman. This addition disturbed him more than he could account for
column6: but finally he decided that it was like an ancient crone whom he had twice actually encountered in the dark tangle of lanes near the abandoned wharves. On those occasions the evil
column7: sardonic
column8: and seemingly unmotivated stare of the beldame had set him almost shivering—especially the first time
column9: when an overgrown rat darting across the shadowed mouth of a neighbouring alley had made him think irrationally of Brown Jenkin. Now
column10: he reflected
column11: those nervous fears were being mirrored in his disordered dreams.

column1: That the influence of the old house was unwholesome
column2: he could not deny; but traces of his early morbid interest still held him there. He argued that the fever alone was responsible for his nightly phantasies
column3: and that when the touch abated he would be free from the monstrous visions. Those visions
column4: however
column5: were of abhorrent vividness and convincingness
column6: and whenever he awaked he retained a vague sense of having undergone much more than he remembered. He was hideously sure that in unrecalled dreams he had talked with both Brown Jenkin and the old woman
column7: and that they had been urging him to go somewhere with them and to meet a third being of greater potency.

column1: Toward the end of March he began to pick up in his mathematics
column2: though other studies bothered him increasingly. He was getting an intuitive knack for solving Riemannian equations
column3: and astonished Professor Upham by his comprehension of fourth-dimensional and other problems which had floored all the rest of the class. One afternoon there was a discussion of possible freakish curvatures in space
column4: and of theoretical points of approach or even contact between our part of the cosmos and various other regions as distant as the farthest stars or the trans-galactic gulfs themselves—or even as fabulously remote as the tentatively conceivable cosmic units beyond the whole Einsteinian space-time continuum. Gilman’s handling of this theme filled everyone with admiration
column5: even though some of his hypothetical illustrations caused an increase in the always plentiful gossip about his nervous and solitary eccentricity. What made the students shake their heads was his sober theory that a man might—given mathematical knowledge admittedly beyond all likelihood of human acquirement—step deliberately from the earth to any other celestial body which might lie at one of an infinity of specific points in the cosmic pattern.

column1: Such a step
column2: he said
column3: would require only two stages; first
column4: a passage out of the three-dimensional sphere we know
column5: and second
column6: a passage back to the three-dimensional sphere at another point
column7: perhaps one of infinite remoteness. That this could be accomplished without loss of life was in many cases conceivable. Any being from any part of three-dimensional space could probably survive in the fourth dimension; and its survival of the second stage would depend upon what alien part of three-dimensional space it might select for its re-entry. Denizens of some planets might be able to live on certain others—even planets belonging to other galaxies
column8: or to similar-dimensional phases of other space-time continua—though of course there must be vast numbers of mutually uninhabitable even though mathematically juxtaposed bodies or zones of space.

column1: It was also possible that the inhabitants of a given dimensional realm could survive entry to many unknown and incomprehensible realms of additional or indefinitely multiplied dimensions—be they within or outside the given space-time continuum—and that the converse would be likewise true. This was a matter for speculation
column2: though one could be fairly certain that the type of mutation involved in a passage from any given dimensional plane to the next higher plane would not be destructive of biological integrity as we understand it. Gilman could not be very clear about his reasons for this last assumption
column3: but his haziness here was more than overbalanced by his clearness on other complex points. Professor Upham especially liked his demonstration of the kinship of higher mathematics to certain phases of magical lore transmitted down the ages from an ineffable antiquity—human or pre-human—whose knowledge of the cosmos and its laws was greater than ours.

column1: Around the first of April Gilman worried considerably because his slow fever did not abate. He was also troubled by what some of his fellow-lodgers said about his sleep-walking. It seemed that he was often absent from his bed
column2: and that the creaking of his floor at certain hours of the night was remarked by the man in the room below. This fellow also spoke of hearing the tread of shod feet in the night; but Gilman was sure he must have been mistaken in this
column3: since shoes as well as other apparel were always precisely in place in the morning. One could develop all sorts of aural delusions in this morbid old house—for did not Gilman himself
column4: even in daylight
column5: now feel certain that noises other than rat-scratchings came from the black voids beyond the slanting wall and above the slanting ceiling? His pathologically sensitive ears began to listen for faint footfalls in the immemorially sealed loft overhead
column6: and sometimes the illusion of such things was agonisingly realistic.

column1: However

column3: though with all his clothing in place. Of this he had been assured by Frank Elwood
column4: the one fellow-student whose poverty forced him to room in this squalid and unpopular house. Elwood had been studying in the small hours and had come up for help on a differential equation
column5: only to find Gilman absent. It had been rather presumptuous of him to open the unlocked door after knocking had failed to rouse a response

column7: though
column8: had Gilman been there—and when told of the matter he wondered where he could have been wandering

column1: As April advanced Gilman’s fever-sharpened ears were disturbed by the whining prayers of a superstitious loomfixer named Joe Mazurewicz
column2: who had a room on the ground floor. Mazurewicz had told long
column3: rambling stories about the ghost of old Keziah and the furry
column4: sharp-fanged
column5: nuzzling thing

column7: when hell’s blackest evil roamed the earth and all the slaves of Satan gathered for nameless rites and deeds. It was always a very bad time in Arkham
column8: even though the fine folks up in Miskatonic Avenue and High and Saltonstall Streets pretended to know nothing about it. There would be bad doings—and a child or two would probably be missing. Joe knew about such things
column9: for his grandmother in the old country had heard tales from her grandmother. It was wise to pray and count one’s beads at this season. For three months Keziah and Brown Jenkin had not been near Joe’s room
column10: nor near Paul Choynski’s room
column11: nor anywhere else—and it meant no good when they held off like that. They must be up to something.

column1: Gilman dropped in at a doctor’s office on the 16th of the month
column2: and was surprised to find his temperature was not as high as he had feared. The physician questioned him sharply
column3: and advised him to see a nerve specialist. On reflection
column4: he was glad he had not consulted the still more inquisitive college doctor. Old Waldron
column5: who had curtailed his activities before
column6: would have made him take a rest—an impossible thing now that he was so close to great results in his equations. He was certainly near the boundary between the known universe and the fourth dimension
column7: and who could say how much farther he might go?

column1: But even as these thoughts came to him he wondered at the source of his strange confidence. Did all of this perilous sense of imminence come from the formulae on the sheets he covered day by day? The soft
column2: stealthy
column3: imaginary footsteps in the sealed loft above were unnerving. And now
column4: too
column5: there was a growing feeling that somebody was constantly persuading him to do something terrible which he could not do. How about the somnambulism? Where did he go sometimes in the night? And what was that faint suggestion of sound which once in a while seemed to trickle through the maddening confusion of identifiable sounds even in broad daylight and full wakefulness? Its rhythm did not correspond to anything on earth
column6: unless perhaps to the cadence of one or two unmentionable Sabbat-chants
column7: and sometimes he feared it corresponded to certain attributes of the vague shrieking or roaring in those wholly alien abysses of dream.

column1: The dreams were meanwhile getting to be atrocious. In the lighter preliminary phase the evil old woman was now of fiendish distinctness
column2: and Gilman knew she was the one who had frightened him in the slums. Her bent back
column3: long nose
column4: and shrivelled chin were unmistakable
column5: and her shapeless brown garments were like those he remembered. The expression on her face was one of hideous malevolence and exultation
column6: and when he awaked he could recall a croaking voice that persuaded and threatened. He must meet the Black Man
column7: and go with them all to the throne of Azathoth at the centre of ultimate Chaos. That was what she said. He must sign in his own blood the book of Azathoth and take a new secret name now that his independent delvings had gone so far. What kept him from going with her and Brown Jenkin and the other to the throne of Chaos where the thin flutes pipe mindlessly was the fact that he had seen the name “Azathoth” in the Necronomicon
column8: and knew it stood for a primal evil too horrible for description.

column1: The old woman always appeared out of thin air near the corner where the downward slant met the inward slant. She seemed to crystallise at a point closer to the ceiling than to the floor
column2: and every night she was a little nearer and more distinct before the dream shifted. Brown Jenkin
column3: too
column4: was always a little nearer at the last
column5: and its yellowish-white fangs glistened shockingly in that unearthly violet phosphorescence. Its shrill loathsome tittering stuck more and more in Gilman’s head
column6: and he could remember in the morning how it had pronounced the words “Azathoth” and “Nyarlathotep”.

column1: In the deeper dreams everything was likewise more distinct
column2: and Gilman felt that the twilight abysses around him were those of the fourth dimension. Those organic entities whose motions seemed least flagrantly irrelevant and unmotivated were probably projections of life-forms from our own planet
column3: including human beings. What the others were in their own dimensional sphere or spheres he dared not try to think. Two of the less irrelevantly moving things—a rather large congeries of iridescent
column4: prolately spheroidal bubbles and a very much smaller polyhedron of unknown colours and rapidly shifting surface angles—seemed to take notice of him and follow him about or float ahead as he changed position among the titan prisms
column5: labyrinths
column6: cube-and-plane clusters
column7: and quasi-buildings; and all the while the vague shrieking and roaring waxed louder and louder
column8: as if approaching some monstrous climax of utterly unendurable intensity.

column1: During the night of April 19–20 the new development occurred. Gilman was half-involuntarily moving about in the twilight abysses with the bubble-mass and the small polyhedron floating ahead
column2: when he noticed the peculiarly regular angles formed by the edges of some gigantic neighbouring prism-clusters. In another second he was out of the abyss and standing tremulously on a rocky hillside bathed in intense
column3: diffused green light. He was barefooted and in his night-clothes
column4: and when he tried to walk discovered that he could scarcely lift his feet. A swirling vapour hid everything but the immediate sloping terrain from sight
column5: and he shrank from the thought of the sounds that might surge out of that vapour.

column1: Then he saw the two shapes laboriously crawling toward him—the old woman and the little furry thing. The crone strained up to her knees and managed to cross her arms in a singular fashion
column2: while Brown Jenkin pointed in a certain direction with a horribly anthropoid fore paw which it raised with evident difficulty. Spurred by an impulse he did not originate
column3: Gilman dragged himself forward along a course determined by the angle of the old woman’s arms and the direction of the small monstrosity’s paw
column4: and before he had shuffled three steps he was back in the twilight abysses. Geometrical shapes seethed around him
column5: and he fell dizzily and interminably. At last he woke in his bed in the crazily angled garret of the eldritch old house.

column1: He was good for nothing that morning
column2: and stayed away from all his classes. Some unknown attraction was pulling his eyes in a seemingly irrelevant direction
column3: for he could not help staring at a certain vacant spot on the floor. As the day advanced the focus of his unseeing eyes changed position
column4: and by noon he had conquered the impulse to stare at vacancy. About two o’clock he went out for lunch
column5: and as he threaded the narrow lanes of the city he found himself turning always to the southeast. Only an effort halted him at a cafeteria in Church Street
column6: and after the meal he felt the unknown pull still more strongly.

column1: He would have to consult a nerve specialist after all—perhaps there was a connexion with his somnambulism—but meanwhile he might at least try to break the morbid spell himself. Undoubtedly he could still manage to walk away from the pull; so with great resolution he headed against it and dragged himself deliberately north along Garrison Street. By the time he had reached the bridge over the Miskatonic he was in a cold perspiration
column2: and he clutched at the iron railing as he gazed upstream at the ill-regarded island whose regular lines of ancient standing stones brooded sullenly in the afternoon sunlight.

column1: Then he gave a start. For there was a clearly visible living figure on that desolate island
column2: and a second glance told him it was certainly the strange old woman whose sinister aspect had worked itself so disastrously into his dreams. The tall grass near her was moving
column3: too
column4: as if some other living thing were crawling close to the ground. When the old woman began to turn toward him he fled precipitately off the bridge and into the shelter of the town’s labyrinthine waterfront alleys. Distant though the island was
column5: he felt that a monstrous and invincible evil could flow from the sardonic stare of that bent
column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held
column2: and only with tremendous resolution could Gilman drag himself into the old house and up the rickety stairs. For hours he sat silent and aimless
column3: with his eyes shifting gradually westward. About six o’clock his sharpened ears caught the whining prayers of Joe Mazurewicz two floors below
column4: and in desperation he seized his hat and walked out into the sunset-golden streets
column5: letting the now directly southward pull carry him where it might. An hour later darkness found him in the open fields beyond Hangman’s Brook
column6: with the glimmering spring stars shining ahead. The urge to walk was gradually changing to an urge to leap mystically into space
column7: and suddenly he realised just where the source of the pull lay.

column1: It was in the sky. A definite point among the stars had a claim on him and was calling him. Apparently it was a point somewhere between Hydra and Argo Navis
column2: and he knew that he had been urged toward it ever since he had awaked soon after dawn. In the morning it had been underfoot; afternoon found it rising in the southeast
column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door
column2: and seemed both anxious and reluctant to whisper some fresh bit of superstition. It was about the witch light. Joe had been out celebrating the night before—it was Patriots’ Day in Massachusetts—and had come home after midnight. Looking up at the house from outside
column3: he had thought at first that Gilman’s window was dark; but then he had seen the faint violet glow within. He wanted to warn the gentleman about that glow
column4: for everybody in Arkham knew it was Keziah’s witch light which played near Brown Jenkin and the ghost of the old crone herself. He had not mentioned this before
column5: but now he must tell about it because it meant that Keziah and her long-toothed familiar were haunting the young gentleman. Sometimes he and Paul Choynski and Landlord Dombrowski thought they saw that light seeping out of cracks in the sealed loft above the young gentleman’s room
column6: but they had all agreed not to talk about that. However
column7: it would be better for the gentleman to take another room and get a crucifix from some good priest like Father Iwanicki.

column1: As the man rambled on Gilman felt a nameless panic clutch at his throat. He knew that Joe must have been half drunk when he came home the night before
column2: yet this mention of a violet light in the garret window was of frightful import. It was a lambent glow of this sort which always played about the old woman and the small furry thing in those lighter
column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses
column4: and the thought that a wakeful second person could see the dream-luminance was utterly beyond sane harbourage. Yet where had the fellow got such an odd notion? Had he himself talked as well as walked around the house in his sleep? No
column5: Joe said
column6: he had not—but he must check up on this. Perhaps Frank Elwood could tell him something
column7: though he hated to ask.

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column2: see a nerve specialist
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest
column4: but he also found himself listening intently for some sound in the closed loft above
column5: and half imagining that an evil violet light seeped down through an infinitesimal crack in the low
column6: slanting ceiling.

column1: That night as Gilman slept the violet light broke upon him with heightened intensity
column2: and the old witch and small furry thing—getting closer than ever before—mocked him with inhuman squeals and devilish gestures. He was glad to sink into the vaguely roaring twilight abysses
column3: though the pursuit of that iridescent bubble-congeries and that kaleidoscopic little polyhedron was menacing and irritating. Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles
column8: and numberless forms of still greater wildness—some of stone and some of metal—which glittered gorgeously in the mixed
column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame
column10: each of a different hue
column11: and at a different height above an infinitely distant curving horizon of low mountains. Behind him tiers of higher terraces towered aloft as far as he could see. The city below stretched away to the limits of vision
column12: and he hoped that no sound would well up from it.

column1: The pavement from which he easily raised himself was of a veined
column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify
column3: and the tiles were cut in bizarre-angled shapes which struck him as less asymmetrical than based on some unearthly symmetry whose laws he could not comprehend. The balustrade was chest-high
column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought
column6: while along the rail were ranged at short intervals little figures of grotesque design and exquisite workmanship. They
column7: like the whole balustrade
column8: seemed to be made of some sort of shining metal whose colour could not be guessed in this chaos of mixed effulgences; and their nature utterly defied conjecture. They represented some ridged
column9: barrel-shaped object with thin horizontal arms radiating spoke-like from a central ring
column10: and with vertical knobs or bulbs projecting from the head and base of the barrel. Each of these knobs was the hub of a system of five long
column11: flat
column12: triangularly tapering arms arranged around it like the arms of a starfish—nearly horizontal
column13: but curving slightly away from the central barrel. The base of the bottom knob was fused to the long railing with so delicate a point of contact that several figures had been broken off and were missing. The figures were about four and a half inches in height
column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column1: When Gilman stood up the tiles felt hot to his bare feet. He was wholly alone
column2: and his first act was to walk to the balustrade and look dizzily down at the endless
column3: Cyclopean city almost two thousand feet below. As he listened he thought a rhythmic confusion of faint musical pipings covering a wide tonal range welled up from the narrow streets beneath
column4: and he wished he might discern the denizens of the place. The sight turned him giddy after a while
column5: so that he would have fallen to the pavement had he not clutched instinctively at the lustrous balustrade. His right hand fell on one of the projecting figures
column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed
column10: he continued to clutch it as his other hand seized a vacant space on the smooth railing.

column1: But now his oversensitive ears caught something behind him
column2: and he looked back across the level terrace. Approaching him softly though without apparent furtiveness were five figures
column3: two of which were the sinister old woman and the fanged
column4: furry little animal. The other three were what sent him unconscious—for they were living entities about eight feet high
column5: shaped precisely like the spiky images on the balustrade
column6: and propelling themselves by a spider-like wriggling of their lower set of starfish-arms.

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed
column2: drenched by a cold perspiration and with a smarting sensation in his face
column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste
column6: as if it were necessary for him to get out of the house as quickly as possible. He did not know where he wished to go
column7: but felt that once more he would have to sacrifice his classes. The odd pull toward that spot in the sky between Hydra and Argo had abated
column8: but another of even greater strength had taken its place. Now he felt that he must go north—infinitely north. He dreaded to cross the bridge that gave a view of the desolate island in the Miskatonic
column9: so went over the Peabody Avenue bridge. Very often he stumbled
column10: for his eyes and ears were chained to an extremely lofty point in the blank blue sky.

column1: After about an hour he got himself under better control
column2: and saw that he was far from the city. All around him stretched the bleak emptiness of salt marshes
column3: while the narrow road ahead led to Innsmouth—that ancient
column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished
column5: he resisted it as he had resisted the other pull
column6: and finally found that he could almost balance the one against the other. Plodding back to town and getting some coffee at a soda fountain
column7: he dragged himself into the public library and browsed aimlessly among the lighter magazines. Once he met some friends who remarked how oddly sunburned he looked
column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant
column9: noting meanwhile that the pull had either lessened or divided itself. After that he killed the time at a cheap cinema show
column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green
column10: and Gilman could see amidst his horror and bewilderment that one of the knobs ended in a jagged break corresponding to its former point of attachment to the dream-railing.

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged
column2: furry thing came again and with a greater distinctness than on any former occasion. This time they actually reached him
column3: and he felt the crone’s withered claws clutching at him. He was pulled out of bed and into empty space
column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief
column5: for presently he was in a crude
column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration
column8: and in the centre were a table and bench
column9: both apparently fastened in place. Small objects of unknown shape and nature were ranged on the tops of the cases
column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling
column13: there presently climbed the hateful little furry thing with the yellow fangs and bearded human face.

column1: The evilly grinning beldame still clutched him
column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod
column6: since there was a clicking whenever he changed position. The man did not speak
column7: and bore no trace of expression on his small
column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table
column9: while the beldame thrust a huge grey quill into Gilman’s right hand. Over everything was a pall of intensely maddening fear
column10: and the climax was reached when the furry thing ran up the dreamer’s clothing to his shoulders and then down his left arm
column11: finally biting him sharply in the wrist just below his cuff. As the blood spurted from this wound Gilman lapsed into a faint.

column1: He awaked on the morning of the 22nd with a pain in his left wrist
column2: and saw that his cuff was brown with dried blood. His recollections were very confused
column3: but the scene with the black man in the unknown space stood out vividly. The rats must have bitten him as he slept
column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door
column5: he saw that the flour on the corridor floor was undisturbed except for the huge prints of the loutish fellow who roomed at the other end of the garret. So he had not been sleep-walking this time. But something would have to be done about those rats. He would speak to the landlord about them. Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall
column6: wedging in a candlestick which seemed of about the right size. His ears were ringing horribly
column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column1: As he bathed and changed clothes he tried to recall what he had dreamed after the scene in the violet-litten space
column2: but nothing definite would crystallise in his mind. That scene itself must have corresponded to the sealed loft overhead
column3: which had begun to attack his imagination so violently

column5: and what had been near her rattling the tin can in a rubbish-heap at the mouth of a squalid courtyard. The crone had seemed to notice him and leer evilly at him—though perhaps this was merely his imagination.

column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column6: and by entering and remaining in such a belt one might preserve one’s life and age indefinitely; never suffering organic metabolism or deterioration except for slight amounts incurred during visits to one’s own or similar planes. One might

column4: the hideous crone seized Gilman by the shoulders
column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him
column6: but in another second he thought he was in a dark
column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours
column9: with the rotting walls of ancient houses towering up on every hand.

column1: Ahead was the robed black man he had seen in the peaked space in the other dream

column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry

column1: On the morning of the 29th Gilman awaked into a maelstrom of horror. The instant he opened his eyes he knew something was terribly wrong

column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them
column7: the more peculiar they seemed; for in addition to those he could recognise as his there were some smaller
column8: almost round markings—such as the legs of a large chair or table might make

Utter bewilderment and the fear of madness racked Gilman as he staggered to the door and saw that there were no muddy prints outside. The more he remembered of his hideous dream the more terrified he felt

column7: livid marks on his throat

column12: he added

column3: they said
column4: been a huge robed negro
