Had he actually slipped outside our sphere to points unguessed and unimaginable? Where—if anywhere—had he been on those nights of daemoniac alienage? The roaring twilight abysses—the green hillside—the blistering terrace—the pulls from the stars—the ultimate black vortex—the black man—the muddy alley and the stairs—the old witch and the fanged

column4: dreaded murmur beyond the noises in the ancient house. Unwholesome recollections of things in the Necronomicon and the Black Book welled up
column5: and he found himself swaying to infandous rhythms said to pertain to the blackest ceremonies of the Sabbat and to have an origin outside the time and space we comprehend.

column3: however
column4: closed his throat. He was not his own master. Had he signed the black man’s book after all?

column2: abnormal hearing caught the distant

column5: and the dancers must be starting in. How could he keep himself from going? What was it that had enmeshed him? column3: kaleidoscopic polyhedron

column3: the low cases of ancient books
column4: the bench and table
column5: the queer objects
column6: and the triangular gulf at one side. On the table lay a small white figure—an infant boy

column4: while the wrinkled face was twisted with insane fury. He felt the chain of the cheap crucifix grinding into his neck

column6: but as she continued her choking he reached feebly in his shirt and drew out the metal symbol

column3: as he turned away

column5: tough of sinew and with four tiny hands of daemoniac dexterity
column6: had been busy while the witch was throttling him

column1: In his dream-delirium Gilman heard the hellish
column2: alien-rhythmed chant of the Sabbat coming from an infinite distance
column3: and knew the black man must be there. Confused memories mixed themselves with his mathematics

column5: but whether he could ever escape through the slanting floor or the long-stopped egress he doubted greatly. Besides
column6: would not an escape from a dream-loft bring him merely into a dream-house—an abnormal projection of the actual place he sought? He was wholly bewildered as to the relation betwixt dream and reality in all his experiences.

column1: The passage through the vague abysses would be frightful
column2: for the Walpurgis-rhythm would be vibrating
column3: and at last he would have to hear that hitherto veiled cosmic pulsing which he so mortally dreaded. Even now he could detect a low
column4: monstrous shaking whose tempo he suspected all too well. At Sabbat-time it always mounted and reached through to the worlds to summon the initiate to nameless rites. Half the chants of the Sabbat were patterned on this faintly overheard pulsing which no earthly ear could endure in its unveiled spatial fulness. Gilman wondered
column5: too
column6: whether he could trust his instinct to take him back to the right part of space. How could he be sure he would not land on that green-litten hillside of a far planet
column7: on the tessellated terrace above the city of tentacled monsters somewhere beyond the galaxy
column8: or in the spiral black vortices of that ultimate void of Chaos wherein reigns the mindless daemon-sultan Azathoth?

column1: Just before he made the plunge the violet light went out and left him in utter blackness. The witch—old Keziah—Nahab—that must have meant her death. And mixed with the distant chant of the Sabbat and the whimpers of Brown Jenkin in the gulf below he thought he heard another and wilder whine from unknown depths. Joe Mazurewicz—the prayers against the Crawling Chaos now turning to an inexplicably triumphant shriek—worlds of sardonic actuality impinging on vortices of febrile dream—Iä! Shub-Niggurath! The Goat with a Thousand Young. . . .
They found Gilman on the floor of his queerly angled old garret room long before dawn
column2: for the terrible cry had brought Desrochers and Choynski and Dombrowski and Mazurewicz at once
column3: and had even wakened the soundly sleeping Elwood in his chair. He was alive
column4: and with open
column5: staring eyes

column7: and on his left ankle was a distressing rat-bite. His clothing was badly rumpled
column8: and Joe’s crucifix was missing. Elwood trembled
column9: afraid even to speculate on what new form his friend’s sleep-walking had taken. Mazurewicz seemed half-dazed because of a “sign” he said he had had in response to his prayers

column1: When the dreamer was settled on his couch in Elwood’s room they sent for Dr. Malkowski—a local practitioner who would repeat no tales where they might prove embarrassing—and he gave Gilman two hypodermic injections which caused him to relax in something like natural drowsiness. During the day the patient regained consciousness at times and whispered his newest dream disjointedly to Elwood. It was a painful process
column2: and at its very start brought out a fresh and disconcerting fact.

column1: Gilman—whose ears had so lately possessed an abnormal sensitiveness—was now stone deaf. Dr. Malkowski
column2: summoned again in haste
column3: told Elwood that both ear-drums were ruptured
column4: as if by the impact of some stupendous sound intense beyond all human conception or endurance. How such a sound could have been heard in the last few hours without arousing all the Miskatonic Valley was more than the honest physician could say.

column1: Elwood wrote his part of the colloquy on paper
column2: so that a fairly easy communication was maintained. Neither knew what to make of the whole chaotic business
column3: and decided it would be better if they thought as little as possible about it. Both
column4: though
column5: agreed that they must leave this ancient and accursed house as soon as it could be arranged. Evening papers spoke of a police raid on some curious revellers in a ravine beyond Meadow Hill just before dawn

column10: but one or two in each street shewing signs of occupancy. In Washington Street there was a row of four or five in excellent repair and with finely-tended lawns and gardens. The most sumptuous of these--with wide terraced parterres extending back the whole way to Lafayette Street--I took to be the home of Old Man Marsh
column11: the afflicted refinery owner.

column1: In all these streets no living thing was visible
column2: and I wondered at the complete absence of cats and dogs from Innsmouth. Another thing which puzzled and disturbed me
column3: even in some of the best-preserved mansions
column4: was the tightly shuttered condition of many third-story and attic windows. Furtiveness and secretiveness seemed universal in this hushed city of alienage and death
column5: and I could not escape the sensation of being watched from ambush on every hand by sly
column6: staring eyes that never shut.

column1: I shivered as the cracked stroke of three sounded from a belfry on my left. Too well did I recall the squat church from which those notes came. Following Washington Street toward the river
column2: I now faced a new zone of former industry and commerce; noting the ruins of a factory ahead
column3: and seeing others
column4: with the traces of an old railway station and covered railway bridge beyond
column5: up the gorge on my right.

column1: The uncertain bridge now before me was posted with a warning sign
column2: but I took the risk and crossed again to the south bank where traces of life reappeared. Furtive
column3: shambling creatures stared cryptically in my direction
column4: and more normal faces eyed me coldly and curiously. Innsmouth was rapidly becoming intolerable
column5: and I turned down Paine Street toward the Square in the hope of getting some vehicle to take me to Arkham before the still-distant starting-time of that sinister bus.

column1: It was then that I saw the tumbledown fire station on my left
column2: and noticed the red faced
column3: bushy-bearded
column4: watery eyed old man in nondescript rags who sat on a bench in front of it talking with a pair of unkempt but not abnormal looking firemen. This
column5: of course
column6: must be Zadok Allen
column7: the half-crazed
column8: liquorish nonagenarian whose tales of old Innsmouth and its shadow were so hideous and incredible.

column1: \﻿West of Arkham the hills rise wild
column2: and there are valleys with deep woods that no axe has ever cut. There are dark narrow glens where the trees slope fantastically
column3: and where thin brooklets trickle without ever having caught the glint of sunlight. On the gentle slopes there are farms
column4: ancient and rocky
column5: with squat
column6: moss-coated cottages brooding eternally over old New England secrets in the lee of great ledges; but these are all vacant now
column7: the wide chimneys crumbling and the shingled sides bulging perilously beneath low gambrel roofs.

column1: The old folk have gone away
column2: and foreigners do not like to live there. French-Canadians have tried it
column3: Italians have tried it
column4: and the Poles have come and departed. It is not because of anything that can be seen or heard or handled
column5: but because of something that is imagined. The place is not good for imagination
column6: and does not bring restful dreams at night. It must be this which keeps the foreigners away
column7: for old Ammi Pierce has never told them of anything he recalls from the strange days. Ammi
column8: whose head has been a little queer for years
column9: is the only one who still remains
column10: or who ever talks of the strange days; and he dares to do this because his house is so near the open fields and the travelled roads around Arkham.

column1: There was once a road over the hills and through the valleys
column2: that ran straight where the blasted heath is now; but people ceased to use it and a new road was laid curving far toward the south. Traces of the old one can still be found amidst the weeds of a returning wilderness
column3: and some of them will doubtless linger even when half the hollows are flooded for the new reservoir. Then the dark woods will be cut down and the blasted heath will slumber far below blue waters whose surface will mirror the sky and ripple in the sun. And the secrets of the strange days will be one with the deep's secrets; one with the hidden lore of old ocean
column4: and all the mystery of primal earth.

column1: When I went into the hills and vales to survey for the new reservoir they told me the place was evil. They told me this in Arkham
column2: and because that is a very old town full of witch legends I thought the evil must be something which grandams had whispered to children through centuries. The name ""blasted heath"" seemed to me very odd and theatrical
column3: and I wondered how it had come into the folklore of a Puritan people. Then I saw that dark westward tangle of glens and slopes for myself
column4: and ceased to wonder at anything beside its own elder mystery. It was morning when I saw it
column5: but shadow lurked always there. The trees grew too thickly
column6: and their trunks were too big for any healthy New England wood. There was too much silence in the dim alleys between them
column7: and the floor was too soft with the dank moss and mattings of infinite years of decay.

column1: In the open spaces
column2: mostly along the line of the old road
column3: there were little hillside farms; sometimes with all the buildings standing
column4: sometimes with only one or two
column5: and sometimes with only a lone chimney or fast-filling cellar. Weeds and briers reigned
column6: and furtive wild things rustled in the undergrowth. Upon everything was a haze of restlessness and oppression; a touch of the unreal and the grotesque
column7: as if some vital element of perspective or chiaroscuro were awry. I did not wonder that the foreigners would not stay
column8: for this was no region to sleep in. It was too much like a landscape of Salvator Rosa; too much like some forbidden woodcut in a tale of terror.

column1: But even all this was not so bad as the blasted heath. I knew it the moment I came upon it at the bottom of a spacious valley; for no other name could fit such a thing
column2: or any other thing fit such a name. It was as if the poet had coined the phrase from having seen this one particular region. It must
column3: I thought as I viewed it
column4: be the outcome of a fire; but why had nothing new ever grown over these five acres of grey desolation that sprawled open to the sky like a great spot eaten by acid in the woods and fields? It lay largely to the north of the ancient road line
column5: but encroached a little on the other side. I felt an odd reluctance about approaching
column6: and did so at last only because my business took me through and past it. There was no vegetation of any kind on that broad expanse
column7: but only a fine grey dust or ash which no wind seemed ever to blow about. The trees near it were sickly and stunted
column8: and many dead trunks stood or lay rotting at the rim. As I walked hurriedly by I saw the tumbled bricks and stones of an old chimney and cellar on my right
column9: and the yawning black maw of an abandoned well whose stagnant vapours played strange tricks with the hues of the sunlight. Even the long
column10: dark woodland climb beyond seemed welcome in contrast
column11: and I marvelled no more at the frightened whispers of Arkham people. There had been no house or ruin near; even in the old days the place must have been lonely and remote. And at twilight
column12: dreading to repass that ominous spot
column13: I walked circuitously back to the town by the curious road on the south. I vaguely wished some clouds would gather
column14: for an odd timidity about the deep skyey voids above had crept into my soul.

column1: In the evening I asked old people in Arkham about the blasted heath
column2: and what was meant by that phrase ""strange days"" which so many evasively muttered. I could not
column3: however
column4: get any good answers except that all the mystery was much more recent than I had dreamed. It was not a matter of old legendry at all
column5: but something within the lifetime of those who spoke. It had happened in the 'eighties
column6: and a family had disappeared or was killed. Speakers would not be exact; and because they all told me to pay no attention to old Ammi Pierce's crazy tales
column7: I sought him out the next morning
column8: having heard that he lived alone in the ancient tottering cottage where the trees first begin to get very thick. It was a fearsomely ancient place
column9: and had begun to exude the faint miasmal odour which clings about houses that have stood too long. Only with persistent knocking could I rouse the aged man
column10: and when he shuffled timidly to the door I could tell he was not glad to see me. He was not so feeble as I had expected; but his eyes drooped in a curious way
column11: and his unkempt clothing and white beard made him seem very worn and dismal.

column1: Not knowing just how he could best be launched on his tales
column2: I feigned a matter of business; told him of my surveying
column3: and asked vague questions about the district. He was far brighter and more educated than I had been led to think
column4: and before I knew it had grasped quite as much of the subject as any man I had talked with in Arkham. He was not like other rustics I had known in the sections where reservoirs were to be. From him there were no protests at the miles of old wood and farmland to be blotted out
column5: though perhaps there would have been had not his home lain outside the bounds of the future lake. Relief was all that he showed; relief at the doom of the dark ancient valleys through which he had roamed all his life. They were better under water now--better under water since the strange days. And with this opening his husky voice sank low
column6: while his body leaned forward and his right forefinger began to point shakily and impressively.

column1: It was then that I heard the story
column2: and as the rambling voice scraped and whispered on I shivered again and again spite the summer day. Often I had to recall the speaker from ramblings
column3: piece out scientific points which he knew only by a fading parrot memory of professors' talk
column4: or bridge over gaps
column5: where his sense of logic and continuity broke down. When he was done I did not wonder that his mind had snapped a trifle
column6: or that the folk of Arkham would not speak much of the blasted heath. I hurried back before sunset to my hotel
column7: unwilling to have the stars come out above me in the open; and the next day returned to Boston to give up my position. I could not go into that dim chaos of old forest and slope again
column8: or face another time that grey blasted heath where the black well yawned deep beside the tumbled bricks and stones. The reservoir will soon be built now
column9: and all those elder secrets will be safe forever under watery fathoms. But even then I do not believe I would like to visit that country by night--at least not when the sinister stars are out; and nothing could bribe me to drink the new city water of Arkham.

column1: It all began
column2: old Ammi said
column3: with the meteorite. Before that time there had been no wild legends at all since the witch trials
column4: and even then these western woods were not feared half so much as the small island in the Miskatonic where the devil held court beside a curious lone altar older than the Indians. These were not haunted woods
column5: and their fantastic dusk was never terrible till the strange days. Then there had come that white noontide cloud
column6: that string of explosions in the air
column7: and that pillar of smoke from the valley far in the wood. And by night all Arkham had heard of the great rock that fell out of the sky and bedded itself in the ground beside the well at the Nahum Gardner place. That was the house which had stood where the blasted heath was to come--the trim white Nahum Gardner house amidst its fertile gardens and orchards.

column1: Nahum had come to town to tell people about the stone
column2: and dropped in at Ammi Pierce's on the way. Ammi was forty then
column3: and all the queer things were fixed very strongly in his mind. He and his wife had gone with the three professors from Miskatonic University who hastened out the next morning to see the weird visitor from unknown stellar space
column4: and had wondered why Nahum had called it so large the day before. It had shrunk
column5: Nahum said as he pointed out the big brownish mound above the ripped earth and charred grass near the archaic well-sweep in his front yard; but the wise men answered that stones do not shrink. Its heat lingered persistently
column6: and Nahum declared it had glowed faintly in the night. The professors tried it with a geologist's hammer and found it was oddly soft. It was
column7: in truth
column8: so soft as to be almost plastic; and they gouged rather than chipped a specimen to take back to the college for testing. They took it in an old pail borrowed from Nahum's kitchen
column9: for even the small piece refused to grow cool. On the trip back they stopped at Ammi's to rest
column10: and seemed thoughtful when Mrs. Pierce remarked that the fragment was growing smaller and burning the bottom of the pail. Truly
column11: it was not large
column12: but perhaps they had taken less than they thought.

column1: The day after that--all this was in June of '82--the professors had trooped out again in a great excitement. As they passed Ammi's they told him what queer things the specimen had done
column2: and how it had faded wholly away when they put it in a glass beaker. The beaker had gone
column3: too
column4: and the wise men talked of the strange stone's affinity for silicon. It had acted quite unbelievably in that well-ordered laboratory; doing nothing at all and showing no occluded gases when heated on charcoal
column5: being wholly negative in the borax bead
column6: and soon proving itself absolutely non-volatile at any producible temperature
column7: including that of the oxy-hydrogen blowpipe. On an anvil it appeared highly malleable
column8: and in the dark its luminosity was very marked. Stubbornly refusing to grow cool
column9: it soon had the college in a state of real excitement; and when upon heating before the spectroscope it displayed shining bands unlike any known colours of the normal spectrum there was much breathless talk of new elements
column10: bizarre optical properties
column11: and other things which puzzled men of science are wont to say when faced by the unknown.

column1: Hot as it was
column2: they tested it in a crucible with all the proper reagents. Water did nothing. Hydrochloric acid was the same. Nitric acid and even aqua regia merely hissed and spattered against its torrid invulnerability. Ammi had difficulty in recalling all these things
column3: but recognized some solvents as I mentioned them in the usual order of use. There were ammonia and caustic soda
column4: alcohol and ether
column5: nauseous carbon disulphide and a dozen others; but although the weight grew steadily less as time passed
column6: and the fragment seemed to be slightly cooling
column7: there was no change in the solvents to show that they had attacked the substance at all. It was a metal
column8: though
column9: beyond a doubt. It was magnetic
column10: for one thing; and after its immersion in the acid solvents there seemed to be faint traces of the Widmanstatten figures found on meteoric iron. When the cooling had grown very considerable
column11: the testing was carried on in glass; and it was in a glass beaker that they left all the chips made of the original fragment during the work. The next morning both chips and beaker were gone without trace
column12: and only a charred spot marked the place on the wooden shelf where they had been.

column1: All this the professors told Ammi as they paused at his door
column2: and once more he went with them to see the stony messenger from the stars
column3: though this time his wife did not accompany him. It had now most certainly shrunk
column4: and even the sober professors could not doubt the truth of what they saw. All around the dwindling brown lump near the well was a vacant space
column5: except where the earth had caved in; and whereas it had been a good seven feet across the day before
column6: it was now scarcely five. It was still hot
column7: and the sages studied its surface curiously as they detached another and larger piece with hammer and chisel. They gouged deeply this time
column8: and as they pried away the smaller mass they saw that the core of the thing was not quite homogeneous.

column1: They had uncovered what seemed to be the side of a large coloured globule embedded in the substance. The colour
column2: which resembled some of the bands in the meteor's strange spectrum
column3: was almost impossible to describe; and it was only by analogy that they called it colour at all. Its texture was glossy
column4: and upon tapping it appeared to promise both brittleness and hollowness. One of the professors gave it a smart blow with a hammer
column5: and it burst with a nervous little pop. Nothing was emitted
column6: and all trace of the thing vanished with the puncturing. It left behind a hollow spherical space about three inches across
column7: and all thought it probable that others would be discovered as the enclosing substance wasted away.

column1: Conjecture was vain; so after a futile attempt to find additional globules by drilling
column2: the seekers left again with their new specimen which proved
column3: however
column4: as baffling in the laboratory as its predecessor. Aside from being almost plastic
column5: having heat
column6: magnetism
column7: and slight luminosity
column8: cooling slightly in powerful acids
column9: possessing an unknown spectrum
column10: wasting away in air
column11: and attacking silicon compounds with mutual destruction as a result
column12: it presented no identifying features whatsoever; and at the end of the tests the college scientists were forced to own that they could not place it. It was nothing of this earth
column13: but a piece of the great outside; and as such dowered with outside properties and obedient to outside laws.

column1: That night there was a thunderstorm
column2: and when the professors went out to Nahum's the next day they met with a bitter disappointment. The stone
column3: magnetic as it had been
column4: must have had some peculiar electrical property; for it had ""drawn the lightning
column5: as Nahum said
column6: with a singular persistence. Six times within an hour the farmer saw the lightning strike the furrow in the front yard
column7: and when the storm was over nothing remained but a ragged pit by the ancient well-sweep
column8: half-choked with a caved-in earth. Digging had borne no fruit
column9: and the scientists verified the fact of the utter vanishment. The failure was total; so that nothing was left to do but go back to the laboratory and test again the disappearing fragment left carefully cased in lead. That fragment lasted a week
column10: at the end of which nothing of value had been learned of it. When it had gone
column11: no residue was left behind
column12: and in time the professors felt scarcely sure they had indeed seen with waking eyes that cryptic vestige of the fathomless gulfs outside; that lone
column13: weird message from other universes and other realms of matter
column14: force
column15: and entity.

column1: As was natural
column2: the Arkham papers made much of the incident with its collegiate sponsoring
column3: and sent reporters to talk with Nahum Gardner and his family. At least one Boston daily also sent a scribe
column4: and Nahum quickly became a kind of local celebrity. He was a lean
column5: genial person of about fifty
column6: living with his wife and three sons on the pleasant farmstead in the valley. He and Ammi exchanged visits frequently
column7: as did their wives; and Ammi had nothing but praise for him after all these years. He seemed slightly proud of the notice his place had attracted
column8: and talked often of the meteorite in the succeeding weeks. That July and August were hot; and Nahum worked hard at his haying in the ten-acre pasture across Chapman's Brook; his rattling wain wearing deep ruts in the shadowy lanes between. The labour tired him more than it had in other years
column9: and he felt that age was beginning to tell on him.

column1: Then fell the time of fruit and harvest. The pears and apples slowly ripened
column2: and Nahum vowed that his orchards were prospering as never before. The fruit was growing to phenomenal size and unwonted gloss
column3: and in such abundance that extra barrels were ordered to handle the future crop. But with the ripening came sore disappointment
column4: for of all that gorgeous array of specious lusciousness not one single jot was fit to eat. Into the fine flavour of the pears and apples had crept a stealthy bitterness and sickishness
column5: so that even the smallest bites induced a lasting disgust. It was the same with the melons and tomatoes
column6: and Nahum sadly saw that his entire crop was lost. Quick to connect events
column7: he declared that the meteorite had poisoned the soil
column8: and thanked Heaven that most of the other crops were in the upland lot along the road.

column1: Winter came early
column2: and was very cold. Ammi saw Nahum less often than usual
column3: and observed that he had begun to look worried. The rest of his family too
column4: seemed to have grown taciturn; and were far from steady in their church-going or their attendance at the various social events of the countryside. For this reserve or melancholy no cause could be found
column5: though all the household confessed now and then to poorer health and a feeling of vague disquiet. Nahum himself gave the most definite statement of anyone when he said he was disturbed about certain footprints in the snow. They were the usual winter prints of red squirrels
column6: white rabbits
column7: and foxes
column8: but the brooding farmer professed to see something not quite right about their nature and arrangement. He was never specific
column9: but appeared to think that they were not as characteristic of the anatomy and habits of squirrels and rabbits and foxes as they ought to be. Ammi listened without interest to this talk until one night when he drove past Nahum's house in his sleigh on the way back from Clark's Comer. There had been a moon
column10: and a rabbit had run across the road
column11: and the leaps of that rabbit were longer than either Ammi or his horse liked. The latter
column12: indeed
column13: had almost run away when brought up by a firm rein. Thereafter Ammi gave Nahum's tales more respect
column14: and wondered why the Gardner dogs seemed so cowed and quivering every morning. They had
column15: it developed
column16: nearly lost the spirit to bark.

column1: In February the McGregor boys from Meadow Hill were out shooting woodchucks
column2: and not far from the Gardner place bagged a very peculiar specimen. The proportions of its body seemed slightly altered in a queer way impossible to describe
column3: while its face had taken on an expression which no one ever saw in a woodchuck before. The boys were genuinely frightened
column4: and threw the thing away at once
column5: so that only their grotesque tales of it ever reached the people of the countryside. But the shying of horses near Nahum's house had now become an acknowledged thing
column6: and all the basis for a cycle of whispered legend was fast taking form.

column1: People vowed that the snow melted faster around Nahum's than it did anywhere else
column2: and early in March there was an awed discussion in Potter's general store at Clark's Corners. Stephen Rice had driven past Gardner's in the morning
column3: and had noticed the skunk-cabbages coming up through the mud by the woods across the road. Never were things of such size seen before
column4: and they held strange colours that could not be put into any words. Their shapes were monstrous
column5: and the horse had snorted at an odour which struck Stephen as wholly unprecedented. That afternoon several persons drove past to see the abnormal growth
column6: and all agreed that plants of that kind ought never to sprout in a healthy world. The bad fruit of the fall before was freely mentioned
column7: and it went from mouth to mouth that there was poison in Nahum's ground. Of course it was the meteorite; and remembering how strange the men from the college had found that stone to be
column8: several farmers spoke about the matter to them.

column1: One day they paid Nahum a visit; but having no love of wild tales and folklore were very conservative in what they inferred. The plants were certainly odd
column2: but all skunk-cabbages are more or less odd in shape and hue. Perhaps some mineral element from the stone had entered the soil
column3: but it would soon be washed away. And as for the footprints and frightened horses--of course this was mere country talk which such a phenomenon as the aerolite would be certain to start. There was really nothing for serious men to do in cases of wild gossip
column4: for superstitious rustics will say and believe anything. And so all through the strange days the professors stayed away in contempt. Only one of them
column5: when given two phials of dust for analysis in a police job over a year and half later
column6: recalled that the queer colour of that skunk-cabbage had been very like one of the anomalous bands of light shown by the meteor fragment in the college spectroscope
column7: and like the brittle globule found imbedded in the stone from the abyss. The samples in this analysis case gave the same odd bands at first
column8: though later they lost the property.

column1: The trees budded prematurely around Nahum's
column2: and at night they swayed ominously in the wind. Nahum's second son Thaddeus
column3: a lad of fifteen
column4: swore that they swayed also when there was no wind; but even the gossips would not credit this. Certainly
column5: however
column6: restlessness was in the air. The entire Gardner family developed the habit of stealthy listening
column7: though not for any sound which they could consciously name. The listening was
column8: indeed
column9: rather a product of moments when consciousness seemed half to slip away. Unfortunately such moments increased week by week
column10: till it became common speech that ""something was wrong with all Nahum's folks."" When the early saxifrage came out it had another strange colour; not quite like that of the skunk-cabbage
column11: but plainly related and equally unknown to anyone who saw it. Nahum took some blossoms to Arkham and showed them to the editor of the Gazette
column12: but that dignitary did no more than write a humorous article about them
column13: in which the dark fears of rustics were held up to polite ridicule. It was a mistake of Nahum's to tell a stolid city man about the way the great
column14: overgrown mourning-cloak butterflies behaved in connection with these saxifrages.

column1: April brought a kind of madness to the country folk
column2: and began that disuse of the road past Nahum's which led to its ultimate abandonment. It was the vegetation. All the orchard trees blossomed forth in strange colours
column3: and through the stony soil of the yard and adjacent pasturage there sprang up a bizarre growth which only a botanist could connect with the proper flora of the region. No sane wholesome colours were anywhere to be seen except in the green grass and leafage; but everywhere were those hectic and prismatic variants of some diseased
column4: underlying primary tone without a place among the known tints of earth. The ""Dutchman's breeches"" became a thing of sinister menace
column5: and the bloodroots grew insolent in their chromatic perversion. Ammi and the Gardners thought that most of the colours had a sort of haunting familiarity
column6: and decided that they reminded one of the brittle globule in the meteor. Nahum ploughed and sowed the ten-acre pasture and the upland lot
column7: but did nothing with the land around the house. He knew it would be of no use
column8: and hoped that the summer's strange growths would draw all the poison from the soil. He was prepared for almost anything now
column9: and had grown used to the sense of something near him waiting to be heard. The shunning of his house by neighbors told on him
column10: of course; but it told on his wife more. The boys were better off
column11: being at school each day; but they could not help being frightened by the gossip. Thaddeus
column12: an especially sensitive youth
column13: suffered the most.

column1: In May the insects came
column2: and Nahum's place became a nightmare of buzzing and crawling. Most of the creatures seemed not quite usual in their aspects and motions
column3: and their nocturnal habits contradicted all former experience. The Gardners took to watching at night--watching in all directions at random for something--they could not tell what. It was then that they owned that Thaddeus had been right about the trees. Mrs. Gardner was the next to see it from the window as she watched the swollen boughs of a maple against a moonlit sky. The boughs surely moved
column4: and there was no wind. It must be the sap. Strangeness had come into everything growing now. Yet it was none of Nahum's family at all who made the next discovery. Familiarity had dulled them
column5: and what they could not see was glimpsed by a timid windmill salesman from Bolton who drove by one night in ignorance of the country legends. What he told in Arkham was given a short paragraph in the Gazette; and it was there that all the farmers
column6: Nahum included
column7: saw it first. The night had been dark and the buggy-lamps faint
column8: but around a farm in the valley which everyone knew from the account must be Nahum's
column9: the darkness had been less thick. A dim though distinct luminosity seemed to inhere in all the vegetation
column10: grass
column11: leaves
column12: and blossoms alike
column13: while at one moment a detached piece of the phosphorescence appeared to stir furtively in the yard near the barn.

column1: The grass had so far seemed untouched
column2: and the cows were freely pastured in the lot near the house
column3: but toward the end of May the milk began to be bad. Then Nahum had the cows driven to the uplands
column4: after which this trouble ceased. Not long after this the change in grass and leaves became apparent to the eye. All the verdure was going grey
column5: and was developing a highly singular quality of brittleness. Ammi was now the only person who ever visited the place
column6: and his visits were becoming fewer and fewer. When school closed the Gardners were virtually cut off from the world
column7: and sometimes let Ammi do their errands in town. They were failing curiously both physically and mentally
column8: and no one was surprised when the news of Mrs. Gardner's madness stole around.

column1: It happened in June
column2: about the anniversary of the meteor's fall
column3: and the poor woman screamed about things in the air which she could not describe. In her raving there was not a single specific noun
column4: but only verbs and pronouns. Things moved and changed and fluttered
column5: and ears tingled to impulses which were not wholly sounds. Something was taken away--she was being drained of something--something was fastening itself on her that ought not to be--someone must make it keep off--nothing was ever still in the night--the walls and windows shifted. Nahum did not send her to the county asylum
column6: but let her wander about the house as long as she was harmless to herself and others. Even when her expression changed he did nothing. But when the boys grew afraid of her
column7: and Thaddeus nearly fainted at the way she made faces at him
column8: he decided to keep her locked in the attic. By July she had ceased to speak and crawled on all fours
column9: and before that month was over Nahum got the mad notion that she was slightly luminous in the dark
column10: as he now clearly saw was the case with the nearby vegetation.

column1: It was a little before this that the horses had stampeded. Something had aroused them in the night
column2: and their neighing and kicking in their stalls had been terrible. There seemed virtually nothing to do to calm them
column3: and when Nahum opened the stable door they all bolted out like frightened woodland deer. It took a week to track all four
column4: and when found they were seen to be quite useless and unmanageable. Something had snapped in their brains
column5: and each one had to be shot for its own good. Nahum borrowed a horse from Ammi for his haying
column6: but found it would not approach the barn. It shied
column7: balked
column8: and whinnied

He had come of late to do nothing but stare into space and obey what his father told him; and Ammi thought that his fate was very merciful. column2: but it burns...it lived in the well...I seen it...a kind of smoke...jest like the flowers last spring...the well shone at night...Thad an' Merwin an' Zenas...everything alive...suckin' the life out of everything...in that stone...it must a' come in that stone pizened the whole place...dun't know what it wants...that round thing them men from the college dug outen the stone...they smashed it...it was the same colour...jest the same

column5: Ammi?...my head's no good...dun't know how long sense I fed her...it'll git her ef we ain't keerful...jest a colour...her face is gittin' to hev that colour sometimes towards night...an' it burns an' sucks...it come from some place whar things ain't as they is here...one o' them professors said so...he was right...look out
column6: Ammi
column7: it'll do suthin' more...sucks the life out...""

column1: But that was all. That which spoke could speak no more because it had completely caved in. Ammi laid a red checked tablecloth over what was left and reeled out the back door into the fields. He climbed the slope to the ten-acre pasture and stumbled home by the north road and the woods. He could not pass that well from which his horses had run away. He had looked at it through the window

column1: Ammi would not have told the men about the well if he had thought they meant to do anything then and there. It was getting toward sunset
column2: and he was anxious to be away. But he could not help glancing nervously at the stony curb by the great sweep

column1: Twilight had now fallen
column2: and lanterns were brought from the house. Then
column3: when it was seen that nothing further could be gained from the well

column5: and could find no convincing common element to link the strange vegetable conditions
column6: the unknown disease of live-stock and humans
column7: and the unaccountable deaths of Merwin and Zenas in the tainted well. They had heard the common country talk

column9: but the illness of persons and animals who had eaten nothing grown in that soil was another matter. Was it the well water? Very possibly. It might be a good idea to analyze it. But what peculiar madness could have made both boys jump into the well? Their deeds were so similar-and the fragments showed that they had both suffered from the grey brittle death. Why was everything so grey and brittle?

column1: It was the coroner
column2: seated near a window overlooking the yard
column3: who first noticed the glow about the well. Night had fully set in
column4: and all the abhorrent grounds seemed faintly luminous with more than the fitful moonbeams; but this new glow was something definite and distinct
column5: and appeared to shoot up from the black pit like a softened ray from a searchlight
column6: giving dull reflections in the little ground pools where the water had been emptied. It had a very queer colour
column7: and as all the men clustered round the window Ammi gave a violent start. For this strange beam of ghastly miasma was to him of no unfamiliar hue. He had seen that colour before
column8: and feared to think what it might mean. He had seen it in the nasty brittle globule in that aerolite two summers ago
column9: had seen it in the crazy vegetation of the springtime
column10: and had thought he had seen it for an instant that very morning against the small barred window of that terrible attic room where nameless things had happened. It had flashed there a second
column11: and a clammy and hateful current of vapour had brushed past him--and then poor Nahum had been taken by something of that colour. He had said so at the last--said it was like the globule and the plants. After that had come the runaway in the yard and the splash in the well and now that well was belching forth to the night a pale insidious beam of the same demoniac tint.

column3: and from a nocturnal exhalation seen as a phosphorescent mist against the black and blasted landscape. It wasn't right--it was against Nature--and he thought of those terrible last words of his stricken friend
column4: ""It come from some place whar things ain't as they is here...one o' them professors said so...""

column5: he whispered. ""They's more to this nor what we know. Nahum said somethin' lived in the well that sucks your life out. He said it must be some'at growed from a round ball like one we all seen in the meteor stone that fell a year ago June. Sucks an' burns
column6: he said
column7: an' is jest a cloud of colour like that light out thar now
column8: that ye can hardly see an' can't tell what it is. Nahum thought it feeds on everything livin' an' gits stronger all the time. He said he seen it this last week. It must be somethin' from away off in the sky like the men from the college last year says the meteor stone was. The way it's made an' the way it works ain't like no way o' God's world. It's some'at from beyond.""

column1: So the men paused indecisively as the light from the well grew stronger and the hitched horses pawed and whinnied in increasing frenzy. It was truly an awful moment; with terror in that ancient and accursed house itself
column2: four monstrous sets of fragments--two from the house and two from the well--in the woodshed behind
column3: and that shaft of unknown and unholy iridescence from the slimy depths in front. Ammi had restrained the driver on impulse

column1: All at once one of the detectives at the window gave a short
column2: sharp gasp. The others looked at him
column3: and then quickly followed his own gaze upward to the point at which its idle straying had been suddenly arrested. There was no need for words. What had been disputed in country gossip was disputable no longer

column1: Not a man breathed for several seconds. Then a cloud of darker depth passed over the moon
column2: and the silhouette of clutching branches faded out momentarily. At this there was a general cry; muffled with awe
column3: but husky and almost identical from every throat. For the terror had not faded with the silhouette
column4: and in a fearsome instant of deeper darkness the watchers saw wriggling at that tree top height a thousand tiny points of faint and unhallowed radiance
column5: tipping each bough like the fire of St. Elmo or the flames that come down on the apostles' heads at Pentecost. It was a monstrous constellation of unnatural light
column6: like a glutted swarm of corpse-fed fireflies dancing hellish sarabands over an accursed marsh

column8: bringing to the minds of the huddled men

column1: It was then that the most horrible impression of all was borne in upon me--the impression which destroyed my last vestige of self-control and sent me running frantically southward past the yawning black doorways and fishily staring windows of that deserted nightmare street. For at a closer glance I saw that the moonlit waters between the reef and the shore were far from empty. They were alive with a teeming horde of shapes swimming inward toward the town; and even at my vast distance and in my single moment of perception I could tell that the bobbing heads and flailing arms were alien and aberrant in a way scarcely to be expressed or consciously formulated.
My frantic running ceased before I had covered a block

One man moved in a positively simian way

column7: however

column7: but I never see mor'n two or three people in it--nobody but those Innsmouth folk. Leaves the square--front of Hammond's Drug Store--at 10 a.m. and 7 p.m. unless they've changed lately. Looks like a terrible rattletrap--I've never been on it.""

column1: That was the first I ever heard of shadowed Innsmouth. Any reference to a town not shown on common maps or listed in recent guidebooks would have interested me

column3: I thought

column1: Innsmouth? Well
column2: it's a queer kind of a town down at the mouth of the Manuxet. Used to be almost a city--quite a port before the War of 1812--but all gone to pieces in the last hundred years or so. No railroad now--B. and M. never went through
column3: and the branch line from Rowley was given up years ago.

column1: More empty houses than there are people
column2: I guess
column3: and no business to speak of except fishing and lobstering. Everybody trades mostly either here or in Arkham or Ipswich. Once they had quite a few mills
column4: but nothing's left now except one gold refinery running on the leanest kind of part time.

column1: That refinery
column2: though
column3: used to be a big thing
column4: and old man Marsh
column5: who owns it
column6: must be richer'n Croesus. Queer old duck
column7: though
column8: and sticks mighty close in his home. He's supposed to have developed some skin disease or deformity late in life that makes him keep out of sight. Grandson of Captain Obed Marsh

column11: come to think of it

column1: And why is everybody so down on Innsmouth? Well
column2: young fellow

column5: mostly--for the last hundred years
column6: I guess

column1: You ought to hear

column4: they call it. It's well above water a good part of the time
column5: and never much below it

column1: That is
column2: sailors that didn't hail from Innsmouth. One of the things they had against old Captain Marsh was that he was supposed to land on it sometimes at night when the tide was right. Maybe he did
column3: for I dare say the rock formation was interesting
column4: and it's just barely possible he was looking for pirate loot and maybe finding it; but there was talk of his dealing with demons there. Fact is
column5: I guess on the whole it was really the Captain that gave the bad reputation to the reef.

column1: That was before the big epidemic of 1846
column2: when over half the folks in Innsmouth was carried off. They never did quite figure out what the trouble was
column3: but it was probably some foreign kind of disease brought from China or somewhere by the shipping. It surely was bad enough--there was riots over it
column4: and all sorts of ghastly doings that I don't believe ever got outside of town--and it left the place in awful shape. Never came back--there can't be more'n 300 or 400 people living there now.

column1: But the real thing behind the way folks feel is simply race prejudice--and I don't say I'm blaming those that hold it. I hate those Innsmouth folks myself
column2: and I wouldn't care to go to their town. I s'pose you know--though I can see you're a Westerner by your talk--what a lot our New England ships used to have to do with queer ports in Africa
column3: Asia
column4: the South Seas
column5: and everywhere else
column6: and what queer kinds of people they sometimes brought back with 'em. You've probably heard about the Salem man that came home with a Chinese wife
column7: and maybe you know there's still a bunch of Fiji Islanders somewhere around Cape Cod.

column1: Well
column2: there must be something like that back of the Innsmouth people. The place always was badly cut off from the rest of the country by marshes and creeks and we can't be sure about the ins and outs of the matter; but it's pretty clear that old Captain Marsh must have brought home some odd specimens when he had all three of his ships in commission back in the twenties and thirties. There certainly is a strange kind of streak in the Innsmouth folks today--I don't know how to explain it but it sort of makes you crawl. You'll notice a little in Sargent if you take his bus. Some of 'em have queer narrow heads with flat noses and bulgy
column3: stary eyes that never seem to shut
column4: and their skin ain't quite right. Rough and scabby
column5: and the sides of the necks are all shriveled or creased up. Get bald
column6: too
column7: very young. The older fellows look the worst--fact is
column8: I don't believe I've ever seen a very old chap of that kind. Guess they must die of looking in the glass! Animals hate 'em--they used to have lots of horse trouble before the autos came in.

column1: Nobody around here or in Arkham or Ipswich will have anything to do with 'em
column2: and they act kind of offish themselves when they come to town or when anyone tries to fish on their grounds. Queer how fish are always thick off Innsmouth Harbour when there ain't any anywhere else around--but just try to fish there yourself and see how the folks chase you off! Those people used to come here on the railroad--walking and taking the train at Rowley after the branch was dropped--but now they use that bus.

column1: Yes
column2: there's a hotel in Innsmouth--called the Gilman House--but I don't believe it can amount to much. I wouldn't advise you to try it. Better stay over here and take the ten o'clock bus tomorrow morning; then you can get an evening bus there for Arkham at eight o'clock. There was a factory inspector who stopped at the Gilman a couple of years ago and he had a lot of unpleasant hints about the place. Seems they get a queer crowd there
column3: for this fellow heard voices in other rooms--though most of 'em was empty--that gave him the shivers. It was foreign talk he thought
column4: but he said the bad thing about it was the kind of voice that sometimes spoke. It sounded so unnatural--slopping like
column5: he said--that he didn't dare undress and go to sleep. Just waited up and lit out the first thing in the morning. The talk went on most all night.

column1: This fellow--Casey
column2: his name was--had a lot to say about how the Innsmouth folk watched him and seemed kind of on guard. He found the Marsh refinery a queer place--it's in an old mill on the lower falls of the Manuxet. What he said tallied up with what I'd heard. Books in bad shape
column3: and no clear account of any kind of dealings. You know it's always been a kind of mystery where the Marshes get the gold they refine. They've never seemed to do much buying in that line
column4: but years ago they shipped out an enormous lot of ingots.

column1: Used to be talk of a queer foreign kind of jewelry that the sailors and refinery men sometimes sold on the sly
column2: or that was seen once or twice on some of the Marsh women-folks. People allowed maybe old Captain Obed traded for it in some heathen port
column3: especially since he always ordered stacks of glass beads and trinkets such as seafaring men used to get for native trade. Others thought and still think he'd found an old pirate cache out on Devil Reef. But here's a funny thing. The old Captain's been dead these sixty years
column4: and there's ain't been a good-sized ship out of the place since the Civil War; but just the same the Marshes still keep on buying a few of those native trade things--mostly glass and rubber gewgaws
column5: they tell me. Maybe the Innsmouth folks like 'em to look at themselves--Gawd knows they've gotten to be about as bad as South Sea cannibals and Guinea savages.

column1: That plague of '46 must have taken off the best blood in the place. Anyway
column2: they're a doubtful lot now
column3: and the Marshes and other rich folks are as bad as any. As I told you
column4: there probably ain't more'n 400 people in the whole town in spite of all the streets they say there are. I guess they're what they call 'white trash' down South--lawless and sly
column5: and full of secret things. They get a lot of fish and lobsters and do exporting by truck. Queer how the fish swarm right there and nowhere else.

column1: Nobody can ever keep track of these people
column2: and state school officials and census men have a devil of a time. You can bet that prying strangers ain't welcome around Innsmouth. I've heard personally of more'n one business or government man that's disappeared there
column3: and there's loose talk of one who went crazy and is out at Danvers now. They must have fixed up some awful scare for that fellow.

column1: That's why I wouldn't go at night if I was you. I've never been there and have no wish to go
column2: but I guess a daytime trip couldn't hurt you--even though the people hereabouts will advise you not to make it. If you're just sightseeing
column3: and looking for old-time stuff
column4: Innsmouth ought to be quite a place for you.""

column3: the garages
column4: and the fire station

column6: as if there were something amiss with anyone too much interested in Innsmouth. At the Y. M. C. A.
column7: where I was stopping

column9: decadent place; and the people at the library shewed much the same attitude. Clearly
column10: in the eyes of the educated

column1: The Essex County histories on the library shelves had very little to say
column2: except that the town was founded in 1643
column3: noted for shipbuilding before the Revolution
column4: a seat of great marine prosperity in the early 19th century
column5: and later a minor factory center using the Manuxet as power. The epidemic and riots of 1846 were very sparsely treated
column6: as if they formed a discredit to the county.

column1: References to decline were few
column2: though the significance of the later record was unmistakable. After the Civil War all industrial life was confined to the Marsh Refining Company
column3: and the marketing of gold ingots formed the only remaining bit of major commerce aside from the eternal fishing. That fishing paid less and less as the price of the commodity fell and large-scale corporations offered competition
column4: but there was never a dearth of fish around Innsmouth Harbour. Foreigners seldom settled there
column5: and there was some discreetly veiled evidence that a number of Poles and Portuguese who had tried it had been scattered in a peculiarly drastic fashion.

column1: Most interesting of all was a glancing reference to the strange jewelry vaguely associated with Innsmouth. It had evidently impressed the whole countryside more than a little
column2: for mention was made of specimens in the museum of Miskatonic University at Arkham
column3: and in the display room of the Newburyport Historical Society. The fragmentary descriptions of these things were bald and prosaic
column4: but they hinted to me an undercurrent of persistent strangeness. Something about them seemed so odd and provocative that I could not put them out of my mind
column5: and despite the relative lateness of the hour I resolved to see the local sample--said to be a large
column6: queerly-proportioned thing evidently meant for a tiara--if it could possibly be arranged.

column1: The librarian gave me a note of introduction to the curator of the Society
column2: a Miss Anna Tilton
column3: who lived nearby
column4: and after a brief explanation that ancient gentlewoman was kind enough to pilot me into the closed building
column5: since the hour was not outrageously late. The collection was a notable one indeed
column6: but in my present mood I had eyes for nothing but the bizarre object which glistened in a corner cupboard under the electric lights.

column1: It took no excessive sensitiveness to beauty to make me literally gasp at the strange
column2: unearthly splendour of the alien
column3: opulent phantasy that rested there on a purple velvet cushion. Even now I can hardly describe what I saw
column4: though it was clearly enough a sort of tiara
column5: as the description had said. It was tall in front
column6: and with a very large and curiously irregular periphery
column7: as if designed for a head of almost freakishly elliptical outline. The material seemed to be predominantly gold
column8: though a weird lighter lustrousness hinted at some strange alloy with an equally beautiful and scarcely identifiable metal. Its condition was almost perfect
column9: and one could have spent hours in studying the striking and puzzlingly untraditional designs--some simply geometrical
column10: and some plainly marine--chased or moulded in high relief on its surface with a craftsmanship of incredible skill and grace.

column1: The longer I looked
column2: the more the thing fascinated me; and in this fascination there was a curiously disturbing element hardly to be classified or accounted for. At first I decided that it was the queer other-worldly quality of the art which made me uneasy. All other art objects I had ever seen either belonged to some known racial or national stream
column3: or else were consciously modernistic defiances of every recognized stream. This tiara was neither. It clearly belonged to some settled technique of infinite maturity and perfection
column4: yet that technique was utterly remote from any--Eastern or Western
column5: ancient or modern--which I had ever heard of or seen exemplified. It was as if the workmanship were that of another planet.

column1: However
column2: I soon saw that my uneasiness had a second and perhaps equally potent source residing in the pictorial and mathematical suggestion of the strange designs. The patterns all hinted of remote secrets and unimaginable abysses in time and space
column3: and the monotonously aquatic nature of the reliefs became almost sinister. Among these reliefs were fabulous monsters of abhorrent grotesqueness and malignity--half ichthyic and half batrachian in suggestion--which one could not dissociate from a certain haunting and uncomfortable sense of pseudomemory
column4: as if they called up some image from deep cells and tissues whose retentive functions are wholly primal and awesomely ancestral. At times I fancied that every contour of these blasphemous fish-frogs was over-flowing with the ultimate quintessence of unknown and inhuman evil.

column1: In odd contrast to the tiara's aspect was its brief and prosy history as related by Miss Tilton. It had been pawned for a ridiculous sum at a shop in State Street in 1873
column2: by a drunken Innsmouth man shortly afterward killed in a brawl. The Society had acquired it directly from the pawnbroker
column3: at once giving it a display worthy of its quality. It was labeled as of probable East-Indian or Indochinese provenance
column4: though the attribution was frankly tentative.

column1: Miss Tilton
column2: comparing all possible hypotheses regarding its origin and its presence in New England
column3: was inclined to believe that it formed part of some exotic pirate hoard discovered by old Captain Obed Marsh. This view was surely not weakened by the insistent offers of purchase at a high price which the Marshes began to make as soon as they knew of its presence
column4: and which they repeated to this day despite the Society's unvarying determination not to sell.

column1: As the good lady shewed me out of the building she made it clear that the pirate theory of the Marsh fortune was a popular one among the intelligent people of the region. Her own attitude toward shadowed Innsmouth--which she never seen--was one of disgust at a community slipping far down the cultural scale
column2: and she assured me that the rumours of devil-worship were partly justified by a peculiar secret cult which had gained force there and engulfed all the orthodox churches.

column1: It was called
column2: she said
column3: ""The Esoteric Order of Dagon
column4: and was undoubtedly a debased
column5: quasi-pagan thing imported from the East a century before
column6: at a time when the Innsmouth fisheries seemed to be going barren. Its persistence among a simple people was quite natural in view of the sudden and permanent return of abundantly fine fishing
column7: and it soon came to be the greatest influence in the town
column8: replacing Freemasonry altogether and taking up headquarters in the old Masonic Hall on New Church Green.

column1: All this
column2: to the pious Miss Tilton
column3: formed an excellent reason for shunning the ancient town of decay and desolation; but to me it was merely a fresh incentive. To my architectural and historical anticipations was now added an acute anthropological zeal
column4: and I could scarcely sleep in my small room at the ""Y"" as the night wore away.

column1: I.
It is true that I have sent six bullets through the head of my best friend
column2: and yet I hope to shew by this statement that I am not his murderer. At first I shall be called a madman—madder than the man I shot in his cell at the Arkham Sanitarium. Later some of my readers will weigh each statement
column3: correlate it with the known facts
column4: and ask themselves how I could have believed otherwise than as I did after facing the evidence of that horror—that thing on the doorstep.

column1: Until then I also saw nothing but madness in the wild tales I have acted on. Even now I ask myself whether I was misled—or whether I am not mad after all. I do not know—but others have strange things to tell of Edward and Asenath Derby
column2: and even the stolid police are at their wits’ ends to account for that last terrible visit. They have tried weakly to concoct a theory of a ghastly jest or warning by discharged servants
column3: yet they know in their hearts that the truth is something infinitely more terrible and incredible.

column1: So I say that I have not murdered Edward Derby. Rather have I avenged him
column2: and in so doing purged the earth of a horror whose survival might have loosed untold terrors on all mankind. There are black zones of shadow close to our daily paths
column3: and now and then some evil soul breaks a passage through. When that happens
column4: the man who knows must strike before reckoning the consequences.

column1: I have known Edward Pickman Derby all his life. Eight years my junior
column2: he was so precocious that we had much in common from the time he was eight and I sixteen. He was the most phenomenal child scholar I have ever known
column3: and at seven was writing verse of a sombre
column4: fantastic
column5: almost morbid cast which astonished the tutors surrounding him. Perhaps his private education and coddled seclusion had something to do with his premature flowering. An only child
column6: he had organic weaknesses which startled his doting parents and caused them to keep him closely chained to their side. He was never allowed out without his nurse
column7: and seldom had a chance to play unconstrainedly with other children. All this doubtless fostered a strange
column8: secretive inner life in the boy
column9: with imagination as his one avenue of freedom.

column1: At any rate
column2: his juvenile learning was prodigious and bizarre; and his facile writings such as to captivate me despite my greater age. About that time I had leanings toward art of a somewhat grotesque cast
column3: and I found in this younger child a rare kindred spirit. What lay behind our joint love of shadows and marvels was
column4: no doubt
column5: the ancient
column6: mouldering
column7: and subtly fearsome town in which we lived—witch-cursed
column8: legend-haunted Arkham
column9: whose huddled
column10: sagging gambrel roofs and crumbling Georgian balustrades brood out the centuries beside the darkly muttering Miskatonic.

column1: As time went by I turned to architecture and gave up my design of illustrating a book of Edward’s daemoniac poems
column2: yet our comradeship suffered no lessening. Young Derby’s odd genius developed remarkably
column3: and in his eighteenth year his collected nightmare-lyrics made a real sensation when issued under the title Azathoth and Other Horrors. He was a close correspondent of the notorious Baudelairean poet Justin Geoffrey
column4: who wrote The People of the Monolith and died screaming in a madhouse in 1926 after a visit to a sinister
column5: ill-regarded village in Hungary.

column1: In self-reliance and practical affairs
column2: however
column3: Derby was greatly retarded because of his coddled existence. His health had improved
column4: but his habits of childish dependence were fostered by overcareful parents; so that he never travelled alone
column5: made independent decisions
column6: or assumed responsibilities. It was early seen that he would not be equal to a struggle in the business or professional arena
column7: but the family fortune was so ample that this formed no tragedy. As he grew to years of manhood he retained a deceptive aspect of boyishness. Blond and blue-eyed
column8: he had the fresh complexion of a child; and his attempts to raise a moustache were discernible only with difficulty. His voice was soft and light
column9: and his pampered
column10: unexercised life gave him a juvenile chubbiness rather than the paunchiness of premature middle age. He was of good height
column11: and his handsome face would have made him a notable gallant had not his shyness held him to seclusion and bookishness.

column1: Derby’s parents took him abroad every summer
column2: and he was quick to seize on the surface aspects of European thought and expression. His Poe-like talents turned more and more toward the decadent
column3: and other artistic sensitivenesses and yearnings were half-aroused in him. We had great discussions in those days. I had been through Harvard
column4: had studied in a Boston architect’s office
column5: had married
column6: and had finally returned to Arkham to practice my profession—settling in the family homestead in Saltonstall St. since my father had moved to Florida for his health. Edward used to call almost every evening
column7: till I came to regard him as one of the household. He had a characteristic way of ringing the doorbell or sounding the knocker that grew to be a veritable code signal
column8: so that after dinner I always listened for the familiar three brisk strokes followed by two more after a pause. Less frequently I would visit at his house and note with envy the obscure volumes in his constantly growing library.

column1: Derby went through Miskatonic University in Arkham
column2: since his parents would not let him board away from them. He entered at sixteen and completed his course in three years
column3: majoring in English and French literature and receiving high marks in everything but mathematics and the sciences. He mingled very little with the other students
column4: though looking enviously at the “daring” or “Bohemian” set—whose superficially “smart” language and meaninglessly ironic pose he aped
column5: and whose dubious conduct he wished he dared adopt.

column1: What he did do was to become an almost fanatical devotee of subterranean magical lore
column2: for which Miskatonic’s library was and is famous. Always a dweller on the surface of phantasy and strangeness
column3: he now delved deep into the actual runes and riddles left by a fabulous past for the guidance or puzzlement of posterity. He read things like the frightful Book of Eibon
column4: the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt
column5: and the forbidden Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred
column6: though he did not tell his parents he had seen them. Edward was twenty when my son and only child was born
column7: and seemed pleased when I named the newcomer Edward Derby Upton
column8: after him.

column1: By the time he was twenty-five Edward Derby was a prodigiously learned man and a fairly well-known poet and fantaisiste
column2: though his lack of contacts and responsibilities had slowed down his literary growth by making his products derivative and overbookish. I was perhaps his closest friend—finding him an inexhaustible mine of vital theoretical topics
column3: while he relied on me for advice in whatever matters he did not wish to refer to his parents. He remained single—more through shyness
column4: inertia
column5: and parental protectiveness than through inclination—and moved in society only to the slightest and most perfunctory extent. When the war came both health and ingrained timidity kept him at home. I went to Plattsburg for a commission
column6: but never got overseas.

column1: So the years wore on. Edward’s mother died when he was thirty-four
column2: and for months he was incapacitated by some odd psychological malady. His father took him to Europe
column3: however
column4: and he managed to pull out of his trouble without visible effects. Afterward he seemed to feel a sort of grotesque exhilaration
column5: as if of partial escape from some unseen bondage. He began to mingle in the more “advanced” college set despite his middle age
column6: and was present at some extremely wild doings—on one occasion paying heavy blackmail (which he borrowed of me) to keep his presence at a certain affair from his father’s notice. Some of the whispered rumours about the wild Miskatonic set were extremely singular. There was even talk of black magic and of happenings utterly beyond credibility.

column1: II.
Edward was thirty-eight when he met Asenath Waite. She was
column2: I judge
column3: about twenty-three at the time; and was taking a special course in mediaeval metaphysics at Miskatonic. The daughter of a friend of mine had met her before—in the Hall School at Kingsport—and had been inclined to shun her because of her odd reputation. She was dark
column4: smallish
column5: and very good-looking except for overprotuberant eyes; but something in her expression alienated extremely sensitive people. It was
column6: however
column7: largely her origin and conversation which caused average folk to avoid her. She was one of the Innsmouth Waites
column8: and dark legends have clustered for generations about crumbling
column9: half-deserted Innsmouth and its people. There are tales of horrible bargains about the year 1850

column2: Innsmouth

column4: and that strange sounds sometimes floated from within as evening drew on. The old man was known to have been a prodigious magical student in his day
column5: and legend averred that he could raise or quell storms at sea according to his whim. I had seen him once or twice in my youth as he came to Arkham to consult forbidden tomes at the college library

column1: The friend whose daughter had gone to school with Asenath Waite repeated many curious things when the news of Edward’s acquaintance with her began to spread about. Asenath
column2: it seemed

column6: and would seem to extract an obscene and zestful irony from her present situation.

column1: Most unusual
column2: though

column4: beyond question

column6: whose eyes blazed and protruded with an alien expression. Asenath often made wild claims about the nature of consciousness and about its independence of the physical frame—or at least from the life-processes of the physical frame. Her crowning rage

column9: she declared
column10: she could not only equal but surpass her father in mastery of unknown forces.

column1: Edward met Asenath at a gathering of “intelligentsia” held in one of the students’ rooms

column7: he said

column1: I.
It is true that I have sent six bullets through the head of my best friend

column4: and ask themselves how I could have believed otherwise than as I did after facing the evidence of that horror—that thing on the doorstep.

column1: So I say that I have not murdered Edward Derby. Rather have I avenged him

column1: I have known Edward Pickman Derby all his life. Eight years my junior

column4: fantastic

column8: secretive inner life in the boy

column1: At any rate

column5: the ancient
column6: mouldering

column2: however

column5: made independent decisions

column1: Derby’s parents took him abroad every summer
column2: and he was quick to seize on the surface aspects of European thought and expression. His Poe-like talents turned more and more toward the decadent
column3: and other artistic sensitivenesses and yearnings were half-aroused in him. We had great discussions in those days. I had been through Harvard
column4: had studied in a Boston architect’s office
column5: had married
column6: and had finally returned to Arkham to practice my profession—settling in the family homestead in Saltonstall St. since my father had moved to Florida for his health. Edward used to call almost every evening

column8: so that after dinner I always listened for the familiar three brisk strokes followed by two more after a pause. Less frequently I would visit at his house and note with envy the obscure volumes in his constantly growing library.

column1: Derby went through Miskatonic University in Arkham
column2: since his parents would not let him board away from them. He entered at sixteen and completed his course in three years

column4: though looking enviously at the “daring” or “Bohemian” set—whose superficially “smart” language and meaninglessly ironic pose he aped

column4: the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt
column5: and the forbidden Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred

column8: after him.

column1: By the time he was twenty-five Edward Derby was a prodigiously learned man and a fairly well-known poet and fantaisiste
column2: though his lack of contacts and responsibilities had slowed down his literary growth by making his products derivative and overbookish. I was perhaps his closest friend—finding him an inexhaustible mine of vital theoretical topics

column4: inertia
column5: and parental protectiveness than through inclination—and moved in society only to the slightest and most perfunctory extent. When the war came both health and ingrained timidity kept him at home. I went to Plattsburg for a commission

column1: So the years wore on. Edward’s mother died when he was thirty-four

Some of the whispered rumours about the wild Miskatonic set were extremely singular. There was even talk of black magic and of happenings utterly beyond credibility.

column3: he said

column1: IV.
Derby had been married more than three years on that August day when I got the telegram from Maine. I had not seen him for two months
column2: but had heard he was away “on business”. Asenath was supposed to be with him
column3: though watchful gossips declared there was someone upstairs in the house behind the doubly curtained windows. They had watched the purchases made by the servants. And now the town marshal of Chesuncook had wired of the draggled madman who stumbled out of the woods with delirious ravings and screamed to me for protection. It was Edward—and he had been just able to recall his own name and my name and address.
