column1: To convey any idea of these monstrosities is impossible. They were of the reptile kind
column2: with body lines suggestion sometimes the crocodile
column3: sometimes the seal
column4: but more often nothing of which either the naturalist or the palaeontologist ever heard. In size they approximated a small man
column5: and their fore-legs bore delicate and evident feet curiously like human hands and fingers. But strangest of all were their heads
column6: which presented a contour violating all known biological principles. To nothing can such things be well compared--in one flash I thought of comparisons as varied as the cat
column7: the bullfrog
column8: the mythic Satyr
column9: and the human being. Not Jove himself had had so colossal and protuberant a forehead
column10: yet the horns and the noselessness and the alligator-like jaw placed things outside all established categories. I debated for a time on the reality of the mummies
column11: half suspecting they were artificial idols; but soon decided they were indeed some palaeogean species which had lived when the nameless city was alive. To crown their grotesqueness
column12: most of them were gorgeously enrobed in the costliest of fabrics
column13: and lavishly laden with ornaments of gold
column14: jewels
column15: and unknown shining metals.

column1: The importance of these crawling creatures must have been vast
column2: for they held first place among the wild designs on the frescoed walls and ceiling. With matchless skill had the artist drawn them in a world of their own
column3: wherein they had cities and gardens fashioned to suit their dimensions; and I could not help but think that their pictured history was allegorical
column4: perhaps showing the progress of the race that worshipped them. These creatures
column5: I said to myself
column6: were to men of the nameless city what the she-wolf was to Rome
column7: or some totem-beast is to a tribe of Indians.

column1: Holding this view
column2: I could trace roughly a wonderful epic of the nameless city; the tale of a mighty seacoast metropolis that ruled the world before Africa rose out of the waves
column3: and of its struggles as the sea shrank away
column4: and the desert crept into the fertile valley that held it. I saw its wars and triumphs
column5: its troubles and defeats
column6: and afterwards its terrible fight against the desert when thousands of its people--here represented in allegory by the grotesque reptiles--were driven to chisel their way down through the rocks in some marvellous manner to another world whereof their prophets had told them. It was all vividly weird and realistic
column7: and its connection with the awesome descent I had made was unmistakable. I even recognized the passages.

column1: As I crept along the corridor toward the brighter light I saw later stages of the painted epic--the leave-taking of the race that had dwelt in the nameless city and the valley around for ten million years; the race whose souls shrank from quitting scenes their bodies had known so long where they had settled as nomads in the earth's youth
column2: hewing in the virgin rock those primal shrines at which they had never ceased to worship. Now that the light was better I studied the pictures more closely and
column3: remembering that the strange reptiles must represent the unknown men
column4: pondered upon the customs of the nameless city. Many things were peculiar and inexplicable. The civilization
column5: which included a written alphabet
column6: had seemingly risen to a higher order than those immeasurably later civilizations of Egypt and Chaldaea
column7: yet there were curious omissions. I could
column8: for example
column9: find no pictures to represent deaths or funeral customs
column10: save such as were related to wars
column11: violence
column12: and plagues; and I wondered at the reticence shown concerning natural death. It was as though an ideal of immortality had been fostered as a cheering illusion.

column1: Still nearer the end of the passage was painted scenes of the utmost picturesqueness and extravagance: contrasted views of the nameless city in its desertion and growing ruin
column2: and of the strange new realm of paradise to which the race had hewed its way through the stone. In these views the city and the desert valley were shewn always by moonlight
column3: golden nimbus hovering over the fallen walls
column4: and half-revealing the splendid perfection of former times
column5: shown spectrally and elusively by the artist. The paradisal scenes were almost too extravagant to be believed
column6: portraying a hidden world of eternal day filled with glorious cities and ethereal hills and valleys. At the very last I thought I saw signs of an artistic anticlimax. The paintings were less skillful
column7: and much more bizarre than even the wildest of the earlier scenes. They seemed to record a slow decadence of the ancient stock
column8: coupled with a growing ferocity toward the outside world from which it was driven by the desert. The forms of the people--always represented by the sacred reptiles--appeared to be gradually wasting away
column9: through their spirit as shewn hovering above the ruins by moonlight gained in proportion. Emaciated priests
column10: displayed as reptiles in ornate robes
column11: cursed the upper air and all who breathed it; and one terrible final scene shewed a primitive-looking man
column12: perhaps a pioneer of ancient Irem
column13: the City of Pillars
column14: torn to pieces by members of the elder race. I remember how the Arabs fear the nameless city
column15: and was glad that beyond this place the grey walls and ceiling were bare.

column1: As I viewed the pageant of mural history I had approached very closely to the end of the low-ceiled hall
column2: and was aware of a gate through which came all of the illuminating phosphorescence. Creeping up to it
column3: I cried aloud in transcendent amazement at what lay beyond; for instead of other and brighter chambers there was only an illimitable void of uniform radiance
column4: such one might fancy when gazing down from the peak of Mount Everest upon a sea of sunlit mist. Behind me was a passage so cramped that I could not stand upright in it; before me was an infinity of subterranean effulgence.

column1: Reaching down from the passage into the abyss was the head of a steep flight of steps--small numerous steps like those of black passages I had traversed--but after a few feet the glowing vapours concealed everything. Swung back open against the left-hand wall of the passage was a massive door of brass
column2: incredibly thick and decorated with fantastic bas-reliefs
column3: which could if closed shut the whole inner world of light away from the vaults and passages of rock. I looked at the step
column4: and for the nonce dared not try them. I touched the open brass door
column5: and could not move it. Then I sank prone to the stone floor
column6: my mind aflame with prodigious reflections which not even a death-like exhaustion could banish.

column1: As I lay still with closed eyes
column2: free to ponder
column3: many things I had lightly noted in the frescoes came back to me with new and terrible significance--scenes representing the nameless city in its heyday--the vegetations of the valley around it
column4: and the distant lands with which its merchants traded. The allegory of the crawling creatures puzzled me by its universal prominence
column5: and I wondered that it would be so closely followed in a pictured history of such importance. In the frescoes the nameless city had been shewn in proportions fitted to the reptiles. I wondered what its real proportions and magnificence had been
column6: and reflected a moment on certain oddities I had noticed in the ruins. I thought curiously of the lowness of the primal temples and of the underground corridor
column7: which were doubtless hewn thus out of deference to the reptile deities there honoured; though it perforce reduced the worshippers to crawling. Perhaps the very rites here involved crawling in imitation of the creatures. No religious theory
column8: however
column9: could easily explain why the level passages in that awesome descent should be as low as the temples--or lower
column10: since one could not even kneel in it. As I thought of the crawling creatures
column11: whose hideous mummified forms were so close to me
column12: I felt a new throb of fear. Mental associations are curious
column13: and I shrank from the idea that except for the poor primitive man torn to pieces in the last painting
column14: mine was the only human form amidst the many relics and symbols of the primordial life.

column1: But as always in my strange and roving existence
column2: wonder soon drove out fear; for the luminous abyss and what it might contain presented a problem worthy of the greatest explorer that a weird world of mystery lay far down that flight of peculiarly small steps I could not doubt
column3: and I hoped to find there those human memorials which the painted corridor had failed to give. The frescoes had pictured unbelievable cities
column4: and valleys in this lower realm
column5: and my fancy dwelt on the rich and colossal ruins that awaited me.

column1: My fears
column2: indeed
column3: concerned the past rather than the future. Not even the physical horror of my position in that cramped corridor of dead reptiles and antediluvian frescoes
column4: miles below the world I knew and faced by another world of eery light and mist
column5: could match the lethal dread I felt at the abysmal antiquity of the scene and its soul. An ancientness so vast that measurement is feeble seemed to leer down from the primal stones and rock-hewn temples of the nameless city
column6: while the very latest of the astounding maps in the frescoes shewed oceans and continents that man has forgotten
column7: with only here and there some vaguely familiar outlines. Of what could have happened in the geological ages since the paintings ceased and the death-hating race resentfully succumbed to decay
column8: no man might say. Life had once teemed in these caverns and in the luminous realm beyond; now I was alone with vivid relics
column9: and I trembled to think of the countless ages through which these relics had kept a silent deserted vigil.

column1: Suddenly there came another burst of that acute fear which had intermittently seized me ever since I first saw the terrible valley and the nameless city under a cold moon
column2: and despite my exhaustion I found myself starting frantically to a sitting posture and gazing back along the black corridor toward the tunnels that rose to the outer world. My sensations were like those which had made me shun the nameless city at night
column3: and were as inexplicable as they were poignant. In another moment
column4: however
column5: I received a still greater shock in the form of a definite sound--the first which had broken the utter silence of these tomb-like depths. It was a deep
column6: low moaning
column7: as of a distant throng of condemned spirits
column8: and came from the direction in which I was staring. Its volume rapidly grew
column9: till it soon reverberated rightfully through the low passage
column10: and at the same time I became conscious of an increasing draught of old air
column11: likewise flowing from the tunnels and the city above. The touch of this air seemed to restore my balance
column12: for I instantly recalled the sudden gusts which had risen around the mouth of the abyss each sunset and sunrise
column13: one of which had indeed revealed the hidden tunnels to me. I looked at my watch and saw that sunrise was near
column14: so bracing myself to resist the gale that was sweeping down to its cavern home as it had swept forth at evening. My fear again waned low
column15: since a natural phenomenon tends to dispel broodings over the unknown.

column1: More and more madly poured the shrieking
column2: moaning night wind into the gulf of the inner earth. I dropped prone again and clutched vainly at the floor for fear of being swept bodily through the open gate into the phosphorescent abyss. Such fury I had not expected
column3: and as I grew aware of an actual slipping of my form toward the abyss I was beset by a thousand new terrors of apprehension and imagination. The malignancy of the blast awakened incredible fancies; once more I compared myself shudderingly to the only human image in that frightful corridor
column4: the man who was torn to pieces by the nameless race
column5: for in the fiendish clawing of the swirling currents there seemed to abide a vindictive rage all the stronger because it was largely impotent. I think I screamed frantically near the last--I was almost mad--of the howling wind-wraiths. I tried to crawl against the murderous invisible torrent
column6: but I could not even hold my own as I was pushed slowly and inexorably toward the unknown world. Finally reason must have wholly snapped; for I fell babbling over and over that unexplainable couplet of the mad Arab Alhazred
column7: who dreamed of the nameless city:

column1: That is not dead which can eternal lie
column2: And with strange aeons even death may die.

column1: Only the grim brooding desert gods know what really took place--what indescribable struggles and scrambles in the dark I endured or what Abaddon guided me back to life
column2: where I must always remember and shiver in the night wind till oblivion--or worse--claims me. Monstrous
column3: unnatural
column4: colossal
column5: was the thing--too far beyond all the ideas of man to be believed except in the silent damnable small hours of the morning when one cannot sleep.

column1: I have said that the fury of the rushing blast was infernal-- cacodaemoniacal--and that its voices were hideous with the pent-up viciousness of desolate eternities. Presently these voices
column2: while still chaotic before me
column3: seemed to my beating brain to take articulate form behind me; and down there in the grave of unnumbered aeon-dead antiquities
column4: leagues below the dawn-lit world of men
column5: I heard the ghastly cursing and snarling of strange-tongued fiends. Turning
column6: I saw outlined against the luminous aether of the abyss that could not be seen against the dusk of the corridor--a nightmare horde of rushing devils; hate distorted
column7: grotesquely panoplied
column8: half transparent devils of a race no man might mistake--the crawling reptiles of the nameless city.

column1: And as the wind died away I was plunged into the ghoul-pooled darkness of earth's bowels; for behind the last of the creatures the great brazen door clanged shut with a deafening peal of metallic music whose reverberations swelled out to the distant world to hail the rising sun as Memnon hails it from the banks of the Nile.
I.
It is true that I have sent six bullets through the head of my best friend
column2: and yet I hope to shew by this statement that I am not his murderer. At first I shall be called a madman—madder than the man I shot in his cell at the Arkham Sanitarium. Later some of my readers will weigh each statement
column3: correlate it with the known facts
column4: and ask themselves how I could have believed otherwise than as I did after facing the evidence of that horror—that thing on the doorstep.

column1: Until then I also saw nothing but madness in the wild tales I have acted on. Even now I ask myself whether I was misled—or whether I am not mad after all. I do not know—but others have strange things to tell of Edward and Asenath Derby
column2: and even the stolid police are at their wits’ ends to account for that last terrible visit. They have tried weakly to concoct a theory of a ghastly jest or warning by discharged servants
column3: yet they know in their hearts that the truth is something infinitely more terrible and incredible.

column1: So I say that I have not murdered Edward Derby. Rather have I avenged him
column2: and in so doing purged the earth of a horror whose survival might have loosed untold terrors on all mankind. There are black zones of shadow close to our daily paths
column3: and now and then some evil soul breaks a passage through. When that happens
column4: the man who knows must strike before reckoning the consequences.

column1: I have known Edward Pickman Derby all his life. Eight years my junior
column2: he was so precocious that we had much in common from the time he was eight and I sixteen. He was the most phenomenal child scholar I have ever known
column3: and at seven was writing verse of a sombre
column4: fantastic
column5: almost morbid cast which astonished the tutors surrounding him. Perhaps his private education and coddled seclusion had something to do with his premature flowering. An only child
column6: he had organic weaknesses which startled his doting parents and caused them to keep him closely chained to their side. He was never allowed out without his nurse
column7: and seldom had a chance to play unconstrainedly with other children. All this doubtless fostered a strange
column8: secretive inner life in the boy
column9: with imagination as his one avenue of freedom.

column1: At any rate
column2: his juvenile learning was prodigious and bizarre; and his facile writings such as to captivate me despite my greater age. About that time I had leanings toward art of a somewhat grotesque cast
column3: and I found in this younger child a rare kindred spirit. What lay behind our joint love of shadows and marvels was
column4: no doubt
column5: the ancient
column6: mouldering
column7: and subtly fearsome town in which we lived—witch-cursed
column8: legend-haunted Arkham
column9: whose huddled
column10: sagging gambrel roofs and crumbling Georgian balustrades brood out the centuries beside the darkly muttering Miskatonic.

column1: As time went by I turned to architecture and gave up my design of illustrating a book of Edward’s daemoniac poems
column2: yet our comradeship suffered no lessening. Young Derby’s odd genius developed remarkably
column3: and in his eighteenth year his collected nightmare-lyrics made a real sensation when issued under the title Azathoth and Other Horrors. He was a close correspondent of the notorious Baudelairean poet Justin Geoffrey
column4: who wrote The People of the Monolith and died screaming in a madhouse in 1926 after a visit to a sinister
column5: ill-regarded village in Hungary.

column1: In self-reliance and practical affairs
column2: however
column3: Derby was greatly retarded because of his coddled existence. His health had improved
column4: but his habits of childish dependence were fostered by overcareful parents; so that he never travelled alone
column5: made independent decisions
column6: or assumed responsibilities. It was early seen that he would not be equal to a struggle in the business or professional arena
column7: but the family fortune was so ample that this formed no tragedy. As he grew to years of manhood he retained a deceptive aspect of boyishness. Blond and blue-eyed
column8: he had the fresh complexion of a child; and his attempts to raise a moustache were discernible only with difficulty. His voice was soft and light
column9: and his pampered
column10: unexercised life gave him a juvenile chubbiness rather than the paunchiness of premature middle age. He was of good height
column11: and his handsome face would have made him a notable gallant had not his shyness held him to seclusion and bookishness.

column1: Derby’s parents took him abroad every summer
column2: and he was quick to seize on the surface aspects of European thought and expression. His Poe-like talents turned more and more toward the decadent
column3: and other artistic sensitivenesses and yearnings were half-aroused in him. We had great discussions in those days. I had been through Harvard
column4: had studied in a Boston architect’s office
column5: had married
column6: and had finally returned to Arkham to practice my profession—settling in the family homestead in Saltonstall St. since my father had moved to Florida for his health. Edward used to call almost every evening
column7: till I came to regard him as one of the household. He had a characteristic way of ringing the doorbell or sounding the knocker that grew to be a veritable code signal
column8: so that after dinner I always listened for the familiar three brisk strokes followed by two more after a pause. Less frequently I would visit at his house and note with envy the obscure volumes in his constantly growing library.

column1: Derby went through Miskatonic University in Arkham
column2: since his parents would not let him board away from them. He entered at sixteen and completed his course in three years
column3: majoring in English and French literature and receiving high marks in everything but mathematics and the sciences. He mingled very little with the other students
column4: though looking enviously at the “daring” or “Bohemian” set—whose superficially “smart” language and meaninglessly ironic pose he aped
column5: and whose dubious conduct he wished he dared adopt.

column1: What he did do was to become an almost fanatical devotee of subterranean magical lore
column2: for which Miskatonic’s library was and is famous. Always a dweller on the surface of phantasy and strangeness
column3: he now delved deep into the actual runes and riddles left by a fabulous past for the guidance or puzzlement of posterity. He read things like the frightful Book of Eibon
column4: the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt
column5: and the forbidden Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred
column6: though he did not tell his parents he had seen them. Edward was twenty when my son and only child was born
column7: and seemed pleased when I named the newcomer Edward Derby Upton
column8: after him.

column1: By the time he was twenty-five Edward Derby was a prodigiously learned man and a fairly well-known poet and fantaisiste
column2: though his lack of contacts and responsibilities had slowed down his literary growth by making his products derivative and overbookish. I was perhaps his closest friend—finding him an inexhaustible mine of vital theoretical topics
column3: while he relied on me for advice in whatever matters he did not wish to refer to his parents. He remained single—more through shyness
column4: inertia
column5: and parental protectiveness than through inclination—and moved in society only to the slightest and most perfunctory extent. When the war came both health and ingrained timidity kept him at home. I went to Plattsburg for a commission
column6: but never got overseas.

column1: So the years wore on. Edward’s mother died when he was thirty-four
column2: and for months he was incapacitated by some odd psychological malady. His father took him to Europe
column3: however
column4: and he managed to pull out of his trouble without visible effects. Afterward he seemed to feel a sort of grotesque exhilaration
column5: as if of partial escape from some unseen bondage. He began to mingle in the more “advanced” college set despite his middle age
column6: and was present at some extremely wild doings—on one occasion paying heavy blackmail (which he borrowed of me) to keep his presence at a certain affair from his father’s notice. Some of the whispered rumours about the wild Miskatonic set were extremely singular. There was even talk of black magic and of happenings utterly beyond credibility.

column1: II.
Edward was thirty-eight when he met Asenath Waite. She was
column2: I judge
column3: about twenty-three at the time; and was taking a special course in mediaeval metaphysics at Miskatonic. The daughter of a friend of mine had met her before—in the Hall School at Kingsport—and had been inclined to shun her because of her odd reputation. She was dark
column4: smallish
column5: and very good-looking except for overprotuberant eyes; but something in her expression alienated extremely sensitive people. It was
column6: however
column7: largely her origin and conversation which caused average folk to avoid her. She was one of the Innsmouth Waites
column8: and dark legends have clustered for generations about crumbling
column9: half-deserted Innsmouth and its people. There are tales of horrible bargains about the year 1850
column10: and of a strange element “not quite human” in the ancient families of the run-down fishing port—tales such as only old-time Yankees can devise and repeat with proper awesomeness.

column1: Asenath’s case was aggravated by the fact that she was Ephraim Waite’s daughter—the child of his old age by an unknown wife who always went veiled. Ephraim lived in a half-decayed mansion in Washington Street
column2: Innsmouth
column3: and those who had seen the place (Arkham folk avoid going to Innsmouth whenever they can) declared that the attic windows were always boarded
column4: and that strange sounds sometimes floated from within as evening drew on. The old man was known to have been a prodigious magical student in his day
column5: and legend averred that he could raise or quell storms at sea according to his whim. I had seen him once or twice in my youth as he came to Arkham to consult forbidden tomes at the college library
column6: and had hated his wolfish
column7: saturnine face with its tangle of iron-grey beard. He had died insane—under rather queer circumstances—just before his daughter (by his will made a nominal ward of the principal) entered the Hall School

column1: The friend whose daughter had gone to school with Asenath Waite repeated many curious things when the news of Edward’s acquaintance with her began to spread about. Asenath
column2: it seemed
column3: had posed as a kind of magician at school; and had really seemed able to accomplish some highly baffling marvels. She professed to be able to raise thunderstorms
column4: though her seeming success was generally laid to some uncanny knack at prediction. All animals markedly disliked her
column5: and she could make any dog howl by certain motions of her right hand. There were times when she displayed snatches of knowledge and language very singular—and very shocking—for a young girl; when she would frighten her schoolmates with leers and winks of an inexplicable kind
column6: and would seem to extract an obscene and zestful irony from her present situation.

column1: Most unusual
column2: though
column3: were the well-attested cases of her influence over other persons. She was
column4: beyond question
column5: a genuine hypnotist. By gazing peculiarly at a fellow-student she would often give the latter a distinct feeling of exchanged personality—as if the subject were placed momentarily in the magician’s body and able to stare half across the room at her real body
column6: whose eyes blazed and protruded with an alien expression. Asenath often made wild claims about the nature of consciousness and about its independence of the physical frame—or at least from the life-processes of the physical frame. Her crowning rage
column7: however
column8: was that she was not a man; since she believed a male brain had certain unique and far-reaching cosmic powers. Given a man’s brain
column9: she declared
column10: she could not only equal but surpass her father in mastery of unknown forces.

column1: Edward met Asenath at a gathering of “intelligentsia” held in one of the students’ rooms
column2: and could talk of nothing else when he came to see me the next day. He had found her full of the interests and erudition which engrossed him most
column3: and was in addition wildly taken with her appearance. I had never seen the young woman
column4: and recalled casual references only faintly
column5: but I knew who she was. It seemed rather regrettable that Derby should become so upheaved about her; but I said nothing to discourage him
column6: since infatuation thrives on opposition. He was not
column7: he said
column8: mentioning her to his father.

column1: In the next few weeks I heard of very little but Asenath from young Derby. Others now remarked Edward’s autumnal gallantry
column2: though they agreed that he did not look even nearly his actual age
column3: or seem at all inappropriate as an escort for his bizarre divinity. He was only a trifle paunchy despite his indolence and self-indulgence
column4: and his face was absolutely without lines. Asenath
column5: on the other hand
column6: had the premature crow’s feet which come from the exercise of an intense will.

column1: About this time Edward brought the girl to call on me
column2: and I at once saw that his interest was by no means one-sided. She eyed him continually with an almost predatory air
column3: and I perceived that their intimacy was beyond untangling. Soon afterward I had a visit from old Mr. Derby
column4: whom I had always admired and respected. He had heard the tales of his son’s new friendship
column5: and had wormed the whole truth out of “the boy”. Edward meant to marry Asenath
column6: and had even been looking at houses in the suburbs. Knowing my usually great influence with his son
column7: the father wondered if I could help to break the ill-advised affair off; but I regretfully expressed my doubts. This time it was not a question of Edward’s weak will but of the woman’s strong will. The perennial child had transferred his dependence from the parental image to a new and stronger image

column1: The wedding was performed a month later—by a justice of the peace
column2: according to the bride’s request. Mr. Derby
column3: at my advice
column4: offered no opposition; and he
column5: my wife
column6: my son
column7: and I attended the brief ceremony—the other guests being wild young people from the college. Asenath had bought the old Crowninshield place in the country at the end of High Street
column8: and they proposed to settle there after a short trip to Innsmouth
column9: whence three servants and some books and household goods were to be brought. It was probably not so much consideration for Edward and his father as a personal wish to be near the college

column11: and its crowd of “sophisticates”
column12: that made Asenath settle in Arkham instead of returning permanently home.

column1: When Edward called on me after the honeymoon I thought he looked slightly changed. Asenath had made him get rid of the undeveloped moustache
column2: but there was more than that. He looked soberer and more thoughtful
column3: his habitual pout of childish rebelliousness being exchanged for a look almost of genuine sadness. I was puzzled to decide whether I liked or disliked the change. Certainly
column4: he seemed for the moment more normally adult than ever before. Perhaps the marriage was a good thing—might not the change of dependence form a start toward actual neutralisation
column5: leading ultimately to responsible independence? He came alone
column6: for Asenath was very busy. She had brought a vast store of books and apparatus from Innsmouth (Derby shuddered as he spoke the name)
column7: and was finishing the restoration of the Crowninshield house and grounds.

column1: Her home in—that town—was a rather disquieting place
column2: but certain objects in it had taught him some surprising things. He was progressing fast in esoteric lore now that he had Asenath’s guidance. Some of the experiments she proposed were very daring and radical—he did not feel at liberty to describe them—but he had confidence in her powers and intentions. The three servants were very queer—an incredibly aged couple who had been with old Ephraim and referred occasionally to him and to Asenath’s dead mother in a cryptic way
column3: and a swarthy young wench who had marked anomalies of feature and seemed to exude a perpetual odour of fish.

column1: III.
For the next two years I saw less and less of Derby. A fortnight would sometimes slip by without the familiar three-and-two strokes at the front door; and when he did call—or when
column2: as happened with increasing infrequency
column3: I called on him—he was very little disposed to converse on vital topics. He had become secretive about those occult studies which he used to describe and discuss so minutely
column4: and preferred not to talk of his wife. She had aged tremendously since her marriage
column5: till now—oddly enough—she seemed the elder of the two. Her face held the most concentratedly determined expression I had ever seen
column6: and her whole aspect seemed to gain a vague
column7: unplaceable repulsiveness. My wife and son noticed it as much as I
column8: and we all ceased gradually to call on her—for which
column9: Edward admitted in one of his boyishly tactless moments
column10: she was unmitigatedly grateful. Occasionally the Derbys would go on long trips—ostensibly to Europe
column11: though Edward sometimes hinted at obscurer destinations.

column1: It was after the first year that people began talking about the change in Edward Derby. It was very casual talk
column2: for the change was purely psychological; but it brought up some interesting points. Now and then
column3: it seemed
column4: Edward was observed to wear an expression and to do things wholly incompatible with his usual flabby nature. For example—although in the old days he could not drive a car

This was the person who had driven my car through the night five months before—the person I had not seen since that brief call when he had forgotten the old-time doorbell signal and stirred such nebulous fears in me—and now he filled me with the same dim feeling of blasphemous alienage and ineffable cosmic hideousness.

column1: EN205\"﻿During the winter of 1927-28 officials of the Federal government made a strange and secret investigation of certain conditions in the ancient Massachusetts seaport of Innsmouth. The public first learned of it in February
column2: when a vast series of raids and arrests occurred
column3: followed by the deliberate burning and dynamiting--under suitable precautions--of an enormous number of crumbling
column4: worm-eaten
column5: and supposedly empty houses along the abandoned waterfront. Uninquiring souls let this occurrence pass as one of the major clashes in a spasmodic war on liquor.

column1: Keener news-followers
column2: however
column3: wondered at the prodigious number of arrests
column4: the abnormally large force of men used in making them
column5: and the secrecy surrounding the disposal of the prisoners. No trials
column6: or even definite charges were reported; nor were any of the captives seen thereafter in the regular gaols of the nation. There were vague statements about disease and concentration camps

column1: Piecing together the scattered records

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape

Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years

column5: were freely spoken of. Indeed

column1: But most of the tales and impressions concerned a relatively late race
column2: of a queer and intricate shape resembling no life-form known to science

column4: they indicated

column1: In its vast libraries were volumes of texts and pictures holding the whole of earth’s annals—histories and descriptions of every species that had ever been or that ever would be

column3: their achievements
column4: their languages
column5: and their psychologies. With this aeon-embracing knowledge
column6: the Great Race chose from every era and life-form such thoughts

column1: In the latter case the course was easier and more material. With suitable mechanical aid a mind would project itself forward in time
column2: feeling its dim
column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then
column4: after preliminary trials
column5: it would seize on the best discoverable representative of the highest of that period’s life-forms; entering the organism’s brain and setting up therein its own vibrations while the displaced mind would strike back to the period of the displacer
column6: remaining in the latter’s body till a reverse process was set up. The projected mind
column7: in the body of the organism of the future
column8: would then pose as a member of the race whose outward form it wore; learning as quickly as possible all that could be learned of the chosen age and its massed information and techniques.

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body
column3: would be carefully guarded. It would be kept from harming the body it occupied
column4: and would be drained of all its knowledge by trained questioners. Often it could be questioned in its own language
column5: when previous quests into the future had brought back records of that language. If the mind came from a body whose language the Great Race could not physically reproduce
column6: clever machines would be made
column7: on which the alien speech could be played as on a musical instrument. The Great Race’s members were immense rugose cones ten feet high
column8: and with head and other organs attached to foot-thick

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off
column2: and when (assuming that it came from a body vastly different from the Great Race’s) it had lost its horror at its unfamiliar temporary form
column3: it was permitted to study its new environment and experience a wonder and wisdom approximating that of its displacer. With suitable precautions
column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen
column7: and to such minds the unveiling of hidden mysteries of earth—closed chapters of inconceivable pasts and dizzying vortices of future time which include the years ahead of their own natural ages—forms always
column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times
column4: great disasters. And it was largely in consequence of two cases of the kind (said the old myths) that mankind had learned what it had concerning the Great Race. Of all things surviving physically and directly from that aeon-distant world
column5: there remained only certain ruins of great stones in far places and under the sea
column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated
column2: so that in most cases only a dream-shadowed blank stretched back to the time of the first exchange. Some minds recalled more than others
column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be
column7: while the myriad minds sent backward were left to die in the horror of strange shapes. Later the race would again face death
column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations

Suppose I did see strange things at night? These were only what I had heard and read of. Suppose I did have odd loathings and perspectives and pseudo-memories? These

column6: though shewing no physical variation

column9: I fancied
column10: used our own familiar alphabet. Most of them worked much more slowly than the general mass of the entities.

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August
column4: did any suggestions of bodily existence begin to harass me. I say harass
column5: because the first phase was a purely abstract though infinitely terrible association of my previously noted body-loathing with the scenes of my visions. For a while my chief concern during dreams was to avoid looking down at myself

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking
column8: I could recall only minute and meaningless scraps of the unknown tongues which my dream-self had mastered

column1: I learned—even before my waking self had studied the parallel cases or the old myths from which the dreams doubtless sprang—that the entities around me were of the world’s greatest race
column2: which had conquered time and had sent exploring minds into every age. I knew
column3: too
column4: that I had been snatched from my age while another used my body in that age
column5: and that a few of the other strange forms housed similarly captured minds. I seemed to talk
column6: in some odd language of claw-clickings
column7: with exiled intellects from every corner of the solar system.

column1: There was a mind from the planet we know as Venus
column2: which would live incalculable epochs to come
column3: and one from an outer moon of Jupiter six million years in the past. Of earthly minds there were some from the winged

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations

column1: The blackfellows have always been full of talk about “great stones with marks on them”
column2: and seem to have a terrible fear of such things. They connect them in some way with their common racial legends about Buddai
column3: the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm
column4: and who will some day awake and eat up the world. There are some very old and half-forgotten tales of enormous underground huts of great stones
column5: where passages lead down and down
column6: and where horrible things have happened. The blackfellows claim that once some warriors
column7: fleeing in battle
column8: went down into one and never came back
column9: but that frightful winds began to blow from the place soon after they went down. However
column10: there usually isn’t much in what these natives say.

column1: But what I have to tell is more than this. Two years ago

column4: and weathered and pitted to the very limit. At first I couldn’t find any of the marks the blackfellows told about

column1: When I saw some

column4: and will enclose the prints for you to see. I turned my information and pictures over to the government at Perth
column5: but they have done nothing with them. Then I met Dr. Boyle

column7: and in time happened to mention the stones. He was enormously interested

column1: Now I can understand how important all this will be to you. Without question we are faced with the remains of an unknown civilisation older than any dreamed of before
column2: and forming a basis for your legends. As a mining engineer
column3: I have some knowledge of geology
column4: and can tell you that these blocks are so ancient they frighten me. They are mostly sandstone and granite

column6: as if this part of the world had been submerged and come up again after long ages—all since these blocks were made and used. It is a matter of hundreds of thousands of years—or heaven knows how much more. I don’t like to think about it.

column1: In view of your previous diligent work in tracking down the legends and everything connected with them
column2: I cannot doubt but that you will want to lead an expedition to the desert and make some archaeological excavations. Both Dr. Boyle and I are prepared to coöperate in such work if you—or organisations known to you—can furnish the funds. I can get together a dozen miners for the heavy digging—the blacks would be of no use
column3: for I’ve found that they have an almost maniacal fear of this particular spot. Boyle and I are saying nothing to others
column4: for you very obviously ought to have precedence in any discoveries or credit.

column1: The place can be reached from Pilbarra in about 4 days by motor tractor—which we’d need for our apparatus. It is somewhat west and south of Warburton’s path of 1873
column2: and 100 miles southeast of Joanna Spring. We could float things up the De Grey River instead of starting from Pilbarra—but all that can be talked over later. Roughly
column3: the stones lie at a point about 22° 3' 14"" South Latitude
column4: 125° 0' 39"" East Longitude. The climate is tropical
column5: and the desert conditions are trying. Any expedition had better be made in winter—June or July or August. I shall welcome further correspondence upon this subject
column6: and am keenly eager to assist in any plan you may devise. After studying your articles I am deeply impressed with the profound significance of the whole matter. Dr. Boyle will write later. When rapid communication is needed
column7: a cable to Perth can be relayed by wireless.

column1: Hoping profoundly for an early message
Believe me
Most faithfully yours
Robert B. F. Mackenzie.
Of the immediate aftermath of this letter

column5: printed reports were sparing; but enough appeared to tell of our quest for reported Australian ruins and to chronicle our various preparatory steps.

column1: Discomfort and expectancy were oddly mingled in most of us when at length our party of eighteen rattled forth over the arid leagues of sand and rock. On Friday
column2: May 31st
column3: we forded a branch of the De Grey and entered the realm of utter desolation. A certain positive terror grew on me as we advanced to this actual site of the elder world behind the legends—a terror of course abetted by the fact that my disturbing dreams and pseudo-memories still beset me with unabated force.

column1: It was on Monday
column2: June 3
column3: that we saw the first of the half-buried blocks. I cannot describe the emotions with which I actually touched—in objective reality—a fragment of Cyclopean masonry in every respect like the blocks in the walls of my dream-buildings. There was a distinct trace of carving—and my hands trembled as I recognised part of a curvilinear decorative scheme made hellish to me through years of tormenting nightmare and baffling research.

column1: A month of digging brought a total of some 1250 blocks in varying stages of wear and disintegration. Most of these were carven megaliths with curved tops and bottoms. A minority were smaller
column2: flatter
column3: plain-surfaced

column6: though

column1: Sometimes
column2: on these walks

column1: An indication of my poor nervous health can be gained from my response to an odd discovery which I made on one of my nocturnal rambles. It was on the evening of July 11th

column6: this one was perfectly square-cut

column8: too

column1: Suddenly I rose
column2: turned
column3: and ran for the camp at top speed. It was a wholly unconscious and irrational flight

column7: half-material
column8: alien Things that festered in earth’s nether abysses and against whose wind-like

column6: Boyle
column7: my son

column1: VI.

I come now to the crucial and most difficult part of my narrative—all the more difficult because I cannot be quite certain of its reality. At times I feel uncomfortably sure that I was not dreaming or deluded; and it is this feeling—in view of the stupendous implications which the objective truth of my experience would raise—which impels me to make this record. My son—a trained psychologist with the fullest and most sympathetic knowledge of my whole case—shall be the primary judge of what I have to tell.
First let me outline the externals of the matter
column2: as those at the camp know them. On the night of July 17–18
column3: after a windy day
column4: I retired early but could not sleep. Rising shortly before eleven
column5: and afflicted as usual with that strange feeling regarding the northeastward terrain
column6: I set out on one of my typical nocturnal walks; seeing and greeting only one person—an Australian miner named Tupper—as I left our precincts. The moon
column7: slightly past full
column8: shone from a clear sky and drenched the ancient sands with a white
column9: leprous radiance which seemed to me somehow infinitely evil. There was no longer any wind
column10: nor did any return for nearly five hours
column11: as amply attested by Tupper and others who did not sleep through the night. The Australian last saw me walking rapidly across the pallid
column12: secret-guarding hillocks toward the northeast.

column1: About 3:30 a.m. a violent wind blew up
column2: waking everyone in camp and felling three of the tents. The sky was unclouded
column3: and the desert still blazed with that leprous moonlight. As the party saw to the tents my absence was noted
column4: but in view of my previous walks this circumstance gave no one alarm. And yet as many as three men—all Australians—seemed to feel something sinister in the air. Mackenzie explained to Prof. Freeborn that this was a fear picked up from blackfellow folklore—the natives having woven a curious fabric of malignant myth about the high winds which at long intervals sweep across the sands under a clear sky. Such winds
column5: it is whispered
column6: blow out of the great stone huts under the ground where terrible things have happened—and are never felt except near places where the big marked stones are scattered. Close to four the gale subsided as suddenly as it had begun
column7: leaving the sand hills in new and unfamiliar shapes.

column1: It was just past five
column2: with the bloated
column3: fungoid moon sinking in the west
column4: when I staggered into camp—hatless
column5: tattered
column6: features scratched and ensanguined
column7: and without my electric torch. Most of the men had returned to bed

column11: roused by the stir

column1: But there was no sleep for me. My psychological state was very extraordinary—different from anything I had previously suffered. After a time I insisted upon talking—nervously and elaborately explaining my condition. I told them I had become fatigued
column2: and had lain down in the sand for a nap. There had
column3: I said
column4: been dreams even more frightful than usual—and when I was awaked by the sudden high wind my overwrought nerves had snapped. I had fled in panic
column5: frequently falling over half-buried stones and thus gaining my tattered and bedraggled aspect. I must have slept long—hence the hours of my absence.

column1: Of anything strange either seen or experienced I hinted absolutely nothing—exercising the greatest self-control in that respect. But I spoke of a change of mind regarding the whole work of the expedition
column2: and earnestly urged a halt in all digging toward the northeast. My reasoning was patently weak—for I mentioned a dearth of blocks
column3: a wish not to offend the superstitious miners

column1: The next day I was up and around the camp
column2: but took no part in the excavations. Seeing that I could not stop the work
column3: I decided to return home as soon as possible for the sake of my nerves
column4: and made my son promise to fly me in the plane to Perth—a thousand miles to the southwest—as soon as he had surveyed the region I wished let alone. If
column5: I reflected
column6: the thing I had seen was still visible
column7: I might decide to attempt a specific warning even at the cost of ridicule. It was just conceivable that the miners who knew the local folklore might back me up. Humouring me

It was the case of the anomalous basalt block all over again—the shifting sand had wiped out every trace. For an instant I half regretted having lost a certain awesome object in my stark fright—but now I know that the loss was merciful. I can still believe my whole experience an illusion—especially if
column9: as I devoutly hope
column10: that hellish abyss is never found.

column1: Wingate took me to Perth July 20
column2: though declining to abandon the expedition and return home. He stayed with me until the 25th

column4: in the cabin of the Empress
column5: I am pondering long and frantically on the entire matter
column6: and have decided that my son at least must be informed. It shall rest with him whether to diffuse the matter more widely. In order to meet any eventuality I have prepared this summary of my background—as already known in a scattered way to others—and will now tell as briefly as possible what seemed to happen during my absence from the camp that hideous night.

column1: Nerves on edge
column2: and whipped into a kind of perverse eagerness by that inexplicable
column3: dread-mingled
column4: pseudo-mnemonic urge toward the northeast
column5: I plodded on beneath the evil
column6: burning moon. Here and there I saw
column7: half-shrouded by the sand
column8: those primal Cyclopean blocks left from nameless and forgotten aeons. The incalculable age and brooding horror of this monstrous waste began to oppress me as never before
column9: and I could not keep from thinking of my maddening dreams
column10: of the frightful legends which lay behind them
column11: and of the present fears of natives and miners concerning the desert and its carven stones.

column1: And yet I plodded on as if to some eldritch rendezvous—more and more assailed by bewildering fancies
column2: compulsions
column3: and pseudo-memories. I thought of some of the possible contours of the lines of stones as seen by my son from the air

column1: The night was windless
column2: and the pallid sand curved upward and downward like frozen waves of the sea. I had no goal

column4: so that each sand-embedded megalith seemed part of endless rooms and corridors of pre-human masonry

column1: I do not know how long or how far—or indeed
column2: in just what direction—I had walked when I first spied the heap of blocks bared by the day’s wind. It was the largest group in one place that I had so far seen
column3: and so sharply did it impress me that the visions of fabulous aeons faded suddenly away. Again there were only the desert and the evil moon and the shards of an unguessed past. I drew close and paused
column4: and cast the added light of my electric torch over the tumbled pile. A hillock had blown away
column5: leaving a low
column6: irregularly round mass of megaliths and smaller fragments some forty feet across and from two to eight feet high.

column1: From the very outset I realised that there was some utterly unprecedented quality about these stones. Not only was the mere number of them quite without parallel

Not that any one differed essentially from the earlier specimens we had found. It was something subtler than that. The impression did not come when I looked at one block alone
column3: but only when I ran my eye over several almost simultaneously. Then
column4: at last
column5: the truth dawned upon me. The curvilinear patterns on many of these blocks were closely related—parts of one vast decorative conception. For the first time in this aeon-shaken waste I had come upon a mass of masonry in its old position—tumbled and fragmentary
column6: it is true
column7: but none the less existing in a very definite sense.

column1: Mounting at a low place
column2: I clambered laboriously over the heap; here and there clearing away the sand with my fingers
column3: and constantly striving to interpret varieties of size
column4: shape
column5: and style
column6: and relationships of design. After a while I could vaguely guess at the nature of the bygone structure
column7: and at the designs which had once stretched over the vast surfaces of the primal masonry. The perfect identity of the whole with some of my dream-glimpses appalled and unnerved me. This was once a Cyclopean corridor thirty feet tall
column8: paved with octagonal blocks and solidly vaulted overhead. There would have been rooms opening off on the right
column9: and at the farther end one of those strange inclined planes would have wound down to still lower depths.

column1: I started violently as these conceptions occurred to me
column2: for there was more in them than the blocks themselves had supplied. How did I know that this level should have been far underground? How did I know that the plane leading upward should have been behind me? How did I know that the long subterrene passage to the Square of Pillars ought to lie on the left one level above me? How did I know that the room of machines
column3: and the rightward-leading tunnel to the central archives
column4: ought to lie two levels below? How did I know that there would be one of those horrible
column5: metal-banded trap-doors at the very bottom
column6: four levels down? Bewildered by this intrusion from the dream-world
column7: I found myself shaking and bathed in a cold perspiration.

column1: Then
column2: as a last
column3: intolerable touch
column4: I felt that faint
column5: insidious stream of cool air trickling upward from a depressed place near the centre of the huge heap. Instantly
column6: as once before
column7: my visions faded
column8: and I saw again only the evil moonlight
column9: the brooding desert
column10: and the spreading tumulus of palaeogean masonry. Something real and tangible
column11: yet fraught with infinite suggestions of nighted mystery

column1: My first thought was of the sinister blackfellow legends of vast underground huts among the megaliths where horrors happen and great winds are born. Then thoughts of my own dreams came back

column3: inconceivable source of age-old myth-cycles and haunting nightmares might I be on the brink of uncovering? It was only for a moment that I hesitated

column1: I seemed to move almost automatically

column3: and struggling with a strength that I had not thought I possessed
column4: I wrenched aside first one titan fragment of stone and then another
column5: till there welled up a strong draught whose dampness contrasted oddly with the desert’s dry air. A black rift began to yawn

column1: I drew out my torch and cast a brilliant beam into the opening. Below me was a chaos of tumbled masonry
column2: sloping roughly down toward the north at an angle of about forty-five degrees
column3: and evidently the result of some bygone collapse from above. Between its surface and the ground level was a gulf of impenetrable blackness at whose upper edge were signs of gigantic
column4: stress-heaved vaulting. At this point
column5: it appeared

column1: In retrospect
column2: the barest idea of a sudden
column3: lone descent into such a doubtful abyss—and at a time when one’s whereabouts were unknown to any living soul—seems like the utter apex of insanity. Perhaps it was—yet that night I embarked without hesitancy upon such a descent. Again there was manifest that lure and driving of fatality which had all along seemed to direct my course. With torch flashing intermittently to save the battery
column4: I commenced a mad scramble down the sinister
column5: Cyclopean incline below the opening—sometimes facing forward as I found good hand and foot holds
column6: and at other times turning to face the heap of megaliths as I clung and fumbled more precariously. In two directions beside me
column7: distant walls of carven
column8: crumbling masonry loomed dimly under the direct beams of my torch. Ahead
column9: however
column10: was only unbroken blackness.

column1: I kept no track of time during my downward scramble. So seething with baffling hints and images was my mind
column2: that all objective matters seemed withdrawn into incalculable distances. Physical sensation was dead
column3: and even fear remained as a wraith-like
column4: inactive gargoyle leering impotently at me. Eventually I reached a level floor strown with fallen blocks

column1: Behind and high above
column2: a faint luminous blur told of the distant moonlit world outside. Some vague shred of caution warned me that I should not let it out of my sight

column4: where the traces of carving were plainest. The littered floor was nearly as hard to traverse as the downward heap had been
column5: but I managed to pick my difficult way. At one place I heaved aside some blocks and kicked away the detritus to see what the pavement was like

column1: Reaching a convenient distance from the wall
column2: I cast the torchlight slowly and carefully over its worn remnants of carving. Some bygone influx of water seemed to have acted on the sandstone surface
column3: while there were curious incrustations which I could not explain. In places the masonry was very loose and distorted
column4: and I wondered how many aeons more this primal
column5: hidden edifice could keep its remaining traces of form amidst earth’s heavings.

column3: intimate familiarity of every detail almost stunned my imagination. That the major attributes of this hoary masonry should be familiar

column8: forgotten iconography could have reproduced each subtle shading and nuance which so persistently
column9: exactly
column10: and unvaryingly besieged my sleeping vision night after night?

column1: For this was no chance or remote resemblance. Definitely and absolutely

column3: aeon-hidden corridor in which I stood was the original of something I knew in sleep as intimately as I knew my own house in Crane Street
column4: Arkham. True

column3: diffused green light. He was barefooted and in his night-clothes
