column1: It was a little before this that the horses had stampeded. Something had aroused them in the night
column2: and their neighing and kicking in their stalls had been terrible. There seemed virtually nothing to do to calm them
column3: and when Nahum opened the stable door they all bolted out like frightened woodland deer. It took a week to track all four
column4: and when found they were seen to be quite useless and unmanageable. Something had snapped in their brains
column5: and each one had to be shot for its own good. Nahum borrowed a horse from Ammi for his haying
column6: but found it would not approach the barn. It shied
column7: balked
column8: and whinnied
column9: and in the end he could do nothing but drive it into the yard while the men used their own strength to get the heavy wagon near enough the hayloft for convenient pitching. And all the while the vegetation was turning grey and brittle. Even the flowers whose hues had been so strange were greying now
column10: and the fruit was coming out grey and dwarfed and tasteless. The asters and golden-rod bloomed grey and distorted
column11: and the roses and zinneas and hollyhocks in the front yard were such blasphemous-looking things that Nahum's oldest boy Zenas cut them down. The strangely puffed insects died about that time
column12: even the bees that had left their hives and taken to the woods.

column1: By September all the vegetation was fast crumbling to a greyish powder
column2: and Nahum feared that the trees would die before the poison was out of the soil. His wife now had spells of terrific screaming
column3: and he and the boys were in a constant state of nervous tension. They shunned people now
column4: and when school opened the boys did not go. But it was Ammi
column5: on one of his rare visits
column6: who first realised that the well water was no longer good. It had an evil taste that was not exactly fetid nor exactly salty
column7: and Ammi advised his friend to dig another well on higher ground to use till the soil was good again. Nahum
column8: however
column9: ignored the warning
column10: for he had by that time become calloused to strange and unpleasant things. He and the boys continued to use the tainted supply
column11: drinking it as listlessly and mechanically as they ate their meagre and ill-cooked meals and did their thankless and monotonous chores through the aimless days. There was something of stolid resignation about them all
column12: as if they walked half in another world between lines of nameless guards to a certain and familiar doom.

column1: Thaddeus went mad in September after a visit to the well. He had gone with a pail and had come back empty-handed
column2: shrieking and waving his arms
column3: and sometimes lapsing into an inane titter or a whisper about ""the moving colours down there."" Two in one family was pretty bad
column4: but Nahum was very brave about it. He let the boy run about for a week until he began stumbling and hurting himself
column5: and then he shut him in an attic room across the hall from his mother's. The way they screamed at each other from behind their locked doors was very terrible
column6: especially to little Merwin
column7: who fancied they talked in some terrible language that was not of earth. Merwin was getting frightfully imaginative
column8: and his restlessness was worse after the shutting away of the brother who had been his greatest playmate.

column1: Almost at the same time the mortality among the livestock commenced. Poultry turned greyish and died very quickly
column2: their meat being found dry and noisome upon cutting. Hogs grew inordinately fat
column3: then suddenly began to undergo loathsome changes which no one could explain. Their meat was of course useless
column4: and Nahum was at his wit's end. No rural veterinary would approach his place
column5: and the city veterinary from Arkham was openly baffled. The swine began growing grey and brittle and falling to pieces before they died
column6: and their eyes and muzzles developed singular alterations. It was very inexplicable
column7: for they had never been fed from the tainted vegetation. Then something struck the cows. Certain areas or sometimes the whole body would be uncannily shrivelled or compressed
column8: and atrocious collapses or disintegrations were common. In the last stages--and death was always the result--there would be a greying and turning brittle like that which beset the hogs. There could be no question of poison
column9: for all the cases occurred in a locked and undisturbed barn. No bites of prowling things could have brought the virus
column10: for what live beast of earth can pass through solid obstacles? It must be only natural disease--yet what disease could wreak such results was beyond any mind's guessing. When the harvest came there was not an animal surviving on the place
column11: for the stock and poultry were dead and the dogs had run away. These dogs
column12: three in number
column13: had all vanished one night and were never heard of again. The five cats had left some time before
column14: but their going was scarcely noticed since there now seemed to be no mice
column15: and only Mrs. Gardner had made pets of the graceful felines.

column1: On the nineteenth of October Nahum staggered into Ammi's house with hideous news. The death had come to poor Thaddeus in his attic room
column2: and it had come in a way which could not be told. Nahum had dug a grave in the railed family plot behind the farm
column3: and had put therein what he found. There could have been nothing from outside
column4: for the small barred window and locked door were intact; but it was much as it had been in the barn. Ammi and his wife consoled the stricken man as best they could
column5: but shuddered as they did so. Stark terror seemed to cling round the Gardners and all they touched
column6: and the very presence of one in the house was a breath from regions unnamed and unnamable. Ammi accompanied Nahum home with the greatest reluctance
column7: and did what he might to calm the hysterical sobbing of little Merwin. Zenas needed no calming. He had come of late to do nothing but stare into space and obey what his father told him; and Ammi thought that his fate was very merciful. Now and then Merwin's screams were answered faintly from the attic
column8: and in response to an inquiring look Nahum said that his wife was getting very feeble. When night approached
column9: Ammi managed to get away; for not even friendship could make him stay in that spot when the faint glow of the vegetation began and the trees may or may not have swayed without wind. It was really lucky for Ammi that he was not more imaginative. Even as things were
column10: his mind was bent ever so slightly; but had he been able to connect and reflect upon all the portents around him he must inevitably have turned a total maniac. In the twilight he hastened home
column11: the screams of the mad woman and the nervous child ringing horribly in his ears.

column1: Three days later Nahum burst into Ammi's kitchen in the early morning
column2: and in the absence of his host stammered out a desperate tale once more
column3: while Mrs. Pierce listened in a clutching fright. It was little Merwin this time. He was gone. He had gone out late at night with a lantern and pail for water
column4: and had never come back. He'd been going to pieces for days
column5: and hardly knew what he was about. Screamed at everything. There had been a frantic shriek from the yard then
column6: but before the father could get to the door the boy was gone. There was no glow from the lantern he had taken
column7: and of the child himself no trace. At the time Nahum thought the lantern and pail were gone too; but when dawn came
column8: and the man had plodded back from his all-night search of the woods and fields

column10: both half-fused
column11: seemed to hint at the remnants of the pail. That was all. Nahum was past imagining
column12: Mrs. Pierce was blank
column13: and Ammi
column14: when he had reached home and heard the tale
column15: could give no guess. Merwin was gone
column16: and there would be no use in telling the people around
column17: who shunned all Gardners now. No use
column18: either

column20: and now Merwin was gone. Something was creeping and creeping and waiting to be seen and heard. Nahum would go soon
column21: and he wanted Ammi to look after his wife and Zenas if they survived him. It must all be a judgment of some sort; though he could not fancy what for
column22: since he had always walked uprightly in the Lord's ways so far as he knew.

column1: For over two weeks Ammi saw nothing of Nahum; and then
column2: worried about what might have happened
column3: he overcame his fears and paid the Gardner place a visit. There was no smoke from the great chimney
column4: and for a moment the visitor was apprehensive of the worst. The aspect of the whole farm was shocking--greyish withered grass and leaves on the ground
column5: vines falling in brittle wreckage from archaic walls and gables
column6: and great bare trees clawing up at the grey November sky with a studied malevolence which Ammi could not but feel had come from some subtle change in the tilt of the branches. But Nahum was alive
column7: after all. He was weak
column8: and lying on a couch in the low-ceiled kitchen
column9: but perfectly conscious and able to give simple orders to Zenas. The room was deadly cold; and as Ammi visibly shivered
column10: the host shouted huskily to Zenas for more wood. Wood
column11: indeed
column12: was sorely needed; since the cavernous fireplace was unlit and empty
column13: with a cloud of soot blowing about in the chill wind that came down the chimney. Presently Nahum asked him if the extra wood had made him any more comfortable
column14: and then Ammi saw what had happened. The stoutest cord had broken at last
column15: and the hapless farmer's mind was proof against more sorrow.

column1: Questioning tactfully

column3: and he changed his line of inquiry. ""Nabby? Why
column4: here she is!"" was the surprised response of poor Nahum

column7: and no sound could be heard from any direction. Of the four doors in sight
column8: only one was locked
column9: and on this he tried various keys of the ring he had taken. The third key proved the right one
column10: and after some fumbling Ammi threw open the low white door.

column1: It was quite dark inside
column2: for the window was small and half-obscured by the crude wooden bars; and Ammi could see nothing at all on the wide-planked floor. The stench was beyond enduring
column3: and before proceeding further he had to retreat to another room and return with his lungs filled with breathable air. When he did enter he saw something dark in the corner
column4: and upon seeing it more clearly he screamed outright. While he screamed he thought a momentary cloud eclipsed the window
column5: and a second later he felt himself brushed as if by some hateful current of vapour. Strange colours danced before his eyes; and had not a present horror numbed him he would have thought of the globule in the meteor that the geologist's hammer had shattered
column6: and of the morbid vegetation that had sprouted in the spring. As it was he thought only of the blasphemous monstrosity which confronted him
column7: and which all too clearly had shared the nameless fate of young Thaddeus and the livestock. But the terrible thing about the horror was that it very slowly and perceptibly moved as it continued to crumble.

column1: Ammi would give me no added particulars of this scene
column2: but the shape in the comer does not reappear in his tale as a moving object. There are things which cannot be mentioned
column3: and what is done in common humanity is sometimes cruelly judged by the law. I gathered that no moving thing was left in that attic room
column4: and that to leave anything capable of motion there would have been a deed so monstrous as to damn any accountable being to eternal torment. Anyone but a stolid farmer would have fainted or gone mad
column5: but Ammi walked conscious through that low doorway and locked the accursed secret behind him. There would be Nahum to deal with now; he must be fed and tended
column6: and removed to some place where he could be cared for.

column1: Commencing his descent of the dark stairs. Ammi heard a thud below him. He even thought a scream had been suddenly choked off
column2: and recalled nervously the clammy vapour which had brushed by him in that frightful room above. What presence had his cry and entry started up? Halted by some vague fear
column3: he heard still further sounds below. Indubitably there was a sort of heavy dragging
column4: and a most detestably sticky noise as of some fiendish and unclean species of suction. With an associative sense goaded to feverish heights
column5: he thought unaccountably of what he had seen upstairs. Good God! What eldritch dream-world was this into which he had blundered? He dared move neither backward nor forward
column6: but stood there trembling at the black curve of the boxed-in staircase. Every trifle of the scene burned itself into his brain. The sounds
column7: the sense of dread expectancy
column8: the darkness
column9: the steepness of the narrow step--and merciful Heaven!--the faint but unmistakable luminosity of all the woodwork in sight; steps
column10: sides
column11: exposed laths
column12: and beams alike.

column1: Then there burst forth a frantic whinny from Ammi's horse outside
column2: followed at once by a clatter which told of a frenzied runaway. In another moment horse and buggy had gone beyond earshot
column3: leaving the frightened man on the dark stairs to guess what had sent them. But that was not all. There had been another sound out there. A sort of liquid splash--water--it must have been the well. He had left Hero untied near it
column4: and a buggy wheel must have brushed the coping and knocked in a stone. And still the pale phosphorescence glowed in that detestably ancient woodwork. God! how old the house was! Most of it built before 1670
column5: and the gambrel roof no later than 1730.

column1: A feeble scratching on the floor downstairs now sounded distinctly

column3: he finished his descent and walked boldly toward the kitchen. But he did not complete the walk

column5: and it was still alive after a fashion. Whether it had crawled or whether it had been dragged by any external forces
column6: Ammi could not say; but the death had been at it. Everything had happened in the last half-hour
column7: but collapse
column8: greying
column9: and disintegration were already far advanced. There was a horrible brittleness
column10: and dry fragments were scaling off. Ammi could not touch it
column11: but looked horrifiedly into the distorted parody that had been a face. ""What was it
column12: Nahum--what was it?"" He whispered
column13: and the cleft
column14: bulging lips were just able to crackle out a final answer.

column1: Nothin'...nothin'...the colour...it burns...cold an' wet
column2: but it burns...it lived in the well...I seen it...a kind of smoke...jest like the flowers last spring...the well shone at night...Thad an' Merwin an' Zenas...everything alive...suckin' the life out of everything...in that stone...it must a' come in that stone pizened the whole place...dun't know what it wants...that round thing them men from the college dug outen the stone...they smashed it...it was the same colour...jest the same
column3: like the flowers an' plants...must a' ben more of 'em...seeds...seeds...they growed...I seen it the fust time this week...must a' got strong on Zenas...he was a big boy
column4: full o' life...it beats down your mind an' then gets ye...burns ye up...in the well water...you was right about that...evil water...Zenas never come back from the well...can't git away...draws ye...ye know summ'at's comin' but tain't no use...I seen it time an' agin senct Zenas was took...whar's Nabby
column5: Ammi?...my head's no good...dun't know how long sense I fed her...it'll git her ef we ain't keerful...jest a colour...her face is gittin' to hev that colour sometimes towards night...an' it burns an' sucks...it come from some place whar things ain't as they is here...one o' them professors said so...he was right...look out
column6: Ammi
column7: it'll do suthin' more...sucks the life out...""

column1: But that was all. That which spoke could speak no more because it had completely caved in. Ammi laid a red checked tablecloth over what was left and reeled out the back door into the fields. He climbed the slope to the ten-acre pasture and stumbled home by the north road and the woods. He could not pass that well from which his horses had run away. He had looked at it through the window
column2: and had seen that no stone was missing from the rim. Then the lurching buggy had not dislodged anything after all--the splash had been something else--something which went into the well after it had done with poor Nahum.

column1: When Ammi reached his house the horses and buggy had arrived before him and thrown his wife into fits of anxiety. Reassuring her without explanations
column2: he set out at once for Arkham and notified the authorities that the Gardner family was no more. He indulged in no details

column8: the medical examiner
column9: and the veterinary who had treated the diseased animals. He went much against his will

column1: The six men drove out in a democrat-wagon
column2: following Ammi's buggy
column3: and arrived at the pest-ridden farmhouse about four o'clock. Used as the officers were to gruesome experiences

column5: but those two crumbling objects were beyond all bounds. No one could look long at them

column3: too
column4: as if some other living thing were crawling close to the ground. When the old woman began to turn toward him he fled precipitately off the bridge and into the shelter of the town’s labyrinthine waterfront alleys. Distant though the island was

column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held

column1: It was in the sky. A definite point among the stars had a claim on him and was calling him. Apparently it was a point somewhere between Hydra and Argo Navis

column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door

column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying

column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest

column6: slanting ceiling.

column1: That night as Gilman slept the violet light broke upon him with heightened intensity
column2: and the old witch and small furry thing—getting closer than ever before—mocked him with inhuman squeals and devilish gestures. He was glad to sink into the vaguely roaring twilight abysses

Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles

column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame

column11: and at a different height above an infinitely distant curving horizon of low mountains. Behind him tiers of higher terraces towered aloft as far as he could see. The city below stretched away to the limits of vision

column1: The pavement from which he easily raised himself was of a veined
column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify

column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought

column7: like the whole balustrade

column10: and with vertical knobs or bulbs projecting from the head and base of the barrel. Each of these knobs was the hub of a system of five long
column11: flat

column13: but curving slightly away from the central barrel. The base of the bottom knob was fused to the long railing with so delicate a point of contact that several figures had been broken off and were missing. The figures were about four and a half inches in height
column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column1: When Gilman stood up the tiles felt hot to his bare feet. He was wholly alone

column4: and he wished he might discern the denizens of the place. The sight turned him giddy after a while

column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed
column10: he continued to clutch it as his other hand seized a vacant space on the smooth railing.

column1: But now his oversensitive ears caught something behind him

column5: shaped precisely like the spiky images on the balustrade
column6: and propelling themselves by a spider-like wriggling of their lower set of starfish-arms.

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed
column2: drenched by a cold perspiration and with a smarting sensation in his face
column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste

column1: After about an hour he got himself under better control

column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished

column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant

column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged

column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief

column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration

column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling

column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod

column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table

column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door

Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall

column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column8: like himself

column3: however

column5: and what had been near her rattling the tin can in a rubbish-heap at the mouth of a squalid courtyard. The crone had seemed to notice him and leer evilly at him—though perhaps this was merely his imagination.

column1: The next day both youths felt very tired
column2: and knew they would sleep like logs when night came. In the evening they drowsily discussed the mathematical studies which had so completely and perhaps harmfully engrossed Gilman

column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column1: Whether a modern student could ever gain similar powers from mathematical research alone
column2: was still to be seen. Success
column3: Gilman added
column4: might lead to dangerous and unthinkable situations; for who could foretell the conditions pervading an adjacent but normally inaccessible dimension? On the other hand

column6: and by entering and remaining in such a belt one might preserve one’s life and age indefinitely; never suffering organic metabolism or deterioration except for slight amounts incurred during visits to one’s own or similar planes. One might
column7: for example

column5: too

column7: too sleepy to argue further

column4: the hideous crone seized Gilman by the shoulders
column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him
column6: but in another second he thought he was in a dark
column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours

column2: while from a lesser distance the old woman was beckoning and grimacing imperiously. Brown Jenkin was rubbing itself with a kind of affectionate playfulness around the ankles of the black man
column3: which the deep mud largely concealed. There was a dark open doorway on the right
column4: to which the black man silently pointed. Into this the grimacing crone started
column5: dragging Gilman after her by his pajama sleeve. There were evil-smelling staircases which creaked ominously
column6: and on which the old woman seemed to radiate a faint violet light; and finally a door leading off a landing. The crone fumbled with the latch and pushed the door open
column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry
column2: and presently the beldame came out of the room bearing a small
column3: senseless form which she thrust at the dreamer as if ordering him to carry it. The sight of this form
column4: and the expression on its face
column5: broke the spell. Still too dazed to cry out
column6: he plunged recklessly down the noisome staircase and into the mud outside; halting only when seized and choked by the waiting black man. As consciousness departed he heard the faint
column7: shrill tittering of the fanged
column8: rat-like abnormality.

column3: sprawled on the now unmade bed. His throat was aching inexplicably

column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them

column7: and lions. And the leader of the caravan wore a head-dress with two horns and a curious disc betwixt the horns.

column2: but only a tiny black kitten to cherish. The plague had not been kind to him
column3: yet had left him this small furry thing to mitigate his sorrow; and when one is very young
column4: one can find great relief in the lively antics of a black kitten. So the boy whom the dark people called Menes smiled more often than he wept as he sate playing with his graceful kitten on the steps of an oddly painted wagon.

column1: Here the old man faltered

column3: and lapsed into a moody and apprehensive silence; glancing nervously over his shoulder and then turning back to stare fascinatedly at the distant black reef. When I spoke to him he did not answer
column4: so I knew I would have to let him finish the bottle. The insane yarn I was hearing interested me profoundly
column5: for I fancied there was contained within it a sort of crude allegory based upon the strangeness of Innsmouth and elaborated by an imagination at once creative and full of scraps of exotic legend. Not for a moment did I believe that the tale had any really substantial foundation; but none the less the account held a hint of genuine terror if only because it brought in references to strange jewels clearly akin to the malign tiara I had seen at Newburyport. Perhaps the ornaments had

column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column1: Mazurewicz was waiting for him at the door
column2: and seemed both anxious and reluctant to whisper some fresh bit of superstition. It was about the witch light. Joe had been out celebrating the night before—it was Patriots’ Day in Massachusetts—and had come home after midnight. Looking up at the house from outside
column3: he had thought at first that Gilman’s window was dark; but then he had seen the faint violet glow within. He wanted to warn the gentleman about that glow
column4: for everybody in Arkham knew it was Keziah’s witch light which played near Brown Jenkin and the ghost of the old crone herself. He had not mentioned this before
column5: but now he must tell about it because it meant that Keziah and her long-toothed familiar were haunting the young gentleman. Sometimes he and Paul Choynski and Landlord Dombrowski thought they saw that light seeping out of cracks in the sealed loft above the young gentleman’s room
column6: but they had all agreed not to talk about that. However
column7: it would be better for the gentleman to take another room and get a crucifix from some good priest like Father Iwanicki.

column1: As the man rambled on Gilman felt a nameless panic clutch at his throat. He knew that Joe must have been half drunk when he came home the night before
column2: yet this mention of a violet light in the garret window was of frightful import. It was a lambent glow of this sort which always played about the old woman and the small furry thing in those lighter
column3: sharper dreams which prefaced his plunge into unknown abysses
column4: and the thought that a wakeful second person could see the dream-luminance was utterly beyond sane harbourage. Yet where had the fellow got such an odd notion? Had he himself talked as well as walked around the house in his sleep? No
column5: Joe said
column6: he had not—but he must check up on this. Perhaps Frank Elwood could tell him something
column7: though he hated to ask.

column1: Fever—wild dreams—somnambulism—illusions of sounds—a pull toward a point in the sky—and now a suspicion of insane sleep-talking! He must stop studying
column2: see a nerve specialist
column3: and take himself in hand. When he climbed to the second story he paused at Elwood’s door but saw that the other youth was out. Reluctantly he continued up to his garret room and sat down in the dark. His gaze was still pulled to the southwest
column4: but he also found himself listening intently for some sound in the closed loft above
column5: and half imagining that an evil violet light seeped down through an infinitesimal crack in the low
column6: slanting ceiling.

column1: That night as Gilman slept the violet light broke upon him with heightened intensity
column2: and the old witch and small furry thing—getting closer than ever before—mocked him with inhuman squeals and devilish gestures. He was glad to sink into the vaguely roaring twilight abysses
column3: though the pursuit of that iridescent bubble-congeries and that kaleidoscopic little polyhedron was menacing and irritating. Then came the shift as vast converging planes of a slippery-looking substance loomed above and below him—a shift which ended in a flash of delirium and a blaze of unknown
column4: alien light in which yellow
column5: carmine
column6: and indigo were madly and inextricably blended.

column1: He was half lying on a high
column2: fantastically balustraded terrace above a boundless jungle of outlandish
column3: incredible peaks
column4: balanced planes
column5: domes
column6: minarets
column7: horizontal discs poised on pinnacles
column8: and numberless forms of still greater wildness—some of stone and some of metal—which glittered gorgeously in the mixed
column9: almost blistering glare from a polychromatic sky. Looking upward he saw three stupendous discs of flame
column10: each of a different hue
column11: and at a different height above an infinitely distant curving horizon of low mountains. Behind him tiers of higher terraces towered aloft as far as he could see. The city below stretched away to the limits of vision
column12: and he hoped that no sound would well up from it.

column1: The pavement from which he easily raised himself was of a veined
column2: polished stone beyond his power to identify
column3: and the tiles were cut in bizarre-angled shapes which struck him as less asymmetrical than based on some unearthly symmetry whose laws he could not comprehend. The balustrade was chest-high
column4: delicate
column5: and fantastically wrought
column6: while along the rail were ranged at short intervals little figures of grotesque design and exquisite workmanship. They
column7: like the whole balustrade
column8: seemed to be made of some sort of shining metal whose colour could not be guessed in this chaos of mixed effulgences; and their nature utterly defied conjecture. They represented some ridged
column9: barrel-shaped object with thin horizontal arms radiating spoke-like from a central ring
column10: and with vertical knobs or bulbs projecting from the head and base of the barrel. Each of these knobs was the hub of a system of five long
column11: flat
column12: triangularly tapering arms arranged around it like the arms of a starfish—nearly horizontal
column13: but curving slightly away from the central barrel. The base of the bottom knob was fused to the long railing with so delicate a point of contact that several figures had been broken off and were missing. The figures were about four and a half inches in height
column14: while the spiky arms gave them a maximum diameter of about two and a half inches.

column1: When Gilman stood up the tiles felt hot to his bare feet. He was wholly alone
column2: and his first act was to walk to the balustrade and look dizzily down at the endless
column3: Cyclopean city almost two thousand feet below. As he listened he thought a rhythmic confusion of faint musical pipings covering a wide tonal range welled up from the narrow streets beneath
column4: and he wished he might discern the denizens of the place. The sight turned him giddy after a while
column5: so that he would have fallen to the pavement had he not clutched instinctively at the lustrous balustrade. His right hand fell on one of the projecting figures
column6: the touch seeming to steady him slightly. It was too much
column7: however
column8: for the exotic delicacy of the metal-work
column9: and the spiky figure snapped off under his grasp. Still half-dazed
column10: he continued to clutch it as his other hand seized a vacant space on the smooth railing.

column1: But now his oversensitive ears caught something behind him
column2: and he looked back across the level terrace. Approaching him softly though without apparent furtiveness were five figures
column3: two of which were the sinister old woman and the fanged
column4: furry little animal. The other three were what sent him unconscious—for they were living entities about eight feet high
column5: shaped precisely like the spiky images on the balustrade
column6: and propelling themselves by a spider-like wriggling of their lower set of starfish-arms.

column1: Gilman awakened in his bed
column2: drenched by a cold perspiration and with a smarting sensation in his face
column3: hands
column4: and feet. Springing to the floor
column5: he washed and dressed in frantic haste
column6: as if it were necessary for him to get out of the house as quickly as possible. He did not know where he wished to go
column7: but felt that once more he would have to sacrifice his classes. The odd pull toward that spot in the sky between Hydra and Argo had abated
column8: but another of even greater strength had taken its place. Now he felt that he must go north—infinitely north. He dreaded to cross the bridge that gave a view of the desolate island in the Miskatonic
column9: so went over the Peabody Avenue bridge. Very often he stumbled
column10: for his eyes and ears were chained to an extremely lofty point in the blank blue sky.

column1: After about an hour he got himself under better control
column2: and saw that he was far from the city. All around him stretched the bleak emptiness of salt marshes
column3: while the narrow road ahead led to Innsmouth—that ancient
column4: half-deserted town which Arkham people were so curiously unwilling to visit. Though the northward pull had not diminished
column5: he resisted it as he had resisted the other pull
column6: and finally found that he could almost balance the one against the other. Plodding back to town and getting some coffee at a soda fountain
column7: he dragged himself into the public library and browsed aimlessly among the lighter magazines. Once he met some friends who remarked how oddly sunburned he looked
column8: but he did not tell them of his walk. At three o’clock he took some lunch at a restaurant
column9: noting meanwhile that the pull had either lessened or divided itself. After that he killed the time at a cheap cinema show
column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green
column10: and Gilman could see amidst his horror and bewilderment that one of the knobs ended in a jagged break corresponding to its former point of attachment to the dream-railing.

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged
column2: furry thing came again and with a greater distinctness than on any former occasion. This time they actually reached him
column3: and he felt the crone’s withered claws clutching at him. He was pulled out of bed and into empty space
column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief
column5: for presently he was in a crude
column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration
column8: and in the centre were a table and bench
column9: both apparently fastened in place. Small objects of unknown shape and nature were ranged on the tops of the cases
column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling
column13: there presently climbed the hateful little furry thing with the yellow fangs and bearded human face.

column1: The evilly grinning beldame still clutched him
column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod
column6: since there was a clicking whenever he changed position. The man did not speak
column7: and bore no trace of expression on his small
column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table
column9: while the beldame thrust a huge grey quill into Gilman’s right hand. Over everything was a pall of intensely maddening fear
column10: and the climax was reached when the furry thing ran up the dreamer’s clothing to his shoulders and then down his left arm
column11: finally biting him sharply in the wrist just below his cuff. As the blood spurted from this wound Gilman lapsed into a faint.

column1: He awaked on the morning of the 22nd with a pain in his left wrist
column2: and saw that his cuff was brown with dried blood. His recollections were very confused
column3: but the scene with the black man in the unknown space stood out vividly. The rats must have bitten him as he slept
column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door
column5: he saw that the flour on the corridor floor was undisturbed except for the huge prints of the loutish fellow who roomed at the other end of the garret. So he had not been sleep-walking this time. But something would have to be done about those rats. He would speak to the landlord about them. Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall
column6: wedging in a candlestick which seemed of about the right size. His ears were ringing horribly
column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column1: As he bathed and changed clothes he tried to recall what he had dreamed after the scene in the violet-litten space

column3: which had begun to attack his imagination so violently

column5: twilight abysses
column6: and of still vaster
column7: blacker abysses beyond them—abysses in which all fixed suggestions of form were absent. He had been taken there by the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron which always dogged him; but they
column8: like himself

column10: barely luminous mist in this farther void of ultimate blackness. Something else had gone on ahead—a larger wisp which now and then condensed into nameless approximations of form—and he thought that their progress had not been in a straight line
column11: but rather along the alien curves and spirals of some ethereal vortex which obeyed laws unknown to the physics and mathematics of any conceivable cosmos. Eventually there had been a hint of vast
column12: leaping shadows
column13: of a monstrous
column14: half-acoustic pulsing
column15: and of the thin

column17: which rules all time and space from a curiously environed black throne at the centre of Chaos.

column1: When the blood was washed away the wrist wound proved very slight
column2: and Gilman puzzled over the location of the two tiny punctures. It occurred to him that there was no blood on the bedspread where he had lain—which was very curious in view of the amount on his skin and cuff. Had he been sleep-walking within his room
column3: and had the rat bitten him as he sat in some chair or paused in some less rational position? He looked in every corner for brownish drops or stains
column4: but did not find any. He had better
column5: he thought

column7: though they were replaced by another sensation even more inexplicable. It was a vague
column8: insistent impulse to fly away from his present situation

column10: it was wholly overruled by the newer and more bewildering urge.

column10: though

column17: the fellow under Gilman’s room

column1: Elwood could not imagine what had set these superstitious creatures gossiping
column2: but supposed their imaginations had been roused by Gilman’s late hours and somnolent walking and talking on the one hand

These simple people were quick to imagine they had seen any odd thing they had heard about. As for a plan of action—Gilman had better move down to Elwood’s room and avoid sleeping alone. Elwood would
column5: if awake
column6: rouse him whenever he began to talk or rise in his sleep. Very soon

column1: Braced up by Elwood’s companionship

column3: but he could sidetrack them with considerable success. During a free period he shewed the queer image to several professors

column4: whose imaginations had become highly excited. Mazurewicz was always trying to make him get a crucifix
column5: and finally forced one upon him which he said had been blessed by the good Father Iwanicki. Desrochers
column6: too

column1: For three days Gilman and Elwood canvassed the local museums in an effort to identify the strange spiky image
column2: but always without success. In every quarter
column3: however
column4: interest was intense; for the utter alienage of the thing was a tremendous challenge to scientific curiosity. One of the small radiating arms was broken off and subjected to chemical analysis
column5: and the result is still talked about in college circles. Professor Ellery found platinum
column6: iron
column7: and tellurium in the strange alloy; but mixed with these were at least three other apparent elements of high atomic weight which chemistry was absolutely powerless to classify. Not only did they fail to correspond with any known element
column8: but they did not even fit the vacant places reserved for probable elements in the periodic system. The mystery remains unsolved to this day
column9: though the image is on exhibition at the museum of Miskatonic University.

column1: On the morning of April 27 a fresh rat-hole appeared in the room where Gilman was a guest
column2: but Dombrowski tinned it up during the day. The poison was not having much effect
column3: for scratchings and scurryings in the walls were virtually undiminished. Elwood was out late that night
column4: and Gilman waited up for him. He did not wish to go to sleep in a room alone—especially since he thought he had glimpsed in the evening twilight the repellent old woman whose image had become so horribly transferred to his dreams. He wondered who she was
column5: and what had been near her rattling the tin can in a rubbish-heap at the mouth of a squalid courtyard. The crone had seemed to notice him and leer evilly at him—though perhaps this was merely his imagination.

column1: The next day both youths felt very tired
column2: and knew they would sleep like logs when night came. In the evening they drowsily discussed the mathematical studies which had so completely and perhaps harmfully engrossed Gilman
column3: and speculated about the linkage with ancient magic and folklore which seemed so darkly probable. They spoke of old Keziah Mason
column4: and Elwood agreed that Gilman had good scientific grounds for thinking she might have stumbled on strange and significant information. The hidden cults to which these witches belonged often guarded and handed down surprising secrets from elder
column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column1: Whether a modern student could ever gain similar powers from mathematical research alone
column2: was still to be seen. Success
column3: Gilman added
column4: might lead to dangerous and unthinkable situations; for who could foretell the conditions pervading an adjacent but normally inaccessible dimension? On the other hand
column5: the picturesque possibilities were enormous. Time could not exist in certain belts of space
column6: and by entering and remaining in such a belt one might preserve one’s life and age indefinitely; never suffering organic metabolism or deterioration except for slight amounts incurred during visits to one’s own or similar planes. One might
column7: for example
column8: pass into a timeless dimension and emerge at some remote period of the earth’s history as young as before.

column1: Whether anybody had ever managed to do this
column2: one could hardly conjecture with any degree of authority. Old legends are hazy and ambiguous
column3: and in historic times all attempts at crossing forbidden gaps seem complicated by strange and terrible alliances with beings and messengers from outside. There was the immemorial figure of the deputy or messenger of hidden and terrible powers—the “Black Man” of the witch-cult
column4: and the “Nyarlathotep” of the Necronomicon. There was
column5: too
column6: the baffling problem of the lesser messengers or intermediaries—the quasi-animals and queer hybrids which legend depicts as witches’ familiars. As Gilman and Elwood retired
column7: too sleepy to argue further
column8: they heard Joe Mazurewicz reel into the house half-drunk
column9: and shuddered at the desperate wildness of his whining prayers.

column1: That night Gilman saw the violet light again. In his dream he had heard a scratching and gnawing in the partitions
column2: and thought that someone fumbled clumsily at the latch. Then he saw the old woman and the small furry thing advancing toward him over the carpeted floor. The beldame’s face was alight with inhuman exultation
column3: and the little yellow-toothed morbidity tittered mockingly as it pointed at the heavily sleeping form of Elwood on the other couch across the room. A paralysis of fear stifled all attempts to cry out. As once before
column4: the hideous crone seized Gilman by the shoulders
column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him
column6: but in another second he thought he was in a dark
column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours
column9: with the rotting walls of ancient houses towering up on every hand.

column1: Ahead was the robed black man he had seen in the peaked space in the other dream
column2: while from a lesser distance the old woman was beckoning and grimacing imperiously. Brown Jenkin was rubbing itself with a kind of affectionate playfulness around the ankles of the black man
column3: which the deep mud largely concealed. There was a dark open doorway on the right
column4: to which the black man silently pointed. Into this the grimacing crone started
column5: dragging Gilman after her by his pajama sleeve. There were evil-smelling staircases which creaked ominously
column6: and on which the old woman seemed to radiate a faint violet light; and finally a door leading off a landing. The crone fumbled with the latch and pushed the door open
column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry
column2: and presently the beldame came out of the room bearing a small
column3: senseless form which she thrust at the dreamer as if ordering him to carry it. The sight of this form
column4: and the expression on its face
column5: broke the spell. Still too dazed to cry out
column6: he plunged recklessly down the noisome staircase and into the mud outside; halting only when seized and choked by the waiting black man. As consciousness departed he heard the faint
column7: shrill tittering of the fanged
column8: rat-like abnormality.

column1: On the morning of the 29th Gilman awaked into a maelstrom of horror. The instant he opened his eyes he knew something was terribly wrong
column2: for he was back in his old garret room with the slanting wall and ceiling
column3: sprawled on the now unmade bed. His throat was aching inexplicably
column4: and as he struggled to a sitting posture he saw with growing fright that his feet and pajama-bottoms were brown with caked mud. For the moment his recollections were hopelessly hazy
column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them
column7: the more peculiar they seemed; for in addition to those he could recognise as his there were some smaller
column8: almost round markings—such as the legs of a large chair or table might make
column9: except that most of them tended to be divided into halves. There were also some curious muddy rat-tracks leading out of a fresh hole and back into it again. Utter bewilderment and the fear of madness racked Gilman as he staggered to the door and saw that there were no muddy prints outside. The more he remembered of his hideous dream the more terrified he felt
column10: and it added to his desperation to hear Joe Mazurewicz chanting mournfully two floors below.

column3: how he got back to his room without making tracks in the hall
column4: and how the muddy

column6: were wholly beyond conjecture. Then there were those dark
column7: livid marks on his throat
column8: as if he had tried to strangle himself. He put his hands up to them
column9: but found that they did not even approximately fit. While they were talking Desrochers dropped in to say that he had heard a terrific clattering overhead in the dark small hours. No

column11: and cautiously descending steps he did not like. It was
column12: he added
column13: a very bad time of year for Arkham. The young gentleman had better be sure to wear the crucifix Joe Mazurewicz had given him. Even the daytime was not safe

column1: Gathering from the grocery boy's map that the best route out of town was southward

column3: hence I saw--after drawing the bolt and finding other fastening in place--it was not a favorable one for forcing. Accordingly abandoning it as a route

column5: and this--though a test proved it to be locked or bolted from the other side--I knew must be my route. If I could gain the roofs of the buildings in Paine Street and descend successfully to the ground level

column1: As I thought of these things I looked out over the squalid sea of decaying roofs below me
column2: now brightened by the beams of a moon not much past full. On the right the black gash of the river-gorge clove the panorama; abandoned factories and railway station clinging barnacle-like to its sides. Beyond it the rusted railway and the Rowley road led off through a flat marshy terrain dotted with islets of higher and dryer scrub-grown land. On the left the creek-threaded country-side was nearer
column3: the narrow road to Ipswich gleaming white in the moonlight. I could not see from my side of the hotel the southward route toward Arkham which I had determined to take.

column1: I was irresolutely speculating on when I had better attack the northward door

column3: when I noticed that the vague noises underfoot had given place to a fresh and heavier creaking of the stairs. A wavering flicker of light shewed through my transom

column1: For a moment I simply held my breath and waited. Eternities seemed to elapse
column2: and the nauseous fishy odour of my environment seemed to mount suddenly and spectacularly. Then the knocking was repeated--continuously
column3: and with growing insistence. I knew that the time for action had come
column4: and forthwith drew the bolt of the northward connecting door
column5: bracing myself for the task of battering it open. The knocking waxed louder
column6: and I hoped that its volume would cover the sound of my efforts. At last beginning my attempt
column7: I lunged again and again at the thin paneling with my left shoulder
column8: heedless of shock or pain. The door resisted even more than I expected
column9: but I did not give in. And all the while the clamour at the outer door increased.

column1: Finally the connecting door gave
column2: but with such a crash that I knew those outside must have heard. Instantly the outside knocking became a violent battering
column3: while keys sounded ominously in the hall doors of the rooms on both sides of me. Rushing through the newly opened connexion
column4: I succeeded in bolting the northerly hall door before the lock could be turned; but even as I did so I heard the hall door of the third room--the one from whose window I had hoped to reach the roof below--being tried with a pass-key.

column1: For an instant I felt absolute despair
column2: since my trapping in a chamber with no window egress seemed complete. A wave of almost abnormal horror swept over me
column3: and invested with a terrible but unexplainable singularity the flashlight-glimpsed dust prints made by the intruder who had lately tried my door from this room. Then
column4: with a dazed automatism which persisted despite hopelessness
column5: I made for the next connecting door and performed the blind motion of pushing at it in an effort to get through and--granting that fastenings might be as providentially intact as in this second room--bolt the hall door beyond before the lock could be turned from outside.

column1: Sheer fortunate chance gave me my reprieve--for the connecting door before me was not only unlocked but actually ajar. In a second I was though
column2: and had my right knee and shoulder against a hall door which was visibly opening inward. My pressure took the opener off guard
column3: for the thing shut as I pushed
column4: so that I could slip the well-conditioned bolt as I had done with the other door. As I gained this respite I heard the battering at the two other doors abate
column5: while a confused clatter came from the connecting door I had shielded with the bedstead. Evidently the bulk of my assailants had entered the southerly room and were massing in a lateral attack. But at the same moment a pass-key sounded in the next door to the north
column6: and I knew that a nearer peril was at hand.

column1: The northward connecting door was wide open
column2: but there was no time to think about checking the already turning lock in the hall. All I could do was to shut and bolt the open connecting door
column3: as well as its mate on the opposite side--pushing a bedstead against the one and a bureau against the other
column4: and moving a washstand in front of the hall door. I must
column5: I saw
column6: trust to such makeshift barriers to shield me till I could get out the window and on the roof of the Paine Street block. But even in this acute moment my chief horror was something apart from the immediate weakness of my defenses. I was shuddering because not one of my pursuers
column7: despite some hideous panting
column8: grunting
column9: and subdued barkings at odd intervals
column10: was uttering an unmuffled or intelligible vocal sound.

column1: As I moved the furniture and rushed toward the windows I heard a frightful scurrying along the corridor toward the room north of me
column2: and perceived that the southward battering had ceased. Plainly
column3: most of my opponents were about to concentrate against the feeble connecting door which they knew must open directly on me. Outside

column1: Surveying the conditions
column2: I chose the more southerly of the two windows as my avenue of escape; planning to land on the inner slope of the roof and make for the nearest sky-light. Once inside one of the decrepit brick structures I would have to reckon with pursuit; but I hoped to descend and dodge in and out of yawning doorways along the shadowed courtyard
column3: eventually getting to Washington Street and slipping out of town toward the south.

column1: The clatter at the northerly connecting door was now terrific
column2: and I saw that the weak panelling was beginning to splinter. Obviously
column3: the besiegers had brought some ponderous object into play as a battering-ram. The bedstead
column4: however
column5: still held firm; so that I had at least a faint chance of making good my escape. As I opened the window I noticed that it was flanked by heavy velour draperies suspended from a pole by brass rings
column6: and also that there was a large projecting catch for the shutters on the exterior. Seeing a possible means of avoiding the dangerous jump
column7: I yanked at the hangings and brought them down

column9: and I saw that the rings and catch would be likely to bear my weight. So

column11: I left behind me forever the morbid and horror-infested fabric of the Gilman House.

column1: I landed safely on the loose slates of the steep roof
column2: and succeeded in gaining the gaping black skylight without a slip. Glancing up at the window I had left

column4: though far across the crumbling chimneys to the north I could see lights ominously blazing in the Order of Dagon Hall
column5: the Baptist church
column6: and the Congregational church which I recalled so shiveringly. There had seemed to be no one in the courtyard below
column7: and I hoped there would be a chance to get away before the spreading of a general alarm. Flashing my pocket lamp into the skylight
column8: I saw that there were no steps down. The distance was slight
column9: however
column10: so I clambered over the brink and dropped; striking a dusty floor littered with crumbling boxes and barrels.

column1: The place was ghoulish-looking
column2: but I was past minding such impressions and made at once for the staircase revealed by my flashlight--after a hasty glance at my watch
column3: which shewed the hour to be 2 a.m. The steps creaked
column4: but seemed tolerably sound; and I raced down past a barnlike second storey to the ground floor. The desolation was complete
column5: and only echoes answered my footfalls. At length I reached the lower hall at the end of which I saw a faint luminous rectangle marking the ruined Paine Street doorway. Heading the other way
column6: I found the back door also open; and darted out and down five stone steps to the grass-grown cobblestones of the courtyard.

column1: The moonbeams did not reach down here
column2: but I could just see my way about without using the flashlight. Some of the windows on the Gilman House side were faintly glowing
column3: and I thought I heard confused sounds within. Walking softly over to the Washington Street side I perceived several open doorways
column4: and chose the nearest as my route out. The hallway inside was black
column5: and when I reached the opposite end I saw that the street door was wedged immovably shut. Resolved to try another building
column6: I groped my way back toward the courtyard
column7: but stopped short when close to the doorway.

column1: For out of an opened door in the Gilman House a large crowd of doubtful shapes was pouring--lanterns bobbing in the darkness
column2: and horrible croaking voices exchanging low cries in what was certainly not English. The figures moved uncertainly
column3: and I realized to my relief that they did not know where I had gone; but for all that they sent a shiver of horror through my frame. Their features were indistinguishable
column4: but their crouching
column5: shambling gait was abominably repellent. And worst of all
column6: I perceived that one figure was strangely robed
column7: and unmistakably surmounted by a tall tiara of a design altogether too familiar. As the figures spread throughout the courtyard
column8: I felt my fears increase. Suppose I could find no egress from this building on the street side? The fishy odour was detestable
column9: and I wondered I could stand it without fainting. Again groping toward the street
column10: I opened a door off the hall and came upon an empty room with closely shuttered but sashless windows. Fumbling in the rays of my flashlight
column11: I found I could open the shutters; and in another moment had climbed outside and was fully closing the aperture in its original manner.

column1: I was now in Washington Street
column2: and for the moment saw no living thing nor any light save that of the moon. From several directions in the distance
column3: however
column4: I could hear the sound of hoarse voices
column5: of footsteps
column6: and of a curious kind of pattering which did not sound quite like footsteps. Plainly I had no time to lose. The points of the compass were clear to me
column7: and I was glad that all the street lights were turned off
column8: as is often the custom on strongly moonlit nights in prosperous rural regions. Some of the sounds came from the south
column9: yet I retained my design of escaping in that direction. There would
column10: I knew
column11: be plenty of deserted doorways to shelter me in case I met any person or group who looked like pursuers.

column1: I walked rapidly
column2: softly
column3: and close to the ruined houses. While hatless and dishevelled after my arduous climb
column4: I did not look especially noticeable; and stood a good chance of passing unheeded if forced to encounter any casual wayfarer.

column1: At Bates Street I drew into a yawning vestibule while two shambling figures crossed in front of me
column2: but was soon on my way again and approaching the open space where Eliot Street obliquely crosses Washington at the intersection of South. Though I had never seen this space
column3: it had looked dangerous to me on the grocery youth's map; since the moonlight would have free play there. There was no use trying to evade it
column4: for any alternative course would involve detours of possibly disastrous visibility and delaying effect. The only thing to do was to cross it boldly and openly; imitating the typical shamble of the Innsmouth folk as best I could
column5: and trusting that no one--or at least no pursuer of mine--would be there.

column1: Just how fully the pursuit was organised--and indeed
column2: just what its purpose might be--I could form no idea. There seemed to be unusual activity in the town
column3: but I judged that the news of my escape from the Gilman had not yet spread. I would
column4: of course
column5: soon have to shift from Washington to some other southward street; for that party from the hotel would doubtless be after me. I must have left dust prints in that last old building
column6: revealing how I had gained the street.

column1: The open space was
column2: as I had expected
column3: strongly moonlit; and I saw the remains of a parklike
column4: iron-railed green in its center. Fortunately no one was about though a curious sort of buzz or roar seemed to be increasing in the direction of Town Square. South Street was very wide
column5: leading directly down a slight declivity to the waterfront and commanding a long view out to sea; and I hoped that no one would be glancing up it from afar as I crossed in the bright moonlight.

column1: My progress was unimpeded
column2: and no fresh sound arose to hint that I had been spied. Glancing about me
column3: I involuntarily let my pace slacken for a second to take in the sight of the sea
column4: gorgeous in the burning moonlight at the street's end. Far out beyond the breakwater was the dim
column5: dark line of Devil Reef
column6: and as I glimpsed it I could not help thinking of all the hideous legends I had heard in the last twenty-four hours--legends which portrayed this ragged rock as a veritable gateway to realms of unfathomed horror and inconceivable abnormality.

column1: Then
column2: without warning
column3: I saw the intermittent flashes of light on the distant reef. They were definite and unmistakable
column4: and awaked in my mind a blind horror beyond all rational proportion. My muscles tightened for panic flight
column5: held in only by a certain unconscious caution and half-hypnotic fascination. And to make matters worse
column6: there now flashed forth from the lofty cupola of the Gilman House
column7: which loomed up to the northeast behind me
column8: a series of analogous though differently spaced gleams which could be nothing less than an answering signal.

column1: Controlling my muscles
column2: and realising afresh--how plainly visible I was
column3: I resumed my brisker and feignedly shambling pace; though keeping my eyes on that hellish and ominous reef as long as the opening of South Street gave me a seaward view. What the whole proceeding meant
column4: I could not imagine; unless it involved some strange rite connected with Devil Reef
column5: or unless some party had landed from a ship on that sinister rock. I now bent to the left around the ruinous green; still gazing toward the ocean as it blazed in the spectral summer moonlight
column6: and watching the cryptical flashing of those nameless
column7: unexplainable beacons.

column1: It was then that the most horrible impression of all was borne in upon me--the impression which destroyed my last vestige of self-control and sent me running frantically southward past the yawning black doorways and fishily staring windows of that deserted nightmare street. For at a closer glance I saw that the moonlit waters between the reef and the shore were far from empty. They were alive with a teeming horde of shapes swimming inward toward the town; and even at my vast distance and in my single moment of perception I could tell that the bobbing heads and flailing arms were alien and aberrant in a way scarcely to be expressed or consciously formulated.
My frantic running ceased before I had covered a block
column2: for at my left I began to hear something like the hue and cry of organised pursuit. There were footsteps and guttural sounds
column3: and a rattling motor wheezed south along Federal Street. In a second all my plans were utterly changed--for if the southward highway were blocked ahead of me
column4: I must clearly find another egress from Innsmouth. I paused and drew into a gaping doorway
column5: reflecting how lucky I was to have left the moonlit open space before these pursuers came down the parallel street.

column1: A second reflection was less comforting. Since the pursuit was down another street
column2: it was plain that the party was not following me directly. It had not seen me
column3: but was simply obeying a general plan of cutting off my escape. This
column4: however
column5: implied that all roads leading out of Innsmouth were similarly patrolled; for the people could not have known what route I intended to take. If this were so
column6: I would have to make my retreat across country away from any road; but how could I do that in view of the marshy and creek-riddled nature of all the surrounding region? For a moment my brain reeled--both from sheer hopelessness and from a rapid increase in the omnipresent fishy odour.

column1: Then I thought of the abandoned railway to Rowley
column2: whose solid line of ballasted
column3: weed-grown earth still stretched off to the northwest from the crumbling station on the edge at the river-gorge. There was just a chance that the townsfolk would not think of that; since its briar-choked desertion made it half-impassable
column4: and the unlikeliest of all avenues for a fugitive to choose. I had seen it clearly from my hotel window and knew about how it lay. Most of its earlier length was uncomfortably visible from the Rowley road
column5: and from high places in the town itself; but one could perhaps crawl inconspicuously through the undergrowth. At any rate
column6: it would form my only chance of deliverance
column7: and there was nothing to do but try it.

column1: Drawing inside the hall of my deserted shelter
column2: I once more consulted the grocery boy's map with the aid of the flashlight. The immediate problem was how to reach the ancient railway; and I now saw that the safest course was ahead to Babson Street; then west to Lafayette--there edging around but not crossing an open space homologous to the one I had traversed--and subsequently back northward and westward in a zigzagging line through Lafayette
column3: Bates
column4: Adam
column5: and Bank streets--the latter skirting the river gorge--to the abandoned and dilapidated station I had seen from my window. My reason for going ahead to Babson was that I wished neither to recross the earlier open space nor to begin my westward course along a cross street as broad as South.

column1: Starting once more
column2: I crossed the street to the right-hand side in order to edge around into Babson as inconspicuously as possible. Noises still continued in Federal Street
column3: and as I glanced behind me I thought I saw a gleam of light near the building through which I had escaped. Anxious to leave Washington Street
column4: I broke into a quiet dogtrot
column5: trusting to luck not to encounter any observing eye. Next the corner of Babson Street I saw to my alarm that one of the houses was still inhabited

column7: and I passed it without disaster.

column1: In Babson Street
column2: which crossed Federal and might thus reveal me to the searchers

column4: uneven buildings; twice pausing in a doorway as the noises behind me momentarily increased. The open space ahead shone wide and desolate under the moon
column5: but my route would not force me to cross it. During my second pause I began to detect a fresh distribution of vague sounds; and upon looking cautiously out from cover beheld a motor car darting across the open space
column6: bound outward along Eliot Street
