column1: As I watched--choked by a sudden rise in the fishy odour after a short abatement--I saw a band of uncouth
column2: crouching shapes loping and shambling in the same direction; and knew that this must be the party guarding the Ipswich road

column4: and one wore a peaked diadem which glistened whitely in the moonlight. The gait of this figure was so odd that it sent a chill through me--for it seemed to me the creature was almost hopping.

column1: When the last of the band was out of sight I resumed my progress; darting around the corner into Lafayette Street
column2: and crossing Eliot very hurriedly lest stragglers of the party be still advancing along that thoroughfare. I did hear some croaking and clattering sounds far off toward Town Square
column3: but accomplished the passage without disaster. My greatest dread was in re-crossing broad and moonlit South Street--with its seaward view--and I had to nerve myself for the ordeal. Someone might easily be looking
column4: and possible Eliot Street stragglers could not fail to glimpse me from either of two points. At the last moment I decided I had better slacken my trot and make the crossing as before in the shambling gait of an average Innsmouth native.

column1: When the view of the water again opened out--this time on my right--I was half-determined not to look at it at all. I could not however
column2: resist; but cast a sidelong glance as I carefully and imitatively shambled toward the protecting shadows ahead. There was no ship visible
column3: as I had half-expected there would be. Instead
column4: the first thing which caught my eye was a small rowboat pulling in toward the abandoned wharves and laden with some bulky
column5: tarpaulin-covered object. Its rowers
column6: though distantly and indistinctly seen
column7: were of an especially repellent aspect. Several swimmers were still discernible; while on the far black reef I could see a faint
column8: steady glow unlike the winking beacon visible before
column9: and of a curious colour which I could not precisely identify. Above the slant roofs ahead and to the right there loomed the tall cupola of the Gilman House

column11: dispelled for a moment by some merciful breeze
column12: now closed in again with maddening intensity.

column1: I had not quite crossed the street when I heard a muttering band advancing along Washington from the north. As they reached the broad open space where I had had my first disquieting glimpse of the moonlit water I could see them plainly only a block away--and was horrified by the bestial abnormality of their faces and the doglike sub-humanness of their crouching gait. One man moved in a positively simian way
column2: with long arms frequently touching the ground; while another figure--robed and tiaraed--seemed to progress in an almost hopping fashion. I judged this party to be the one I had seen in the Gilman's courtyard--the one
column3: therefore
column4: most closely on my trail. As some of the figures turned to look in my direction I was transfixed with fright
column5: yet managed to preserve the casual
column6: shambling gait I had assumed. To this day I do not know whether they saw me or not. If they did
column7: my stratagem must have deceived them
column8: for they passed on across the moonlit space without varying their course--meanwhile croaking and jabbering in some hateful guttural patois I could not identify.

column1: Once more in shadow
column2: I resumed my former dog-trot past the leaning and decrepit houses that stared blankly into the night. Having crossed to the western sidewalk I rounded the nearest corner into Bates Street where I kept close to the buildings on the southern side. I passed two houses shewing signs of habitation
column3: one of which had faint lights in upper rooms
column4: yet met with no obstacle. As I turned into Adams Street I felt measurably safer
column5: but received a shook when a man reeled out of a black doorway directly in front of me. He proved
column6: however
column7: too hopelessly drunk to be a menace; so that I reached the dismal ruins of the Bank Street warehouses in safety.

column1: No one was stirring in that dead street beside the river-gorge
column2: and the roar of the waterfalls quite drowned my foot steps. It was a long dog-trot to the ruined station
column3: and the great brick warehouse walls around me seemed somehow more terrifying than the fronts of private houses. At last I saw the ancient arcaded station--or what was left of it--and made directly for the tracks that started from its farther end.

column1: The rails were rusty but mainly intact
column2: and not more than half the ties had rotted away. Walking or running on such a surface was very difficult; but I did my best
column3: and on the whole made very fair time. For some distance the line kept on along the gorge's brink

column5: I would use it; if not

column1: The vast
column2: barnlike length of the old bridge gleamed spectrally in the moonlight
column3: and I saw that the ties were safe for at least a few feet within. Entering
column4: I began to use my flashlight
column5: and was almost knocked down by the cloud of bats that flapped past me. About half-way across there was a perilous gap in the ties which I feared for a moment would halt me; but in the end I risked a desperate jump which fortunately succeeded.

column1: I was glad to see the moonlight again when I emerged from that macabre tunnel. The old tracks crossed River Street at grade
column2: and at once veered off into a region increasingly rural and with less and less of Innsmouth's abhorrent fishy odour. Here the dense growth of weeds and briers hindered me and cruelly tore at my clothes
column3: but I was none the less glad that they were there to give me concealment in case of peril. I knew that much of my route must be visible from the Rowley road.

column1: The marshy region began very abruptly
column2: with the single track on a low
column3: grassy embankment where the weedy growth was somewhat thinner. Then came a sort of island of higher ground
column4: where the line passed through a shallow open cut choked with bushes and brambles. I was very glad of this partial shelter
column5: since at this point the Rowley road was uncomfortably near according to my window view. At the end of the cut it would cross the track and swerve off to a safer distance; but meanwhile I must be exceedingly careful. I was by this time thankfully certain that the railway itself was not patrolled.

column1: Just before entering the cut I glanced behind me
column2: but saw no pursuer. The ancient spires and roofs of decaying Innsmouth gleamed lovely and ethereal in the magic yellow moonlight
column3: and I thought of how they must have looked in the old days before the shadow fell. Then
column4: as my gaze circled inland from the town
column5: something less tranquil arrested my notice and held me immobile for a second.

column1: What I saw--or fancied I saw--was a disturbing suggestion of undulant motion far to the south; a suggestion which made me conclude that a very large horde must be pouring out of the city along the level Ipswich road. The distance was great and I could distinguish nothing in detail; but I did not at all like the look of that moving column. It undulated too much
column2: and glistened too brightly in the rays of the now westering moon. There was a suggestion of sound
column3: too
column4: though the wind was blowing the other way--a suggestion of bestial scraping and bellowing even worse than the muttering of the parties I had lately overheard.

column1: All sorts of unpleasant conjectures crossed my mind. I thought of those very extreme Innsmouth types said to be hidden in crumbling
column2: centuried warrens near the waterfront; I thought
column3: too

column5: as well as those presumably covering other roads
column6: the number of my pursuers must be strangely large for a town as depopulated as Innsmouth.

column1: Whence could come the dense personnel of such a column as I now beheld? Did those ancient
column2: unplumbed warrens teem with a twisted
column3: uncatalogued
column4: and unsuspected life? Or had some unseen ship indeed landed a legion of unknown outsiders on that hellish reef? Who were they? Why were they here? And if such a column of them was scouring the Ipswich road
column5: would the patrols on the other roads be likewise augmented?

column1: I had entered the brush-grown cut and was struggling along at a very slow pace when that damnable fishy odour again waxed dominant. Had the wind suddenly changed eastward
column2: so that it blew in from the sea and over the town? It must have

column4: since I now began to hear shocking guttural murmurs from that hitherto silent direction. There was another sound
column5: too--a kind of wholesale
column6: colossal flopping or pattering which somehow called up images of the most detestable sort. It made me think illogically of that unpleasantly undulating column on the far-off Ipswich road.

column1: And then both stench and sounds grew stronger
column2: so that I paused shivering and grateful for the cut's protection. It was here
column3: I recalled
column4: that the Rowley road drew so close to the old railway before crossing westward and diverging. Something was coming along that road
column5: and I must lie low till its passage and vanishment in the distance. Thank heaven these creatures employed no dogs for tracking--though perhaps that would have been impossible amidst the omnipresent regional odour. Crouched in the bushes of that sandy cleft I felt reasonably safe
column6: even though I knew the searchers would have to cross the track in front of me not much more than a hundred yards away. I would be able to see them
column7: but they could not
column8: except by a malign miracle
column9: see me.

column1: All at once I began dreading to look at them as they passed. I saw the close moonlit space where they would surge by

column1: The stench waxed overpowering
column2: and the noises swelled to a bestial babel of croaking
column3: baying and barking without the least suggestion of human speech. Were these indeed the voices of my pursuers? Did they have dogs after all? So far I had seen none of the lower animals in Innsmouth. That flopping or pattering was monstrous--I could not look upon the degenerate creatures responsible for it. I would keep my eyes shut till the sound receded toward the west. The horde was very close now--air foul with their hoarse snarlings

column4: haunted

column2: far places. For them are the catacombs of Ptolemais
column3: and the carven mausolea of the nightmare countries. They climb to the moonlit towers of ruined Rhine castles
column4: and falter down black cobwebbed steps beneath the scattered stones of forgotten cities in Asia. The haunted wood and the desolate mountain are their shrines
column5: and they linger around the sinister monoliths on uninhabited islands. But the true epicure in the terrible
column6: to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence
column7: esteems most of all the ancient

column9: solitude
column10: grotesqueness
column11: and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous.

column1: Most horrible of all sights are the little unpainted wooden houses remote from travelled ways
column2: usually squatted upon some damp
column3: grassy slope or leaning against some gigantic outcropping of rock. Two hundred years and more they have leaned or squatted there
column4: while the vines have crawled and the trees have swelled and spread. They are almost hidden now in lawless luxuriances of green and guardian shrouds of shadow; but the small-paned windows still stare shockingly
column5: as if blinking through a lethal stupor which wards off madness by dulling the memory of unutterable things.

column1: In such houses have dwelt generations of strange people
column2: whose like the world has never seen. Seized with a gloomy and fanatical belief which exiled them from their kind
column3: their ancestors sought the wilderness for freedom. There the scions of a conquering race indeed flourished free from the restrictions of their fellows
column4: but cowered in an appalling slavery to the dismal phantasms of their own minds. Divorced from the enlightenment of civilisation
column5: the strength of these Puritans turned into singular channels; and in their isolation

column1: Remote in the desert of Araby lies the nameless city
column2: crumbling and inarticulate
column3: its low walls nearly hidden by the sands of uncounted ages. It must have been thus before the first stones of Memphis were laid
column4: and while the bricks of Babylon were yet unbaked. There is no legend so old as to give it a name
column5: or to recall that it was ever alive; but it is told of in whispers around campfires and muttered about by grandams in the tents of sheiks so that all the tribes shun it without wholly knowing why. It was of this place that Abdul Alhazred the mad poet dreamed of the night before he sang his unexplained couplet:

column1: That is not dead which can eternal lie
column2: And with strange aeons death may die.

column1: I should have known that the Arabs had good reason for shunning the nameless city

column1: For hours I waited

And then in a moment of indescribable emotion I did see it.

column6: vivid

column1: There was in this singular caravan a little boy with no father or mother
column2: but only a tiny black kitten to cherish. The plague had not been kind to him
column3: yet had left him this small furry thing to mitigate his sorrow; and when one is very young

column4: for of all that gorgeous array of specious lusciousness not one single jot was fit to eat. Into the fine flavour of the pears and apples had crept a stealthy bitterness and sickishness
column5: so that even the smallest bites induced a lasting disgust. It was the same with the melons and tomatoes
column6: and Nahum sadly saw that his entire crop was lost. Quick to connect events
column7: he declared that the meteorite had poisoned the soil
column8: and thanked Heaven that most of the other crops were in the upland lot along the road.

column1: Winter came early
column2: and was very cold. Ammi saw Nahum less often than usual
column3: and observed that he had begun to look worried. The rest of his family too
column4: seemed to have grown taciturn; and were far from steady in their church-going or their attendance at the various social events of the countryside. For this reserve or melancholy no cause could be found
column5: though all the household confessed now and then to poorer health and a feeling of vague disquiet. Nahum himself gave the most definite statement of anyone when he said he was disturbed about certain footprints in the snow. They were the usual winter prints of red squirrels
column6: white rabbits
column7: and foxes
column8: but the brooding farmer professed to see something not quite right about their nature and arrangement. He was never specific
column9: but appeared to think that they were not as characteristic of the anatomy and habits of squirrels and rabbits and foxes as they ought to be. Ammi listened without interest to this talk until one night when he drove past Nahum's house in his sleigh on the way back from Clark's Comer. There had been a moon
column10: and a rabbit had run across the road
column11: and the leaps of that rabbit were longer than either Ammi or his horse liked. The latter
column12: indeed
column13: had almost run away when brought up by a firm rein. Thereafter Ammi gave Nahum's tales more respect
column14: and wondered why the Gardner dogs seemed so cowed and quivering every morning. They had
column15: it developed
column16: nearly lost the spirit to bark.

column1: In February the McGregor boys from Meadow Hill were out shooting woodchucks
column2: and not far from the Gardner place bagged a very peculiar specimen. The proportions of its body seemed slightly altered in a queer way impossible to describe
column3: while its face had taken on an expression which no one ever saw in a woodchuck before. The boys were genuinely frightened
column4: and threw the thing away at once
column5: so that only their grotesque tales of it ever reached the people of the countryside. But the shying of horses near Nahum's house had now become an acknowledged thing
column6: and all the basis for a cycle of whispered legend was fast taking form.

column1: People vowed that the snow melted faster around Nahum's than it did anywhere else
column2: and early in March there was an awed discussion in Potter's general store at Clark's Corners. Stephen Rice had driven past Gardner's in the morning
column3: and had noticed the skunk-cabbages coming up through the mud by the woods across the road. Never were things of such size seen before
column4: and they held strange colours that could not be put into any words. Their shapes were monstrous
column5: and the horse had snorted at an odour which struck Stephen as wholly unprecedented. That afternoon several persons drove past to see the abnormal growth
column6: and all agreed that plants of that kind ought never to sprout in a healthy world. The bad fruit of the fall before was freely mentioned
column7: and it went from mouth to mouth that there was poison in Nahum's ground. Of course it was the meteorite; and remembering how strange the men from the college had found that stone to be
column8: several farmers spoke about the matter to them.

column1: One day they paid Nahum a visit; but having no love of wild tales and folklore were very conservative in what they inferred. The plants were certainly odd
column2: but all skunk-cabbages are more or less odd in shape and hue. Perhaps some mineral element from the stone had entered the soil
column3: but it would soon be washed away. And as for the footprints and frightened horses--of course this was mere country talk which such a phenomenon as the aerolite would be certain to start. There was really nothing for serious men to do in cases of wild gossip
column4: for superstitious rustics will say and believe anything. And so all through the strange days the professors stayed away in contempt. Only one of them
column5: when given two phials of dust for analysis in a police job over a year and half later
column6: recalled that the queer colour of that skunk-cabbage had been very like one of the anomalous bands of light shown by the meteor fragment in the college spectroscope
column7: and like the brittle globule found imbedded in the stone from the abyss. The samples in this analysis case gave the same odd bands at first
column8: though later they lost the property.

column1: The trees budded prematurely around Nahum's
column2: and at night they swayed ominously in the wind. Nahum's second son Thaddeus
column3: a lad of fifteen
column4: swore that they swayed also when there was no wind; but even the gossips would not credit this. Certainly
column5: however
column6: restlessness was in the air. The entire Gardner family developed the habit of stealthy listening
column7: though not for any sound which they could consciously name. The listening was
column8: indeed
column9: rather a product of moments when consciousness seemed half to slip away. Unfortunately such moments increased week by week
column10: till it became common speech that ""something was wrong with all Nahum's folks."" When the early saxifrage came out it had another strange colour; not quite like that of the skunk-cabbage
column11: but plainly related and equally unknown to anyone who saw it. Nahum took some blossoms to Arkham and showed them to the editor of the Gazette
column12: but that dignitary did no more than write a humorous article about them
column13: in which the dark fears of rustics were held up to polite ridicule. It was a mistake of Nahum's to tell a stolid city man about the way the great
column14: overgrown mourning-cloak butterflies behaved in connection with these saxifrages.

column1: April brought a kind of madness to the country folk
column2: and began that disuse of the road past Nahum's which led to its ultimate abandonment. It was the vegetation. All the orchard trees blossomed forth in strange colours
column3: and through the stony soil of the yard and adjacent pasturage there sprang up a bizarre growth which only a botanist could connect with the proper flora of the region. No sane wholesome colours were anywhere to be seen except in the green grass and leafage; but everywhere were those hectic and prismatic variants of some diseased
column4: underlying primary tone without a place among the known tints of earth. The ""Dutchman's breeches"" became a thing of sinister menace
column5: and the bloodroots grew insolent in their chromatic perversion. Ammi and the Gardners thought that most of the colours had a sort of haunting familiarity
column6: and decided that they reminded one of the brittle globule in the meteor. Nahum ploughed and sowed the ten-acre pasture and the upland lot
column7: but did nothing with the land around the house. He knew it would be of no use
column8: and hoped that the summer's strange growths would draw all the poison from the soil. He was prepared for almost anything now
column9: and had grown used to the sense of something near him waiting to be heard. The shunning of his house by neighbors told on him
column10: of course; but it told on his wife more. The boys were better off
column11: being at school each day; but they could not help being frightened by the gossip. Thaddeus
column12: an especially sensitive youth
column13: suffered the most.

column1: In May the insects came
column2: and Nahum's place became a nightmare of buzzing and crawling. Most of the creatures seemed not quite usual in their aspects and motions
column3: and their nocturnal habits contradicted all former experience. The Gardners took to watching at night--watching in all directions at random for something--they could not tell what. It was then that they owned that Thaddeus had been right about the trees. Mrs. Gardner was the next to see it from the window as she watched the swollen boughs of a maple against a moonlit sky. The boughs surely moved
column4: and there was no wind. It must be the sap. Strangeness had come into everything growing now. Yet it was none of Nahum's family at all who made the next discovery. Familiarity had dulled them
column5: and what they could not see was glimpsed by a timid windmill salesman from Bolton who drove by one night in ignorance of the country legends. What he told in Arkham was given a short paragraph in the Gazette; and it was there that all the farmers
column6: Nahum included
column7: saw it first. The night had been dark and the buggy-lamps faint
column8: but around a farm in the valley which everyone knew from the account must be Nahum's
column9: the darkness had been less thick. A dim though distinct luminosity seemed to inhere in all the vegetation
column10: grass
column11: leaves
column12: and blossoms alike
column13: while at one moment a detached piece of the phosphorescence appeared to stir furtively in the yard near the barn.

column1: The grass had so far seemed untouched
column2: and the cows were freely pastured in the lot near the house
column3: but toward the end of May the milk began to be bad. Then Nahum had the cows driven to the uplands
column4: after which this trouble ceased. Not long after this the change in grass and leaves became apparent to the eye. All the verdure was going grey
column5: and was developing a highly singular quality of brittleness. Ammi was now the only person who ever visited the place
column6: and his visits were becoming fewer and fewer. When school closed the Gardners were virtually cut off from the world
column7: and sometimes let Ammi do their errands in town. They were failing curiously both physically and mentally
column8: and no one was surprised when the news of Mrs. Gardner's madness stole around.

column1: It happened in June
column2: about the anniversary of the meteor's fall
column3: and the poor woman screamed about things in the air which she could not describe. In her raving there was not a single specific noun
column4: but only verbs and pronouns. Things moved and changed and fluttered
column5: and ears tingled to impulses which were not wholly sounds. Something was taken away--she was being drained of something--something was fastening itself on her that ought not to be--someone must make it keep off--nothing was ever still in the night--the walls and windows shifted. Nahum did not send her to the county asylum
column6: but let her wander about the house as long as she was harmless to herself and others. Even when her expression changed he did nothing. But when the boys grew afraid of her
column7: and Thaddeus nearly fainted at the way she made faces at him
column8: he decided to keep her locked in the attic. By July she had ceased to speak and crawled on all fours
column9: and before that month was over Nahum got the mad notion that she was slightly luminous in the dark
column10: as he now clearly saw was the case with the nearby vegetation.

column1: It was a little before this that the horses had stampeded. Something had aroused them in the night
column2: and their neighing and kicking in their stalls had been terrible. There seemed virtually nothing to do to calm them
column3: and when Nahum opened the stable door they all bolted out like frightened woodland deer. It took a week to track all four
column4: and when found they were seen to be quite useless and unmanageable. Something had snapped in their brains
column5: and each one had to be shot for its own good. Nahum borrowed a horse from Ammi for his haying
column6: but found it would not approach the barn. It shied
column7: balked
column8: and whinnied
column9: and in the end he could do nothing but drive it into the yard while the men used their own strength to get the heavy wagon near enough the hayloft for convenient pitching. And all the while the vegetation was turning grey and brittle. Even the flowers whose hues had been so strange were greying now
column10: and the fruit was coming out grey and dwarfed and tasteless. The asters and golden-rod bloomed grey and distorted
column11: and the roses and zinneas and hollyhocks in the front yard were such blasphemous-looking things that Nahum's oldest boy Zenas cut them down. The strangely puffed insects died about that time
column12: even the bees that had left their hives and taken to the woods.

column1: By September all the vegetation was fast crumbling to a greyish powder
column2: and Nahum feared that the trees would die before the poison was out of the soil. His wife now had spells of terrific screaming
column3: and he and the boys were in a constant state of nervous tension. They shunned people now
column4: and when school opened the boys did not go. But it was Ammi
column5: on one of his rare visits
column6: who first realised that the well water was no longer good. It had an evil taste that was not exactly fetid nor exactly salty
column7: and Ammi advised his friend to dig another well on higher ground to use till the soil was good again. Nahum
column8: however
column9: ignored the warning
column10: for he had by that time become calloused to strange and unpleasant things. He and the boys continued to use the tainted supply
column11: drinking it as listlessly and mechanically as they ate their meagre and ill-cooked meals and did their thankless and monotonous chores through the aimless days. There was something of stolid resignation about them all
column12: as if they walked half in another world between lines of nameless guards to a certain and familiar doom.

column1: Thaddeus went mad in September after a visit to the well. He had gone with a pail and had come back empty-handed
column2: shrieking and waving his arms
column3: and sometimes lapsing into an inane titter or a whisper about ""the moving colours down there."" Two in one family was pretty bad
column4: but Nahum was very brave about it. He let the boy run about for a week until he began stumbling and hurting himself
column5: and then he shut him in an attic room across the hall from his mother's. The way they screamed at each other from behind their locked doors was very terrible
column6: especially to little Merwin
column7: who fancied they talked in some terrible language that was not of earth. Merwin was getting frightfully imaginative
column8: and his restlessness was worse after the shutting away of the brother who had been his greatest playmate.

column1: Almost at the same time the mortality among the livestock commenced. Poultry turned greyish and died very quickly
column2: their meat being found dry and noisome upon cutting. Hogs grew inordinately fat
column3: then suddenly began to undergo loathsome changes which no one could explain. Their meat was of course useless
column4: and Nahum was at his wit's end. No rural veterinary would approach his place
column5: and the city veterinary from Arkham was openly baffled. The swine began growing grey and brittle and falling to pieces before they died
column6: and their eyes and muzzles developed singular alterations. It was very inexplicable
column7: for they had never been fed from the tainted vegetation. Then something struck the cows. Certain areas or sometimes the whole body would be uncannily shrivelled or compressed
column8: and atrocious collapses or disintegrations were common. In the last stages--and death was always the result--there would be a greying and turning brittle like that which beset the hogs. There could be no question of poison
column9: for all the cases occurred in a locked and undisturbed barn. No bites of prowling things could have brought the virus
column10: for what live beast of earth can pass through solid obstacles? It must be only natural disease--yet what disease could wreak such results was beyond any mind's guessing. When the harvest came there was not an animal surviving on the place
column11: for the stock and poultry were dead and the dogs had run away. These dogs
column12: three in number
column13: had all vanished one night and were never heard of again. The five cats had left some time before
column14: but their going was scarcely noticed since there now seemed to be no mice
column15: and only Mrs. Gardner had made pets of the graceful felines.

column1: On the nineteenth of October Nahum staggered into Ammi's house with hideous news. The death had come to poor Thaddeus in his attic room
column2: and it had come in a way which could not be told. Nahum had dug a grave in the railed family plot behind the farm
column3: and had put therein what he found. There could have been nothing from outside
column4: for the small barred window and locked door were intact; but it was much as it had been in the barn. Ammi and his wife consoled the stricken man as best they could
column5: but shuddered as they did so. Stark terror seemed to cling round the Gardners and all they touched
column6: and the very presence of one in the house was a breath from regions unnamed and unnamable. Ammi accompanied Nahum home with the greatest reluctance
column7: and did what he might to calm the hysterical sobbing of little Merwin. Zenas needed no calming. He had come of late to do nothing but stare into space and obey what his father told him; and Ammi thought that his fate was very merciful. Now and then Merwin's screams were answered faintly from the attic
column8: and in response to an inquiring look Nahum said that his wife was getting very feeble. When night approached
column9: Ammi managed to get away; for not even friendship could make him stay in that spot when the faint glow of the vegetation began and the trees may or may not have swayed without wind. It was really lucky for Ammi that he was not more imaginative. Even as things were
column10: his mind was bent ever so slightly; but had he been able to connect and reflect upon all the portents around him he must inevitably have turned a total maniac. In the twilight he hastened home
column11: the screams of the mad woman and the nervous child ringing horribly in his ears.

column1: Three days later Nahum burst into Ammi's kitchen in the early morning
column2: and in the absence of his host stammered out a desperate tale once more
column3: while Mrs. Pierce listened in a clutching fright. It was little Merwin this time. He was gone. He had gone out late at night with a lantern and pail for water
column4: and had never come back. He'd been going to pieces for days
column5: and hardly knew what he was about. Screamed at everything. There had been a frantic shriek from the yard then
column6: but before the father could get to the door the boy was gone. There was no glow from the lantern he had taken
column7: and of the child himself no trace. At the time Nahum thought the lantern and pail were gone too; but when dawn came
column8: and the man had plodded back from his all-night search of the woods and fields
column9: he had found some very curious things near the well. There was a crushed and apparently somewhat melted mass of iron which had certainly been the lantern; while a bent handle and twisted iron hoops beside it
column10: both half-fused
column11: seemed to hint at the remnants of the pail. That was all. Nahum was past imagining
column12: Mrs. Pierce was blank
column13: and Ammi
column14: when he had reached home and heard the tale
column15: could give no guess. Merwin was gone
column16: and there would be no use in telling the people around
column17: who shunned all Gardners now. No use
column18: either
column19: in telling the city people at Arkham who laughed at everything. Thad was gone
column20: and now Merwin was gone. Something was creeping and creeping and waiting to be seen and heard. Nahum would go soon
column21: and he wanted Ammi to look after his wife and Zenas if they survived him. It must all be a judgment of some sort; though he could not fancy what for
column22: since he had always walked uprightly in the Lord's ways so far as he knew.

column1: For over two weeks Ammi saw nothing of Nahum; and then
column2: worried about what might have happened
column3: he overcame his fears and paid the Gardner place a visit. There was no smoke from the great chimney
column4: and for a moment the visitor was apprehensive of the worst. The aspect of the whole farm was shocking--greyish withered grass and leaves on the ground
column5: vines falling in brittle wreckage from archaic walls and gables
column6: and great bare trees clawing up at the grey November sky with a studied malevolence which Ammi could not but feel had come from some subtle change in the tilt of the branches. But Nahum was alive
column7: after all. He was weak
column8: and lying on a couch in the low-ceiled kitchen
column9: but perfectly conscious and able to give simple orders to Zenas. The room was deadly cold; and as Ammi visibly shivered
column10: the host shouted huskily to Zenas for more wood. Wood
column11: indeed
column12: was sorely needed; since the cavernous fireplace was unlit and empty
column13: with a cloud of soot blowing about in the chill wind that came down the chimney. Presently Nahum asked him if the extra wood had made him any more comfortable
column14: and then Ammi saw what had happened. The stoutest cord had broken at last
column15: and the hapless farmer's mind was proof against more sorrow.

column1: Questioning tactfully
column2: Ammi could get no clear data at all about the missing Zenas. ""In the well--he lives in the well--"" was all that the clouded father would say. Then there flashed across the visitor's mind a sudden thought of the mad wife
column3: and he changed his line of inquiry. ""Nabby? Why
column4: here she is!"" was the surprised response of poor Nahum
column5: and Ammi soon saw that he must search for himself. Leaving the harmless babbler on the couch
column6: he took the keys from their nail beside the door and climbed the creaking stairs to the attic. It was very close and noisome up there
column7: and no sound could be heard from any direction. Of the four doors in sight
column8: only one was locked
column9: and on this he tried various keys of the ring he had taken. The third key proved the right one
column10: and after some fumbling Ammi threw open the low white door.

column1: It was quite dark inside
column2: for the window was small and half-obscured by the crude wooden bars; and Ammi could see nothing at all on the wide-planked floor. The stench was beyond enduring
column3: and before proceeding further he had to retreat to another room and return with his lungs filled with breathable air. When he did enter he saw something dark in the corner
column4: and upon seeing it more clearly he screamed outright. While he screamed he thought a momentary cloud eclipsed the window
column5: and a second later he felt himself brushed as if by some hateful current of vapour. Strange colours danced before his eyes; and had not a present horror numbed him he would have thought of the globule in the meteor that the geologist's hammer had shattered
column6: and of the morbid vegetation that had sprouted in the spring. As it was he thought only of the blasphemous monstrosity which confronted him
column7: and which all too clearly had shared the nameless fate of young Thaddeus and the livestock. But the terrible thing about the horror was that it very slowly and perceptibly moved as it continued to crumble.

column1: Ammi would give me no added particulars of this scene
column2: but the shape in the comer does not reappear in his tale as a moving object. There are things which cannot be mentioned
column3: and what is done in common humanity is sometimes cruelly judged by the law. I gathered that no moving thing was left in that attic room
column4: and that to leave anything capable of motion there would have been a deed so monstrous as to damn any accountable being to eternal torment. Anyone but a stolid farmer would have fainted or gone mad
column5: but Ammi walked conscious through that low doorway and locked the accursed secret behind him. There would be Nahum to deal with now; he must be fed and tended
column6: and removed to some place where he could be cared for.

column1: Commencing his descent of the dark stairs. Ammi heard a thud below him. He even thought a scream had been suddenly choked off
column2: and recalled nervously the clammy vapour which had brushed by him in that frightful room above. What presence had his cry and entry started up? Halted by some vague fear
column3: he heard still further sounds below. Indubitably there was a sort of heavy dragging
column4: and a most detestably sticky noise as of some fiendish and unclean species of suction. With an associative sense goaded to feverish heights
column5: he thought unaccountably of what he had seen upstairs. Good God! What eldritch dream-world was this into which he had blundered? He dared move neither backward nor forward
column6: but stood there trembling at the black curve of the boxed-in staircase. Every trifle of the scene burned itself into his brain. The sounds
column7: the sense of dread expectancy
column8: the darkness
column9: the steepness of the narrow step--and merciful Heaven!--the faint but unmistakable luminosity of all the woodwork in sight; steps
column10: sides
column11: exposed laths
column12: and beams alike.

column1: Then there burst forth a frantic whinny from Ammi's horse outside
column2: followed at once by a clatter which told of a frenzied runaway. In another moment horse and buggy had gone beyond earshot
column3: leaving the frightened man on the dark stairs to guess what had sent them. But that was not all. There had been another sound out there. A sort of liquid splash--water--it must have been the well. He had left Hero untied near it
column4: and a buggy wheel must have brushed the coping and knocked in a stone. And still the pale phosphorescence glowed in that detestably ancient woodwork. God! how old the house was! Most of it built before 1670
column5: and the gambrel roof no later than 1730.

column1: A feeble scratching on the floor downstairs now sounded distinctly
column2: and Ammi's grip tightened on a heavy stick he had picked up in the attic for some purpose. Slowly nerving himself
column3: he finished his descent and walked boldly toward the kitchen. But he did not complete the walk
column4: because what he sought was no longer there. It had come to meet him
column5: and it was still alive after a fashion. Whether it had crawled or whether it had been dragged by any external forces
column6: Ammi could not say; but the death had been at it. Everything had happened in the last half-hour
column7: but collapse
column8: greying
column9: and disintegration were already far advanced. There was a horrible brittleness
column10: and dry fragments were scaling off. Ammi could not touch it
column11: but looked horrifiedly into the distorted parody that had been a face. ""What was it
column12: Nahum--what was it?"" He whispered
column13: and the cleft
column14: bulging lips were just able to crackle out a final answer.

column1: Nothin'...nothin'...the colour...it burns...cold an' wet
column2: but it burns...it lived in the well...I seen it...a kind of smoke...jest like the flowers last spring...the well shone at night...Thad an' Merwin an' Zenas...everything alive...suckin' the life out of everything...in that stone...it must a' come in that stone pizened the whole place...dun't know what it wants...that round thing them men from the college dug outen the stone...they smashed it...it was the same colour...jest the same
column3: like the flowers an' plants...must a' ben more of 'em...seeds...seeds...they growed...I seen it the fust time this week...must a' got strong on Zenas...he was a big boy
column4: full o' life...it beats down your mind an' then gets ye...burns ye up...in the well water...you was right about that...evil water...Zenas never come back from the well...can't git away...draws ye...ye know summ'at's comin' but tain't no use...I seen it time an' agin senct Zenas was took...whar's Nabby
column5: Ammi?...my head's no good...dun't know how long sense I fed her...it'll git her ef we ain't keerful...jest a colour...her face is gittin' to hev that colour sometimes towards night...an' it burns an' sucks...it come from some place whar things ain't as they is here...one o' them professors said so...he was right...look out
column6: Ammi
column7: it'll do suthin' more...sucks the life out...""

column1: But that was all. That which spoke could speak no more because it had completely caved in. Ammi laid a red checked tablecloth over what was left and reeled out the back door into the fields. He climbed the slope to the ten-acre pasture and stumbled home by the north road and the woods. He could not pass that well from which his horses had run away. He had looked at it through the window
column2: and had seen that no stone was missing from the rim. Then the lurching buggy had not dislodged anything after all--the splash had been something else--something which went into the well after it had done with poor Nahum.

column1: When Ammi reached his house the horses and buggy had arrived before him and thrown his wife into fits of anxiety. Reassuring her without explanations
column2: he set out at once for Arkham and notified the authorities that the Gardner family was no more. He indulged in no details
column3: but merely told of the deaths of Nahum and Nabby
column4: that of Thaddeus being already known
column5: and mentioned that the cause seemed to be the same strange ailment which had killed the live-stock. He also stated that Merwin and Zenas had disappeared. There was considerable questioning at the police station
column6: and in the end Ammi was compelled to take three officers to the Gardner farm
column7: together with the coroner
column8: the medical examiner
column9: and the veterinary who had treated the diseased animals. He went much against his will
column10: for the afternoon was advancing and he feared the fall of night over that accursed place
column11: but it was some comfort to have so many people with him.

column1: The six men drove out in a democrat-wagon
column2: following Ammi's buggy
column3: and arrived at the pest-ridden farmhouse about four o'clock. Used as the officers were to gruesome experiences
column4: not one remained unmoved at what was found in the attic and under the red checked tablecloth on the floor below. The whole aspect of the farm with its grey desolation was terrible enough
column5: but those two crumbling objects were beyond all bounds. No one could look long at them
column6: and even the medical examiner admitted that there was very little to examine. Specimens could be analysed
column7: of course
column8: so he busied himself in obtaining them--and here it develops that a very puzzling aftermath occurred at the college laboratory where the two phials of dust were finally taken. Under the spectroscope both samples gave off an unknown spectrum
column9: in which many of the baffling bands were precisely like those which the strange meteor had yielded in the previous year. The property of emitting this spectrum vanished in a month
column10: the dust thereafter consisting mainly of alkaline phosphates and carbonates.

column1: Ammi would not have told the men about the well if he had thought they meant to do anything then and there. It was getting toward sunset
column2: and he was anxious to be away. But he could not help glancing nervously at the stony curb by the great sweep
column3: and when a detective questioned him he admitted that Nahum had feared something down there so much so that he had never even thought of searching it for Merwin or Zenas. After that nothing would do but that they empty and explore the well immediately
column4: so Ammi had to wait trembling while pail after pail of rank water was hauled up and splashed on the soaking ground outside. The men sniffed in disgust at the fluid
column5: and toward the last held their noses against the foetor they were uncovering. It was not so long a job as they had feared it would be

column1: Assuming that I was sane and awake
column2: my experience on that night was such as has befallen no man before. It was
column3: moreover
column4: a frightful confirmation of all I had sought to dismiss as myth and dream. Mercifully there is no proof

column6: but chance and the shifting sand have so far saved them from finding it. Now I must formulate some definitive statement—not only for the sake of my own mental balance
column7: but to warn such others as may read it seriously.

column1: These pages—much in whose earlier parts will be familiar to close readers of the general and scientific press—are written in the cabin of the ship that is bringing me home. I shall give them to my son
column2: Prof. Wingate Peaslee of Miskatonic University—the only member of my family who stuck to me after my queer amnesia of long ago
column3: and the man best informed on the inner facts of my case. Of all living persons
column4: he is least likely to ridicule what I shall tell of that fateful night. I did not enlighten him orally before sailing
column5: because I think he had better have the revelation in written form. Reading and re-reading at leisure will leave with him a more convincing picture than my confused tongue could hope to convey. He can do as he thinks best with this account—shewing it
column6: with suitable comment
column7: to any quarters where it will be likely to accomplish good. It is for the sake of such readers as are unfamiliar with the earlier phases of my case that I am prefacing the revelation itself with a fairly ample summary of its background.

column1: My name is Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee
column2: and those who recall the newspaper tales of a generation back—or the letters and articles in psychological journals six or seven years ago—will know who and what I am. The press was filled with the details of my strange amnesia in 1908–13
column3: and much was made of the traditions of horror
column4: madness
column5: and witchcraft which lurk behind the ancient Massachusetts town then and now forming my place of residence. Yet I would have it known that there is nothing whatever of the mad or sinister in my heredity and early life. This is a highly important fact in view of the shadow which fell so suddenly upon me from outside sources. It may be that centuries of dark brooding had given to crumbling
column6: whisper-haunted Arkham a peculiar vulnerability as regards such shadows—though even this seems doubtful in the light of those other cases which I later came to study. But the chief point is that my own ancestry and background are altogether normal. What came
column7: came from somewhere else—where
column8: I even now hesitate to assert in plain words.

column1: I am the son of Jonathan and Hannah (Wingate) Peaslee

column3: and came back to Miskatonic as Instructor of Political Economy in 1895. For thirteen years more my life ran smoothly and happily. I married Alice Keezar of Haverhill in 1896

column1: It was on Thursday
column2: May 14

column1: The collapse occurred about 10:20 a.m.
column2: while I was conducting a class in Political Economy VI—history and present tendencies of economics—for juniors and a few sophomores. I began to see strange shapes before my eyes
column3: and to feel that I was in a grotesque room other than the classroom. My thoughts and speech wandered from my subject
column4: and the students saw that something was gravely amiss. Then I slumped down
column5: unconscious in my chair
column6: in a stupor from which no one could arouse me. Nor did my rightful faculties again look out upon the daylight of our normal world for five years
column7: four months

column1: It is
column2: of course

column4: though removed to my home at 27 Crane St. and given the best of medical attention. At 3 a.m. May 15 my eyes opened and I began to speak
column5: but before long the doctors and my family were thoroughly frightened by the trend of my expression and language. It was clear that I had no remembrance of my identity or of my past

column1: Even my speech seemed awkward and foreign. I used my vocal organs clumsily and gropingly
column2: and my diction had a curiously stilted quality
column3: as if I had laboriously learned the English language from books. The pronunciation was barbarously alien
column4: whilst the idiom seemed to include both scraps of curious archaism and expressions of a wholly incomprehensible cast. Of the latter one in particular was very potently—even terrifiedly—recalled by the youngest of the physicians twenty years afterward. For at that late period such a phrase began to have an actual currency—first in England and then in the United States—and though of much complexity and indisputable newness
column5: it reproduced in every least particular the mystifying words of the strange Arkham patient of 1908.

column10: art

column6: customs

column1: As soon as permitted
column2: I haunted the college library at all hours; and shortly began to arrange for those odd travels
column3: and special courses at American and European universities

column1: Of real friendliness
column2: however
column3: I encountered little. Something in my aspect and speech seemed to excite vague fears and aversions in everyone I met
column4: as if I were a being infinitely removed from all that is normal and healthful. This idea of a black
column5: hidden horror connected with incalculable gulfs of some sort of distance was oddly widespread and persistent. My own family formed no exception. From the moment of my strange waking my wife had regarded me with extreme horror and loathing
column6: vowing that I was some utter alien usurping the body of her husband. In 1910 she obtained a legal divorce

column1: Only my second son Wingate seemed able to conquer the terror and repulsion which my change aroused. He indeed felt that I was a stranger

column3: and the courts gave me his custody. In succeeding years he helped me with the studies to which I was driven
column4: and today at thirty-five he is a professor of psychology at Miskatonic. But I do not wonder at the horror I caused—for certainly
column5: the mind
column6: voice
column7: and facial expression of the being that awaked on May 15

column1: I will not attempt to tell much of my life from 1908 to 1913
column2: since readers may glean all the outward essentials—as I largely had to do—from files of old newspapers and scientific journals. I was given charge of my funds
column3: and spent them slowly and on the whole wisely
column4: in travel and in study at various centres of learning. My travels
column5: however
column6: were singular in the extreme; involving long visits to remote and desolate places. In 1909 I spent a month in the Himalayas
column7: and in 1911 aroused much attention through a camel trip into the unknown deserts of Arabia. What happened on those journeys I have never been able to learn. During the summer of 1912 I chartered a ship and sailed in the Arctic north of Spitzbergen
column8: afterward shewing signs of disappointment. Later in that year I spent weeks alone beyond the limits of previous or subsequent exploration in the vast limestone cavern systems of western Virginia—black labyrinths so complex that no retracing of my steps could even be considered.

column1: My sojourns at the universities were marked by abnormally rapid assimilation
column2: as if the secondary personality had an intelligence enormously superior to my own. I have found
column3: also
column4: that my rate of reading and solitary study was phenomenal. I could master every detail of a book merely by glancing over it as fast as I could turn the leaves; while my skill at interpreting complex figures in an instant was veritably awesome. At times there appeared almost ugly reports of my power to influence the thoughts and acts of others
column5: though I seemed to have taken care to minimise displays of this faculty.

column5: Ludvig Prinn’s De Vermis Mysteriis

column3: since all the recollections I gave were casual

column1: When the doctor reached my house he found me unconscious in the sitting-room—in an easy-chair with a table drawn up before it. On the polished table-top were scratches shewing where some heavy object had rested. The queer machine was gone

column1: II.
My reabsorption into normal life was a painful and difficult process. The loss of over five years creates more complications than can be imagined
column2: and in my case there were countless matters to be adjusted. What I heard of my actions since 1908 astonished and disturbed me
column3: but I tried to view the matter as philosophically as I could. At last regaining custody of my second son Wingate
column4: I settled down with him in the Crane Street house and endeavoured to resume teaching—my old professorship having been kindly offered me by the college.

column1: I began work with the February
column3: term
column4: and kept at it just a year. By that time I realised how badly my experience had shaken me. Though perfectly sane—I hoped—and with no flaw in my original personality
column5: I had not the nervous energy of the old days. Vague dreams and queer ideas continually haunted me
column6: and when the outbreak of the world war turned my mind to history I found myself thinking of periods and events in the oddest possible fashion. My conception of time—my ability to distinguish between consecutiveness and simultaneousness—seemed subtly disordered; so that I formed chimerical notions about living in one age and casting one’s mind all over eternity for knowledge of past and future ages.

column1: The war gave me strange impressions of remembering some of its far-off consequences—as if I knew how it was coming out and could look back upon it in the light of future information. All such quasi-memories were attended with much pain
column2: and with a feeling that some artificial psychological barrier was set against them. When I diffidently hinted to others about my impressions I met with varied responses. Some persons looked uncomfortably at me
column3: but men in the mathematics department spoke of new developments in those theories of relativity—then discussed only in learned circles—which were later to become so famous. Dr. Albert Einstein
column4: they said
column5: was rapidly reducing time to the status of a mere dimension.

column1: But the dreams and disturbed feelings gained on me
column2: so that I had to drop my regular work in 1915. Certain of the impressions were taking an annoying shape—giving me the persistent notion that my amnesia had formed some unholy sort of exchange; that the secondary personality had indeed been an intruding force from unknown regions
column3: and that my own personality had suffered displacement. Thus I was driven to vague and frightful speculations concerning the whereabouts of my true self during the years that another had held my body. The curious knowledge and strange conduct of my body’s late tenant troubled me more and more as I learned further details from persons
column4: papers
column5: and magazines. Queernesses that had baffled others seemed to harmonise terribly with some background of black knowledge which festered in the chasms of my subconscious. I began to search feverishly for every scrap of information bearing on the studies and travels of that other one during the dark years.

column1: Not all of my troubles were as semi-abstract as this. There were the dreams—and these seemed to grow in vividness and concreteness. Knowing how most would regard them
column2: I seldom mentioned them to anyone but my son or certain trusted psychologists
column3: but eventually I commenced a scientific study of other cases in order to see how typical or non-typical such visions might be among amnesia victims. My results
column4: aided by psychologists
column5: historians
column6: anthropologists
column7: and mental specialists of wide experience
column8: and by a study that included all records of split personalities from the days of daemoniac-possession legends to the medically realistic present
column9: at first bothered me more than they consoled me.

column1: I soon found that my dreams had indeed no counterpart in the overwhelming bulk of true amnesia cases. There remained
column2: however
column3: a tiny residue of accounts which for years baffled and shocked me with their parallelism to my own experience. Some of them were bits of ancient folklore; others were case-histories in the annals of medicine; one or two were anecdotes obscurely buried in standard histories. It thus appeared that
column4: while my special kind of affliction was prodigiously rare
column5: instances of it had occurred at long intervals ever since the beginning of man’s annals. Some centuries might contain one
column6: two
column7: or three cases; others none—or at least none whose record survived.

column1: The essence was always the same—a person of keen thoughtfulness seized with a strange secondary life and leading for a greater or lesser period an utterly alien existence typified at first by vocal and bodily awkwardness
column2: and later by a wholesale acquisition of scientific
column3: historic
column4: artistic
column5: and anthropological knowledge; an acquisition carried on with feverish zest and with a wholly abnormal absorptive power. Then a sudden return of the rightful consciousness
column6: intermittently plagued ever after with vague unplaceable dreams suggesting fragments of some hideous memory elaborately blotted out. And the close resemblance of those nightmares to my own—even in some of the smallest particulars—left no doubt in my mind of their significantly typical nature. One or two of the cases had an added ring of faint
column7: blasphemous familiarity
column8: as if I had heard of them before through some cosmic channel too morbid and frightful to contemplate. In three instances there was specific mention of such an unknown machine as had been in my house before the second change.

column1: Another thing that cloudily worried me during my investigation was the somewhat greater frequency of cases where a brief
column2: elusive glimpse of the typical nightmares was afforded to persons not visited with well-defined amnesia. These persons were largely of mediocre mind or less—some so primitive that they could scarcely be thought of as vehicles for abnormal scholarship and preternatural mental acquisitions. For a second they would be fired with alien force—then a backward lapse and a thin
column3: swift-fading memory of un-human horrors.

column1: There had been at least three such cases during the past half century—one only fifteen years before. Had something been groping blindly through time from some unsuspected abyss in Nature? Were these faint cases monstrous
column2: sinister experiments of a kind and authorship utterly beyond sane belief? Such were a few of the formless speculations of my weaker hours—fancies abetted by myths which my studies uncovered. For I could not doubt but that certain persistent legends of immemorial antiquity
column3: apparently unknown to the victims and physicians connected with recent amnesia cases
column4: formed a striking and awesome elaboration of memory lapses such as mine.

column1: Of the nature of the dreams and impressions which were growing so clamorous I still almost fear to speak. They seemed to savour of madness
column2: and at times I believed I was indeed going mad. Was there a special type of delusion afflicting those who had suffered lapses of memory? Conceivably
column3: the efforts of the subconscious mind to fill up a perplexing blank with pseudo-memories might give rise to strange imaginative vagaries. This
column4: indeed (though an alternative folklore theory finally seemed to me more plausible)
column5: was the belief of many of the alienists who helped me in my search for parallel cases
column6: and who shared my puzzlement at the exact resemblances sometimes discovered. They did not call the condition true insanity
column7: but classed it rather among neurotic disorders. My course in trying to track it down and analyse it
column8: instead of vainly seeking to dismiss or forget it
column9: they heartily endorsed as correct according to the best psychological principles. I especially valued the advice of such physicians as had studied me during my possession by the other personality.

column1: My first disturbances were not visual at all
column2: but concerned the more abstract matters which I have mentioned. There was
column3: too

column5: as if my eyes would find it something utterly alien and inconceivably abhorrent. When I did glance down and behold the familiar human shape in quiet grey or blue clothing I always felt a curious relief

column1: It was a long time before I correlated any of these disappointed feelings with the fleeting visual impressions which began to develop. The first such correlation had to do with the odd sensation of an external
column2: artificial restraint on my memory. I felt that the snatches of sight I experienced had a profound and terrible meaning

column5: and with it desperate efforts to place the fragmentary dream-glimpses in the chronological and spatial pattern.

column1: The glimpses themselves were at first merely strange rather than horrible. I would seem to be in an enormous vaulted chamber whose lofty stone groinings were well-nigh lost in the shadows overhead. In whatever time or place the scene might be
column2: the principle of the arch was known as fully and used as extensively as by the Romans. There were colossal round windows and high arched doors
column3: and pedestals or tables each as tall as the height of an ordinary room. Vast shelves of dark wood lined the walls
column4: holding what seemed to be volumes of immense size with strange hieroglyphs on their backs. The exposed stonework held curious carvings
column5: always in curvilinear mathematical designs
column6: and there were chiselled inscriptions in the same characters that the huge books bore. The dark granite masonry was of a monstrous megalithic type
column7: with lines of convex-topped blocks fitting the concave-bottomed courses which rested upon them. There were no chairs
column8: but the tops of the vast pedestals were littered with books
column9: papers
column10: and what seemed to be writing materials—oddly figured jars of a purplish metal
column11: and rods with stained tips. Tall as the pedestals were
column12: I seemed at times able to view them from above. On some of them were great globes of luminous crystal serving as lamps
column13: and inexplicable machines formed of vitreous tubes and metal rods. The windows were glazed
column14: and latticed with stout-looking bars. Though I dared not approach and peer out them
column15: I could see from where I was the waving tops of singular fern-like growths. The floor was of massive octagonal flagstones
column16: while rugs and hangings were entirely lacking.

column1: Later I had visions of sweeping through Cyclopean corridors of stone
column2: and up and down gigantic inclined planes of the same monstrous masonry. There were no stairs anywhere
column3: nor was any passageway less than thirty feet wide. Some of the structures through which I floated must have towered into the sky for thousands of feet. There were multiple levels of black vaults below
column4: and never-opened trap-doors
column5: sealed down with metal bands and holding dim suggestions of some special peril. I seemed to be a prisoner
column6: and horror hung broodingly over everything I saw. I felt that the mocking curvilinear hieroglyphs on the walls would blast my soul with their message were I not guarded by a merciful ignorance.

column1: Still later my dreams included vistas from the great round windows
column2: and from the titanic flat roof
column3: with its curious gardens
column4: wide barren area
column5: and high
column6: scalloped parapet of stone

column8: each in its garden

column10: but few were less than five hundred feet square or a thousand feet high. Many seemed so limitless that they must have had a frontage of several thousand feet

column13: and most of them embodied the oddly curvilinear type of masonry noticeable in the building that held me. Roofs were flat and garden-covered
column14: and tended to have scalloped parapets. Sometimes there were terraces and higher levels

column1: In certain places I beheld enormous dark cylindrical towers which climbed far above any of the other structures. These appeared to be of a totally unique nature
column2: and shewed signs of prodigious age and dilapidation. They were built of a bizarre type of square-cut basalt masonry
column3: and tapered slightly toward their rounded tops. Nowhere in any of them could the least traces of windows or other apertures save huge doors be found. I noticed also some lower buildings—all crumbling with the weathering of aeons—which resembled these dark cylindrical towers in basic architecture. Around all these aberrant piles of square-cut masonry there hovered an inexplicable aura of menace and concentrated fear
column4: like that bred by the sealed trap-doors.

column4: and past other cities as strange as the one which persistently haunted me. I saw monstrous constructions of black or iridescent stone in glades and clearings where perpetual twilight reigned

column6: towering vegetation. Once I saw an area of countless miles strown with age-blasted basaltic ruins whose architecture had been like that of the few windowless
column7: round-topped towers in the haunting city. And once I saw the sea—a boundless steamy expanse beyond the colossal stone piers of an enormous town of domes and arches. Great shapeless suggestions of shadow moved over it

column1: Piecing together the scattered records
column2: ancient and modern
column3: anthropological and medical
column4: I found a fairly consistent mixture of myth and hallucination whose scope and wildness left me utterly dazed. Only one thing consoled me—the fact that the myths were of such early existence. What lost knowledge could have brought pictures of the Palaeozoic or Mesozoic landscape into these primitive fables
column5: I could not even guess

Cases of amnesia no doubt created the general myth-pattern—but afterward the fanciful accretions of the myths must have reacted on amnesia sufferers and coloured their pseudo-memories. I myself had read and heard all the early tales during my memory lapse—my quest had amply proved that. Was it not natural
column8: then
