column1: Hot as it was
column2: they tested it in a crucible with all the proper reagents. Water did nothing. Hydrochloric acid was the same. Nitric acid and even aqua regia merely hissed and spattered against its torrid invulnerability. Ammi had difficulty in recalling all these things
column3: but recognized some solvents as I mentioned them in the usual order of use. There were ammonia and caustic soda
column4: alcohol and ether
column5: nauseous carbon disulphide and a dozen others; but although the weight grew steadily less as time passed
column6: and the fragment seemed to be slightly cooling
column7: there was no change in the solvents to show that they had attacked the substance at all. It was a metal
column8: though
column9: beyond a doubt. It was magnetic
column10: for one thing; and after its immersion in the acid solvents there seemed to be faint traces of the Widmanstatten figures found on meteoric iron. When the cooling had grown very considerable
column11: the testing was carried on in glass; and it was in a glass beaker that they left all the chips made of the original fragment during the work. The next morning both chips and beaker were gone without trace
column12: and only a charred spot marked the place on the wooden shelf where they had been.

column1: All this the professors told Ammi as they paused at his door
column2: and once more he went with them to see the stony messenger from the stars
column3: though this time his wife did not accompany him. It had now most certainly shrunk
column4: and even the sober professors could not doubt the truth of what they saw. All around the dwindling brown lump near the well was a vacant space
column5: except where the earth had caved in; and whereas it had been a good seven feet across the day before
column6: it was now scarcely five. It was still hot
column7: and the sages studied its surface curiously as they detached another and larger piece with hammer and chisel. They gouged deeply this time
column8: and as they pried away the smaller mass they saw that the core of the thing was not quite homogeneous.

column1: They had uncovered what seemed to be the side of a large coloured globule embedded in the substance. The colour
column2: which resembled some of the bands in the meteor's strange spectrum
column3: was almost impossible to describe; and it was only by analogy that they called it colour at all. Its texture was glossy
column4: and upon tapping it appeared to promise both brittleness and hollowness. One of the professors gave it a smart blow with a hammer
column5: and it burst with a nervous little pop. Nothing was emitted
column6: and all trace of the thing vanished with the puncturing. It left behind a hollow spherical space about three inches across
column7: and all thought it probable that others would be discovered as the enclosing substance wasted away.

column1: Conjecture was vain; so after a futile attempt to find additional globules by drilling
column2: the seekers left again with their new specimen which proved
column3: however
column4: as baffling in the laboratory as its predecessor. Aside from being almost plastic
column5: having heat
column6: magnetism
column7: and slight luminosity
column8: cooling slightly in powerful acids
column9: possessing an unknown spectrum
column10: wasting away in air
column11: and attacking silicon compounds with mutual destruction as a result
column12: it presented no identifying features whatsoever; and at the end of the tests the college scientists were forced to own that they could not place it. It was nothing of this earth
column13: but a piece of the great outside; and as such dowered with outside properties and obedient to outside laws.

column1: That night there was a thunderstorm
column2: and when the professors went out to Nahum's the next day they met with a bitter disappointment. The stone
column3: magnetic as it had been
column4: must have had some peculiar electrical property; for it had ""drawn the lightning
column5: as Nahum said
column6: with a singular persistence. Six times within an hour the farmer saw the lightning strike the furrow in the front yard
column7: and when the storm was over nothing remained but a ragged pit by the ancient well-sweep
column8: half-choked with a caved-in earth. Digging had borne no fruit
column9: and the scientists verified the fact of the utter vanishment. The failure was total; so that nothing was left to do but go back to the laboratory and test again the disappearing fragment left carefully cased in lead. That fragment lasted a week
column10: at the end of which nothing of value had been learned of it. When it had gone
column11: no residue was left behind
column12: and in time the professors felt scarcely sure they had indeed seen with waking eyes that cryptic vestige of the fathomless gulfs outside; that lone
column13: weird message from other universes and other realms of matter
column14: force
column15: and entity.

column1: As was natural
column2: the Arkham papers made much of the incident with its collegiate sponsoring
column3: and sent reporters to talk with Nahum Gardner and his family. At least one Boston daily also sent a scribe
column4: and Nahum quickly became a kind of local celebrity. He was a lean
column5: genial person of about fifty
column6: living with his wife and three sons on the pleasant farmstead in the valley. He and Ammi exchanged visits frequently
column7: as did their wives; and Ammi had nothing but praise for him after all these years. He seemed slightly proud of the notice his place had attracted
column8: and talked often of the meteorite in the succeeding weeks. That July and August were hot; and Nahum worked hard at his haying in the ten-acre pasture across Chapman's Brook; his rattling wain wearing deep ruts in the shadowy lanes between. The labour tired him more than it had in other years
column9: and he felt that age was beginning to tell on him.

column1: Then fell the time of fruit and harvest. The pears and apples slowly ripened
column2: and Nahum vowed that his orchards were prospering as never before. The fruit was growing to phenomenal size and unwonted gloss
column3: and in such abundance that extra barrels were ordered to handle the future crop. But with the ripening came sore disappointment
column4: for of all that gorgeous array of specious lusciousness not one single jot was fit to eat. Into the fine flavour of the pears and apples had crept a stealthy bitterness and sickishness
column5: so that even the smallest bites induced a lasting disgust. It was the same with the melons and tomatoes
column6: and Nahum sadly saw that his entire crop was lost. Quick to connect events
column7: he declared that the meteorite had poisoned the soil
column8: and thanked Heaven that most of the other crops were in the upland lot along the road.

column1: Winter came early
column2: and was very cold. Ammi saw Nahum less often than usual
column3: and observed that he had begun to look worried. The rest of his family too
column4: seemed to have grown taciturn; and were far from steady in their church-going or their attendance at the various social events of the countryside. For this reserve or melancholy no cause could be found
column5: though all the household confessed now and then to poorer health and a feeling of vague disquiet. Nahum himself gave the most definite statement of anyone when he said he was disturbed about certain footprints in the snow. They were the usual winter prints of red squirrels
column6: white rabbits
column7: and foxes
column8: but the brooding farmer professed to see something not quite right about their nature and arrangement. He was never specific
column9: but appeared to think that they were not as characteristic of the anatomy and habits of squirrels and rabbits and foxes as they ought to be. Ammi listened without interest to this talk until one night when he drove past Nahum's house in his sleigh on the way back from Clark's Comer. There had been a moon
column10: and a rabbit had run across the road
column11: and the leaps of that rabbit were longer than either Ammi or his horse liked. The latter
column12: indeed
column13: had almost run away when brought up by a firm rein. Thereafter Ammi gave Nahum's tales more respect
column14: and wondered why the Gardner dogs seemed so cowed and quivering every morning. They had
column15: it developed
column16: nearly lost the spirit to bark.

column1: In February the McGregor boys from Meadow Hill were out shooting woodchucks
column2: and not far from the Gardner place bagged a very peculiar specimen. The proportions of its body seemed slightly altered in a queer way impossible to describe
column3: while its face had taken on an expression which no one ever saw in a woodchuck before. The boys were genuinely frightened
column4: and threw the thing away at once
column5: so that only their grotesque tales of it ever reached the people of the countryside. But the shying of horses near Nahum's house had now become an acknowledged thing
column6: and all the basis for a cycle of whispered legend was fast taking form.

column1: People vowed that the snow melted faster around Nahum's than it did anywhere else
column2: and early in March there was an awed discussion in Potter's general store at Clark's Corners. Stephen Rice had driven past Gardner's in the morning
column3: and had noticed the skunk-cabbages coming up through the mud by the woods across the road. Never were things of such size seen before
column4: and they held strange colours that could not be put into any words. Their shapes were monstrous
column5: and the horse had snorted at an odour which struck Stephen as wholly unprecedented. That afternoon several persons drove past to see the abnormal growth
column6: and all agreed that plants of that kind ought never to sprout in a healthy world. The bad fruit of the fall before was freely mentioned
column7: and it went from mouth to mouth that there was poison in Nahum's ground. Of course it was the meteorite; and remembering how strange the men from the college had found that stone to be
column8: several farmers spoke about the matter to them.

column1: One day they paid Nahum a visit; but having no love of wild tales and folklore were very conservative in what they inferred. The plants were certainly odd
column2: but all skunk-cabbages are more or less odd in shape and hue. Perhaps some mineral element from the stone had entered the soil
column3: but it would soon be washed away. And as for the footprints and frightened horses--of course this was mere country talk which such a phenomenon as the aerolite would be certain to start. There was really nothing for serious men to do in cases of wild gossip
column4: for superstitious rustics will say and believe anything. And so all through the strange days the professors stayed away in contempt. Only one of them
column5: when given two phials of dust for analysis in a police job over a year and half later
column6: recalled that the queer colour of that skunk-cabbage had been very like one of the anomalous bands of light shown by the meteor fragment in the college spectroscope
column7: and like the brittle globule found imbedded in the stone from the abyss. The samples in this analysis case gave the same odd bands at first
column8: though later they lost the property.

column1: The trees budded prematurely around Nahum's
column2: and at night they swayed ominously in the wind. Nahum's second son Thaddeus
column3: a lad of fifteen
column4: swore that they swayed also when there was no wind; but even the gossips would not credit this. Certainly
column5: however
column6: restlessness was in the air. The entire Gardner family developed the habit of stealthy listening
column7: though not for any sound which they could consciously name. The listening was
column8: indeed
column9: rather a product of moments when consciousness seemed half to slip away. Unfortunately such moments increased week by week
column10: till it became common speech that ""something was wrong with all Nahum's folks."" When the early saxifrage came out it had another strange colour; not quite like that of the skunk-cabbage
column11: but plainly related and equally unknown to anyone who saw it. Nahum took some blossoms to Arkham and showed them to the editor of the Gazette
column12: but that dignitary did no more than write a humorous article about them
column13: in which the dark fears of rustics were held up to polite ridicule. It was a mistake of Nahum's to tell a stolid city man about the way the great
column14: overgrown mourning-cloak butterflies behaved in connection with these saxifrages.

column1: April brought a kind of madness to the country folk
column2: and began that disuse of the road past Nahum's which led to its ultimate abandonment. It was the vegetation. All the orchard trees blossomed forth in strange colours
column3: and through the stony soil of the yard and adjacent pasturage there sprang up a bizarre growth which only a botanist could connect with the proper flora of the region. No sane wholesome colours were anywhere to be seen except in the green grass and leafage; but everywhere were those hectic and prismatic variants of some diseased
column4: underlying primary tone without a place among the known tints of earth. The ""Dutchman's breeches"" became a thing of sinister menace
column5: and the bloodroots grew insolent in their chromatic perversion. Ammi and the Gardners thought that most of the colours had a sort of haunting familiarity
column6: and decided that they reminded one of the brittle globule in the meteor. Nahum ploughed and sowed the ten-acre pasture and the upland lot
column7: but did nothing with the land around the house. He knew it would be of no use
column8: and hoped that the summer's strange growths would draw all the poison from the soil. He was prepared for almost anything now
column9: and had grown used to the sense of something near him waiting to be heard. The shunning of his house by neighbors told on him
column10: of course; but it told on his wife more. The boys were better off
column11: being at school each day; but they could not help being frightened by the gossip. Thaddeus
column12: an especially sensitive youth
column13: suffered the most.

column1: In May the insects came
column2: and Nahum's place became a nightmare of buzzing and crawling. Most of the creatures seemed not quite usual in their aspects and motions
column3: and their nocturnal habits contradicted all former experience. The Gardners took to watching at night--watching in all directions at random for something--they could not tell what. It was then that they owned that Thaddeus had been right about the trees. Mrs. Gardner was the next to see it from the window as she watched the swollen boughs of a maple against a moonlit sky. The boughs surely moved
column4: and there was no wind. It must be the sap. Strangeness had come into everything growing now. Yet it was none of Nahum's family at all who made the next discovery. Familiarity had dulled them
column5: and what they could not see was glimpsed by a timid windmill salesman from Bolton who drove by one night in ignorance of the country legends. What he told in Arkham was given a short paragraph in the Gazette; and it was there that all the farmers
column6: Nahum included
column7: saw it first. The night had been dark and the buggy-lamps faint
column8: but around a farm in the valley which everyone knew from the account must be Nahum's
column9: the darkness had been less thick. A dim though distinct luminosity seemed to inhere in all the vegetation
column10: grass
column11: leaves
column12: and blossoms alike
column13: while at one moment a detached piece of the phosphorescence appeared to stir furtively in the yard near the barn.

column1: The grass had so far seemed untouched
column2: and the cows were freely pastured in the lot near the house
column3: but toward the end of May the milk began to be bad. Then Nahum had the cows driven to the uplands
column4: after which this trouble ceased. Not long after this the change in grass and leaves became apparent to the eye. All the verdure was going grey
column5: and was developing a highly singular quality of brittleness. Ammi was now the only person who ever visited the place
column6: and his visits were becoming fewer and fewer. When school closed the Gardners were virtually cut off from the world
column7: and sometimes let Ammi do their errands in town. They were failing curiously both physically and mentally
column8: and no one was surprised when the news of Mrs. Gardner's madness stole around.

column1: It happened in June
column2: about the anniversary of the meteor's fall
column3: and the poor woman screamed about things in the air which she could not describe. In her raving there was not a single specific noun
column4: but only verbs and pronouns. Things moved and changed and fluttered
column5: and ears tingled to impulses which were not wholly sounds. Something was taken away--she was being drained of something--something was fastening itself on her that ought not to be--someone must make it keep off--nothing was ever still in the night--the walls and windows shifted. Nahum did not send her to the county asylum
column6: but let her wander about the house as long as she was harmless to herself and others. Even when her expression changed he did nothing. But when the boys grew afraid of her
column7: and Thaddeus nearly fainted at the way she made faces at him
column8: he decided to keep her locked in the attic. By July she had ceased to speak and crawled on all fours
column9: and before that month was over Nahum got the mad notion that she was slightly luminous in the dark
column10: as he now clearly saw was the case with the nearby vegetation.

column1: It was a little before this that the horses had stampeded. Something had aroused them in the night
column2: and their neighing and kicking in their stalls had been terrible. There seemed virtually nothing to do to calm them
column3: and when Nahum opened the stable door they all bolted out like frightened woodland deer. It took a week to track all four
column4: and when found they were seen to be quite useless and unmanageable. Something had snapped in their brains
column5: and each one had to be shot for its own good. Nahum borrowed a horse from Ammi for his haying
column6: but found it would not approach the barn. It shied
column7: balked
column8: and whinnied
column9: and in the end he could do nothing but drive it into the yard while the men used their own strength to get the heavy wagon near enough the hayloft for convenient pitching. And all the while the vegetation was turning grey and brittle. Even the flowers whose hues had been so strange were greying now
column10: and the fruit was coming out grey and dwarfed and tasteless. The asters and golden-rod bloomed grey and distorted
column11: and the roses and zinneas and hollyhocks in the front yard were such blasphemous-looking things that Nahum's oldest boy Zenas cut them down. The strangely puffed insects died about that time
column12: even the bees that had left their hives and taken to the woods.

column1: By September all the vegetation was fast crumbling to a greyish powder
column2: and Nahum feared that the trees would die before the poison was out of the soil. His wife now had spells of terrific screaming
column3: and he and the boys were in a constant state of nervous tension. They shunned people now
column4: and when school opened the boys did not go. But it was Ammi
column5: on one of his rare visits
column6: who first realised that the well water was no longer good. It had an evil taste that was not exactly fetid nor exactly salty
column7: and Ammi advised his friend to dig another well on higher ground to use till the soil was good again. Nahum
column8: however
column9: ignored the warning
column10: for he had by that time become calloused to strange and unpleasant things. He and the boys continued to use the tainted supply
column11: drinking it as listlessly and mechanically as they ate their meagre and ill-cooked meals and did their thankless and monotonous chores through the aimless days. There was something of stolid resignation about them all
column12: as if they walked half in another world between lines of nameless guards to a certain and familiar doom.

column1: Thaddeus went mad in September after a visit to the well. He had gone with a pail and had come back empty-handed
column2: shrieking and waving his arms
column3: and sometimes lapsing into an inane titter or a whisper about ""the moving colours down there."" Two in one family was pretty bad
column4: but Nahum was very brave about it. He let the boy run about for a week until he began stumbling and hurting himself
column5: and then he shut him in an attic room across the hall from his mother's. The way they screamed at each other from behind their locked doors was very terrible
column6: especially to little Merwin
column7: who fancied they talked in some terrible language that was not of earth. Merwin was getting frightfully imaginative
column8: and his restlessness was worse after the shutting away of the brother who had been his greatest playmate.

column1: Almost at the same time the mortality among the livestock commenced. Poultry turned greyish and died very quickly
column2: their meat being found dry and noisome upon cutting. Hogs grew inordinately fat
column3: then suddenly began to undergo loathsome changes which no one could explain. Their meat was of course useless
column4: and Nahum was at his wit's end. No rural veterinary would approach his place
column5: and the city veterinary from Arkham was openly baffled. The swine began growing grey and brittle and falling to pieces before they died
column6: and their eyes and muzzles developed singular alterations. It was very inexplicable
column7: for they had never been fed from the tainted vegetation. Then something struck the cows. Certain areas or sometimes the whole body would be uncannily shrivelled or compressed
column8: and atrocious collapses or disintegrations were common. In the last stages--and death was always the result--there would be a greying and turning brittle like that which beset the hogs. There could be no question of poison
column9: for all the cases occurred in a locked and undisturbed barn. No bites of prowling things could have brought the virus
column10: for what live beast of earth can pass through solid obstacles? It must be only natural disease--yet what disease could wreak such results was beyond any mind's guessing. When the harvest came there was not an animal surviving on the place
column11: for the stock and poultry were dead and the dogs had run away. These dogs
column12: three in number
column13: had all vanished one night and were never heard of again. The five cats had left some time before
column14: but their going was scarcely noticed since there now seemed to be no mice
column15: and only Mrs. Gardner had made pets of the graceful felines.

column1: On the nineteenth of October Nahum staggered into Ammi's house with hideous news. The death had come to poor Thaddeus in his attic room
column2: and it had come in a way which could not be told. Nahum had dug a grave in the railed family plot behind the farm
column3: and had put therein what he found. There could have been nothing from outside
column4: for the small barred window and locked door were intact; but it was much as it had been in the barn. Ammi and his wife consoled the stricken man as best they could
column5: but shuddered as they did so. Stark terror seemed to cling round the Gardners and all they touched
column6: and the very presence of one in the house was a breath from regions unnamed and unnamable. Ammi accompanied Nahum home with the greatest reluctance
column7: and did what he might to calm the hysterical sobbing of little Merwin. Zenas needed no calming. He had come of late to do nothing but stare into space and obey what his father told him; and Ammi thought that his fate was very merciful. Now and then Merwin's screams were answered faintly from the attic
column8: and in response to an inquiring look Nahum said that his wife was getting very feeble. When night approached
column9: Ammi managed to get away; for not even friendship could make him stay in that spot when the faint glow of the vegetation began and the trees may or may not have swayed without wind. It was really lucky for Ammi that he was not more imaginative. Even as things were
column10: his mind was bent ever so slightly; but had he been able to connect and reflect upon all the portents around him he must inevitably have turned a total maniac. In the twilight he hastened home
column11: the screams of the mad woman and the nervous child ringing horribly in his ears.

column1: Three days later Nahum burst into Ammi's kitchen in the early morning
column2: and in the absence of his host stammered out a desperate tale once more
column3: while Mrs. Pierce listened in a clutching fright. It was little Merwin this time. He was gone. He had gone out late at night with a lantern and pail for water
column4: and had never come back. He'd been going to pieces for days
column5: and hardly knew what he was about. Screamed at everything. There had been a frantic shriek from the yard then
column6: but before the father could get to the door the boy was gone. There was no glow from the lantern he had taken
column7: and of the child himself no trace. At the time Nahum thought the lantern and pail were gone too; but when dawn came
column8: and the man had plodded back from his all-night search of the woods and fields
column9: he had found some very curious things near the well. There was a crushed and apparently somewhat melted mass of iron which had certainly been the lantern; while a bent handle and twisted iron hoops beside it
column10: both half-fused
column11: seemed to hint at the remnants of the pail. That was all. Nahum was past imagining
column12: Mrs. Pierce was blank
column13: and Ammi
column14: when he had reached home and heard the tale
column15: could give no guess. Merwin was gone
column16: and there would be no use in telling the people around
column17: who shunned all Gardners now. No use
column18: either
column19: in telling the city people at Arkham who laughed at everything. Thad was gone
column20: and now Merwin was gone. Something was creeping and creeping and waiting to be seen and heard. Nahum would go soon
column21: and he wanted Ammi to look after his wife and Zenas if they survived him. It must all be a judgment of some sort; though he could not fancy what for
column22: since he had always walked uprightly in the Lord's ways so far as he knew.

column1: For over two weeks Ammi saw nothing of Nahum; and then
column2: worried about what might have happened
column3: he overcame his fears and paid the Gardner place a visit. There was no smoke from the great chimney
column4: and for a moment the visitor was apprehensive of the worst. The aspect of the whole farm was shocking--greyish withered grass and leaves on the ground
column5: vines falling in brittle wreckage from archaic walls and gables
column6: and great bare trees clawing up at the grey November sky with a studied malevolence which Ammi could not but feel had come from some subtle change in the tilt of the branches. But Nahum was alive
column7: after all. He was weak
column8: and lying on a couch in the low-ceiled kitchen
column9: but perfectly conscious and able to give simple orders to Zenas. The room was deadly cold; and as Ammi visibly shivered
column10: the host shouted huskily to Zenas for more wood. Wood
column11: indeed
column12: was sorely needed; since the cavernous fireplace was unlit and empty
column13: with a cloud of soot blowing about in the chill wind that came down the chimney. Presently Nahum asked him if the extra wood had made him any more comfortable
column14: and then Ammi saw what had happened. The stoutest cord had broken at last
column15: and the hapless farmer's mind was proof against more sorrow.

column1: Questioning tactfully
column2: Ammi could get no clear data at all about the missing Zenas. ""In the well--he lives in the well--"" was all that the clouded father would say. Then there flashed across the visitor's mind a sudden thought of the mad wife
column3: and he changed his line of inquiry. ""Nabby? Why
column4: here she is!"" was the surprised response of poor Nahum
column5: and Ammi soon saw that he must search for himself. Leaving the harmless babbler on the couch
column6: he took the keys from their nail beside the door and climbed the creaking stairs to the attic. It was very close and noisome up there
column7: and no sound could be heard from any direction. Of the four doors in sight
column8: only one was locked
column9: and on this he tried various keys of the ring he had taken. The third key proved the right one
column10: and after some fumbling Ammi threw open the low white door.

column1: It was quite dark inside
column2: for the window was small and half-obscured by the crude wooden bars; and Ammi could see nothing at all on the wide-planked floor. The stench was beyond enduring
column3: and before proceeding further he had to retreat to another room and return with his lungs filled with breathable air. When he did enter he saw something dark in the corner
column4: and upon seeing it more clearly he screamed outright. While he screamed he thought a momentary cloud eclipsed the window
column5: and a second later he felt himself brushed as if by some hateful current of vapour. Strange colours danced before his eyes; and had not a present horror numbed him he would have thought of the globule in the meteor that the geologist's hammer had shattered
column6: and of the morbid vegetation that had sprouted in the spring. As it was he thought only of the blasphemous monstrosity which confronted him
column7: and which all too clearly had shared the nameless fate of young Thaddeus and the livestock. But the terrible thing about the horror was that it very slowly and perceptibly moved as it continued to crumble.

column1: Ammi would give me no added particulars of this scene
column2: but the shape in the comer does not reappear in his tale as a moving object. There are things which cannot be mentioned
column3: and what is done in common humanity is sometimes cruelly judged by the law. I gathered that no moving thing was left in that attic room
column4: and that to leave anything capable of motion there would have been a deed so monstrous as to damn any accountable being to eternal torment. Anyone but a stolid farmer would have fainted or gone mad
column5: but Ammi walked conscious through that low doorway and locked the accursed secret behind him. There would be Nahum to deal with now; he must be fed and tended
column6: and removed to some place where he could be cared for.

column1: Commencing his descent of the dark stairs. Ammi heard a thud below him. He even thought a scream had been suddenly choked off
column2: and recalled nervously the clammy vapour which had brushed by him in that frightful room above. What presence had his cry and entry started up? Halted by some vague fear
column3: he heard still further sounds below. Indubitably there was a sort of heavy dragging
column4: and a most detestably sticky noise as of some fiendish and unclean species of suction. With an associative sense goaded to feverish heights
column5: he thought unaccountably of what he had seen upstairs. Good God! What eldritch dream-world was this into which he had blundered? He dared move neither backward nor forward
column6: but stood there trembling at the black curve of the boxed-in staircase. Every trifle of the scene burned itself into his brain. The sounds
column7: the sense of dread expectancy
column8: the darkness
column9: the steepness of the narrow step--and merciful Heaven!--the faint but unmistakable luminosity of all the woodwork in sight; steps
column10: sides
column11: exposed laths
column12: and beams alike.

column1: Then there burst forth a frantic whinny from Ammi's horse outside
column2: followed at once by a clatter which told of a frenzied runaway. In another moment horse and buggy had gone beyond earshot
column3: leaving the frightened man on the dark stairs to guess what had sent them. But that was not all. There had been another sound out there. A sort of liquid splash--water--it must have been the well. He had left Hero untied near it
column4: and a buggy wheel must have brushed the coping and knocked in a stone. And still the pale phosphorescence glowed in that detestably ancient woodwork. God! how old the house was! Most of it built before 1670
column5: and the gambrel roof no later than 1730.

column1: A feeble scratching on the floor downstairs now sounded distinctly
column2: and Ammi's grip tightened on a heavy stick he had picked up in the attic for some purpose. Slowly nerving himself
column3: he finished his descent and walked boldly toward the kitchen. But he did not complete the walk
column4: because what he sought was no longer there. It had come to meet him
column5: and it was still alive after a fashion. Whether it had crawled or whether it had been dragged by any external forces

column1: Remote in the desert of Araby lies the nameless city
column2: crumbling and inarticulate
column3: its low walls nearly hidden by the sands of uncounted ages. It must have been thus before the first stones of Memphis were laid

column5: or to recall that it was ever alive; but it is told of in whispers around campfires and muttered about by grandams in the tents of sheiks so that all the tribes shun it without wholly knowing why. It was of this place that Abdul Alhazred the mad poet dreamed of the night before he sang his unexplained couplet:

column1: That is not dead which can eternal lie
column2: And with strange aeons death may die.

column1: The dreams were wholly beyond the pale of sanity

column14: timbre

column4: wide-planked floor with evil expectancy in its tiny

column7: sharp

column7: sardonic

column4: however

column1: Toward the end of March he began to pick up in his mathematics

column4: and of theoretical points of approach or even contact between our part of the cosmos and various other regions as distant as the farthest stars or the trans-galactic gulfs themselves—or even as fabulously remote as the tentatively conceivable cosmic units beyond the whole Einsteinian space-time continuum. Gilman’s handling of this theme filled everyone with admiration
column5: even though some of his hypothetical illustrations caused an increase in the always plentiful gossip about his nervous and solitary eccentricity. What made the students shake their heads was his sober theory that a man might—given mathematical knowledge admittedly beyond all likelihood of human acquirement—step deliberately from the earth to any other celestial body which might lie at one of an infinity of specific points in the cosmic pattern.

column1: Such a step
column2: he said
column3: would require only two stages; first
column4: a passage out of the three-dimensional sphere we know
column5: and second
column6: a passage back to the three-dimensional sphere at another point

Any being from any part of three-dimensional space could probably survive in the fourth dimension; and its survival of the second stage would depend upon what alien part of three-dimensional space it might select for its re-entry. Denizens of some planets might be able to live on certain others—even planets belonging to other galaxies

This was a matter for speculation

Professor Upham especially liked his demonstration of the kinship of higher mathematics to certain phases of magical lore transmitted down the ages from an ineffable antiquity—human or pre-human—whose knowledge of the cosmos and its laws was greater than ours.

column3: and advised him to see a nerve specialist. On reflection

column5: who had curtailed his activities before
column6: would have made him take a rest—an impossible thing now that he was so close to great results in his equations. He was certainly near the boundary between the known universe and the fourth dimension

column2: stealthy
column3: imaginary footsteps in the sealed loft above were unnerving. And now
column4: too

And what was that faint suggestion of sound which once in a while seemed to trickle through the maddening confusion of identifiable sounds even in broad daylight and full wakefulness? Its rhythm did not correspond to anything on earth
column6: unless perhaps to the cadence of one or two unmentionable Sabbat-chants

column3: long nose
column4: and shrivelled chin were unmistakable
column5: and her shapeless brown garments were like those he remembered. The expression on her face was one of hideous malevolence and exultation
column6: and when he awaked he could recall a croaking voice that persuaded and threatened. He must meet the Black Man

He must sign in his own blood the book of Azathoth and take a new secret name now that his independent delvings had gone so far. What kept him from going with her and Brown Jenkin and the other to the throne of Chaos where the thin flutes pipe mindlessly was the fact that he had seen the name “Azathoth” in the Necronomicon
column8: and knew it stood for a primal evil too horrible for description.

column1: The old woman always appeared out of thin air near the corner where the downward slant met the inward slant. She seemed to crystallise at a point closer to the ceiling than to the floor
column2: and every night she was a little nearer and more distinct before the dream shifted. Brown Jenkin
column3: too
column4: was always a little nearer at the last
column5: and its yellowish-white fangs glistened shockingly in that unearthly violet phosphorescence. Its shrill loathsome tittering stuck more and more in Gilman’s head
column6: and he could remember in the morning how it had pronounced the words “Azathoth” and “Nyarlathotep”.

column4: prolately spheroidal bubbles and a very much smaller polyhedron of unknown colours and rapidly shifting surface angles—seemed to take notice of him and follow him about or float ahead as he changed position among the titan prisms
column5: labyrinths
column6: cube-and-plane clusters
column7: and quasi-buildings; and all the while the vague shrieking and roaring waxed louder and louder
column8: as if approaching some monstrous climax of utterly unendurable intensity.

column1: During the night of April 19–20 the new development occurred. Gilman was half-involuntarily moving about in the twilight abysses with the bubble-mass and the small polyhedron floating ahead

column3: diffused green light. He was barefooted and in his night-clothes
column4: and when he tried to walk discovered that he could scarcely lift his feet. A swirling vapour hid everything but the immediate sloping terrain from sight
column5: and he shrank from the thought of the sounds that might surge out of that vapour.

column2: while Brown Jenkin pointed in a certain direction with a horribly anthropoid fore paw which it raised with evident difficulty. Spurred by an impulse he did not originate
column3: Gilman dragged himself forward along a course determined by the angle of the old woman’s arms and the direction of the small monstrosity’s paw
column4: and before he had shuffled three steps he was back in the twilight abysses. Geometrical shapes seethed around him
column5: and he fell dizzily and interminably. At last he woke in his bed in the crazily angled garret of the eldritch old house.

column1: He was good for nothing that morning

column3: for he could not help staring at a certain vacant spot on the floor. As the day advanced the focus of his unseeing eyes changed position
column4: and by noon he had conquered the impulse to stare at vacancy. About two o’clock he went out for lunch

Undoubtedly he could still manage to walk away from the pull; so with great resolution he headed against it and dragged himself deliberately north along Garrison Street. By the time he had reached the bridge over the Miskatonic he was in a cold perspiration
column2: and he clutched at the iron railing as he gazed upstream at the ill-regarded island whose regular lines of ancient standing stones brooded sullenly in the afternoon sunlight.

column3: too

column6: ancient figure in brown.

column1: The southeastward pull still held
column2: and only with tremendous resolution could Gilman drag himself into the old house and up the rickety stairs. For hours he sat silent and aimless
column3: with his eyes shifting gradually westward. About six o’clock his sharpened ears caught the whining prayers of Joe Mazurewicz two floors below

column3: and now it was roughly south but wheeling toward the west. What was the meaning of this new thing? Was he going mad? How long would it last? Again mustering his resolution
column4: Gilman turned and dragged himself back to the sinister old house.

column10: seeing the inane performance over and over again without paying any attention to it.

column1: About nine at night he drifted homeward and stumbled into the ancient house. Joe Mazurewicz was whining unintelligible prayers
column2: and Gilman hastened up to his own garret chamber without pausing to see if Elwood was in. It was when he turned on the feeble electric light that the shock came. At once he saw there was something on the table which did not belong there
column3: and a second look left no room for doubt. Lying on its side—for it could not stand up alone—was the exotic spiky figure which in his monstrous dream he had broken off the fantastic balustrade. No detail was missing. The ridged
column4: barrel-shaped centre
column5: the thin
column6: radiating arms
column7: the knobs at each end
column8: and the flat
column9: slightly outward-curving starfish-arms spreading from those knobs—all were there. In the electric light the colour seemed to be a kind of iridescent grey veined with green
column10: and Gilman could see amidst his horror and bewilderment that one of the knobs ended in a jagged break corresponding to its former point of attachment to the dream-railing.

column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged
column2: furry thing came again and with a greater distinctness than on any former occasion. This time they actually reached him
column3: and he felt the crone’s withered claws clutching at him. He was pulled out of bed and into empty space
column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief
column5: for presently he was in a crude
column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration
column8: and in the centre were a table and bench
column9: both apparently fastened in place. Small objects of unknown shape and nature were ranged on the tops of the cases
column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling
column13: there presently climbed the hateful little furry thing with the yellow fangs and bearded human face.

column1: The evilly grinning beldame still clutched him
column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod
column6: since there was a clicking whenever he changed position. The man did not speak
column7: and bore no trace of expression on his small
column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table
column9: while the beldame thrust a huge grey quill into Gilman’s right hand. Over everything was a pall of intensely maddening fear
column10: and the climax was reached when the furry thing ran up the dreamer’s clothing to his shoulders and then down his left arm
column11: finally biting him sharply in the wrist just below his cuff. As the blood spurted from this wound Gilman lapsed into a faint.

column1: He awaked on the morning of the 22nd with a pain in his left wrist
column2: and saw that his cuff was brown with dried blood. His recollections were very confused
column3: but the scene with the black man in the unknown space stood out vividly. The rats must have bitten him as he slept
column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door
column5: he saw that the flour on the corridor floor was undisturbed except for the huge prints of the loutish fellow who roomed at the other end of the garret. So he had not been sleep-walking this time. But something would have to be done about those rats. He would speak to the landlord about them. Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall
column6: wedging in a candlestick which seemed of about the right size. His ears were ringing horribly
column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column1: As he bathed and changed clothes he tried to recall what he had dreamed after the scene in the violet-litten space

column5: twilight abysses

column7: blacker abysses beyond them—abysses in which all fixed suggestions of form were absent. He had been taken there by the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron which always dogged him; but they
column8: like himself

column10: barely luminous mist in this farther void of ultimate blackness. Something else had gone on ahead—a larger wisp which now and then condensed into nameless approximations of form—and he thought that their progress had not been in a straight line
column11: but rather along the alien curves and spirals of some ethereal vortex which obeyed laws unknown to the physics and mathematics of any conceivable cosmos. Eventually there had been a hint of vast
column12: leaping shadows
column13: of a monstrous
column14: half-acoustic pulsing
column15: and of the thin
column16: monotonous piping of an unseen flute—but that was all. Gilman decided he had picked up that last conception from what he had read in the Necronomicon about the mindless entity Azathoth
column17: which rules all time and space from a curiously environed black throne at the centre of Chaos.

column1: When the blood was washed away the wrist wound proved very slight

column3: and had the rat bitten him as he sat in some chair or paused in some less rational position? He looked in every corner for brownish drops or stains
column4: but did not find any. He had better
column5: he thought

column7: though they were replaced by another sensation even more inexplicable. It was a vague
column8: insistent impulse to fly away from his present situation
column9: but held not a hint of the specific direction in which he wished to fly. As he picked up the strange spiky image on the table he thought the older northward pull grew a trifle stronger; but even so
column10: it was wholly overruled by the newer and more bewildering urge.

column7: haggard aspect

column17: the fellow under Gilman’s room

These simple people were quick to imagine they had seen any odd thing they had heard about. As for a plan of action—Gilman had better move down to Elwood’s room and avoid sleeping alone. Elwood would
column5: if awake
column6: rouse him whenever he began to talk or rise in his sleep. Very soon

column1: Braced up by Elwood’s companionship
column2: Gilman attended classes that day. Strange urges still tugged at him
column3: but he could sidetrack them with considerable success. During a free period he shewed the queer image to several professors
column4: all of whom were intensely interested
column5: though none of them could shed any light upon its nature or origin. That night he slept on a couch which Elwood had had the landlord bring to the second-story room
column6: and for the first time in weeks was wholly free from disquieting dreams. But the feverishness still hung on
column7: and the whines of the loomfixer were an unnerving influence.

column1: During the next few days Gilman enjoyed an almost perfect immunity from morbid manifestations. He had
column2: Elwood said
column3: shewed no tendency to talk or rise in his sleep; and meanwhile the landlord was putting rat-poison everywhere. The only disturbing element was the talk among the superstitious foreigners
column4: whose imaginations had become highly excited. Mazurewicz was always trying to make him get a crucifix
column5: and finally forced one upon him which he said had been blessed by the good Father Iwanicki. Desrochers
column6: too

column9: and claimed that his door had been softly tried

column1: For three days Gilman and Elwood canvassed the local museums in an effort to identify the strange spiky image
column2: but always without success. In every quarter
column3: however
column4: interest was intense; for the utter alienage of the thing was a tremendous challenge to scientific curiosity. One of the small radiating arms was broken off and subjected to chemical analysis
column5: and the result is still talked about in college circles. Professor Ellery found platinum
column6: iron
column7: and tellurium in the strange alloy; but mixed with these were at least three other apparent elements of high atomic weight which chemistry was absolutely powerless to classify. Not only did they fail to correspond with any known element
column8: but they did not even fit the vacant places reserved for probable elements in the periodic system. The mystery remains unsolved to this day
column9: though the image is on exhibition at the museum of Miskatonic University.

column1: On the morning of April 27 a fresh rat-hole appeared in the room where Gilman was a guest
column2: but Dombrowski tinned it up during the day. The poison was not having much effect
column3: for scratchings and scurryings in the walls were virtually undiminished. Elwood was out late that night
column4: and Gilman waited up for him. He did not wish to go to sleep in a room alone—especially since he thought he had glimpsed in the evening twilight the repellent old woman whose image had become so horribly transferred to his dreams. He wondered who she was
column5: and what had been near her rattling the tin can in a rubbish-heap at the mouth of a squalid courtyard. The crone had seemed to notice him and leer evilly at him—though perhaps this was merely his imagination.

column1: The next day both youths felt very tired
column2: and knew they would sleep like logs when night came. In the evening they drowsily discussed the mathematical studies which had so completely and perhaps harmfully engrossed Gilman
column3: and speculated about the linkage with ancient magic and folklore which seemed so darkly probable. They spoke of old Keziah Mason
column4: and Elwood agreed that Gilman had good scientific grounds for thinking she might have stumbled on strange and significant information. The hidden cults to which these witches belonged often guarded and handed down surprising secrets from elder
column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column1: Whether a modern student could ever gain similar powers from mathematical research alone
column2: was still to be seen. Success
column3: Gilman added
column4: might lead to dangerous and unthinkable situations; for who could foretell the conditions pervading an adjacent but normally inaccessible dimension? On the other hand
column5: the picturesque possibilities were enormous. Time could not exist in certain belts of space
column6: and by entering and remaining in such a belt one might preserve one’s life and age indefinitely; never suffering organic metabolism or deterioration except for slight amounts incurred during visits to one’s own or similar planes. One might
column7: for example
column8: pass into a timeless dimension and emerge at some remote period of the earth’s history as young as before.

column1: Whether anybody had ever managed to do this
column2: one could hardly conjecture with any degree of authority. Old legends are hazy and ambiguous
column3: and in historic times all attempts at crossing forbidden gaps seem complicated by strange and terrible alliances with beings and messengers from outside. There was the immemorial figure of the deputy or messenger of hidden and terrible powers—the “Black Man” of the witch-cult
column4: and the “Nyarlathotep” of the Necronomicon. There was
column5: too
column6: the baffling problem of the lesser messengers or intermediaries—the quasi-animals and queer hybrids which legend depicts as witches’ familiars. As Gilman and Elwood retired
column7: too sleepy to argue further
column8: they heard Joe Mazurewicz reel into the house half-drunk
column9: and shuddered at the desperate wildness of his whining prayers.

column1: That night Gilman saw the violet light again. In his dream he had heard a scratching and gnawing in the partitions
column2: and thought that someone fumbled clumsily at the latch. Then he saw the old woman and the small furry thing advancing toward him over the carpeted floor. The beldame’s face was alight with inhuman exultation
column3: and the little yellow-toothed morbidity tittered mockingly as it pointed at the heavily sleeping form of Elwood on the other couch across the room. A paralysis of fear stifled all attempts to cry out. As once before
column4: the hideous crone seized Gilman by the shoulders
column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him
column6: but in another second he thought he was in a dark
column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours
column9: with the rotting walls of ancient houses towering up on every hand.

column1: Ahead was the robed black man he had seen in the peaked space in the other dream
column2: while from a lesser distance the old woman was beckoning and grimacing imperiously. Brown Jenkin was rubbing itself with a kind of affectionate playfulness around the ankles of the black man
column3: which the deep mud largely concealed. There was a dark open doorway on the right
column4: to which the black man silently pointed. Into this the grimacing crone started
column5: dragging Gilman after her by his pajama sleeve. There were evil-smelling staircases which creaked ominously
column6: and on which the old woman seemed to radiate a faint violet light; and finally a door leading off a landing. The crone fumbled with the latch and pushed the door open
column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry
column2: and presently the beldame came out of the room bearing a small
column3: senseless form which she thrust at the dreamer as if ordering him to carry it. The sight of this form
column4: and the expression on its face
column5: broke the spell. Still too dazed to cry out
column6: he plunged recklessly down the noisome staircase and into the mud outside; halting only when seized and choked by the waiting black man. As consciousness departed he heard the faint
column7: shrill tittering of the fanged
column8: rat-like abnormality.

column1: On the morning of the 29th Gilman awaked into a maelstrom of horror. The instant he opened his eyes he knew something was terribly wrong
column2: for he was back in his old garret room with the slanting wall and ceiling
column3: sprawled on the now unmade bed. His throat was aching inexplicably
column4: and as he struggled to a sitting posture he saw with growing fright that his feet and pajama-bottoms were brown with caked mud. For the moment his recollections were hopelessly hazy
column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them
column7: the more peculiar they seemed; for in addition to those he could recognise as his there were some smaller
column8: almost round markings—such as the legs of a large chair or table might make
column9: except that most of them tended to be divided into halves. There were also some curious muddy rat-tracks leading out of a fresh hole and back into it again. Utter bewilderment and the fear of madness racked Gilman as he staggered to the door and saw that there were no muddy prints outside. The more he remembered of his hideous dream the more terrified he felt
column10: and it added to his desperation to hear Joe Mazurewicz chanting mournfully two floors below.

column1: Descending to Elwood’s room he roused his still-sleeping host and began telling of how he had found himself
column2: but Elwood could form no idea of what might really have happened. Where Gilman could have been
column3: how he got back to his room without making tracks in the hall
column4: and how the muddy
column5: furniture-like prints came to be mixed with his in the garret chamber
column6: were wholly beyond conjecture. Then there were those dark
column7: livid marks on his throat
column8: as if he had tried to strangle himself. He put his hands up to them
column9: but found that they did not even approximately fit. While they were talking Desrochers dropped in to say that he had heard a terrific clattering overhead in the dark small hours. No
column10: there had been no one on the stairs after midnight—though just before midnight he had heard faint footfalls in the garret
column11: and cautiously descending steps he did not like. It was
column12: he added
column13: a very bad time of year for Arkham. The young gentleman had better be sure to wear the crucifix Joe Mazurewicz had given him. Even the daytime was not safe
column14: for after dawn there had been strange sounds in the house—especially a thin
column15: childish wail hastily choked off.

column1: Gilman mechanically attended classes that morning
column2: but was wholly unable to fix his mind on his studies. A mood of hideous apprehension and expectancy had seized him
column3: and he seemed to be awaiting the fall of some annihilating blow. At noon he lunched at the University Spa
column4: picking up a paper from the next seat as he waited for dessert. But he never ate that dessert; for an item on the paper’s first page left him limp
column5: wild-eyed
column6: and able only to pay his check and stagger back to Elwood’s room.

column1: There had been a strange kidnapping the night before in Orne’s Gangway
column2: and the two-year-old child of a clod-like laundry worker named Anastasia Wolejko had completely vanished from sight. The mother
column3: it appeared
column4: had feared the event for some time; but the reasons she assigned for her fear were so grotesque that no one took them seriously. She had
column5: she said
column6: seen Brown Jenkin about the place now and then ever since early in March
column7: and knew from its grimaces and titterings that little Ladislas must be marked for sacrifice at the awful Sabbat on Walpurgis-Night. She had asked her neighbour Mary Czanek to sleep in the room and try to protect the child
column8: but Mary had not dared. She could not tell the police
column9: for they never believed such things. Children had been taken that way every year ever since she could remember. And her friend Pete Stowacki would not help because he wanted the child out of the way anyhow.

column1: But what threw Gilman into a cold perspiration was the report of a pair of revellers who had been walking past the mouth of the gangway just after midnight. They admitted they had been drunk
column2: but both vowed they had seen a crazily dressed trio furtively entering the dark passageway. There had
column3: they said
column4: been a huge robed negro
column5: a little old woman in rags
column6: and a young white man in his night-clothes. The old woman had been dragging the youth
column7: while around the feet of the negro a tame rat was rubbing and weaving in the brown mud.

column1: Gilman sat in a daze all the afternoon
column2: and Elwood—who had meanwhile seen the papers and formed terrible conjectures from them—found him thus when he came home. This time neither could doubt but that something hideously serious was closing in around them. Between the phantasms of nightmare and the realities of the objective world a monstrous and unthinkable relationship was crystallising
column3: and only stupendous vigilance could avert still more direful developments. Gilman must see a specialist sooner or later
column4: but not just now
column5: when all the papers were full of this kidnapping business.

column1: Just what had really happened was maddeningly obscure
column2: and for a moment both Gilman and Elwood exchanged whispered theories of the wildest kind. Had Gilman unconsciously succeeded better than he knew in his studies of space and its dimensions? Had he actually slipped outside our sphere to points unguessed and unimaginable? Where—if anywhere—had he been on those nights of daemoniac alienage? The roaring twilight abysses—the green hillside—the blistering terrace—the pulls from the stars—the ultimate black vortex—the black man—the muddy alley and the stairs—the old witch and the fanged
column3: furry horror—the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron—the strange sunburn—the wrist wound—the unexplained image—the muddy feet—the throat-marks—the tales and fears of the superstitious foreigners—what did all this mean? To what extent could the laws of sanity apply to such a case?

column1: There was no sleep for either of them that night
column2: but next day they both cut classes and drowsed. This was April 30th
column3: and with the dusk would come the hellish Sabbat-time which all the foreigners and the superstitious old folk feared. Mazurewicz came home at six o’clock and said people at the mill were whispering that the Walpurgis-revels would be held in the dark ravine beyond Meadow Hill where the old white stone stands in a place queerly void of all plant-life. Some of them had even told the police and advised them to look there for the missing Wolejko child
column4: but they did not believe anything would be done. Joe insisted that the poor young gentleman wear his nickel-chained crucifix
column5: and Gilman put it on and dropped it inside his shirt to humour the fellow.

column1: Late at night the two youths sat drowsing in their chairs
column2: lulled by the rhythmical praying of the loomfixer on the floor below. Gilman listened as he nodded
column3: his preternaturally sharpened hearing seeming to strain for some subtle
column4: dreaded murmur beyond the noises in the ancient house. Unwholesome recollections of things in the Necronomicon and the Black Book welled up
column5: and he found himself swaying to infandous rhythms said to pertain to the blackest ceremonies of the Sabbat and to have an origin outside the time and space we comprehend.

column1: Presently he realised what he was listening for—the hellish chant of the celebrants in the distant black valley. How did he know so much about what they expected? How did he know the time when Nahab and her acolyte were due to bear the brimming bowl which would follow the black cock and the black goat? He saw that Elwood had dropped asleep
column2: and tried to call out and waken him. Something
column3: however
column4: closed his throat. He was not his own master. Had he signed the black man’s book after all?

column1: Then his fevered
column2: abnormal hearing caught the distant
column3: windborne notes. Over miles of hill and field and alley they came
column4: but he recognised them none the less. The fires must be lit
column5: and the dancers must be starting in. How could he keep himself from going? What was it that had enmeshed him? Mathematics—folklore—the house—old Keziah—Brown Jenkin . . . and now he saw that there was a fresh rat-hole in the wall near his couch. Above the distant chanting and the nearer praying of Joe Mazurewicz came another sound—a stealthy
column6: determined scratching in the partitions. He hoped the electric lights would not go out. Then he saw the fanged

column1: The screaming twilight abysses flashed before him
column2: and he felt himself helpless in the formless grasp of the iridescent bubble-congeries. Ahead raced the small
column3: kaleidoscopic polyhedron
column4: and all through the churning void there was a heightening and acceleration of the vague tonal pattern which seemed to foreshadow some unutterable and unendurable climax. He seemed to know what was coming—the monstrous burst of Walpurgis-rhythm in whose cosmic timbre would be concentrated all the primal
column5: ultimate space-time seethings which lie behind the massed spheres of matter and sometimes break forth in measured reverberations that penetrate faintly to every layer of entity and give hideous significance throughout the worlds to certain dreaded periods.

column2: violet-litten peaked space with the slanting floor
column3: the low cases of ancient books
column4: the bench and table
column5: the queer objects
column6: and the triangular gulf at one side. On the table lay a small white figure—an infant boy
column7: unclothed and unconscious—while on the other side stood the monstrous
column8: leering old woman with a gleaming
column9: grotesque-hafted knife in her right hand
column10: and a queerly proportioned pale metal bowl covered with curiously chased designs and having delicate lateral handles in her left. She was intoning some croaking ritual in a language which Gilman could not understand

column4: grotesque knife above the small white victim as high as her right hand could reach. The fanged
column5: furry thing began tittering a continuation of the unknown ritual
column6: while the witch croaked loathsome responses. Gilman felt a gnawing
column7: poignant abhorrence shoot through his mental and emotional paralysis

column1: In an instant he had edged up the slanting floor around the end of the table and wrenched the knife from the old woman’s claws; sending it clattering over the brink of the narrow triangular gulf. In another instant

They were alive with a teeming horde of shapes swimming inward toward the town; and even at my vast distance and in my single moment of perception I could tell that the bobbing heads and flailing arms were alien and aberrant in a way scarcely to be expressed or consciously formulated.
My frantic running ceased before I had covered a block

column1: Piecing together the scattered records

column1: Primal myth and modern delusion joined in their assumption that mankind is only one—perhaps the least—of the highly evolved and dominant races of this planet’s long and largely unknown career. Things of inconceivable shape

Some had come down from the stars; a few were as old as the cosmos itself; others had arisen swiftly from terrene germs as far behind the first germs of our life-cycle as those germs are behind ourselves. Spans of thousands of millions of years

column3: extra-sensory way till it approached the desired period. Then

column1: Meanwhile the displaced mind
column2: thrown back to the displacer’s age and body

column1: When the captive mind’s amazement and resentment had worn off

column4: and in exchange for suitable services
column5: it was allowed to rove all over the habitable world in titan airships or on the huge boat-like atomic-engined vehicles which traversed the great roads
column6: and to delve freely into the libraries containing the records of the planet’s past and future. This reconciled many captive minds to their lot; since none were other than keen

column8: despite the abysmal horrors often unveiled
column9: the supreme experience of life.

column1: Now and then certain captives were permitted to meet other captive minds seized from the future—to exchange thoughts with consciousnesses living a hundred or a thousand or a million years before or after their own ages. And all were urged to write copiously in their own languages of themselves and their respective periods; such documents to be filed in the great central archives.
It may be added that there was one sad special type of captive whose privileges were far greater than those of the majority. These were the dying permanent exiles
column2: whose bodies in the future had been seized by keen-minded members of the Great Race who
column3: faced with death
column4: sought to escape mental extinction. Such melancholy exiles were not as common as might be expected
column5: since the longevity of the Great Race lessened its love of life—especially among those superior minds capable of projection. From cases of the permanent projection of elder minds arose many of those lasting changes of personality noticed in later history—including mankind’s.

column1: As for the ordinary cases of exploration—when the displacing mind had learned what it wished in the future
column2: it would build an apparatus like that which had started its flight and reverse the process of projection. Once more it would be in its own body in its own age
column3: while the lately captive mind would return to that body of the future to which it properly belonged. Only when one or the other of the bodies had died during the exchange was this restoration impossible. In such cases
column4: of course
column5: the exploring mind had—like those of the death-escapers—to live out an alien-bodied life in the future; or else the captive mind—like the dying permanent exiles—had to end its days in the form and past age of the Great Race.

column1: This fate was least horrible when the captive mind was also of the Great Race—a not infrequent occurrence
column2: since in all its periods that race was intensely concerned with its own future. The number of dying permanent exiles of the Great Race was very slight—largely because of the tremendous penalties attached to displacements of future Great Race minds by the moribund. Through projection
column3: arrangements were made to inflict these penalties on the offending minds in their new future bodies—and sometimes forced re-exchanges were effected. Complex cases of the displacement of exploring or already captive minds by minds in various regions of the past had been known and carefully rectified. In every age since the discovery of mind-projection
column4: a minute but well-recognised element of the population consisted of Great Race minds from past ages
column5: sojourning for a longer or shorter while.

column1: When a captive mind of alien origin was returned to its own body in the future
column2: it was purged by an intricate mechanical hypnosis of all it had learned in the Great Race’s age—this because of certain troublesome consequences inherent in the general carrying forward of knowledge in large quantities. The few existing instances of clear transmission had caused
column3: and would cause at known future times

column6: and parts of the text of the frightful Pnakotic Manuscripts.

column1: Thus the returning mind reached its own age with only the faintest and most fragmentary visions of what it had undergone since its seizure. All memories that could be eradicated were eradicated

column3: and the chance joining of memories had at rare times brought hints of the forbidden past to future ages. There probably never was a time when groups or cults did not secretly cherish certain of these hints. In the Necronomicon the presence of such a cult among human beings was suggested—a cult that sometimes gave aid to minds voyaging down the aeons from the days of the Great Race.

column1: And meanwhile the Great Race itself waxed well-nigh omniscient
column2: and turned to the task of setting up exchanges with the minds of other planets
column3: and of exploring their pasts and futures. It sought likewise to fathom the past years and origin of that black
column4: aeon-dead orb in far space whence its own mental heritage had come—for the mind of the Great Race was older than its bodily form. The beings of a dying elder world
column5: wise with the ultimate secrets
column6: had looked ahead for a new world and species wherein they might have long life; and had sent their minds en masse into that future race best adapted to house them—the cone-shaped things that peopled our earth a billion years ago. Thus the Great Race came to be

column8: yet would live through another forward migration of its best minds into the bodies of others who had a longer physical span ahead of them.

column1: Such was the background of intertwined legend and hallucination. When

column1: At times the parallelism of so many cases in so many distant ages continued to worry me as it had at first

Probably all the other victims whose cases were like mine had had a long and familiar knowledge of the tales I had learned only when in my secondary state. When these victims had lost their memory
column3: they had associated themselves with the creatures of their household myths—the fabulous invaders supposed to displace men’s minds—and had thus embarked upon quests for knowledge which they thought they could take back to a fancied
column4: non-human past. Then when their memory returned
column5: they reversed the associative process and thought of themselves as the former captive minds instead of as the displacers. Hence the dreams and pseudo-memories following the conventional myth-pattern.

column1: Despite the seeming cumbrousness of these explanations
column2: they came finally to supersede all others in my mind—largely because of the greater weakness of any rival theory. And a substantial number of eminent psychologists and anthropologists gradually agreed with me. The more I reflected
column3: the more convincing did my reasoning seem; till in the end I had a really effective bulwark against the visions and impressions which still assailed me. Suppose I did see strange things at night? These were only what I had heard and read of. Suppose I did have odd loathings and perspectives and pseudo-memories? These
column4: too

column1: Fortified by this philosophy

column1: All this time my own part in the dreams seemed to be that of a disembodied consciousness with a range of vision wider than the normal; floating freely about
column2: yet confined to the ordinary avenues and speeds of travel. Not until August

column1: And then the morbid temptation to look down at myself became greater and greater
column2: till one night I could not resist it. At first my downward glance revealed nothing whatever. A moment later I perceived that this was because my head lay at the end of a flexible neck of enormous length. Retracting this neck and gazing down very sharply
column3: I saw the scaly
column4: rugose
column5: iridescent bulk of a vast cone ten feet tall and ten feet wide at the base. That was when I waked half of Arkham with my screaming as I plunged madly up from the abyss of sleep.

column1: Only after weeks of hideous repetition did I grow half-reconciled to these visions of myself in monstrous form. In the dreams I now moved bodily among the other unknown entities
column2: reading terrible books from the endless shelves and writing for hours at the great tables with a stylus managed by the green tentacles that hung down from my head. Snatches of what I read and wrote would linger in my memory. There were horrible annals of other worlds and other universes
column3: and of stirrings of formless life outside of all universes. There were records of strange orders of beings which had peopled the world in forgotten pasts
column4: and frightful chronicles of grotesque-bodied intelligences which would people it millions of years after the death of the last human being. And I learned of chapters in human history whose existence no scholar of today has ever suspected. Most of these writings were in the language of the hieroglyphs; which I studied in a queer way with the aid of droning machines
column5: and which was evidently an agglutinative speech with root systems utterly unlike any found in human languages. Other volumes were in other unknown tongues learned in the same queer way. A very few were in languages I knew. Extremely clever pictures
column6: both inserted in the records and forming separate collections
column7: aided me immensely. And all the time I seemed to be setting down a history of my own age in English. On waking
column8: I could recall only minute and meaningless scraps of the unknown tongues which my dream-self had mastered
