column1: Only his tendency toward a dazed stupor prevented him from screaming aloud. This fusion of dream and reality was too much to bear. Still dazed
column2: he clutched at the spiky thing and staggered downstairs to Landlord Dombrowski’s quarters. The whining prayers of the superstitious loomfixer were still sounding through the mouldy halls
column3: but Gilman did not mind them now. The landlord was in
column4: and greeted him pleasantly. No
column5: he had not seen that thing before and did not know anything about it. But his wife had said she found a funny tin thing in one of the beds when she fixed the rooms at noon
column6: and maybe that was it. Dombrowski called her
column7: and she waddled in. Yes
column8: that was the thing. She had found it in the young gentleman’s bed—on the side next the wall. It had looked very queer to her
column9: but of course the young gentleman had lots of queer things in his room—books and curios and pictures and markings on paper. She certainly knew nothing about it.

column1: So Gilman climbed upstairs again in a mental turmoil
column2: convinced that he was either still dreaming or that his somnambulism had run to incredible extremes and led him to depredations in unknown places. Where had he got this outré thing? He did not recall seeing it in any museum in Arkham. It must have been somewhere
column3: though; and the sight of it as he snatched it in his sleep must have caused the odd dream-picture of the balustraded terrace. Next day he would make some very guarded inquiries—and perhaps see the nerve specialist.

column1: Meanwhile he would try to keep track of his somnambulism. As he went upstairs and across the garret hall he sprinkled about some flour which he had borrowed—with a frank admission as to its purpose—from the landlord. He had stopped at Elwood’s door on the way
column2: but had found all dark within. Entering his room
column3: he placed the spiky thing on the table
column4: and lay down in complete mental and physical exhaustion without pausing to undress. From the closed loft above the slanting ceiling he thought he heard a faint scratching and padding
column5: but he was too disorganised even to mind it. That cryptical pull from the north was getting very strong again
column6: though it seemed now to come from a lower place in the sky.

column1: In the dazzling violet light of dream the old woman and the fanged
column2: furry thing came again and with a greater distinctness than on any former occasion. This time they actually reached him
column3: and he felt the crone’s withered claws clutching at him. He was pulled out of bed and into empty space
column4: and for a moment he heard a rhythmic roaring and saw the twilight amorphousness of the vague abysses seething around him. But that moment was very brief
column5: for presently he was in a crude
column6: windowless little space with rough beams and planks rising to a peak just above his head
column7: and with a curious slanting floor underfoot. Propped level on that floor were low cases full of books of every degree of antiquity and disintegration
column8: and in the centre were a table and bench
column9: both apparently fastened in place. Small objects of unknown shape and nature were ranged on the tops of the cases
column10: and in the flaming violet light Gilman thought he saw a counterpart of the spiky image which had puzzled him so horribly. On the left the floor fell abruptly away
column11: leaving a black triangular gulf out of which
column12: after a second’s dry rattling
column13: there presently climbed the hateful little furry thing with the yellow fangs and bearded human face.

column1: The evilly grinning beldame still clutched him
column2: and beyond the table stood a figure he had never seen before—a tall
column3: lean man of dead black colouration but without the slightest sign of negroid features; wholly devoid of either hair or beard
column4: and wearing as his only garment a shapeless robe of some heavy black fabric. His feet were indistinguishable because of the table and bench
column5: but he must have been shod
column6: since there was a clicking whenever he changed position. The man did not speak
column7: and bore no trace of expression on his small
column8: regular features. He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table
column9: while the beldame thrust a huge grey quill into Gilman’s right hand. Over everything was a pall of intensely maddening fear
column10: and the climax was reached when the furry thing ran up the dreamer’s clothing to his shoulders and then down his left arm
column11: finally biting him sharply in the wrist just below his cuff. As the blood spurted from this wound Gilman lapsed into a faint.

column1: He awaked on the morning of the 22nd with a pain in his left wrist
column2: and saw that his cuff was brown with dried blood. His recollections were very confused
column3: but the scene with the black man in the unknown space stood out vividly. The rats must have bitten him as he slept
column4: giving rise to the climax of that frightful dream. Opening the door
column5: he saw that the flour on the corridor floor was undisturbed except for the huge prints of the loutish fellow who roomed at the other end of the garret. So he had not been sleep-walking this time. But something would have to be done about those rats. He would speak to the landlord about them. Again he tried to stop up the hole at the base of the slanting wall
column6: wedging in a candlestick which seemed of about the right size. His ears were ringing horribly
column7: as if with the residual echoes of some horrible noise heard in dreams.

column1: As he bathed and changed clothes he tried to recall what he had dreamed after the scene in the violet-litten space
column2: but nothing definite would crystallise in his mind. That scene itself must have corresponded to the sealed loft overhead
column3: which had begun to attack his imagination so violently
column4: but later impressions were faint and hazy. There were suggestions of the vague
column5: twilight abysses
column6: and of still vaster
column7: blacker abysses beyond them—abysses in which all fixed suggestions of form were absent. He had been taken there by the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron which always dogged him; but they
column8: like himself
column9: had changed to wisps of milky
column10: barely luminous mist in this farther void of ultimate blackness. Something else had gone on ahead—a larger wisp which now and then condensed into nameless approximations of form—and he thought that their progress had not been in a straight line
column11: but rather along the alien curves and spirals of some ethereal vortex which obeyed laws unknown to the physics and mathematics of any conceivable cosmos. Eventually there had been a hint of vast
column12: leaping shadows
column13: of a monstrous
column14: half-acoustic pulsing
column15: and of the thin
column16: monotonous piping of an unseen flute—but that was all. Gilman decided he had picked up that last conception from what he had read in the Necronomicon about the mindless entity Azathoth

column1: On the morning of April 27 a fresh rat-hole appeared in the room where Gilman was a guest

column5: and what had been near her rattling the tin can in a rubbish-heap at the mouth of a squalid courtyard. The crone had seemed to notice him and leer evilly at him—though perhaps this was merely his imagination.

column5: forgotten aeons; and it was by no means impossible that Keziah had actually mastered the art of passing through dimensional gates. Tradition emphasises the uselessness of material barriers in halting a witch’s motions; and who can say what underlies the old tales of broomstick rides through the night?

column3: Gilman added

column6: and by entering and remaining in such a belt one might preserve one’s life and age indefinitely; never suffering organic metabolism or deterioration except for slight amounts incurred during visits to one’s own or similar planes. One might
column7: for example

column5: too

column3: and the little yellow-toothed morbidity tittered mockingly as it pointed at the heavily sleeping form of Elwood on the other couch across the room. A paralysis of fear stifled all attempts to cry out. As once before
column4: the hideous crone seized Gilman by the shoulders
column5: yanking him out of bed and into empty space. Again the infinitude of the shrieking twilight abysses flashed past him
column6: but in another second he thought he was in a dark
column7: muddy
column8: unknown alley of foetid odours
column9: with the rotting walls of ancient houses towering up on every hand.

column1: Ahead was the robed black man he had seen in the peaked space in the other dream
column2: while from a lesser distance the old woman was beckoning and grimacing imperiously. Brown Jenkin was rubbing itself with a kind of affectionate playfulness around the ankles of the black man

column4: to which the black man silently pointed. Into this the grimacing crone started
column5: dragging Gilman after her by his pajama sleeve. There were evil-smelling staircases which creaked ominously
column6: and on which the old woman seemed to radiate a faint violet light; and finally a door leading off a landing. The crone fumbled with the latch and pushed the door open
column7: motioning to Gilman to wait and disappearing inside the black aperture.

column1: The youth’s oversensitive ears caught a hideous strangled cry

column3: senseless form which she thrust at the dreamer as if ordering him to carry it. The sight of this form
column4: and the expression on its face
column5: broke the spell. Still too dazed to cry out

column7: shrill tittering of the fanged
column8: rat-like abnormality.

column1: On the morning of the 29th Gilman awaked into a maelstrom of horror. The instant he opened his eyes he knew something was terribly wrong
column2: for he was back in his old garret room with the slanting wall and ceiling

column4: and as he struggled to a sitting posture he saw with growing fright that his feet and pajama-bottoms were brown with caked mud. For the moment his recollections were hopelessly hazy
column5: but he knew at least that he must have been sleep-walking. Elwood had been lost too deeply in slumber to hear and stop him. On the floor were confused muddy prints
column6: but oddly enough they did not extend all the way to the door. The more Gilman looked at them
column7: the more peculiar they seemed; for in addition to those he could recognise as his there were some smaller
column8: almost round markings—such as the legs of a large chair or table might make
column9: except that most of them tended to be divided into halves. There were also some curious muddy rat-tracks leading out of a fresh hole and back into it again. Utter bewilderment and the fear of madness racked Gilman as he staggered to the door and saw that there were no muddy prints outside. The more he remembered of his hideous dream the more terrified he felt
column10: and it added to his desperation to hear Joe Mazurewicz chanting mournfully two floors below.

column1: Descending to Elwood’s room he roused his still-sleeping host and began telling of how he had found himself
column2: but Elwood could form no idea of what might really have happened. Where Gilman could have been
column3: how he got back to his room without making tracks in the hall
column4: and how the muddy

column7: livid marks on his throat
column8: as if he had tried to strangle himself. He put his hands up to them

column10: there had been no one on the stairs after midnight—though just before midnight he had heard faint footfalls in the garret
column11: and cautiously descending steps he did not like. It was
column12: he added
column13: a very bad time of year for Arkham. The young gentleman had better be sure to wear the crucifix Joe Mazurewicz had given him. Even the daytime was not safe
column14: for after dawn there had been strange sounds in the house—especially a thin
column15: childish wail hastily choked off.

column1: Gilman mechanically attended classes that morning

column3: and he seemed to be awaiting the fall of some annihilating blow. At noon he lunched at the University Spa

column5: wild-eyed

column1: There had been a strange kidnapping the night before in Orne’s Gangway
column2: and the two-year-old child of a clod-like laundry worker named Anastasia Wolejko had completely vanished from sight. The mother
column3: it appeared

column5: she said

column7: and knew from its grimaces and titterings that little Ladislas must be marked for sacrifice at the awful Sabbat on Walpurgis-Night. She had asked her neighbour Mary Czanek to sleep in the room and try to protect the child
column8: but Mary had not dared. She could not tell the police
column9: for they never believed such things. Children had been taken that way every year ever since she could remember. And her friend Pete Stowacki would not help because he wanted the child out of the way anyhow.

column2: but both vowed they had seen a crazily dressed trio furtively entering the dark passageway. There had
column3: they said
column4: been a huge robed negro
column5: a little old woman in rags
column6: and a young white man in his night-clothes. The old woman had been dragging the youth
column7: while around the feet of the negro a tame rat was rubbing and weaving in the brown mud.

This time neither could doubt but that something hideously serious was closing in around them. Between the phantasms of nightmare and the realities of the objective world a monstrous and unthinkable relationship was crystallising

column4: but not just now
column5: when all the papers were full of this kidnapping business.

column1: Just what had really happened was maddeningly obscure
column2: and for a moment both Gilman and Elwood exchanged whispered theories of the wildest kind. Had Gilman unconsciously succeeded better than he knew in his studies of space and its dimensions? Had he actually slipped outside our sphere to points unguessed and unimaginable? Where—if anywhere—had he been on those nights of daemoniac alienage? The roaring twilight abysses—the green hillside—the blistering terrace—the pulls from the stars—the ultimate black vortex—the black man—the muddy alley and the stairs—the old witch and the fanged
column3: furry horror—the bubble-congeries and the little polyhedron—the strange sunburn—the wrist wound—the unexplained image—the muddy feet—the throat-marks—the tales and fears of the superstitious foreigners—what did all this mean? To what extent could the laws of sanity apply to such a case?

column1: There was no sleep for either of them that night

column3: and with the dusk would come the hellish Sabbat-time which all the foreigners and the superstitious old folk feared. Mazurewicz came home at six o’clock and said people at the mill were whispering that the Walpurgis-revels would be held in the dark ravine beyond Meadow Hill where the old white stone stands in a place queerly void of all plant-life. Some of them had even told the police and advised them to look there for the missing Wolejko child

column5: and Gilman put it on and dropped it inside his shirt to humour the fellow.

column1: Late at night the two youths sat drowsing in their chairs

column3: his preternaturally sharpened hearing seeming to strain for some subtle
column4: dreaded murmur beyond the noises in the ancient house. Unwholesome recollections of things in the Necronomicon and the Black Book welled up
column5: and he found himself swaying to infandous rhythms said to pertain to the blackest ceremonies of the Sabbat and to have an origin outside the time and space we comprehend.

column1: Presently he realised what he was listening for—the hellish chant of the celebrants in the distant black valley. How did he know so much about what they expected? How did he know the time when Nahab and her acolyte were due to bear the brimming bowl which would follow the black cock and the black goat? He saw that Elwood had dropped asleep
column2: and tried to call out and waken him. Something
column3: however
column4: closed his throat. He was not his own master. Had he signed the black man’s book after all?

column2: abnormal hearing caught the distant
column3: windborne notes. Over miles of hill and field and alley they came
column4: but he recognised them none the less. The fires must be lit
column5: and the dancers must be starting in. How could he keep himself from going? What was it that had enmeshed him? Mathematics—folklore—the house—old Keziah—Brown Jenkin . . . and now he saw that there was a fresh rat-hole in the wall near his couch. Above the distant chanting and the nearer praying of Joe Mazurewicz came another sound—a stealthy
column6: determined scratching in the partitions. He hoped the electric lights would not go out. Then he saw the fanged
column7: bearded little face in the rat-hole—the accursed little face which he at last realised bore such a shocking
column8: mocking resemblance to old Keziah’s—and heard the faint fumbling at the door.

column1: The screaming twilight abysses flashed before him
column2: and he felt himself helpless in the formless grasp of the iridescent bubble-congeries. Ahead raced the small
column3: kaleidoscopic polyhedron
column4: and all through the churning void there was a heightening and acceleration of the vague tonal pattern which seemed to foreshadow some unutterable and unendurable climax. He seemed to know what was coming—the monstrous burst of Walpurgis-rhythm in whose cosmic timbre would be concentrated all the primal
column5: ultimate space-time seethings which lie behind the massed spheres of matter and sometimes break forth in measured reverberations that penetrate faintly to every layer of entity and give hideous significance throughout the worlds to certain dreaded periods.

column1: But all this vanished in a second. He was again in the cramped
column2: violet-litten peaked space with the slanting floor
column3: the low cases of ancient books
column4: the bench and table
column5: the queer objects
column6: and the triangular gulf at one side. On the table lay a small white figure—an infant boy
column7: unclothed and unconscious—while on the other side stood the monstrous
column8: leering old woman with a gleaming
column9: grotesque-hafted knife in her right hand
column10: and a queerly proportioned pale metal bowl covered with curiously chased designs and having delicate lateral handles in her left. She was intoning some croaking ritual in a language which Gilman could not understand
column11: but which seemed like something guardedly quoted in the Necronomicon.

column3: noticing as he did so its comparative lightness. At the same moment the disgusting form of Brown Jenkin scrambled up over the brink of the triangular black gulf on his left. The crone now motioned him to hold the bowl in a certain position while she raised the huge
column4: grotesque knife above the small white victim as high as her right hand could reach. The fanged
column5: furry thing began tittering a continuation of the unknown ritual
column6: while the witch croaked loathsome responses. Gilman felt a gnawing
column7: poignant abhorrence shoot through his mental and emotional paralysis
column8: and the light metal bowl shook in his grasp. A second later the downward motion of the knife broke the spell completely

column1: In an instant he had edged up the slanting floor around the end of the table and wrenched the knife from the old woman’s claws; sending it clattering over the brink of the narrow triangular gulf. In another instant
column2: however
column3: matters were reversed; for those murderous claws had locked themselves tightly around his own throat
column4: while the wrinkled face was twisted with insane fury. He felt the chain of the cheap crucifix grinding into his neck
column5: and in his peril wondered how the sight of the object itself would affect the evil creature. Her strength was altogether superhuman
column6: but as she continued her choking he reached feebly in his shirt and drew out the metal symbol
column7: snapping the chain and pulling it free.

column2: and her grip relaxed long enough to give Gilman a chance to break it entirely. He pulled the steel-like claws from his neck
column3: and would have dragged the beldame over the edge of the gulf had not the claws received a fresh access of strength and closed in again. This time he resolved to reply in kind
column4: and his own hands reached out for the creature’s throat. Before she saw what he was doing he had the chain of the crucifix twisted about her neck
column5: and a moment later he had tightened it enough to cut off her breath. During her last struggle he felt something bite at his ankle

column1: Whether he had killed the ancient crone he did not know
column2: but he let her rest on the floor where she had fallen. Then
column3: as he turned away
column4: he saw on the table a sight which nearly snapped the last thread of his reason. Brown Jenkin
column5: tough of sinew and with four tiny hands of daemoniac dexterity
column6: had been busy while the witch was throttling him
column7: and his efforts had been in vain. What he had prevented the knife from doing to the victim’s chest

column1: In his dream-delirium Gilman heard the hellish
column2: alien-rhythmed chant of the Sabbat coming from an infinite distance
column3: and knew the black man must be there. Confused memories mixed themselves with his mathematics
column4: and he believed his subconscious mind held the angles which he needed to guide him back to the normal world—alone and unaided for the first time. He felt sure he was in the immemorially sealed loft above his own room
column5: but whether he could ever escape through the slanting floor or the long-stopped egress he doubted greatly. Besides
column6: would not an escape from a dream-loft bring him merely into a dream-house—an abnormal projection of the actual place he sought? He was wholly bewildered as to the relation betwixt dream and reality in all his experiences.

column1: The passage through the vague abysses would be frightful
column2: for the Walpurgis-rhythm would be vibrating
column3: and at last he would have to hear that hitherto veiled cosmic pulsing which he so mortally dreaded. Even now he could detect a low
column4: monstrous shaking whose tempo he suspected all too well. At Sabbat-time it always mounted and reached through to the worlds to summon the initiate to nameless rites. Half the chants of the Sabbat were patterned on this faintly overheard pulsing which no earthly ear could endure in its unveiled spatial fulness. Gilman wondered
column5: too
column6: whether he could trust his instinct to take him back to the right part of space. How could he be sure he would not land on that green-litten hillside of a far planet
column7: on the tessellated terrace above the city of tentacled monsters somewhere beyond the galaxy
column8: or in the spiral black vortices of that ultimate void of Chaos wherein reigns the mindless daemon-sultan Azathoth?

column1: Just before he made the plunge the violet light went out and left him in utter blackness. The witch—old Keziah—Nahab—that must have meant her death. And mixed with the distant chant of the Sabbat and the whimpers of Brown Jenkin in the gulf below he thought he heard another and wilder whine from unknown depths. Joe Mazurewicz—the prayers against the Crawling Chaos now turning to an inexplicably triumphant shriek—worlds of sardonic actuality impinging on vortices of febrile dream—Iä! Shub-Niggurath! The Goat with a Thousand Young. . . .
They found Gilman on the floor of his queerly angled old garret room long before dawn
column2: for the terrible cry had brought Desrochers and Choynski and Dombrowski and Mazurewicz at once
column3: and had even wakened the soundly sleeping Elwood in his chair. He was alive
column4: and with open
column5: staring eyes
column6: but seemed largely unconscious. On his throat were the marks of murderous hands
column7: and on his left ankle was a distressing rat-bite. His clothing was badly rumpled
column8: and Joe’s crucifix was missing. Elwood trembled
column9: afraid even to speculate on what new form his friend’s sleep-walking had taken. Mazurewicz seemed half-dazed because of a “sign” he said he had had in response to his prayers

column1: When the dreamer was settled on his couch in Elwood’s room they sent for Dr. Malkowski—a local practitioner who would repeat no tales where they might prove embarrassing—and he gave Gilman two hypodermic injections which caused him to relax in something like natural drowsiness. During the day the patient regained consciousness at times and whispered his newest dream disjointedly to Elwood. It was a painful process
column2: and at its very start brought out a fresh and disconcerting fact.

column1: Gilman—whose ears had so lately possessed an abnormal sensitiveness—was now stone deaf. Dr. Malkowski
column2: summoned again in haste
column3: told Elwood that both ear-drums were ruptured
column4: as if by the impact of some stupendous sound intense beyond all human conception or endurance. How such a sound could have been heard in the last few hours without arousing all the Miskatonic Valley was more than the honest physician could say.

column1: Elwood wrote his part of the colloquy on paper
column2: so that a fairly easy communication was maintained. Neither knew what to make of the whole chaotic business
column3: and decided it would be better if they thought as little as possible about it. Both
column4: though
column5: agreed that they must leave this ancient and accursed house as soon as it could be arranged. Evening papers spoke of a police raid on some curious revellers in a ravine beyond Meadow Hill just before dawn
column6: and mentioned that the white stone there was an object of age-long superstitious regard. Nobody had been caught
column7: but among the scattering fugitives had been glimpsed a huge negro. In another column it was stated that no trace of the missing child Ladislas Wolejko had been found.

column3: but paid little attention to them. Then
column4: long after both he and Gilman had retired

column6: turned on the lights
column7: and rushed over to his guest’s couch. The occupant was emitting sounds of veritably inhuman nature
column8: as if racked by some torment beyond description. He was writhing under the bedclothes
column9: and a great red stain was beginning to appear on the blankets.

column2: but gradually the screaming and writhing subsided. By this time Dombrowski
column3: Choynski
column4: Desrochers

column1: II.
The Tale of Inspector Legrasse.

column8: soul-chilling chants and dancing devil-flames; and
column9: the frightened messenger added
column10: the people could stand it no more.

column1: So a body of twenty police
column2: filling two carriages and an automobile
column3: had set out in the late afternoon with the shivering squatter as a guide. At the end of the passable road they alighted
column4: and for miles splashed on in silence through the terrible cypress woods where day never came. Ugly roots and malignant hanging nooses of Spanish moss beset them
column5: and now and then a pile of dank stones or fragment of a rotting wall intensified by its hint of morbid habitation a depression which every malformed tree and every fungous islet combined to create. At length the squatter settlement
column6: a miserable huddle of huts
column7: hove in sight; and hysterical dwellers ran out to cluster around the group of bobbing lanterns. The muffled beat of tom-toms was now faintly audible far

column9: too
column10: seemed to filter through the pale undergrowth beyond endless avenues of forest night. Reluctant even to be left alone again
column11: each one of the cowed squatters refused point-blank to advance another inch toward the scene of unholy worship

column1: The region now entered by the police was one of traditionally evil repute
column2: substantially unknown and untraversed by white men. There were legends of a hidden lake unglimpsed by mortal sight
column3: in which dwelt a huge
column4: formless white polypous thing with luminous eyes; and squatters whispered that bat-winged devils flew up out of caverns in inner earth to worship it at midnight. They said it had been there before D’Iberville
column5: before La Salle
column6: before the Indians
column7: and before even the wholesome beasts and birds of the woods. It was nightmare itself
column8: and to see it was to die. But it made men dream
column9: and so they knew enough to keep away. The present voodoo orgy was
column10: indeed
column11: on the merest fringe of this abhorred area
column12: but that location was bad enough; hence perhaps the very place of the worship had terrified the squatters more than the shocking sounds and incidents.

column1: Only poetry or madness could do justice to the noises heard by Legrasse’s men as they ploughed on through the black morass toward the red glare and the muffled tom-toms. There are vocal qualities peculiar to men
column2: and vocal qualities peculiar to beasts; and it is terrible to hear the one when the source should yield the other. Animal fury and orgiastic licence here whipped themselves to daemoniac heights by howls and squawking ecstasies that tore and reverberated through those nighted woods like pestilential tempests from the gulfs of hell. Now and then the less organised ululation would cease
column3: and from what seemed a well-drilled chorus of hoarse voices would rise in sing-song chant that hideous phrase or ritual:

column1: “Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn.”
Then the men
column2: having reached a spot where the trees were thinner
column3: came suddenly in sight of the spectacle itself. Four of them reeled
column4: one fainted
column5: and two were shaken into a frantic cry which the mad cacophony of the orgy fortunately deadened. Legrasse dashed swamp water on the face of the fainting man
column6: and all stood trembling and nearly hypnotised with horror.

column1: In a natural glade of the swamp stood a grassy island of perhaps an acre’s extent
column2: clear of trees and tolerably dry. On this now leaped and twisted a more indescribable horde of human abnormality than any but a Sime or an Angarola could paint. Void of clothing
column3: this hybrid spawn were braying
column4: bellowing
column5: and writhing about a monstrous ring-shaped bonfire; in the centre of which
column6: revealed by occasional rifts in the curtain of flame
column7: stood a great granite monolith some eight feet in height; on top of which
column8: incongruous with its diminutiveness
column9: rested the noxious carven statuette. From a wide circle of ten scaffolds set up at regular intervals with the flame-girt monolith as a centre hung
column10: head downward
column11: the oddly marred bodies of the helpless squatters who had disappeared. It was inside this circle that the ring of worshippers jumped and roared
column12: the general direction of the mass motion being from left to right in endless Bacchanal between the ring of bodies and the ring of fire.

column1: It may have been only imagination and it may have been only echoes which induced one of the men
column2: an excitable Spaniard

column4: Joseph D. Galvez

column6: and of a glimpse of shining eyes and a mountainous white bulk beyond the remotest trees—but I suppose he had been hearing too much native superstition.

column1: Actually
column2: the horrified pause of the men was of comparatively brief duration. Duty came first; and although there must have been nearly a hundred mongrel celebrants in the throng

column6: whom he forced to dress in haste and fall into line between two rows of policemen. Five of the worshippers lay dead

column8: of course

column1: Examined at headquarters after a trip of intense strain and weariness
column2: the prisoners all proved to be men of a very low
column3: mixed-blooded
column4: and mentally aberrant type. Most were seamen
column5: and a sprinkling of negroes and mulattoes
column6: largely West Indians or Brava Portuguese from the Cape Verde Islands
column7: gave a colouring of voodooism to the heterogeneous cult. But before many questions were asked
column8: it became manifest that something far deeper and older than negro fetichism was involved. Degraded and ignorant as they were

column1: They worshipped
column2: so they said
column3: the Great Old Ones who lived ages before there were any men
column4: and who came to the young world out of the sky. Those Old Ones were gone now
column5: inside the earth and under the sea; but their dead bodies had told their secrets in dreams to the first men
column6: who formed a cult which had never died. This was that cult
column7: and the prisoners said it had always existed and always would exist
column8: hidden in distant wastes and dark places all over the world until the time when the great priest Cthulhu
column9: from his dark house in the mighty city of R’lyeh under the waters
column10: should rise and bring the earth again beneath his sway. Some day he would call
column11: when the stars were ready
column12: and the secret cult would always be waiting to liberate him.

column1: Meanwhile no more must be told. There was a secret which even torture could not extract. Mankind was not absolutely alone among the conscious things of earth
column2: for shapes came out of the dark to visit the faithful few. But these were not the Great Old Ones. No man had ever seen the Old Ones. The carven idol was great Cthulhu
column3: but none might say whether or not the others were precisely like him. No one could read the old writing now
column4: but things were told by word of mouth. The chanted ritual was not the secret—that was never spoken aloud
column5: only whispered. The chant meant only this: “In his house at R’lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.”

column1: Only two of the prisoners were found sane enough to be hanged
column2: and the rest were committed to various institutions. All denied a part in the ritual murders
column3: and averred that the killing had been done by Black Winged Ones which had come to them from their immemorial meeting-place in the haunted wood. But of those mysterious allies no coherent account could ever be gained. What the police did extract
column4: came mainly from an immensely aged mestizo named Castro
column5: who claimed to have sailed to strange ports and talked with undying leaders of the cult in the mountains of China.

column1: Old Castro remembered bits of hideous legend that paled the speculations of theosophists and made man and the world seem recent and transient indeed. There had been aeons when other Things ruled on the earth
column2: and They had had great cities. Remains of Them
column3: he said the deathless Chinamen had told him
column4: were still to be found as Cyclopean stones on islands in the Pacific. They all died vast epochs of time before men came
column5: but there were arts which could revive Them when the stars had come round again to the right positions in the cycle of eternity. They had
column6: indeed
column7: come themselves from the stars
column8: and brought Their images with Them.

column1: These Great Old Ones
column2: Castro continued
column3: were not composed altogether of flesh and blood. They had shape—for did not this star-fashioned image prove it?—but that shape was not made of matter. When the stars were right
column4: They could plunge from world to world through the sky; but when the stars were wrong
column5: They could not live. But although They no longer lived
column6: They would never really die. They all lay in stone houses in Their great city of R’lyeh
column7: preserved by the spells of mighty Cthulhu for a glorious resurrection when the stars and the earth might once more be ready for Them. But at that time some force from outside must serve to liberate Their bodies. The spells that preserved Them intact likewise prevented Them from making an initial move
column8: and They could only lie awake in the dark and think whilst uncounted millions of years rolled by. They knew all that was occurring in the universe
column9: but Their mode of speech was transmitted thought. Even now They talked in Their tombs. When
column10: after infinities of chaos
column11: the first men came
column12: the Great Old Ones spoke to the sensitive among them by moulding their dreams; for only thus could Their language reach the fleshly minds of mammals.

column1: Then
column2: whispered Castro
column3: those first men formed the cult around small idols which the Great Ones shewed them; idols brought in dim aeras from dark stars. That cult would never die till the stars came right again
column4: and the secret priests would take great Cthulhu from His tomb to revive His subjects and resume His rule of earth. The time would be easy to know
column5: for then mankind would have become as the Great Old Ones; free and wild and beyond good and evil
column6: with laws and morals thrown aside and all men shouting and killing and revelling in joy. Then the liberated Old Ones would teach them new ways to shout and kill and revel and enjoy themselves
column7: and all the earth would flame with a holocaust of ecstasy and freedom. Meanwhile the cult
column8: by appropriate rites
column9: must keep alive the memory of those ancient ways and shadow forth the prophecy of their return.

column1: In the elder time chosen men had talked with the entombed Old Ones in dreams
column2: but then something had happened. The great stone city R’lyeh
column3: with its monoliths and sepulchres
column4: had sunk beneath the waves; and the deep waters
column5: full of the one primal mystery through which not even thought can pass
column6: had cut off the spectral intercourse. But memory never died
column7: and high-priests said that the city would rise again when the stars were right. Then came out of the earth the black spirits of earth
column8: mouldy and shadowy
column9: and full of dim rumours picked up in caverns beneath forgotten sea-bottoms. But of them old Castro dared not speak much. He cut himself off hurriedly
column10: and no amount of persuasion or subtlety could elicit more in this direction. The size of the Old Ones
column11: too
column12: he curiously declined to mention. Of the cult
column13: he said that he thought the centre lay amid the pathless deserts of Arabia
column14: where Irem
column15: the City of Pillars
column16: dreams hidden and untouched. It was not allied to the European witch-cult
column17: and was virtually unknown beyond its members. No book had ever really hinted of it
column18: though the deathless Chinamen said that there were double meanings in the Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred which the initiated might read as they chose
column19: especially the much-discussed couplet:

column1: “That is not dead which can eternal lie
And with strange aeons even death may die.”
Legrasse
column2: deeply impressed and not a little bewildered
column3: had inquired in vain concerning the historic affiliations of the cult. Castro
column4: apparently
column5: had told the truth when he said that it was wholly secret. The authorities at Tulane University could shed no light upon either cult or image
column6: and now the detective had come to the highest authorities in the country and met with no more than the Greenland tale of Professor Webb.

column1: The feverish interest aroused at the meeting by Legrasse’s tale
column2: corroborated as it was by the statuette
column3: is echoed in the subsequent correspondence of those who attended; although scant mention occurs in the formal publications of the society. Caution is the first care of those accustomed to face occasional charlatanry and imposture. Legrasse for some time lent the image to Professor Webb
column4: but at the latter’s death it was returned to him and remains in his possession
column5: where I viewed it not long ago. It is truly a terrible thing
column6: and unmistakably akin to the dream-sculpture of young Wilcox.

column1: That my uncle was excited by the tale of the sculptor I did not wonder
column2: for what thoughts must arise upon hearing
column3: after a knowledge of what Legrasse had learned of the cult
column4: of a sensitive young man who had dreamed not only the figure and exact hieroglyphics of the swamp-found image and the Greenland devil tablet
column5: but had come in his dreams upon at least three of the precise words of the formula uttered alike by Esquimau diabolists and mongrel Louisianans? Professor Angell’s instant start on an investigation of the utmost thoroughness was eminently natural; though privately I suspected young Wilcox of having heard of the cult in some indirect way
column6: and of having invented a series of dreams to heighten and continue the mystery at my uncle’s expense. The dream-narratives and cuttings collected by the professor were
column7: of course
column8: strong corroboration; but the rationalism of my mind and the extravagance of the whole subject led me to adopt what I thought the most sensible conclusions. So
column9: after thoroughly studying the manuscript again and correlating the theosophical and anthropological notes with the cult narrative of Legrasse
column10: I made a trip to Providence to see the sculptor and give him the rebuke I thought proper for so boldly imposing upon a learned and aged man.

column1: Wilcox still lived alone in the Fleur-de-Lys Building in Thomas Street
column2: a hideous Victorian imitation of seventeenth-century Breton architecture which flaunts its stuccoed front amidst the lovely colonial houses on the ancient hill
column3: and under the very shadow of the finest Georgian steeple in America. I found him at work in his rooms
column4: and at once conceded from the specimens scattered about that his genius is indeed profound and authentic. He will
column5: I believe
column6: some time be heard from as one of the great decadents; for he has crystallised in clay and will one day mirror in marble those nightmares and phantasies which Arthur Machen evokes in prose
column7: and Clark Ashton Smith makes visible in verse and in painting.

column1: Dark
column2: frail
column3: and somewhat unkempt in aspect
column4: he turned languidly at my knock and asked me my business without rising. When I told him who I was
column5: he displayed some interest; for my uncle had excited his curiosity in probing his strange dreams
column6: yet had never explained the reason for the study. I did not enlarge his knowledge in this regard
column7: but sought with some subtlety to draw him out. In a short time I became convinced of his absolute sincerity
column8: for he spoke of the dreams in a manner none could mistake. They and their subconscious residuum had influenced his art profoundly
column9: and he shewed me a morbid statue whose contours almost made me shake with the potency of its black suggestion. He could not recall having seen the original of this thing except in his own dream bas-relief
column10: but the outlines had formed themselves insensibly under his hands. It was

column12: the giant shape he had raved of in delirium. That he really knew nothing of the hidden cult

column14: he soon made clear; and again I strove to think of some way in which he could possibly have received the weird impressions.

column1: He talked of his dreams in a strangely poetic fashion; making me see with terrible vividness the damp Cyclopean city of slimy green stone—whose geometry
column2: he oddly said
column3: was all wrong—and hear with frightened expectancy the ceaseless
column4: half-mental calling from underground: “Cthulhu fhtagn”
column5: “Cthulhu fhtagn”. These words had formed part of that dread ritual which told of dead Cthulhu’s dream-vigil in his stone vault at R’lyeh
column6: and I felt deeply moved despite my rational beliefs. Wilcox
column7: I was sure
column8: had heard of the cult in some casual way
column9: and had soon forgotten it amidst the mass of his equally weird reading and imagining. Later
column10: by virtue of its sheer impressiveness
column11: it had found subconscious expression in dreams
column12: in the bas-relief
column13: and in the terrible statue I now beheld; so that his imposture upon my uncle had been a very innocent one. The youth was of a type
column14: at once slightly affected and slightly ill-mannered
column15: which I could never like; but I was willing enough now to admit both his genius and his honesty. I took leave of him amicably
column16: and wish him all the success his talent promises.

column1: The matter of the cult still remained to fascinate me
column2: and at times I had visions of personal fame from researches into its origin and connexions. I visited New Orleans
column3: talked with Legrasse and others of that old-time raiding-party
column4: saw the frightful image
column5: and even questioned such of the mongrel prisoners as still survived. Old Castro
column6: unfortunately
column7: had been dead for some years. What I now heard so graphically at first-hand
column8: though it was really no more than a detailed confirmation of what my uncle had written
column9: excited me afresh; for I felt sure that I was on the track of a very real
column10: very secret
column11: and very ancient religion whose discovery would make me an anthropologist of note. My attitude was still one of absolute materialism
column12: as I wish it still were

column1: One thing I began to suspect
column2: and which I now fear I know
column3: is that my uncle’s death was far from natural. He fell on a narrow hill street leading up from an ancient waterfront swarming with foreign mongrels
column4: after a careless push from a negro sailor. I did not forget the mixed blood and marine pursuits of the cult-members in Louisiana
column5: and would not be surprised to learn of secret methods and poison needles as ruthless and as anciently known as the cryptic rites and beliefs. Legrasse and his men
column6: it is true
column7: have been let alone; but in Norway a certain seaman who saw things is dead. Might not the deeper inquiries of my uncle after encountering the sculptor’s data have come to sinister ears? I think Professor Angell died because he knew too much
column8: or because he was likely to learn too much. Whether I shall go as he did remains to be seen
column9: for I have learned much now.

column1: III.
The Madness from the Sea.
If heaven ever wishes to grant me a boon
column2: it will be a total effacing of the results of a mere chance which fixed my eye on a certain stray piece of shelf-paper. It was nothing on which I would naturally have stumbled in the course of my daily round
column3: for it was an old number of an Australian journal
column4: the Sydney Bulletin for April 18
column5: 1925. It had escaped even the cutting bureau which had at the time of its issuance been avidly collecting material for my uncle’s research.

column1: I had largely given over my inquiries into what Professor Angell called the “Cthulhu Cult”
column2: and was visiting a learned friend in Paterson
column3: New Jersey; the curator of a local museum and a mineralogist of note. Examining one day the reserve specimens roughly set on the storage shelves in a rear room of the museum
column4: my eye was caught by an odd picture in one of the old papers spread beneath the stones. It was the Sydney Bulletin I have mentioned
column5: for my friend has wide affiliations in all conceivable foreign parts; and the picture was a half-tone cut of a hideous stone image almost identical with that which Legrasse had found in the swamp.

column1: Eagerly clearing the sheet of its precious contents
column2: I scanned the item in detail; and was disappointed to find it of only moderate length. What it suggested
column3: however
column4: was of portentous significance to my flagging quest; and I carefully tore it out for immediate action. It read as follows:

column1: MYSTERY DERELICT FOUND AT SEA
Vigilant Arrives With Helpless Armed New Zealand Yacht in Tow.
One Survivor and Dead Man Found Aboard. Tale of
Desperate Battle and Deaths at Sea.
Rescued Seaman Refuses
Particulars of Strange Experience.
Odd Idol Found in His Possession. Inquiry
to Follow.
The Morrison Co.’s freighter Vigilant
column2: bound from Valparaiso
column3: arrived this morning at its wharf in Darling Harbour
column4: having in tow the battled and disabled but heavily armed steam yacht Alert of Dunedin
column5: N. Z.
column6: which was sighted April 12th in S. Latitude 34° 21'
column7: W. Longitude 152° 17' with one living and one dead man aboard.

column1: The Vigilant left Valparaiso March 25th
column2: and on April 2nd was driven considerably south of her course by exceptionally heavy storms and monster waves. On April 12th the derelict was sighted; and though apparently deserted
column3: was found upon boarding to contain one survivor in a half-delirious condition and one man who had evidently been dead for more than a week. The living man was clutching a horrible stone idol of unknown origin
column4: about a foot in height
column5: regarding whose nature authorities at Sydney University
column6: the Royal Society
column7: and the Museum in College Street all profess complete bafflement
column8: and which the survivor says he found in the cabin of the yacht
column9: in a small carved shrine of common pattern.

column1: This man
column2: after recovering his senses
column3: told an exceedingly strange story of piracy and slaughter. He is Gustaf Johansen
column4: a Norwegian of some intelligence
column5: and had been second mate of the two-masted schooner Emma of Auckland
column6: which sailed for Callao February 20th with a complement of eleven men. The Emma
column7: he says

column9: and on March 22nd

column11: W. Longitude 128° 34'

column5: it appears

column9: and speaks only of their falling into a rock chasm. Later
column10: it seems

Our Auckland correspondent gives the Emma and her crew an excellent reputation

column1: This was all
column2: together with the picture of the hellish image; but what a train of ideas it started in my mind! Here were new treasuries of data on the Cthulhu Cult
column3: and evidence that it had strange interests at sea as well as on land. What motive prompted the hybrid crew to order back the Emma as they sailed about with their hideous idol? What was the unknown island on which six of the Emma’s crew had died
column4: and about which the mate Johansen was so secretive? What had the vice-admiralty’s investigation brought out
column5: and what was known of the noxious cult in Dunedin? And most marvellous of all
column6: what deep and more than natural linkage of dates was this which gave a malign and now undeniable significance to the various turns of events so carefully noted by my uncle?

column1: March 1st—our February 28th according to the International Date Line—the earthquake and storm had come. From Dunedin the Alert and her noisome crew had darted eagerly forth as if imperiously summoned
column2: and on the other side of the earth poets and artists had begun to dream of a strange
column3: dank Cyclopean city whilst a young sculptor had moulded in his sleep the form of the dreaded Cthulhu. March 23d the crew of the Emma landed on an unknown island and left six men dead; and on that date the dreams of sensitive men assumed a heightened vividness and darkened with dread of a giant monster’s malign pursuit
column4: whilst an architect had gone mad and a sculptor had lapsed suddenly into delirium! And what of this storm of April 2nd—the date on which all dreams of the dank city ceased

column6: star-born Old Ones and their coming reign; their faithful cult and their mastery of dreams? Was I tottering on the brink of cosmic horrors beyond man’s power to bear? If so
column7: they must be horrors of the mind alone
column8: for in some way the second of April had put a stop to whatever monstrous menace had begun its siege of mankind’s soul.

column1: That evening
column2: after a day of hurried cabling and arranging
column3: I bade my host adieu and took a train for San Francisco. In less than a month I was in Dunedin; where

column1: Shaken with such a mental revolution as I had never before known
column2: I now resolved to visit Mate Johansen in Oslo. Sailing for London

column4: I discovered
